it must be impermanent, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). Because it possesses resistance, this is the reason (*hetu*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like coarse earth and so forth, which possess resistance."
That is to say, earth, water, and fire. This is a reason that contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*).

Among the categories (*padārtha*), [the property of being] "that which is apprehended by the sense-faculties of form" [is the reason], because it is admitted that they are apprehended by the sense-faculties of form, just like earth, water, fire, and wind.

Next, among the various categories (*padārtha*), we shall examine those things that lack material resistance (*apratigha*). Those things lacking material resistance consist of: within the category of substance (*dravya*), space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*diś*), self (*ātman*), and mind (*manas*);

and within the category of quality (*guṇa*), solidity (*khara*) and so forth. In these categories, the subject (*dharmin*) is "those things lacking material resistance. The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that "they must all possess material resistance.

The reason (*hetu*) is "because they are apprehended by the sense organs of form (*rūpīndriya-grāhya*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like earth, water, fire, and wind. This [reason] also exists [in the subject].
The dharma is a reason that contradicts its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, those things they grasp—such as non-substantial qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth—are subsumed under non-existence, like flowers in the sky and the like.

Furthermore, [the text] below establishes a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to refute the various propositions that there exists a self-nature (*svabhāva*) external to and distinct from consciousness. The two formal arguments are as stated in the text.
It may be established that [the categories] are not real qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth; that is to say, they are not qualities or activities subsumed under the category of "real" (*dravya*).

As for the phrase "not being real substances and so forth," it means they are not the three categories—real substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karman*)—subsumed under the category of "existent" (*sat*).

Because those [proponents] maintain that the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of these categories are definitively distinct, they do not subsume one another. To employ "sky-flowers" and "barren women's children" as examples of similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is intended to establish their reality.
This means that apart from consciousness, there is fundamentally nothing; it does not mean that it reveals *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

This incurs the fault of the probandum (*sādhyadharma*) being unestablished for the subject (*dharmin*), because while the proving factor (*sādhana*) exists, the thing to be proven (*sādhya*) is non-existent.

That which they grasp as "existence" (sattā) must be distinct from substance (*dravya*) and so forth; therefore, its nature as existence is merely a false conceptual construction. Regarding the phrase "that which they grasp":

the first formal argument (*prayoga*) accepts its nature as existence in order to refute its being distinct from substance and so forth. This reveals the fault of the predicate (*viśeṣya*) not being established for the opponent.
The formal argument may be understood accordingly. The subsequent argument accepts its being distinct from substance and so forth in order to refute [its nature as existence].

Regarding its non-existence as an entity (*abhāva-svabhāva*), there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). Since this "existent dharma" (the subject) is devoid of real universal existence (*mahāsattā*), it would follow that the thesis (*pakṣa*) is itself non-existent.

This is because the reason (*hetu*)—namely, "because it is admitted to be distinct from substance and so forth"—is like the examples of absolute non-existence, such as the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
"Suppose there is... and so forth. This provides an example to refute [the opponent's position]. First, one phrase presents the exemplar (*dṛṣṭānta*): "Suppose there is existence.

Apart from existence, there is no separate nature of existence. The subsequent phrase presents the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*): How could there be a separate "greatness" (*mahat*) apart from substance (*dravya*) and the rest? The section beginning with "If apart from...

employs a method of refutation through alternating affirmation and negation (*anujñā-pratiṣedha*). The preceding sentence affirms: "There is a property (*dharma*) above," which refers to substance and the rest.

The phrase "possessing nature" (*sattva*) below refers to "great existence" (*mahāsattva*). The following sentence is a concessive argument regarding non-existence, such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.
Since that [non-existence] is already negated by the two preceding sentences, the final sentence serves as a concluding reprimand.

Furthermore, because those [factors] they grasp as real—namely substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*)—[are not established], the nature of commonality and difference (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) is merely a conventional designation.

In the passage beginning "Furthermore, those... below, the commonality and difference are refuted; the first two phrases briefly state the externalist position. The initial text refers to the nature of substance, quality, and action.

This refers precisely to the nature of sameness and difference (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*). When they speak of "sameness and difference," they are discussing sameness and difference with respect to substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and activities (*karman*).
Furthermore, they maintain that there exists a distinct nature of sameness and difference apart from substances, qualities, and activities. This is certainly not logically tenable. (One sentence)

"General Refutation. "Do not [assert] this below" refers to the refutation of the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) of the opponent's position. "This also below" fully presents the opponent's fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*).

The word "this" (*idam*) refers to the property-possessor (*dharmin*), namely "sameness and difference" (*tulyatvātulyatva*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it does not have the nature of substance, quality, or action (*dravya-guṇa-karma-svabhāva*).

This statement means that there exists a distinct essence apart from substance, quality, and action. "Because it is different from substance and so forth" is the reason (*hetu*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like qualities and actions," etc.
The single character "wu" (not) is precisely a term of negation. The word "yi" (also) follows from the preceding phrase regarding "great existence" (*mahāsattā*).

That [opponent] maintains that apart from substance, quality, and action, there exists a separate category of "great existence"; now, the same applies to the category of "sameness-and-difference" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). Therefore, it says "also.

Furthermore, [the argument] proceeds downward to show that even in the case of substances and so forth, there should likewise be no distinct "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so on; this is raised as an example to refute [the opponent's position].

First, let us provide an example. Furthermore, the two terms "should" (*yìng*) carry over from what precedes. If one were to claim that the categories of "sameness" (*sāmānya*) and "difference" (*viśeṣa*) exist as distinct entities separate from substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karman*), then the category of "sameness" would not be subsumed under the category of "sameness.

Moreover, the category of "substance" would not be subsumed under the category of "substance," because it would possess a nature different from [the definition of] substance, just like a quality (*guṇa*).
The wording and phrasing in the text are repetitive and dense, making the meaning difficult to clarify; therefore, I shall now establish the meaning term by term.
They are existent phenomena (*dharma*). Taken as mutual homologues (*sapakṣa*), they together constitute three proofs (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, the category of quality (*guṇapada*) should not be subsumed under the category of non-quality, because it differs from the nature of quality, just like action (*karman*). This is established by analogy with the category of action.

Following this principle, eight sets of three members [of inference] are established for substance (*dravya*) and the others; the various natures such as earth and so forth are subsumed under the category of quality, namely solidity, moisture, warmth, and...

"Movement. The substance of earth and so forth is subsumed under the category of "realities," namely earth, water, fire, and wind. Taking solidity as the *dharmin* (the subject possessing properties), the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is not subsumed under non-solidity.
The reason (*hetu*) is "because it is different from the substance of earth. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is "like moisture.

Since each word serves as the *dharmin* for the others, they are said to "mutually interrogate one another. "In accordance with this" refers to the preceding categories of reality, quality, and activity; it is just as [explained] above.
The final two lines cite the example and then refute it by inversion. The first line cites the example;
because the preceding eleven types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are extensive in both text and meaning, this single line summarizes and restates them. The subsequent line refutes through inversion:

just as there is no separate "reality-nature" (*tattva*) external to reality itself, so too, by way of analogy, there should be no separate [nature] external to substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), or activity (*karman*).

Regarding the nature of identity and difference: if one departs from the preceding [position], it is refuted through alternating affirmation and negation. The first phrase is an affirmative reversal; the second phrase is a negative affirmation.
The following two phrases constitute the refutation by negation; the final phrase concludes the refutation.

Furthermore, the category of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) as maintained by them—up to the point where it is argued that it is not substantially existent due to the aforementioned reasoning—is also untenable.

Regarding the phrase "Moreover, they... below, a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute conjunction; this syllogism may be understood accordingly. Regarding the phrase "They admit... below, it further refutes [the position] by means of a *prasanga* (reductio ad absurdum). Regarding the phrase "Even if one maintains... below, it refutes [the position] by means of both concession and denial (*anujñā-pratiṣedha*).

However, those [categories] such as "substance" (dravya) and so forth are not objects of cognition that exist independently of consciousness; this is because they are admitted to be objects of knowledge, like the hair of a tortoise and similar examples.

Now, from the words "However, those... onwards, there is a general refutation of all the propositions regarding the object-condition (*ālambana*). The six categories beginning with "substance" are the subject (*dharmin*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is:

"They are not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as having a substantially existent self-nature independent of consciousness. The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because they are admitted to be objects of knowledge."

It is like the hair of a tortoise and similar examples. They maintain that the six categories of phenomena possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that exists separately from their designations and is apprehended as an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by the self.
Now, this is refuted by means of the word "non-. The hair of a tortoise is an object of false mental consciousness and is not apprehended through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
it is used as a homologous example (*dṛṣṭānta*) to refute the claim that those six categories of phenomena are apprehended through direct perception.

Furthermore, wisdom that takes reality as its object does not take that which is separated from consciousness (up to) what is produced by false conjunction as its object; thus it is like the wisdom of reality and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the "lower" [objects], the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute the cognizing wisdom: such cognizing wisdom is not subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

First, the formal argument is established based on wisdom that takes reality as its object; the remaining five are established by analogy. As for "produced by false conjunction," it means it is produced by the false conjunction of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).
Therefore, the categories such as "substance" (dravya) and so forth in the Vaiśeṣika school are likewise merely conceptual constructs devised according to subjective sentiment.
The final two phrases provide a concluding rebuke; the word "also" (亦) contrasts with what was previously stated regarding the Sāṃkhya school.
There are those who maintain that there is a single Great Īśvara (up to: he too should produce [effects] instantaneously because he is eternal).
This constitutes the third refutation of the Great Īśvara. First, the tenet is stated: this is the doctrine held by the *bhasmaka* (ash-smearing) heretics.

They maintain that this deity is the cause of all things, that his essence is real, that he is omnipresent, and that he is eternal; thus, he possesses these four attributes and is able to produce all phenomena.

In refuting [the opponent's position], one first refutes it by means of the producer (*janaka*) through a series of successive reversals, and subsequently refutes the producer itself. First, one refutes permanence by means of the producer:

if that which produces an effect were permanent, it would necessarily be impermanent because it possesses functional activity (*kāritra*). Next, one refutes omnipresence (*vibhu*) by means of impermanence:
since it perishes as soon as it arises, it lacks the property of motion; therefore, there is no possibility for it to move from this location to another place. Next...

Because that which is not pervasive cannot refute the real. The essence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is pervasive, and its nature is truly real; the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is not pervasive, and its nature is not truly real.

Since its essence is inferior, it cannot refute that which can produce [phenomena]. The first phrase restates the [opponent’s] position; the second phrase refutes it. That which is permanent should exist at all times;
that which is pervasive should be present in all places; possessing all functional capacities, it should produce all phenomena instantaneously. [It must] depend upon...

Regarding "desiring to refute": this is the refutation of the [opponent's] defense. The defense states: "Although the essence is eternal, omnipresent, and endowed with all functional capacities, it only arises when waiting for the desires of sentient beings and the convergence of conditions;
therefore, there is no fault of [the effect] arising instantaneously. Regarding "contradicting [the first point]": this refutes the fault of contradicting the teachings.
If one waits for the conditions of desire, although the fault of suddenness is avoided, it nevertheless contradicts your own fundamental tenet.

Alternatively, if desire is [admitted to be] inferior, then the conditions of desire need not be awaited, and [the effect] should likewise arise all at once. Why is this? Because the cause, Maheśvara, is eternally present;
when causes and conditions are fully assembled, phenomena ought to arise instantaneously.
The refutation of other views that there exists a Great Brahmā, Time, Space, and so forth—which hold these to be the originators of all phenomena—is identical to this [refutation].
Four examples are used to refute other attachments. First, the names are listed and their tenets described. Regarding "Great Brahmā":
this refers to the Vedic teachers who reckon Brahmā to be the progenitor of all things, capable of creating all animate and inanimate entities; therefore, they designate him as eternal.
It is the cause of *nirvāṇa*. As for "time" (*kāla*): it refers to the immediate dispersal of the non-Buddhists who maintain that all phenomena arise from time;
therefore, time is eternal, it is the cause of the myriad things, and it is the cause of *nirvāṇa*. As for "direction" (*dis*): this refers to the teachers of the theory of direction (*dig-vādins*).
They hold that humans are born from direction, humans are born within heaven and earth, and after death they return to direction; therefore, direction is eternal, it is one, and so forth.
Regarding the "original limit" (pūrvakoṭi): this refers to the calculation of the teacher Andhaka, who asserts that at the very beginning of the world there was only a great expanse of water.
At that time, a great Andhaka emerged, shaped like a chicken egg and golden in color all around. When it ripened, it split into two halves.
The upper section is heaven; the lower section is earth. From between them, all myriad things are produced.

As for "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*), it is the reckoning of the proponents of causelessness (*ahetuvādin*): they hold that all myriad things arise and perish spontaneously, without cause and without condition;

therefore, this [spontaneity] is eternal and produces all things, serving as the cause of *nirvāṇa*. As for "space" (*ākāśa*), it refers to the proponents of the power of speech (*vākkaraṇavādin*), who say that space—

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the cause of all phenomena. There is another dharma that is real and permanent, which successively gives rise to all dharmas; therefore, emptiness is the cause of all phenomena.
As for "the self" (*ātman*), this refers to the proponents of the theory of self (*ātmavādin*), who maintain that there exists a sentient being (*sattva*).
The self (jīva), the living being (jantu), the nourisher (poṣa), the person (pudgala)—because such things as these are truly and eternally existent, the eye is able to see forms;
one should know that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise. Regarding the word "etcetera" (ādi): it includes the theories of past-action causality (pūrvakṛtahetuvāda) and so forth.
As for the phrase "all are refuted in the same manner": this means they are to be refuted by analogy with the preceding refutation.

There are others who hold the biased attachment that the *vidyā-sthānas* (fields of knowledge) are eternal, [claiming they are] like jars, garments, and so forth, because they depend upon various conditions.

Fifth is the refutation of the theory of sound (*śabda-vāda*). First, the position is stated: "The *vidyā-sthānas*" refers to the five *vidyā-sthānas*, namely: Hetu-vidyā (Logic), Śabda-vidyā (Grammar), and so on.

Regarding the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*), the science of crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*), and the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*): that which is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is fixed and unchanging;
its measurement is non-erroneous, and it illuminates both the past and the present. Therefore, they maintain that sound is eternal. Because of sound, all phenomena are designated and expressed;

furthermore, they maintain that the nature of all sound is eternal, not produced from conditions, but manifested in dependence upon them. It is only at the time of manifestation that it possesses the capacity for expression.

Manifestation: Just as bells and drums await the striking-stick to resound, metal and stone await the hammering to ring out, and strings and flutes await the fingers to produce sound, so too do words and meanings await verbal expression to become manifest.
[The opponent’s position] is refuted below. Next is the refutation: first, a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute the *Abhidharmadīpa*.
Next, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute other [types of] sound, as in the text.
There are non-Buddhists who maintain that the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of earth, water, fire, and wind, although impermanent, exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*).

Sixth, the refutation of the Lokāyata treatises. First, their tenets are set forth: namely, the Cārvākas (Lokāyatikas) who calculate that all phenomena, such as form and mind, are composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Earth possesses four atoms; water possesses three, excluding odor; fire possesses two, color and touch; and wind possesses only one, touch.
Therefore, these four atoms are real and eternal, capable of producing coarse matter (*audārika-rūpa*). This is what is called "coarse."
"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the "son-atom" (*putra-paramāṇu*). "Caused by measure" (*pramāṇa-hetuka*) refers to the "parent-atoms" (*pitṛ-paramāṇu*).
The initial ultimate atoms are called the parents; the collection that produces coarse form is called the son-atom. Although the son-atom is impermanent, it does not transcend the parents;
therefore, it is substantially existent (*dravyasat*). Within this [system], there are four assertions: that the ultimate atom is substantial, permanent, and capable of producing coarse form.
The coarse matter that is produced does not exceed the dimensions of its cause. "Exceeding" means to go beyond or to transgress;
thus, it is said that it neither exceeds nor transgresses. That [position] is also irrational. Why? (Up to: How can it be said that atoms are permanent?

That [position] is also refuted below in nine sections. First, the cause is refuted as being minute (*aṇu*). First, three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established to refute three types of attachment.
The first cognition refutes substantiality by means of having spatial parts (*sapradeśatva*). "Ants moving" refers to their movement in formation; that is, an ant-line (*antavyūha*).

The second cognition refutes its inability to produce an effect by means of lacking spatial parts. The third cognition refutes it by means of having functional activity capable of producing [an effect].
This refutes the permanence [of the cause].
Furthermore, the produced effect does not exceed the magnitude of its cause; [if it did,] being apprehended by the material sense faculties would contradict your own tenets.

Moreover, as for the "produced effect" below: four points refute that the effect does not exceed the magnitude of its cause. Furthermore, the produced effect is a *dharmin* (subject); it is not [merely] named...
Regarding the thesis that coarse matter does not exceed the measure of its cause, the reason is "because it does not exceed the measure of its cause," with the example being "like an atom.
Below this, the fault of contradiction is pointed out: since an atom is extremely subtle, it is not apprehended by the sensory faculties such as the eye;

if one claims that coarse resultant matter does not exceed the measure of its cause, then it would be identical to an atom and likewise not apprehended by the sensory faculties. This contradicts one's own school’s tenet regarding coarse matter.

This refers to that which is apprehended by the physical sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*). First, there is the fault of contradicting one's own doctrine; second, there is the fault of contradicting direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Since they postulate that cause and effect are distinct, and that the producer and the produced are different, the following passages all refute [this view] through the mutual analysis of cause and effect.

If it is argued that [the subtle] is like gross resultant matter because it is conjoined with dimensions and qualities (guṇa), and because there is no distinction in the locus of gross resultant matter—this fifth point refutes [the position] by showing the confusion of gross and subtle regarding dimensions and qualities. "If it is argued" below introduces a counter-argument; "dimension" refers to the dimension of the cause.

"Quality" refers to gross quality (*audārika-guṇa*). Because it does not exceed the measure of its cause, it is not gross; however, because it is conjoined with gross qualities, it appears as if gross.

For this reason, it is that which is apprehended by the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya-grāhya*). Regarding the "apprehended [object]" below, a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute it: the "resultant form" (*kārya-rūpa*) that is the subject of the thesis (*dharmin*)... [is as follows].
[Thesis: Grossness does not combine with qualities; [Reason: because it shares the same dimension as its cause; [Example: like an atom (*paramāṇu*).

This reason—"because it shares the same dimension as its cause"—refutes that the resultant form is gross, for it cannot be established as gross. Alternatively, the atom itself would be the subject (*dharmin*) and must likewise combine with the quality of grossness;
[Reason: because there is no difference in location; [Example: like gross resultant form. This [reason] is based on "there being no difference in location."
If [the effect] were to destroy the extremely subtle [atoms], it would follow that what is subtle is not subtle; coarse and subtle would be conflated, and cause and effect could not be distinguished.
If one claims that the resultant form (kāyavarṇa) is omnipresent within its own causes, then for this reason it too would not be apprehended by the sense organs.
Sixth, refuting [the opponent's view] by means of the pervasiveness of the effect within its own cause. First, the counter-argument is restated:
"Pervasive in its own cause" means that the produced effect, which is matter (rūpa), is pervasive throughout the atoms (paramāṇu) of its own productive cause.

Because the causal atoms are numerous and not one, the effect may be called coarse and can thus be apprehended by the material sense faculties. Now, the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute it: The effect-matter is...
There is a dharma whose substance ought not to be a single entity, because its locations are distinct, just like the cause of "being located.

As for "distinct locations," it means that each individual atom (paramāṇu) abides in its own position. If one claims that the effect pervades its causes, then since the substance of the causes is manifold and not one, the substance of the effect—just like the causes—should also not be one. Because the causes are distinct, a coarse object cannot be established.

Since the effect is like the cause, it likewise cannot be established as gross. For this reason, it also cannot be apprehended as a result of matter (*rūpa*). Both faults are identical to those mentioned previously.

Having previously refuted the capacity to produce [consciousness] by citing the three conditions as examples, we now refute the atom itself by adducing the reason that it does not bear its own aspect;
together these constitute a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to demonstrate that atoms are not the five [objects of consciousness].

Regarding the objective sphere of consciousness (*vijñāna-viṣaya*): some maintain that each individual atom (*paramāṇu*) of form and so forth, up to its specific characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), exists substantially as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Others maintain [the following]. First, the [opponent's] position is restated: they claim that atoms do not aggregate. [The author] then refutes the [notion of] aggregation as being the object-condition. The [opponent's] thesis is stated: "Atoms do not aggregate."

At that time, because its substance is subtle and spherical, it is not the object-domain of the five consciousnesses. In the state of collective aggregation, through mutual support among various [atoms], a coarse appearance arises;
since this appearance is not separate from the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), it is substantially existent. It serves as the objective condition (*ālambana*) for this [consciousness].
The arising of a coarse appearance means that [the consciousness] arises bearing that appearance. That the appearance is substantially existent means that the perception relies upon it to arise. (2)
Since the conditions are complete, it serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses.
Their position is incorrect, because if [the atoms] were to coalesce into a single cognition, that cognition would have to perceive all objects simultaneously.
That [position] is refuted by the following: the first sentence provides a general negation; "and collectively" (*sāmagryā*) and below provide the explanation.

That is to say, since the atoms (*paramāṇu*)—whether aggregated or not yet aggregated—are one in essence, how could their collective aggregation serve as the objective condition (*ālambana*)? The treatise says: "Aggregation is like hardness and so forth;

even with respect to visual consciousness and the rest, it is a condition but not an objective condition, because it is admitted to have the characteristics of atoms. Regarding "jars, bowls," and so forth, this refutes a further counter-argument. He...

Furthermore, you argue that there is a distinct production of the cognitive aspect (buddhi-lakṣaṇa) based on conditions such as jars and bowls, thereby attempting to defend the position that cognition carries the image of those objects.
We now refute this: objects such as jars and bowls are composed of atoms; these atoms are spherical and uniform, their essence being without distinction.

For that reason, the consciousnesses that take those aspects as their objects should likewise have no distinction; thus, the meaning of "bearing those aspects" remains unestablished. The treatise states:

"The aspects of the cognitions of jars, bowls, and so forth, should have no distinction according to that [opponent's] position. It is not the case that they are distinct because of a distinction in shape, for a distinction in shape is not real."

Regarding their collective aggregation: [the opponent] again attempts to refute this by proposing an alternative theory. That theory holds that even atoms possess differentiation. Now, we cite and refute it as follows:

If, in the state of collective aggregation, atoms were to produce a distinct coarse aspect that serves as the object of this consciousness, then each individual atom in the state of collective aggregation would necessarily abandon its own subtle, spherical, and minute aspect. Why must they abandon it? Because it is not [the case].

A consciousness that perceives coarse characteristics (*sthūla-nimitta*) may take subtle characteristics (*sūkṣma-nimitta*) as its object. Why does it not take subtle objects? Lest a consciousness directed toward one object should take another object as its domain.

Regarding the term "other" (*anya*): various sensory objects are called "others" in relation to one another. For example, an eye-consciousness perceiving visible form (*rūpa*) might [otherwise] perceive sound (*śabda*) and so forth.
If other consciousnesses were able to perceive other objects, then a single consciousness would have to perceive all objects.
If even granting the existence of atoms leads to this fault, how much more so when there are no real external atoms?

The phrase "if one grants [their existence]" concludes the argument by way of comparison, as the text explains. Therefore, it is fully established that the objective conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) of the five consciousnesses are not external forms and so forth. This principle is thoroughly proven.

From this, it is known with certainty that what is transformed by one's own consciousness (up to the point of) the seeing [aspect] arises in dependence upon that [object], because it bears its aspect.
From "By this" onwards, the internal object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is revealed. "By this" refers back to the preceding discussion;

since the external form and so forth previously mentioned do not exist as real entities, one knows that the consciousness transforms itself into aspects resembling the objects of form and so forth, which serve as the objects for the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness.
It is a true object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) because it possesses two meanings: being relied upon for the arising of the seeing [aspect], and arising while bearing its image.

"Seeing" refers to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*). "That" refers to that which resembles form and so forth; it signifies that which has substantial reality and the capacity to produce consciousness. "Bearing" has two meanings.
The first is "direct grasping" (*sākṣāt-parigraha*), which means that the cognizing mind directly grasps the object while cognizing it.

The second is "transformative grasping" (*pariṇāma-parigraha*), which means that the cognizing mind transforms and gives rise to an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) while cognizing it. This objective aspect also has two meanings: first, the "essential characteristic aspect" (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*);
and second, the "manifested form aspect" (*ākāra-lakṣaṇa*). When the five consciousnesses cognize an object, they pertain only to the latter of these two meanings. That is to say, regarding...

The five consciousnesses manifest and carry the images of form and so forth within their own substance, such that they become the objects of the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) of the eye-consciousness and the others.

Therefore, the treatise states: "Internal form appears as if external; it serves as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for consciousness. This is because we admit that its image resides within consciousness and because it is capable of producing consciousness."
However, when consciousness transforms [objects], it does so according to their size; therefore, it is said that the atom (*paramāṇu*) is the limit of form.
Yet, below this, it clarifies that the images transformed by consciousness are not composed of atoms. That is to say, when the five consciousnesses transform forms and so forth:
According to the magnitude of their respective original substances, [the images] appear immediately upon contact; the size and form of what appears correspond to those original substances.
It is not that a multitude of atoms (*paramāṇu*) are separately transformed and then combine to constitute a single object. [This is stated] to refute the objection. The objection says:
"It may be granted that the transformation of consciousness into forms and so forth occurs instantaneously; however, since the sūtras speak of 'atoms,' how can this not be [the case]?"

This is contradictory. The commentary explains: For those who cling to the notion that coarse matter possesses a substantial reality, the Buddha taught the atom (*paramāṇu*) in order to cause them to dismantle it;

it does not mean that atoms exist substantially. Following this teaching, the various masters employ analytical meditation (*parikalpa*) to gradually eliminate the object into seven parts each, until it reaches a point where it can no longer be divided.
Furthermore, an objection is raised: as previously stated, if the atom definitely possesses spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*), it must be [divisible].
[Question: "Analysis. Now, why do you further say that it cannot be analyzed? [Answer: The commentary states: "Although these [atoms], such as the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), are thus described...
Below this, it says: As the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states: "Observe the nature of earth: grossly it is the great earth; subtly it is minute dust.
Reaching the *anuvicira* (neighboring-void) atom, analyze the characteristics of the boundaries of that ultimate atom's form into seven parts. If one further analyzes the *anuvicira*, then..."
Because they are truly empty, it is said that the atom (*paramāṇu*) is the limit of form (*rūpa*).
From this, one should know that all resistant forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*) are manifestations of consciousness and are not composed of atoms.
From this point downward, the conclusion is reached: having established that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), those externalist theories are refuted.
Since other non-resistant forms (*apratigha-rūpa*) belong to this same category, they may be described as truly existent material phenomena (*rūpadharma*).

Regarding "the rest lack the lower": this refutes non-resistant form (*apratigha-rūpa*) by means of a prior analogy. Alternatively, "the rest lack the lower" is refuted by means of formal inference (*pramāṇa*). The formal argument is as follows:

Non-resistant form, which is the subject (*dharmin*), is definitely not substantially existent (*dravyasat*), such is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is admitted to be non-resistant. The example (*udāharaṇa*) is: like the mind and mental factors (*citta-caittas*).
Are informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) form not truly existent?
[The text] refutes informative and non-informative form below. "Informative" means to manifest, to display;

it refers to the two types of action—body and speech—which manifest the goodness or evil of the mind. "Non-informative" refers to the remainder of mental action (*manas-karman*). [The opponent] raises an objection, saying: "There is informative [form]."

The two objects of form and sound include [visible and audible] matter; non-informative matter is included within the category of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*). Are these various material phenomena not substantially existent?
Why are they not substantially existent? Furthermore, if bodily informative matter were substantially existent, what would its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) be?

This is not [the case] below. This is a general refutation and a general inquiry. First, regarding "below" in the context of the body: this refers to the inquiry concerning bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) among manifest forms (*vijñapti-rūpa*).
If one says it is shape, then it would not be substantially existent, because it can be analyzed; for instance, atoms (*paramāṇu*) such as length and so forth cannot be apprehended.
If one says that [the preceding argument] separately refutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), it first refutes shape (*saṃsthāna*). Shape refers to dimensions such as long and short.

There is a school of tenets that maintains that shape constitutes bodily intimation; however, when long and short dimensions are analyzed down to their ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), no dimension of shape can be found upon those atoms.
If it is argued that this motion is also not substantially existent—up to the point where it is said that if cessation depended on a cause, it would not be cessation—next, motion is refuted.

"Motion" refers to physical action, such as contracting and extending, bending and stretching, looking down and looking up. The Saṃmitīya school maintains that motion constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
It perishes immediately upon arising and does not reach another location, because the sense of moving or shifting cannot be apprehended. [This is] common [to both positions].
Śrīlāta says: We maintain that bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) is a distinct shape (*saṃsthāna*), and not motion as its essence.

This is because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) perish in each moment. The two subsequent lines of the verse explain this point in succession. Why is it that they perish immediately upon arising?
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) perish without depending on a cause. They are like a flash of lightning, appearing and perishing simultaneously.

How is it that the perishing of phenomena does not depend on a cause? The coming together of conditions is called arising; the separation of conditions is called perishing. If perishing were to depend on a cause, it would not be [truly] perishing.

If it is claimed that there exists a form (*rūpa*) which is neither color (*varṇa*) nor shape (*saṃsthāna*), yet is produced by the mind and is capable of moving the hands and other limbs, and is thus termed "bodily informative action" (*kāyavijñapti-karman*);
we shall next refute the claim that it is produced by the mental factors (*caitta*). First, we state the opponent's position: It is not color, meaning it is not colors such as blue or yellow;
it is not shape, meaning it is not shapes such as long or short. The intention is that there exists a form not subsumed under either color or shape, which is the power of the mind.
Regarding that which is produced by [the mind]: it is said that because this can move the hands and so forth, it is called bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*).
This reasoning is also incorrect; for if this were movement, one should know that it would belong to the categories of sound, odor, taste, or tangible objects, rather than being manifest.

Next, the refutation of motion (*iṅgana*). The meaning of the refutation is as before. As for the cause of motion, it is wind. Since the nature of wind has no substantial entity (*anātman*), what could it possibly indicate?
Furthermore, wind belongs to the category of the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*), and the tangible is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), not encompassing the wholesome or unwholesome.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Bodily and vocal informative acts (*vijñapti-karman*) encompass all three natures. This shows that [motion] is not manifest [action]. By extension, the other two objects [smell and taste] are likewise not bodily manifest action. The above clarifies form (*rūpa*).

By analogy with these cases of tangible objects, odors, and tastes—and because sound consists solely of vocal intimation—it is known that the five sensory objects are all not bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti-karman*).
Therefore, bodily informative action is certainly not substantially existent.

Therefore, below the section on the body (*kāya*), the [discussion of] the formation and destruction of the aggregates is concluded. However, because the mind acts as the cause that causes consciousness to undergo transformation (up to the point where it) represents the mind, it is metaphorically termed "bodily intimation" (*kāyavijñapti*).

Now, below the section on the mind, the correct principle is set forth. In the Mahāyāna, this is based on the mind’s transformation, which differs from the Hīnayāna. Here, "mind" refers to the sixth [consciousness].
"Consciousness" refers to the eighth [consciousness]. It is called "bodily intimation" because it takes the mental consciousness as its cause;

being uniquely predominant in moving the body and initiating speech, it causes the hands and other [limbs] manifested by the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to cease and arise again in succession, similar to their predecessor, as they transition to another location.
Although there is no actual movement, it appears to have action, representing the goodness or evil of the mind; thus it is metaphorically named "bodily intimation. It does not mean...
[The view that] it exists separately from the mind is [rejected].
Verbal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) is also not substantially existent as the nature of sound, because [the existence of] external resistant form (*bāhyapratigha-rūpa*) has already been refuted above.

Regarding "Verbal intimation" and below: next, verbal intimation is refuted. The first phrase directly refutes its lack of substantial reality. "In a single moment" and below provides the explanation. One moment... [text fragment].

Although that sound is substantially existent, its characteristic is extremely subtle because it lacks the capacity for signification. This first phrase, even while granting its substantial existence, denies its capacity for signification.
The subsequent phrase, "many moments," etc., grants its capacity for signification but denies its substantial existence. The section beginning with "externally existing" follows the previous example;
since sound belongs to the category of the resistant (*sapratigha*), it has already been refuted previously and should not be clung to here.

However, because it is due to the mind, consciousness transforms and appears as sound (up to the point where it is designated by the provisional name "vocal intimation"); this does not contradict the principle.
The phrase "However, because it is due to... below serves to state the correct doctrine; it should be understood according to the preceding [explanation].
Since the manifest (*vijñapti*) is in reality non-existent, how could the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) be real?
Having thus refuted the unmanifest by taking the manifest as an example, [the text continues:
however, because it is established based on the limits of wholesome or unwholesome volition (*cetanā*) and its actual manifestation, it is a conventional existence (*prajñaptisat*).

Now, based on the following, the correct meaning is set forth: "volition" (*cetanā*) refers to volition among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), and "aspiration" (*praṇidhāna*) refers to desire (*chanda*) among the object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣabhūmika*).

This means that the boundaries and limits of volition and aspiration—whether wholesome or unwholesome—as they associate with the sixth consciousness, are such that they alone are most predominant in moving the body and initiating speech;
it is based on this that the name "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) is provisionally established. Regarding this, the following provides a detailed analysis and explanation.
"Letter" (vyañjana) refers to the unmanifest (avijñapti). Wholesome or unwholesome bodily and vocal actions are that which is produced; volition (cetanā) is that which produces it.

"Growth" (puṣṭi) refers to the stage of maturation when the seeds are about to manifest as active states (pravṛtti). If they have already manifested, they belong to the manifest (vijñapti); however, while they are about to manifest, they are still termed unmanifest.

This explanation is based on the state of distraction (vikṣipta-citta), encompassing both wholesome and unwholesome positions. In the case of meditative concentration (samādhi), it is defined in terms of the present.

Regarding the establishment [of non-informative action] in the state of mental formation through volition: because within meditative concentration the manifest characteristics do not appear externally, but are known only by oneself, it is also called "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*).

This is explained from the perspective of the virtuous state of the concentrated mind; whether as seeds or as manifest activity, both are established based on volition, and therefore they are not substantially existent.
The World-Honored One stated in the sūtras that there are three types of karma; does this not contradict the sūtra which negates bodily and vocal karma?
[The author] first raises an objection below: he raises the objection based on the premise that among the three types of karma, one exists while two do not, yet now speaks only of the mind.
To deny the existence of body and speech would surely contradict the sūtras.

It is not that they are denied as non-existent; rather, it is said that they are not matter (*rūpa*) [up to] because they are results of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), and for this reason they are also called the "path" (*mārga*).
"Not excluding the lower" is the explanation. The first two phrases provide a direct answer; "not being form" means that all [three types] have volition (*cetanā*) as their intrinsic nature.
"Able to move the lower" clarifies that all three kinds of volition are termed "action" (*karman*). "Deliberation" refers to the volition of deliberation (*saṃtīraṇa-cetanā*);

"decision" refers to the volition of determination (*niścaya-cetanā*); and "mind" refers to the sixth consciousness. These two types of volition are associated with the mind and are capable of moving the mind; thus they are so described.
It is called "mental karma" (*manas-karman*). If the essence of volition (*cetanā*) is movement, it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
If it refers to the karmas of the three—body, speech, and mind—it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Regarding the word "karma" in the phrase "giving rise to":

the meaning of volition as "karma" is "constructive activity. Regarding the phrase "this is deliberative": this body and speech are the traversing and proceeding of deliberative and decisive volition.

It is called the "Path" (*mārga*) because it is that which is trodden, and because it serves as the cause for present bodily and verbal actions that can lead to and produce future fruits of suffering or pleasure;

thus, it is both "trod upon" (*lǐ*) and "penetrating" (*tōng*). Therefore, it is named the Path. "Path" is synonymous with "road" and "penetration. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, which asks:
"What is meant by 'paths of action' (*karmapatha*)? It answers: "The mind itself is the action (*karman*); because it proceeds within [the body and speech], it is therefore called a path of action."
Among the three [factors] that precede [the actual action], and among the seven that follow it, three are karma but not paths, while seven are both karma and paths.

That which is "intention itself as karma" refers to volition (*cetanā*) belonging to the mental level (*manobhūmi*). Among these, "that which proceeds" refers to the proceeding of the body and so forth;

thus, one should know that the body and so forth, being what the mind proceeds toward, are called paths of karma (*karmapatha*). Regarding the phrase "the preceding factors," etc., this distinguishes the sequence of their arising.

Regarding the sequence of arising as set forth in the text: while the order of the written text places the actions of body and speech first and the three mental actions last, the actual order of their arising places the three mental actions first and the actions of body and speech last. Because the stage of the mind arises first, they are called the "preceding actions" (*pūrvagama*);
because they are listed last in the text, they are called the "three subsequent ones. Because they subsequently move the body and speech, they are called the "subsequent actions. Thus says the text.
They are listed at the beginning; thus, they are called the "first seven. The middle character [of the term] is merely an auxiliary particle, meaning simply "in these seven and among these three.
However, the intent of the treatise is that the [last] three are karma but not the path because they are neither body nor speech;
those which are both karma and the path are so called because the two karmas of body and speech are what are practiced by the karma of mind, and are therefore further named the path. Now...
The ability to penetrate the meaning of the words and establish the intended meaning is also called the "path" (*mārga*). Therefore, the latter three [paths] extend to the body and speech;
thus it is said that they "can penetrate the seven. The former seven are karma, yet they also function as mental activities; therefore, the treatise states that they are "both karma and path."
Therefore, the first seven courses of action also have volition (*cetanā*) as their intrinsic nature.
Thus, [the text] concludes below that it is not only mental action that has volition as its intrinsic nature; the substance of both bodily and vocal actions is also volition.
As for the "seven actions," these are the wholesome and unwholesome actions consisting of three of the body and four of speech.

Alternatively, because bodily and vocal intimation are produced by volition (*cetanā*), they are metaphorically designated as "action" (*karman*); and because they are traversed by volition, they are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*).
Alternatively, [the text] below explains the two intimations of body and speech: the former refers to the volition that moves the body and initiates speech, which is termed "action";

this [latter] refers to the bodily and vocal intimations produced by that volition, which are metaphorically named "action" because they are initiated by internal volition. Thus, they are [traversed] by volition.
Because they are both [the basis and] the action, they are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*). This is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
From this, one should know that there is in reality no external form; there is only internal consciousness which transforms and arises as if it were form.
From this point downward, [the author] concludes that form is merely a transformation of consciousness.

Having finished refuting the reality of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) above, he now addresses the non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), which likewise do not exist as substantial entities; rather, they are merely provisionally established based on the various states (*avasthā*) of matter and so forth.
It does not descend [into other categories]. It refutes [its] non-correspondence. First, the general name is explained: "correspondence" (saṃprayoga) means the sense of harmony and conformity.

Because this [dharma] is not a cognitive subject (ālambaka), it does not correspond with the mind (citta). Because it is neither universally wholesome nor defiled, it does not correspond with mental factors (caitta).

Furthermore, because it is not substantially obstructive, it does not correspond with matter (rūpa). Moreover, because it possesses arising and ceasing, it does not correspond with the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).

Distinguishing these fourteen factors—namely, acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the maturation of non-conception (*āsaṃjñika*), birth (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), change (*jarā*), impermanence (*anityatā*), the group of names (*nāmakāya*), the group of phrases (*padakāya*), and the group of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*)—they are called "non-associated" (*viprayukta*).
First, there is a general refutation and a general inquiry; the following three lines explain why they are not real entities, as they are not like [the other conditioned phenomena].

The following phrase clarifies that [the self] does not possess a real, substantial entity. The subsequent phrase clarifies that it is not something distinct from matter (rūpa) and mind (citta), having a separate function.

By means of this phrase, the conclusion is reached: "But based on... below, which clarifies that [the designation of a self] is a provisional construction (prajñapti) based upon the various states (avasthā) of matter and mind.

This meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is not something distinct from matter, mind, or mental factors (up to the point where it is said that, like other conventional phenomena, it lacks a real substantial entity).

This section below explains and establishes the preceding three points by means of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the first valid cognition, it states: "This" refers to acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and so forth;

these are the subject (*dharmin*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they do not possess a real substantial entity or function distinct from matter, mind, or mental factors, because it is admitted that they are subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*).

The reason (*hetu*) is as in the analogy of matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth. This establishes the thesis that [this entity] is not distinct from matter, mind, and so forth, thereby demonstrating that it does not possess a separate function apart from matter, mind, and so forth.
Next, the formal inference (*pramāṇa*) again takes these very characters as the subject (*dharmin*).

The reason is that they are not subsumed under mind or mental factors (*caitta*); this demonstrates that they certainly do not possess a substantially existent essence (*dravyasat*). The subsequent inference likewise takes these...

The term "existent phenomenon" (*dharma*) is used here as an analogy for other conventional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) to demonstrate that this [self] is also a conventional designation based upon various states.

"Other real phenomena" refers to matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth; "other conventional phenomena" refers to things such as reflections in a mirror or the moon in water, which are conventionally designated based upon the true moon and its physical form.
Furthermore, how do they know that acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) possess a real substantial function distinct from form, mind, and so forth?
The phrase "Furthermore, they... introduces a specific explanation of acquisition and non-acquisition; first, the Mahāyāna objection is raised.
Because it is stated in the *Sūtra*, as it says: "Thus [it is]... up to... accomplished or unaccomplished. This statement reveals the attainment (*prāpti*) and non-attainment (*aprāpti*).

The remainder of the *Sūtra* provides the answer from the perspective of other vehicles regarding the *pudgala*—here translated as "one who repeatedly takes on rebirth" (*saṃsārin*). As for the ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*):

right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*); right mindfulness and right concentration constitute the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhiskandha*); and right view [constitutes the aggregate of wisdom].

Right thought and right effort constitute the aggregate of wisdom; right liberation constitutes the aggregate of liberation; and right knowledge constitutes the aggregate of the vision and knowledge of liberation.
These ten are precisely the fivefold dharma-body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa). Regarding "accomplishment and non-accomplishment" below:

The two terms "establishment" (*siddhi*) mentioned in the Sūtra correctly manifest "acquisition" (*prāpti*), while the two terms "non-establishment" (*asiddhi*) manifest "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*).
Therefore, it is known that these possess both substantial entity (*dravya*) and function (*vṛtti*).
The Sūtra does not state that these [factors] are distinct from form, mind, and so forth; rather, it establishes that there must necessarily be seeds of the wholesome and so on in the present.

Regarding the phrase "the Sūtra does not state" below: the first sentence refutes the citation of the Sūtra as being inappropriate. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "it also states" below: this cites an example to refute [the opponent's position]. As for the "seven treasures":

the minister of military affairs, the minister of the treasury, the woman-treasure, the elephant-treasure, and the horse-treasure—these constitute the bodies of others, such as those who possess the power of *rddhi*.

The Jewel and the Wheel-Jewel are insentient (*acetana*). If you claim that [merely] obtaining them constitutes accomplishment, how could a Wheel-Turning King truly accomplish another's body or an insentient object?

The phrase "If you say... below serves to refute this defense; the first clause restates the opponent’s argument, while the section beginning with "In regard to the wholesome... [proceeds with the refutation].

Refutation. If it is argued that a Wheel-turning King possesses sovereign power over the [seven] treasures and is thus figuratively said to "attain" them, then since he likewise possesses sovereign power over wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, why not allow that he is figuratively said to "attain" those as well? Why then do you insist that this is a literal attainment?

"If it is argued... and so forth, further refuting the defense; the first phrase restates the defensive argument. "How can one know... and so forth, is the refutation. If it is argued that the seven treasures are...

Regarding that which can be provisionally designated as "present": how could one know that the wholesome and so forth do not exist in the present? The second phrase explains by way of contrast that they do exist in the present;

for there is no principle whereby a real dharma could be divorced from existing in the present. The single phrase "present" further explains that the seeds of the wholesome and so forth are real and not provisional.
This statement means that the seeds of good and evil are dharmas of the present, and they are substantially existent, not...
This is a mere designation (*prajñapti*). Why do you insist that the seven treasures are present while they must be designated?

If the seven treasures are present yet can be designated, then seeds, being present as well, should also be designated. How then can you insist that they constitute a real attainment (*dravya-lābha*)?
Furthermore, what superior function does "acquisition" (prāpti) have with respect to dharmas? [This continues] until: "If it depends on other causes to be acquired, then it has no function.

Furthermore, the section beginning with "Moreover, acquisition... provides a refutation through logical interrogation. The first phrase is the interrogative inquiry; the section beginning with "If one says... is the refutation.

If one says that because sentient beings possess this acquisition, they are able to give rise to all dharmas, then there would be no need for cultivation and realization, and they should give rise to unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) phenomena.
And thus one accomplishes the Path of the Sage. Furthermore, if all insentient things were characterized by non-attainment, they should never arise at all.

How is it, then, that we currently perceive grasses and trees sprouting in spring and growing in summer? Moreover, those things not yet attained or already lost would both be cases of non-attainment, and thus they too should never arise again.

How can it be that what has not yet been attained is attained, and what has already been lost is regained? If [the opponent] claims that although there is no present attainment of what was previously unattained or lost, it arises again at a later time because it is caused by an innate "possession" (*prāpti*) that has existed since beginningless time, we refute this:
if that were so, it would be identical to the "single-cause theory" of those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and thus contradict your own [tenets].
It is taught that [phenomena] arise from two causes and conditions, and furthermore, they possess the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Consequently, the three natures should manifest simultaneously.
To this, the opponent offers a defense: "Although they possess the three natures, they must await other causes—whether wholesome or unwholesome—before arising. Now, we refute this:
if other causes arise spontaneously, then [the theory of] "attaining" them becomes useless.
If "acquisition" (prāpti) were the cause for not losing a dharma, then [the acquisition] and the dharma itself would both be useless.
If one says "acquisition," this refutes the cause for non-loss. [The opponent] then argues: Acquisition is the cause for the non-loss of a dharma; as for the dharma—

This refers to the dharmas of wholesome and unwholesome karma. "Obtainment" (*prāpti*) means obtaining the rope [of continuity]. In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), fascicle 7, part 3, it is stated that according to the Sarvāstivāda school, there is established the "obtainment of obtainment" (*prāptiprāpti*).
Gradually, by means of the subsequent obtainment, one obtains the prior obtainment; thus, past karma is able to reach into the future.
Therefore, within the Sarvāstivāda school, karma enters the past and can extend into the future. When the body dies and [the present] ceases, the future retribution arises.

Just as one karma is established, it is acquired through a "great acquisition" (*mahāprāpti*) which acquires the dharma of the karma; furthermore, through a "small acquisition" (*parīttaprāpti*), it acquires that great acquisition.
In the second moment, through three great acquisitions, one acquires the two preceding acquisitions as well as the dharma of the karma. At the first...
They are attained through mindfulness, for they are all established as dharmas. Furthermore, there are three minor attainments (*prāpti*) which attain the three preceding major ones;
thus, at the first moment, nine dharmas are accomplished, and at the third moment, twenty-seven dharmas are accomplished.

This meaning of attainment—whether it be manifest action (*vijñapti*) or non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) arising from the explanation of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)—ensures that even if one has performed actions over hundreds of thousands of eons, they are not forgotten, because of this attainment.
It is because the cord is not severed that this occurs; therefore, it is said that "it is not lost. All sentient beings take this as their cause to accomplish various dharmas, such as the wholesome.
[The phrase] "all that is inferior" is refuted. The accomplishment of dharmas is accomplished by sentient beings; what purpose would there be in "attaining" them?
Since acquisition (*prāpti*) is ultimately non-existent, non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is likewise non-existent.
Having established this, the following serves as an analogy to refute non-acquisition.
Nevertheless, based upon sentient beings, the various states (*avasthā*) of dharmas can be established, up to the three types of present manifestation and possession (*samanvāgama*).
Now, based on what follows, the correct meaning is set forth. First, the attainment of the three kinds of accomplishment is explained to clarify "attainment" (*prāpti*).

This refers to all defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), all indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*), and innate wholesome phenomena (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-dharma*) that manifest without the exertion of effort.
Those seeds, if they have not been suppressed by śamatha, if they have not been permanently destroyed by the noble path,
and if their wholesome qualities have not been suppressed by wrong views— as in the case of one who has severed the roots of goodness—
are said to be "accomplished as seeds. This applies to wholesome dharmas produced through application and to a portion of the indeterminate.
Phenomena (*dharma*) that are grasped by the conditions for their arising and whose seeds are intensified are called "accomplishment through mastery" (*vaśitā-sampad*).
If present phenomena manifest and proceed according to their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is called "accomplishment through actualization" (*samudācāra-sampad*).

The phrase "reversing this, one establishes the name 'non-accomplishment'" (up to) "...because one has not yet accomplished the various noble dharmas" reverses the preceding [section] to clarify non-possession (*aprāpti*) and non-accomplishment (*asamanvāgama*), explicitly revealing non-possession as the text describes. The section beginning with "this type of...
points to the detailed exposition to conclude the summary; by citing one instance, it encompasses all others.
Furthermore, how is it known that there exists a real *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) distinct from form, mind, and so forth?
It is as explained below regarding *sabhāgatā*: "Sabhāgatā" refers to the commonality among sentient beings born in various respective places within the same realm (*dhātu*).

Sharing the same destiny, the same birth, the same category, status, nature, form, and so forth—due to this mutual similarity in various respects, it is called "homogeneity" (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and is also termed "homogeneity of sentient beings" (*sattva-sabhāga*). First, the Mahāyāna question:
Because it is stated in the sūtras; as the sūtra states: "This is the generic similarity (*nikāyasabhāga*) of this deity, this is the generic similarity of this person," and so forth at length.
Next, the other vehicle [the Sautrāntika] replies:
This sūtra does not state that there is a real, distinct generic similarity apart from form, mind, and so forth; thus, the proof is unestablished.
Below this passage in the sutra, the author refutes the improper citation of scripture.
[The opponent argues: "If [the self] is identical to cognition because speech arises from it... [The author replies: "Since that is not the case for him, how could it be so for this?"

If it were the same as the previous case, the argument would be refuted by citing that very position. First, the position is restated: "Knowledge" refers to cognitive understanding; "speech" refers to verbal expression.

"Homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) means that their objects are equal. If [it is argued that] homogeneity arises because knowledge and speech are identical and the objects are consequently equal— [End of segment]

The critique by way of example states: "If the objects of grass and trees were identical, they would likewise possess a commonality (*sabhāgatā*), and they would likewise give rise to a common cognition and expression.
Now, although the objects of grass and trees are identical, they lack a commonality, and no common cognition or expression arises.

Thus, sentient beings do not give rise to common cognitions and expressions based on the identity of their objects, nor does a real commonality exist. Furthermore, below this, it refutes [the opponent] by means of an infinite regress.
As stated in the text:

if it is argued that [the *sabhāgatā*] arises as a cause for the desire to act in concert (*samāna-kārya-icchā*), then what is the necessity of separately asserting the existence of a real *sabhāgatā*?

The phrase "if it is argued" below introduces the refutation by restating the opponent's position. First, the position is restated: "acting in concert" means having the same object of activity; "desire in concert" means having the same...
Aspiration and desire arise through the homogeneous factor (*sabhāgatā*) acting as their cause; it is only then that aspirations and desires for common activities emerge.

Therefore, one should know that the claim that the homogeneous factor exists substantially is refuted by the following reasoning: when habits become established as a nature, they arise from the inclinations and desires [of sentient beings]. Why, then, must one insist on positing a separate entity?
However, based on the distinctions among the similar states of the bodies and minds of sentient beings, "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) is conventionally established.

Now, from the passage beginning with "However, based on the lower [categories]," the correct meaning is set forth. "Similarity of body and mind" is the meaning of "same" (*sama*). "Part" (*bhāga*) refers to the cause.
"Distinctions among states" refers to such categories as the class of gods, the class of humans, and so forth; since each class is not singular, they are distinguished according to their types.
"Aggregation" (*skandha*) means that things are categorized according to their kind.
Furthermore, how is it known that there exists a real life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) distinct from visible form, mind, and so forth?

It is as explained below regarding the life-faculty: the life-faculty is the continuous maintenance of the three factors—consciousness, breath, and warmth—throughout the duration of a single lifetime.
The uninterrupted continuity of retribution is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). This is a provisional designation based upon the seeds of the eighth consciousness. First, a Mahāyāna inquiry:

because it is stated in the sūtras; as the sūtra says, "One should know that among the triad of vitality, warmth, and consciousness, what is called the life-faculty is designated as 'vitality' (*āyus*)."
Next, the other vehicle responds:
This scripture does not state that there is a real entity of life-force (jīva) distinct from matter, mind, and so forth; thus, the proof is unestablished.
In the following section of this scripture, the citation of another sutra is shown to be inappropriate.

Furthermore, it has already been established that matter (*rūpa*) is not distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*). [This continues] until: "it should be like feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, and thus the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not real.

Below this, an example is raised to refute [the opponent's position]. A formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute the claim that matter is not distinct from consciousness; this was already fully established previously. Heat (*uṣman*) is a dharma of matter;
by analogy, one should know that the life-faculty likewise does not exist apart from consciousness. This is clarified by a single inference. If it is... [as follows]:
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) does not exist apart from consciousness. The life-faculty is an existent phenomenon; it is our thesis that it does not exist separately apart from consciousness.

This is because it is not different from consciousness—this is the reason. The corroborative example is like heat. Next, a single formal inference clarifies that if it were to exist apart from consciousness, it would not be the life-faculty.

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is a functional entity (*dharmin*). It is not a real life-faculty; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is that it exists as something distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*). If this is so, how is it that the Sūtra speaks of three factors [as the causes of this consciousness]? This shall be explained in detail later.

"If that is so," and so forth, consists of three rounds of question and answer resolving an objection. The first question asks: "If vitality (*āyuṣka*) and warmth (*uṣman*) are both consciousness (*vijñāna*), one should simply say 'consciousness.

Why does the Sūtra speak of the triad of vitality, warmth, and consciousness? The answer begins with "The meanings are distinct": although they are all consciousness, [their specific functions differ].

In terms of their meaning, there are three: the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the *ālaya-vijñāna* is called "warmth" (*uṣman*); the seeds (*bīja*) of this consciousness are called "life-force" (*āyus*);

and the active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) of this consciousness is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). This is analogous to the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*), which are categorized according to whether wholesome or unwholesome dharmas have already arisen or have not yet arisen.

In terms of their meaning, they are explained as four, yet they are but a single vigor (*vīrya*). Next, the question is asked: "Although three are explained in terms of their meaning, there is but a single consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Since there is no mind in the state of non-mentation (*acittaka*), there should likewise be no life-force (*āyus*) or warmth (*uṣman*).

Why, then, does the Sūtra say that life-force does not perish and is not separated from warmth? Is it not [the case that] one is 'down'? The answer is: "In the state of non-mentation, consciousness..."
Because it does not depart from the body, life-force (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*) likewise do not cease. Regarding the phrase "Since this is so," the three subsequent questions state:

"Since this is so" refers back to the fact that consciousness does not depart from the body; this is called the state of having mind (*sacittaka*). What, then, is meant by the state of being without mind (*acittaka*)? Regarding the phrase "That ceases," the answer is:

in the state of being without mind, it is only the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) that cease, not the eighth [consciousness]. Proof that this consciousness exists is as will be cited later through scripture and reasoning.

This consciousness is sufficient to serve as the substance of the realms, destinies, and births; there is no need to laboriously maintain the separate assertion that there is a real life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Below this, the conclusion summarizes [the preceding] and indicates the essence [of the argument] to refute [false] attachments.
However, based on the seeds that directly produce this consciousness—up until the point of their abiding—it is conventionally established as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Now, following the subsequent passage, the correct meaning is revealed. The word "this" (*idam*) excludes the seeds of other consciousnesses; the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) excludes associated mental factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*);
and the term "seeds" (*bīja*) excludes manifest states (*pravṛtti*). Those excluded are all not the life-faculty. Here, we take the seeds of the eighth [consciousness] that directly produce it.
Son, these seeds are projected by prior wholesome and unwholesome karma. Since karma is not uniform, the seeds projected by it also differ.
Their duration is determined according to their causes. Based upon these seeds, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is conventionally established.

Furthermore, how is it known that the two mindless absorptions (*acittaka-samāpatti*) and the maturation of the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) distinct from matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth?
It is as follows: in explaining the two mindless absorptions and the maturation of non-perception, first, the Mahāyāna objection is raised.
If it lacked real existence, it would be unable to prevent the mind and mental factors from arising.

[The text says] "if there were none," to which the other vehicle responds; the text answers in reverse, meaning that only by having a real dharma distinct from consciousness can one prevent the mind and so forth from arising.
If there were a distinct, real dharma in the state of non-consciousness (as in the case of a dam or embankment), even a conventional designation could serve to obstruct [the flow].

"If there were not" below [in the text] takes up the opponent's position and provides an example to refute it. First, "should there not be" below takes up the position; then, "since that already" below provides the example.
[This] refutes [the objection]. Furthermore, by negating the lower [position], it cites the conventional to refute the real.

That is to say, when practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because this wholesome seed exists within the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of that concentration, the concentration itself is also termed "wholesome."

This refers to the cultivation of the lower [state], which clarifies the correct meaning. First, the two mindless states are explained. Regarding the preparatory application (*prayoga*): this refers to the preliminary means prior to meditative concentration.

At the time one is actually in concentration, the mind and mental factors are quiescent, and there is no longer any aversion, expectation, or aspiration. Therefore, aversion and expectation exist only during the stage of preparatory application.
As for the distinction between the two concentrations, they differ in their aversion and expectation; as for the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), it is merely...
