One becomes weary of the first six types of non-permanently active mind and mental factors; furthermore, in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one is additionally weary of the seventh type, the defiled permanently active mind and mental factors.
Moreover, the bases (*āśraya*) of these two attainments differ: one relies on non-Buddhist teachings, while the other relies on the Noble Teachings. Their realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*) differ:
[the former] pertains to the five levels of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), while [the latter] pertains to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Their modes of attention (*manasikāra*) also differ.
One seeks to extinguish [defilements], while the other seeks temporary rest; based on this difference, two meditative attainments are provisionally established.

In the case of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), one first seeks the fruit of non-conception; it is established as "attainment" (*samāpatti*) based on its being a resultant state (*vipāka*). Thus, it receives the name "resultant attainment."

Below [the section on] the non-percipient realm (*asaṃjñin*), next is the explanation of the maturation (*vipāka*) of the non-percipient state. This refers to seeking the fruit of non-perception during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).

One grasps that heaven as the most ultimate state of tranquility and the locus of true liberation, and because one generates a superior aspiration and yearns to attain it, this differs from the meditative attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
While the latter exists in the causal stage, this exists only as the fruit; while the former involves cultivation, this...

It is without activity. That belongs to the mind; this belongs to form. It is a provisional designation for this state in which all innate, non-constant, coarse, and mobile minds and mental factors have ceased.
Therefore, these three dharmas are also not substantially existent.
From "Therefore, this" below, the text concludes that the three dharmas are not real.
*Cheng weishi lun zikao*, Scroll One.
From the *Cheng weishi lun zikao*, Fascicle Two.
Recorded by the disciple Da-hui of the Lianju Monastery in Lin’an, Wulin.

Furthermore, how is it known that the various conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) distinct from matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth?
Furthermore, as follows: refuting arising, abiding, change, and cessation. First, the Mahāyāna inquiry:
because it is taught in the sūtras; as the sūtra says, "There are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned," and so forth, at length.
Below the Sūtra [section], the answer from the other vehicles follows. Regarding the "three conditioned [phenomena]":

this refers to all dharmas—whether form (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*)—bound to the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness; these all belong to the conditioned. Regarding the "characteristics of the conditioned":

this refers to the four characteristics of arising, abiding, change, and cessation. Because conditioned phenomena undergo impermanence and ceaseless transformation due to these four, these four are termed "conditioned."

This serves as the characteristic [of conditioned phenomena]. Since the Sūtra teaches that there are three characteristics of the conditioned for conditioned things, it is proven that these characteristics exist separately from matter and mind.
This Sūtra does not state that matter, mind, and so forth possess a real intrinsic nature (svabhāva); therefore, using that as proof is unestablished.
Below this, the sūtra refutes [the opponent's position]. First, it rebuts the improper citation of scripture:

the sixth case-ending does not signify a distinct entity (pṛthak-svabhāva); otherwise, the characteristic of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa) would have to be a different entity from that which is characterized (lakṣya).

It is not merely the genitive case. It is distinguished by three further instances of refutation, all of which refute the notion that the subject (the capacity) and the object (the referent) are distinct entities.
The "sixth sound" refers to the sixth among the eight grammatical cases (*vibhakti*), namely the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*). The *Weishi kaimeng* (Introduction to Consciousness-Only) states:

"The [grammatical categories] are substance, object, instrument, point of departure, purpose, locus, and vocative. The term used here corresponds precisely to the "locus" (*adhi-karaṇa*) within those [categories], specifically the genitive suffix. This means "belonging to" or "connected to."

This is both a summary and a synthesis. First, it directly refutes [the opponent] by stating: one cannot, based on this word "capacity" (neng), express that the capacity and its object are distinct entities.

The second line refutes by analogy; it states: the essence of form and mind is itself form and mind. Since the former does not use the word "capacity" to express a distinction, how could this be otherwise?
Furthermore, the phrase beginning with "not the capacity" directly refutes the "characteristic of capacity" (nengxiang). That is to say:

The four characteristics, such as arising (*jāti*), are the characterized (*lakṣya*), namely the three conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). The word "not" (*na*) refutes the fixed distinction between the characteristic and the characterized.

The subsequent phrase applies this same refutation by analogy to qualities such as solidity (*khara*), as well as moisture, warmth, and motion; to the elements such as earth, as well as water, fire, and wind.

The word "not" refutes the notion that there is no solidity and so forth external to earth and the other elements. Furthermore, the phrase "if there were... introduces a concessive objection, which is then refuted by the subsequent phrase through the same analogy.
The characteristics of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) refer to non-arising, non-ceasing, and so forth. The objects characterized by the unconditioned refer to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.

The word "should" (*yīng*) here is used as a negative particle. To say "should be different" (*yīng yì*) is a rhetorical inversion that actually signifies "not different. Since those unconditioned factors—the subject and the object—are not different, [the characteristic and the characterized are likewise not different].

How is this so? Furthermore, if characteristics such as arising were to exist simultaneously with their substance (*dravya*), then the functions of abiding, change, and cessation could not operate concurrently.

Moreover, in the section below on "arising," the existence of a substantial nature (*svabhāva*) in the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) is refuted; whereas above, it was assumed that the various conditioned characteristics are distinct from matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
There exists an external, real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The first phrase restates the opponent's position; the second phrase refutes that nature by means of its functions.

Since the functions do not arise simultaneously, the nature cannot exist as a simultaneous entity. If [the opponent] were to argue below that "because they are contradictory, the functions do not arise all at once, yet the nature exists as a simultaneous entity," [the author] then establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) below to refute it, demonstrating that the nature should not exist as a simultaneous entity. The functions such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth are the subject (*dharmin*).

The thesis cannot be established all at once because the reason is contradictory, just as with the essence (*svabhāva*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The essence of arising and so forth is a subject;

it also should not exist simultaneously [with its functions], because the reason is contradictory, just as with the function (*vṛtti*). Furthermore, below the section on "abiding" (*sthiti*), the essence is used to refute the function:

based on the foregoing formal argument, since the essence does not exist simultaneously, the functions of abiding, change, and cessation should likewise not exist simultaneously. There are others who...

When multiplied by the four characteristics and applied to the three periods of time, [the characteristic of] arising belongs to the future, while the three—abiding, change, and cessation—are held to be identical to the present.
Since these three do not coexist, how can they be held to be identical to the present?

The essence of both the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) is inherently existent... (up to) furthermore, it would follow that the production (*utpāda*) and so forth are useless.

Regarding "the characteristic" and below, both the essence and function of the characteristic and the characterized are refuted together. The first phrase restates the opponent’s position; the second phrase clarifies this by applying the same logic.

That the functions of the characteristic and the characterized are functional entities (*dharmin*), that they are both inherently existent (*pakṣa*), and that they lack a distinct nature (*hetu*) constitute the reason.
It is like the substance; therefore, it is said that the function must likewise be so. This clarifies that if one is established, both are established.

If the function were to exist simultaneously, it would further contradict the preceding statement that "function does not arise all at once. The section beginning with "If one says... refutes the alternative position.

The first sentence [of the opponent] maintains that, regarding the dependence on further causes and conditions, the function's non-simultaneous arising is established. The second sentence refutes this, stating: "The causes and conditions upon which it depends should..."

It is not inherently existent. Since its function is not inherently existent, its essence (*tattva*) must likewise be so. The subject and object, as well as their characteristics and functions, are phenomena that exist;

they should therefore belong to the thesis that they are not inherently existent, because they further depend upon causes and conditions. This is illustrated by the analogy of the essence of the subject and object.

Why? Because their nature and characteristics are identical. This clarifies that when refuted, both are refuted together. Since both essence and function are neither inherently existent, this is consistent with the original [thesis].

This contradicts the principle of simultaneous existence (*sahabhū*). Furthermore, the text below refutes the preceding position by stating that if one maintains this, then the [factors] such as "arising" (*jāti*) would be useless;
for causes and conditions would arise by themselves and cease by themselves, having no relation to arising and so forth.
Therefore, it is criticized here as being useless.
Because the characterized (lakṣya) exists eternally, yet its conjunction with arising and so forth [is observed], and because no cause for their mutual difference can be found.
Below the section on the "characterized," a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is established to demonstrate that the characteristic and the characterized are not different in essence.

The inference is stated as follows: The three conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are the subject (*dharmin*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they are conjoined with arising and so forth, which are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because that which is characterized (lakṣya) exists eternally, it serves as the reason; for example, like the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta).

Since the unconditioned, which is characterized, exists eternally and yet does not combine with arising and so forth, this proves that the conditioned, which is characterized, must likewise exist eternally and should also not combine with arising and so forth.

When the substance of the agent and the object are distinct, one may discuss their conjunction; however, here, taking the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as being of the same category, it is said that it does not conjoin with arising and so forth.
This is because it refutes the notion that there are separate arising and so forth that come to conjoin with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Thus, when discussing arising and ceasing within conditioned phenomena, it clarifies that these do not exist separately from matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
Furthermore, because the past and future are neither present nor eternal (up to this point), what they maintain is irrational from both advancing and retreating perspectives.
Furthermore, "going down" [refers to] establishing a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to refute the claim that the past and future lack real existence; the formal argument is as stated in the text.

Because the four characteristics are contrasted with the [three] time periods, refuting the three times is equivalent to refuting the four characteristics. Regarding "arising is named," this refutes the inappropriateness of arising in relation to the time periods. Arising...

The first four lines below [the heading] refute [the opponent's position] by examining the present and the future. The last two lines below "If it ceases" refute it by examining existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, the four lines below "Moreover, if it ceases" refute it by examining identity and difference. Therefore, the section beginning with "Thus, that...
concludes the refutation by examining the progression and regression; since arising occurs in the future and cessation occurs in the present, it is said to be "illogical."
However, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) exist by the power of causes and conditions; [the passage] up to "the last one is non-existent" means they exist in the past.

The section beginning with "However, there is" sets forth the correct principle. The first six phrases indicate the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): existence and non-existence correspond to arising (*utpāda*) and cessation (*nirodha*); temporary existence corresponds to duration (*sthiti*) and change (*anyathātva*).
The eight phrases beginning with "originally non-existent" explain the four characteristics: that which suddenly exists where there was nothing is called arising. Its characteristic...

What appears as a continuity is called "abiding" (*sthiti*); what undergoes momentary transformation is called "change" (*anyathātva*); and what transforms from existence into non-existence is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).
The first three [characteristics] are common to the two time periods [past and future], whereas this [characteristic of change] is distinct from those encountered in other vehicles.
How can that which is a non-existent phenomenon serve as a characteristic for conditioned phenomena?

How does the following passage resolve this objection? First, the difficulty is established by asking: "Cessation is a non-existent phenomenon; how can it function as a characteristic for conditioned phenomena?"
"What fault is there in designating this as a subsequent unconditioned characteristic? (up to: "Although both are termed 'manifestation' (*vijñapti*), their manifestations differ.

Regarding "manifesting this" and below, he answers directly by way of manifestation. Regarding "the manifestation of arising" and below, he first clarifies the four characteristics of a moment (*kṣaṇa*).

The manifestation of arising now exists; the manifestation of cessation has not yet ceased; the manifestation of change refers to transformation and alteration; the manifestation of duration refers to non-longevity.
[This concludes] the remote application; thus, the following section provides the conclusion.
These four characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are provisionally established based on a single moment (*kṣaṇa*)—up to this point—it is shown that all four characteristics are merely provisional designations.

Next, the four characteristics over the course of a lifetime (*ekakāla*) are explained. "This is based on" below concludes the preceding [section]. "Over the course of a lifetime" below introduces the subsequent [section]. "First, there is" below...
This is the explicit explanation. "Initial existence" refers to the time of birth; "subsequent non-existence" refers to the time of death.
The subsequent state being like the former is called "similarity. The absence of interruption in between is termed "continuity. The gradual alteration [of that continuity] is called "transformation."
Therefore, a sutra says: "At twenty, one declines from the state of ten; this continues until sixty. From day to month, year to season, every thought-moment undergoes transformation.
Thus, below this, [the text] uses the term "provisionally established" to refute the notion of real existence held by other vehicles.
Furthermore, how is it known that there exist real sets of names (nāma-kāya), phrases (pada-kāya), and phonemes (vyañjana-kāya) that express and signify distinct forms, minds, and so forth?
This is as follows. First, the Mahāyāna inquiry refutes the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes.
Because it is stated in the sūtras; as the sūtra says, the Buddha attained rare sets of names, phrases, and syllables.
[The opponent asks: "In the sūtra below, other vehicles respond. [The author replies:
This sūtra does not state that there exist real names and so forth distinct from matter, mind, and the rest; therefore, as evidence, this is unestablished.
Below this, the sūtra refutes [the opponent's position]. First, it rebukes the citation of fallacies:
if names, phrases, and syllables were substantially distinct from sound, they would—like form and so forth—not be actual signifiers.

Below the section on "names," the refutation is established through formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as in the text. Even granting that they are distinct from sound, their status as non-signifiers is denied.
This means: "If sound can produce names (nāma), phrases (pada), and phonemes (vyañjana)" [up to] "this [sound] is sufficient to express [meaning]; what use are names and so forth?
The phrase "if sound" and below refutes the claim that sound can produce names and so forth. The first sentence restates the opponent's position; they maintain that sound is the producer.
Names, phrases, and syllables are that which is produced; that which is produced serves as the expressive agent (*vācaka*).
Since the expressive agent and its object are distinct, one further calculates that names and so forth exist substantially as entities separate from sound. Below this, [the text] refutes this:

since this sound itself possesses melodic contours and inflections sufficient to serve as the expressive agent, what need is there to produce names and so forth as the expressive agent? This refutation establishes that sound does not necessarily produce names.
These serve as the designators.
If it is argued that because the phonetic modulations upon the sound [are distinct], there must be a separate real entity existing apart from the location of the color-form;
this is the refutation of the attempted defense. The first phrase restates the defense: based on the aforementioned admission that the phonetic modulations can serve as [designators]...

[The opponent] asserts that it is the expressive [factors]. Now, the defense is offered: "The modulations and inflections of sound are precisely what I call the essence of names, phrases, and syllables;
they are distinct from sound yet exist as real entities. Below, this is refuted by analogy:

"Regarding shape and dimension—meaning inflections such as long and short—if those were distinct from color and existed separately, then these modulations of sound should likewise be so. Since they are not so, how can this [be the case]?"
Why is this so? This refutation [shows that] names and so forth do not exist as real entities distinct from sound.
If it is argued that [names arise] from the modulations of phonemes within sound, then—just as in that case—names and so forth should not be produced separately from the sound itself.

"If it is argued that... and so forth refutes the counter-argument. The counter-argument is presented by means of an analogy: it claims that the sounds of phonemes are like the sounds of stringed instruments or pipes and are not themselves expressive;

yet, one still wishes to establish that names and so forth are produced as the expressive agents. "This should be... and so forth establishes formal syllogisms (pramāṇa) to refute [the position] simultaneously.

The sound of phonemes is a phenomenon that possesses intrinsic nature (*dharmin*). It does not separately produce names (*nāman*) and so forth; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). Because it is not a signifier (*vācaka*), it is the reason (*hetu*).
The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like the sound of strings or pipes. This restates the subsequent point: the sound of strings and pipes is not a signifier, yet it cannot produce names and so forth.
Since it has been proven that sounds (*śabda*) are neither signifiers (*vācaka*) nor capable of producing names (*nāman*) and so forth,

who says that they are definitively incapable of signifying [objects], or that they do not separately produce the real entities of the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*)?
Furthermore, who says that the Mahāyāna is inferior? This is a challenge based on the preceding [argument].

Since the sounds of strings and pipes in other vehicles are not expressive (*vācaka*), this serves as a metaphor for how vocal tones and sounds are not expressive. Now, the intent of the challenge is this: the sounds of strings and pipes can also be expressive.

Just as when a person hears a sound, they discern and understand musical notes such as *gong* and *shang*, thereby proving that vocal tones and sounds are indeed expressive. Why [is this not the case]?

Using the names of arising things and so forth, if the sound is low, the proponents of other vehicles establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as a rebuttal: "The sound of strings and pipes is the subject (*dharmin*); it lacks the function of signification (*abhidhāna-vyāpāra*), this is the thesis (*pakṣa*);
because it is an insentient phenomenon (*jaḍa-dharma*), this is the reason (*hetu*); for example, like the sound of a wind-bell. "It should exist" means, conversely, that it does not exist.
Above, the sound of strings and pipes was used as a metaphor for sounds of similar tonal quality; here, the sound of a wind-bell is used as a metaphor for sounds similar to those of strings.

The sounds of flutes and pipes—these three all lack the capacity for signification (*abhidhāna*). It is necessarily the arising of names (*nāman*) and so forth that constitutes the capacity for signification.

This [point] should be refuted by restating the opponent's position below: since it is claimed that strings, flutes, wind-chimes, and bells lack the capacity for signification and do not produce names and so forth, then these melodic sounds, like those two types of sound [the previous examples], would likewise not separately produce names, phrases, and syllables (*pada-vyañjana*). The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) for this refutation is as stated above.

If it were held that only the sound of speech can produce names and so forth, then—O you who love the gods—the Proponents of Distinct Entities (Vaiśeṣika) would maintain that the expressive [word] is something other than speech;

this is not the case for others. If [it is argued] that only the lower [vehicles] hold such views, then the higher Mahāyāna schools counter-argue that the wind of the strings cannot produce names and so forth.

This establishes that vocal sounds do not produce names and so forth. Now, the proponents of other vehicles (the Śrāvakas) maintain that the strings and the wind are insentient and thus cannot produce names and so forth;
rather, it is only vocal sound, which belongs to a sentient being, that can produce names and so forth. The following section of the Mahāyāna text cites and refutes this position.
Since it has already been granted that speech alone is capable of producing [names and so forth], why is it not granted that speech alone is capable of expressing [meaning]?

Why must names and so forth be produced for there to be expression? What is the reasoning behind this? The first phrase presents the objection from the perspective of other vehicles (*anyayāna*); the second phrase offers a defense against this discrepancy.

The Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*) answers sequentially based on the distinction between the general and the specific: that which expresses is indeed speech, because it is commonly understood by humans and devas throughout the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

It is called "distinctive speech" (*viśeṣa-vāc*) because it is capable of expressing meaning and is restricted solely to the second dhyāna and above. Since light serves as the medium for expression, it is termed "distinctive speech.
Because it does not extend to the lower realms, it is said to be "not otherwise."

However, based on the distinctions in the temporal phases (*avasthā*) of vocal sound, the phonemes (*vyañjana*)—which are the syllables (*akṣara*)—serve as the basis for these two [names and phrases].

Now, following the phrase "however, based on," the correct principle is set forth. Question: Since sound itself is the expressive agent (*vācaka*), how can there be distinct categories such as names and so forth?
Answer: It is said: based on the distinctions in the temporal phases of vocal sound; for example, in the Sanskrit word *kṛtuka*, if the two syllables are pronounced separately... [text continues]

That which is designated by the eyes is called the "status of a word" (*pada-vyañjana*). When two words are combined and pronounced to express the essence of the eye, it is called the "status of a name" (*nāma-vyañjana*).
If one further adds *asali-ba* (existence), it is called "the eye with outflows" (*sāsrava-cakṣus*), and this is called the "status of a phrase" (*vākya-vyañjana*).

Thus, names and so forth are established based on these statuses. As for their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): for example, when one says "fire," it expresses only the intrinsic nature of burning and heat.

Regarding the distinction: it is like the term "incense smoke," which excludes fire from grasses, trees, and so forth. As for the word, it is the written character that serves as the basis for the two [name and phrase].

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks: "What is called a 'name-group' (*nāmakāya*)? It refers to the designation based on the intrinsic nature of phenomena and the designation based on their specific characteristics.
Through pervasive conceptualization, it establishes mere ideation in accordance with verbal expression; this is called a name-group. Thus it is said.

What is the group of phrases (*padakāya*)? It refers to all the various designations of phenomena established based on their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), as well as the establishment of qualities, faults, and the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of affliction and purification; this is called the group of phrases.
What is the group of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*)? It refers to all sets of syllables (*akṣara*) that serve as the basis for the groups of names and phrases; this is called the group of phonemes.

Although these three [factors]—name, phrase, and syllable—are not distinct entities apart from sound, they each have their own differences even when subsumed within the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).

Regarding the passage "These three... and below, this clarifies that they are neither identical nor separate: they are not separate because they exist as specific states (avasthā), yet they are not identical because they possess distinct characteristics.

Although they are neither identical nor separate, there is a difference between the conventional and the real: sound is a real dharma (dravyadharma), whereas names and so forth are merely provisional designations (prajñapti). Regarding the passage "By this... and below:

The distinction in the determination of the objects (*ālambana*) of the two unimpeded knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is as follows: the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) takes names and so forth as its object;

the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) takes actual sound as its object. Regarding the classification according to the three aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), sound is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the base of sound (*śabda-āyatana*), and the element of sound (*śabda-dhātu*).
Names and so forth are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the base of mental phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*), and the element of mental phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*).
Furthermore, based on this land, names, phrases, and syllables—up to and including subtle odors, tastes, and so forth—are established as the three [categories].
Now, based on the lower [level], the question asks: "If the curvature within sound constitutes the teaching, then the curvature within form should also be able to constitute the teaching.
The answer says: "Based on this land for now: 'The true essence of the teaching in this region / Is pure and resides in audible sound.'"

Therefore, if it were to pervade other lands, all six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) would be applicable; these, such as light and so forth, are precisely the sense objects of form, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmaviṣaya*).

All of these can be established as names, phrases, and syllables, as taught in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* and other scriptures. They are provisionally established based on sound, thereby distinguishing them from the attachments of other vehicles which hold them to be substantially existent.

Some maintain that the *anuśaya* (latent dispositions) are distinct from the mind and mental factors, and are subsumed under the *viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind).

Others maintain [they are not]. [The following] separately refutes [the view that] the *anuśaya* are [dissociated]: the *anuśaya* refers to the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*). They "follow" (*anu*) sentient beings and "lie dormant" (*śayana*) within the *ālayavijñāna*.
Alternatively, they are called *anuśaya* because they increase [in strength] (*anuśerate*) or because they augment faults.

That too is unreasonable, because they are designated as "greed" and so forth; just as manifest greed and the like are not non-associated [conditioned phenomena], those [others] are likewise untenable.
This refutes them. The formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) is as stated in the text.
Any assertion that there exist other distinct non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) should be rejected in accordance with the same reasoning applied above.
The section "Refuting the Distinct [Factors]" below follows this model to refute the remaining non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). These include:

flux (*pravṛtti*), distinctness (*anyathātva*), association (*samyoga*), momentum (*java*), succession (*anupūrvi*), time (*kāla*), direction (*deśa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), the nature of conjunction (*sāmagrī*), and the nature of non-conjunction (*asāmagrī*). Phenomena (*dharma*) themselves are originally faultless; it is due to attachment that they become erroneous.
Therefore, one refutes the conceptual clinging (*saṃjñā*), not the phenomena themselves. This concludes the refutation of the non-associated formations.
No determinate, real existence apart from form, mind, and so forth can be found among the various unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

[The phrase] "the various unconditioned" below refutes the three types of unconditioned phenomena—namely, space (*ākāśa*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—by first refuting them collectively.
Furthermore, regarding the fact that determinate dharmas are briefly of three kinds (up to): "therefore, one must not cling to the idea that unconditioned phenomena definitely exist.

Starting from "Furthermore, regarding the fact that... [the text] cites examples to clarify through contrast. That which is known by direct perception, such as matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*): matter possesses substantial resistance, while mind possesses objective cognition;
these can be known by worldly wisdom. That which is utilized in the present, such as a jar or a garment: [a jar] contains and preserves, while [a garment] covers.
The obstruction of form [is] for the sake of concealing ugliness; it is also known by worldly wisdom (*loka-jñāna*) without depending on inference (*anumāna*). "Eye, ear, etc.

refers to the nose, tongue, and body—that is, the five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*), which are the purified four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni viśuddhāni*). These cannot be seen by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*);

rather, because they possess the function of generating consciousness (*vijñāna*) according to their respective [bases], one infers and realizes them through the measurement of that function. The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the opposite of this; it is not worldly.

This is known by wisdom; it is not established through inference (*anumāna*). This reveals that the noble ones (*ārya*) directly realize [it] through immediate perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*). Therefore, it is refuted by stating:

"It cannot be grasped by ordinary sentiment or worldly wisdom as being substantially existent apart from consciousness. Regarding the phrase "Even if granted," this refutes substantial existence. As for "that which has utility":

even if its substantial existence were conceded, one establishes a formal argument (*prayoga*) to refute it by means of impermanence (*anityatā*). That which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the subject (*dharmin*); it should...

This is the thesis that [conditioned phenomena] are impermanent. The reason is that they possess functional utility, as illustrated by the examples of the eye, ear, and so forth. Because they possess functional utility, they are impermanent;
conversely, this clarifies that unconditioned phenomena are truly permanent, yet they do not exist as substantial entities apart from form and mind.
However, because all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are of the nature of objects of knowledge, [they] lack a real unconditioned nature apart from form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth.

The passage beginning with "However, all... clarifies that unconditioned phenomena do not exist as real entities separate from form and mind. The formal proof (*pramāṇa*) is established according to the text.

Previously, it was stated that unconditioned phenomena are not commonly known by the world in the same way that form and mind are presently perceived; now, within the formal proof, it is established that unconditioned phenomena are...
Regarding the nature of the knowable, such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), there appears to be a contradiction between earlier and later statements. However, this is not the case.

The former [passage] refers to form and mind as being known by worldly knowledge (*loka-jñāna*), whereas the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not known by worldly knowledge. The present [passage], however, refers to the unconditioned as being realized by noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*).
Therefore, it employs form and mind—known by worldly knowledge—as a concordant example (*dṛṣṭānta*) to illustrate that the unconditioned is known by noble wisdom. This is the intended meaning.

It is not indiscriminate. Regarding that which is manifested by form, mind, and so forth: when conditions are lacking and [a phenomenon] does not arise, the principle of the emptiness of its nature is revealed.
Furthermore, are space and so forth one or many?
Furthermore, below the section on "empty space," [the text] provides a general inquiry based on the categories of "one" and "many":
"If its essence were one and pervasive of all places, [it would follow that] where there is [space], they should intermingle; where there is no [space], it should not be pervasive."

If the substance [of space] is inferior [to that of other things], it is separately refuted that the substance of space is one. First, the meaning of space is set forth: its substance is one, it is all-pervasive, and it is capable of containing.

Following this, it is refuted according to the capacity [of the opponent's claims]. First, the first phrase refutes "oneness. This refers to the "concordant factors," namely: large and small, square and round, and so forth.
By combining [with others], it becomes many; this [argument] refutes its pervasiveness by means of its being unitary. The following line refutes its pervasiveness:

if it were definitively one, the meaning of pervasion would not be established, because that which is conjoined with one place would not be conjoined with others. This refutes its pervasiveness by means of its being unitary.

Otherwise, if one attempts to defend both its unity and its pervasiveness, the refutation of that defense states: if it were both one and pervasive, then all phenomena would have to mutually pervade one another.

If all phenomena do not mutually pervade one another, then the principle of a single universal pervasion remains unestablished. This [argument] uses the fact that phenomena do not mutually pervade to simultaneously refute the notion of a single universal pervasion.
Regarding the phrase "if it is claimed," this is a further defense. If space were to conjoin with phenomena, then there would be the aforementioned fault of multiple substantial bodies;
furthermore, if other things did not so conjoin, there would be the three faults of mutual pervasion. Now, it is said that space does not [conjoin with phenomena].

If [space] were conjoined with phenomena, its single essence would be omnipresent and thus everything would be established as space. If it were not conjoined with phenomena, then space would be space by itself and all phenomena would be phenomena by themselves;
in that case, the meaning of "receptivity" would not be established. To refute this through formal logic (*pramāṇa*), one cannot establish receptivity: Space is a functional entity (*dharmin*);
it must not be receptive (*pakṣa*), because it is not conjoined with phenomena (*hetu*); for example, like other unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Furthermore, "below form" [the text] again refutes both unity and pervasiveness. The preceding section refuted [form] by means of space containing form; this section refutes [it] by means of form containing space.
If they were mixed, they would not be one; if they were absent, they would not be pervasive. This refutes both unity and pervasiveness by means of existence and non-existence.

When the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of a particular category (*nikāya*) and a particular grade (*prakāra*) are severed—up to [the point where] it is logically necessary that their substance (*tattva*) be one—the following refutes the other two unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
First, it refutes "one category. "Category" refers to categories such as greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and so forth.

"Grade" refers to the superior, middling, and inferior grades. "Fetters" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the fivefold division of upper and lower realms. [This is] the analytical discernment (*pravicaya*).

"Cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the severing of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) through discernment by means of wisdom. "Cessation not through discernment" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) refers to the time when phenomena do not arise due to the absence of their conditions, rather than through discernment by wisdom;
at that time, the principle of intrinsic emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) is revealed, and this is termed cessation not through discernment. The meaning of its refutation is as stated in the text.
If its essence were manifold, it would possess distinct categories; furthermore, space (ākāśa) would not be all-pervasive or capable of containing all things.

[The argument] "if its essence were below" establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to refute the manifold nature. First, the inference generally refutes the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

**Thesis:** The unconditioned phenomena, such as space, are not substantially real unconditioned phenomena. **Reason:** Because they possess distinct categories. **Example:** Like form (*rūpa*) and so forth. [Regarding] space...

Below, a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is established to specifically refute that space is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): Space is a functional entity (*dharmin*); it is not [unconditioned] because its nature consists of pervasive containment (*sādhya*).
The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it possesses categories" (*pakṣadharmatva*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: "like form and so forth."

The claim of other schools that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) exist substantially apart from the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) should be refuted according to the previous [arguments].

Regarding the "other schools" mentioned below, this refers to the three types of unconditioned phenomena held by those schools; they should be refuted by applying the same examples concerning unity and plurality as before.
Furthermore, since all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are asserted to lack cause and effect, they should—like a rabbit’s horn—not exist as something distinct from the mind and its associates.

The passage beginning with "Furthermore, all... refutes the reality of unconditioned phenomena. Here, by taking the absence of cause and effect as the reason (*hetu*), the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) establishes the general refutation of the attachment to unconditioned phenomena as being separate from the mind.
However, the sūtras state that there are unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma), such as space (ākāśa) and so forth; briefly, there are two kinds.
The phrase "However, the sūtras... serves to clarify the correct meaning and provides a general enumeration of these two types.
First, based on the transformation of consciousness, there is a provisional designation [of existence] (up to) the provisional designation of permanence as being without change.

"Based on the lower" clarifies the provisional designation based on the transformation of consciousness. The first phrase indicates that it refers to the transformation through the discrimination of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
"That which was formerly... explains this: initially, one discriminates by hearing names; through the perfuming of names and phrases, one repeatedly cultivates contemplation.
[The power of] force. When subsequent minds and mental factors arise, they manifest as resembling the characteristics of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

This is observed and transformed in accordance with consciousness; it is an "object consisting solely of images" (*kevala-pratibimba-viṣaya*). Regarding the passage below, [the author] addresses a potential objection. Question:

The essence of the unconditioned is eternal, yet the characteristics now transformed [by consciousness] arise and perish in accordance with the mind. How can you say they are eternal? Explanation: As for the phrase "similar in succession," it is because the preceding [moment] induces [the succeeding one].

Regarding "later": because the later resembles the former, there is no change; because this and that are identical, although it is not truly eternal, it may be designated as such by way of conventional metaphor.
Second, [the establishment] based on the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena), provisionally designated as such because it is the true principle of these phenomena.

Regarding "second, based on," this clarifies the provisional designation based upon *dharmatā*. The first phrase provides the heading; the section beginning with "namely, emptiness" provides the explanation. First, it presents the *dharmatā* upon which [the designation] relies.

The first phrase points to its essence: "emptiness and selflessness. This refers to the observing wisdom (*prajñā*) that performs the observation; "suchness" (*tathatā*) refers to that which is observed.
This reveals the true principle. Regarding the phrase "existence and non-existence," etc., it demonstrates the meaning.

That which is "neither identical to nor different from all phenomena" means that all phenomena are the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), while this *dharmatā* is the ultimate (*paramārtha*); therefore, they are said to be not identical.

Since *tathatā* pervades all things and all things do not depart from *tathatā*, they are said to be not different. Regarding the phrase "this phenomenon," etc., the name is established based on the principle. As for "*dharmatā*," it refers to...

The true principle upon which all phenomena depend is called "space" (*ākāśa*) because it is free from all obstructions; it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*) because its principle is not false or inverted. [The phrase] "free from all...
and so forth next clarifies that these are merely provisional designations. This demonstrates that based on a single principle, various names are provisionally established. All obstructions...
“Obstruction” refers to all phenomena, both material and mental. “The power of discernment” refers to the power of wisdom and contemplation.
“Defilement” refers to the afflictions and attachments that act as hindrances. “Ultimate realization” refers to the truth realized and attained.
“Not by means of [causes]” refers to the nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity, which is manifested through the absence of conditions; that is, when the conditions for all phenomena are removed.

The principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) is revealed. Regarding the cessation of the sensations of suffering and pleasure: in the fourth dhyāna, equanimity and mindfulness are purified;

suffering and pleasure are suddenly abandoned, and the conflicting mind does not engage. Regarding the non-functioning of perception and sensation: in the ninth successive attainment (*anupūrva-samāpatti*), the non-permanent and the permanently defiled minds and mental factors cease;
this is called the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). These five are all provisionally established based upon *tathatā* (suchness). *Tathatā*...

Thus, even "Tathatā" (Suchness) is a provisional designation, for it is like raising a voice to stop an echo. This refutes the denial [of reality] below; it reveals that the name "Tathatā" is also a conventional construction.
To diminish is to deny existence; to augment is to cling to existence. Do not call an illusion "real," nor call that which is not false "true.
Although there are names such as "emptiness" and "reality," they are established as designations to dispel emotional attachments.
Unlike other schools which [assert that] apart from form, mind, and so forth, [there exist unconditioned phenomena], the various unconditioned phenomena are not definitively real.
"Not like the lower [schools]" concludes the refutation of unconditioned phenomena mentioned above.
The various phenomena grasped by non-Buddhists and those of other vehicles (up to the point "are also like illusory things") do not truly exist.

The section on "Non-Buddhists" below uses the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to generally demonstrate that the various phenomena grasped by non-Buddhists and those of other vehicles do not exist apart from the mind, nor do they possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

The "apprehended object" (*grāhya*) and the "apprehending subject" (*grāhaka*) are the two parts of appearance and perception (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*); "this" and "that" refer to the objective essence (*ālambana*).
Regarding the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*): the first inference demonstrates that the apprehended object does not exist apart from consciousness;

the second inference demonstrates that the perceiving subject does not take an external substance as its object, but takes only internal objects; the third inference demonstrates that mind and mental factors exist like illusions and are not substantially real.
The three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are all as stated in the text. Above, it was said that external objects do not exist and the internal mind is not empty;

fearing that those who cling to them might reckon the mind to be real, [the text] dispels this by means of its being like an illusion. Thus, the refutation of all phenomena across the five positions is complete.

"In order to dispel the false attachment [to the existence of] mind and mental factors apart from [objects], [the text says: '...just as the attachment to external objects is also an attachment to dharmas.

The phrase 'in order to dispel' below explains a potential objection. The question asks: 'Above, you refuted that external objects do not exist, and extensively explained that the internal mind is not non-existent.'"
Now, why do you say that [all things] are also like illusions? The intent of this explanation can be understood.
However, there are briefly two types of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*): [the former] exists conventionally, while the latter—due to false conceptual construction—is definitely non-existent.

"However, all the following [passages] summarize the breadth and omit the details. Their explanations of the meaning are the same as those for the previously mentioned 'clinging to a self,' differing only in that they concern the 'self' and 'dharmas.

The section beginning with 'Both arising together' clarifies the characteristics of innate [afflictions]. The section beginning with 'This, moreover' clarifies the characteristics of clinging. The section beginning with 'These two' clarifies the characteristics of abandonment.

The section beginning with 'Discriminative' clarifies the characteristics of discriminatively arisen [afflictions]. The section beginning with 'This also' clarifies the characteristics of clinging. These two..."

"Below" clarifies the characteristics of cessation. "Thus, below" concludes the determination of existence or non-existence by way of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the fundamental substance (*vastu*). "Therefore, below" summarizes deluded attachment.
"However, 'like' and so forth, below" determines existence or non-existence by way of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Therefore, the World-Honored One said, "Maitreya, you should know" (up to) "the dependent nature is like illusions and so forth.

The passage from "therefore, the World-Honored One" downward cites scriptural authority to establish the formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) as it appears in the text. The two lines beginning with "The objects of all consciousnesses" clarify that there is no basis apart from mind.

The two lines beginning with "Like illusions and so forth" clarify that [the dependent nature] cannot be grasped as real. This concludes the refutation of the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
In this way, because the externalists and those of other vehicles maintain that the functioning of conditions must necessarily depend upon a substantially real entity, [the text] concludes below:
it reveals that both the self and dharmas are not substantially real apart from consciousness. Therefore, regarding "the mind" below, it concludes by distinguishing external dharmas:
the first phrase concludes that the substantial form (rūpa) external to the mind is not a direct object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); the second phrase...
A conditioned phenomenon must necessarily possess a real substance and an objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) as its object-field to serve as an object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

This is because, at present, those mental states and mental factors within that collection [of consciousness] do not take other collections as their objects, just as [a thing] is not an object when it is subsumed under a different collection.

Now, the following section establishes the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to distinguish the mind from external objects, showing that they are not direct objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), as stated in the text. Regarding "this and that":

the primary mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) together constitute a single aggregate; when these various consciousnesses are compared with one another, they mutually function as "this" and "that.
As for "not being an object condition," this is like the case where visual consciousness, in relation to sound, is said not to have it as its object.

The mental factors (*caitta*) that arise in the same assemblage (*samprayukta*) are also not the direct objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), because their own-natures (*svabhāva*) are distinct, just like other things that are not apprehended.

[The phrase] "In the same assemblage" and below establishes the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to exclude the mental factors. They are also not the direct objective conditions for the mind-king, as stated in the text.

Regarding "because their own-natures are distinct": this is because both the mind-king and the mental factors each possess their own respective self-verifying nature (*svasaṃvitti*). Regarding "like other things that are not apprehended": [this means they are not apprehended by the mind-king].
Just as sound is not an object of the eye, so too the mind of that [external] aggregate is not an object for this [internal] aggregate.
From this, one should know that there are truly no external objects; there is only internal consciousness arising in the likeness of external objects.

From this point downward, the conclusion is drawn. Starting from the distant and proceeding toward the intimate, it is shown that [consciousness] not only does not take external phenomena as its object, but also does not take an external mind as its object.
Furthermore, it does not take what is external to the sovereign (the primary consciousness) within its own aggregate as its object.

Since even this sovereign does not take its own objects as its object, and the mind itself does not take the mind as its object, we know that in reality there are no external objects; there is only the internal mind appearing as if it were external.
The object arises. This concludes the preceding verse, intending to show that [the object] is a transformation of consciousness.
Therefore, it is said in a verse of the Sūtra (up to): "Because the mind is disturbed and turbid by habitual tendencies, it evolves appearing as those [objects]."
Therefore, below, the scriptural citations are introduced as in the text.
Some raise this objection: "If there is no [external object] apart from consciousness (until the point where it asks), how can one say that the mind evolves appearing as an external object?
Below this, the difficulties are resolved. First, the objection: this objection arises by following up on the word "appearing" (*sādṛśya*) mentioned above; it is a counter-argument to the heading.

It is said that if there were no real self or dharmas, even the conventional (prajñapti) would not exist. This is explained as follows: first the principle (*dharma*), then the analogy. "True fire" represents the real entity; "resembling fire" represents the semblance-entity;

and "the qualities of fierceness and redness" represent the common attributes. Then, "it may be... concludes [the argument]. The phrase "conventionally designated as 'ox' and so forth" establishes another analogy.
The section beginning with "self and dharmas" applies this by way of example to establish the conclusion. Thus, because there exists the conventional and the semblance, [the conventional exists].
There must also be a reality; if there were no reality, there could be no semblance. How then can it be said that [cognition] arises as a semblance of external objects? This objection is circular.
That objection is irrational, for apart from consciousness, neither the self nor dharmas exist, and thus even conventional designations such as "fire" would both fail to be established.

The objection is difficult to resolve. The answer is as follows: The first phrase refers back to the general refutation [of the previous position]. The second sentence generally indicates that neither the "category" (*jāti*) nor the "substance" (*dravya*) is established.

"Category" (*jāti*) refers to a semblance of a category; it is a semblance of a thing (*vastu*). For instance, the fierceness and redness of a person resemble those of fire, and thus they are called a "category.
The fierceness and redness of fire are substantially existent, and thus they are called "substance."

The principle of metaphorical designation regarding clothing and other such things is not established (up to: one should also metaphorically designate the names of fire and so forth for water and so forth).

Regarding "based on a category" (*jāti*), first the basis of the category within the refutation of the analogy is addressed. The initial phrase restates the opponent's position and rejects it in general. From "the intensity and redness" (*tīvra-ārakta*) onwards, there is a specific refutation.

"Intensity" (*tīvra*) refers to the power of fire; "redness" (*ārakta*) refers to its color. It transforms from arising to maturation, and through transformation, it passes from existence to non-existence.

This is designated as "virtue" (*guṇa*). "Fierce" (*tīkṣṇa*) refers to the nature of fire, while "red" (*rakta*) refers to its color; thus, there are two types of categories, namely the categories of fierceness and redness, as well as virtue.
However, while the categories of fierceness and redness exist in actual fire, the virtue of fierceness and redness does not exist as a category.
Therefore, while fierceness and redness belong to the category of existence, virtue is not common [to all]. If there were no such common virtue...
This is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*). Water lacks the quality of fire; why then is it not called "fire"? Because water also possesses the property of being fierce and red.
If you argue that although fierceness and so forth are not qualities belonging to the same category [as fire], we nonetheless observe them existing separately from one another, [we reply:]...

"If it is argued that... [The text] cites the opponent's defense, saying: "Although the quality of being fierce and red is not of the same category, those whose complexion is red must be fierce by nature, and those who are fierce by nature must have a red complexion; this is similar to fire, where the two are inseparable as one entity.

Therefore, the name 'fire' may be applied metaphorically to such a person. "This too... [The text] refutes this: "We observe that there are people who are fierce but not red, and [others who are] red..."
Because they are not intense.
Since categories (jāti) possess no qualities and are mutually distinct, one knows that metaphorical designations (prajñapti) do not depend on categories for their establishment.
[The phrase] "Since categories... concludes that they do not depend on categories.
The principle of a metaphorical designation based on a real entity is also untenable (up to: there is the same fault as before regarding the lack of a common metaphorical designation).
Regarding "based on a real entity" below: next, the reliance on a real entity is refuted. A "real entity" refers to the quality of intense redness (*tīvra-lohita-guṇa*).

The first phrase cites the opponent's position and refutes it in general. Regarding "intense redness" below: this specifically refutes [the claim]. The first phrase indicates that the quality of intense redness is not shared by both the person and the fire; that is to say, "intense... [and so forth].

Below, this further explains that [the qualities] are not shared. Herein, the refutation is also based on the absence of common attributes. The intense redness of a person has matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) as its substance and resides in dependence upon the person.
The intense redness of fire has the subtle element of fire (*tejo-dhātu*), the subtle element of color, and the subtle element of touch as its substance and resides in dependence upon the fire.
Since the substances of the attributes of the person and the fire reside in different bases, the person does not possess the fire.
The quality [of fire] can be metaphorically designated; the fault is the same as [the case of] speaking of water.

If it is argued that because the human and the fire share a similarity in quality, [this applies]—up to the point where it is said that this metaphorical designation is not established based on reality.
"If it is argued that [the metaphor] is permissible because their qualities are similar," this is the citation of a counter-argument. "This principle is also [invalid]," this is the refutation.
For one speaks only of a person who resembles fire, not of a person who resembles qualities. "Therefore," this concludes that [the metaphor] does not rely on reality.

Furthermore, if a designation must necessarily rely upon a real entity to be established (up to the point where it concludes), one thus knows that conventional designations do not rely upon real entities.

"Furthermore, [the section] below" next refutes the dharmas. First, the provisional thesis is restated and generally criticized. Regarding "The 'real' refers to... and so forth: first, the characteristics of the real are set forth.
"The 'real' refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)" means the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a dharma, such as the solidity of earth or the moisture of water, and so on. This is...
"Attained by non-conceptual direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*); both conventional cognition (*jñāna*) and its verbal expression (*abhilāpa*) are not its object.

This statement means that neither the true aspect (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) nor the conventional aspect (*saṃvṛti-lakṣaṇa*) are objects attained by conventional cognition or its verbal expression; it precisely clarifies that the conventional does not depend upon the true.

The following section, beginning with "As for the conventional," provides a further explanation. "Conventional cognition" refers to the conceptualizing mind that forms mental constructions and interpretations. "Verbal expression" refers to that which signifies...
Regarding the statement that "the bodies of meaning, names, and phrases do not apprehend specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)," this is as follows:

the five consciousnesses and the first moment of the clearly manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are both direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*) that apprehend the specific characteristics of phenomena. However, when subsequent moments of mental consciousness arise, they are minds characterized by conceptualization (*savikalpa*) that carry names and phrases;
these operate only with respect to the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of form and so forth. As for "common characteristics," it means:
All phenomena are characterized by impermanence, selflessness, and so forth; these are obtained through conceptualization, inference, and conventional cognition (*prajñapti-jñāna*).

Nor is it the case that this [conventional cognition] is inferior; for although conventional cognition does not apprehend the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is no separate means of designation that establishes a specific characteristic as the basis for conventionality.
This statement in general indicates that conventional cognition does not express the ultimate (*paramārtha*). Conventional cognition...
It arises solely based on mental verbalization (*manojalpa-śabda*). Where mental verbalization does not reach, this wisdom does not function. The signifier refers to speech and wisdom;
the signified refers to the meaning and the object. Therefore, one should know that the following section concludes that the conventional (*prajñapti*) does not depend upon the ultimate (*tattva*).
Therefore, it functions solely based on what appears to be an object; thus, that objection is not consistent with correct reasoning.
From "By this" onwards, the correct position is set forth. "What appears to be an object" refers to the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

"Superimposition" means that after the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) has cognized the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there subsequently arises an inferential cognition (*anumāna*) which manifests a reflected image. This is...

[This refers to] superimposition (*samāropa*). Since the aforementioned conceptual cognition (*prajñapti-jñāna*) is established neither by relying on the real entity (*bhūta-vastu*) nor by relying on a semblance of an entity (*pratibimba*), it is known that it functions solely by relying on a superimposed semblance of characteristics.
Question: Previously it was stated that it does not rely on a semblance of an entity, yet now it is said that it relies solely on a semblance of an entity.

How are these two statements to be reconciled? Answer: Regarding the term "semblance" used previously, it referred to a mutual resemblance between entities, such as brass resembling [gold]. However, here...

"Gold. This is a case of "resemblance. Regarding this term "resemblance," it refers to the appearance of the reflected image (*pratibimba*) produced by the transformation of consciousness; it is called "resemblance" because one superimposes the status of an external object upon it.
Therefore, while the previous [term] "category" (*jāti*) must be refuted, this term "resemblance" must be accepted. Thus, the following section concludes by responding to the prior objection.

"However, based on the transformation of consciousness, one counters and dispels false attachments" (up to "therefore, regarding what is transformed by consciousness, one metaphorically designates it as 'self' and 'dharmas'").

The phrase "however, based on" clarifies that the term "resembling" (*sādṛśya*) is used because of the dispelling of attachment. The phrase "consequently" cites scriptural evidence to conclude by returning to the word "metaphorical" (*prajñapti*) from the opening chapter.
This completes the explanation of the first three phrases.
Although the images transformed by consciousness are of immeasurable kinds, the types of consciousness that perform this transformation are only three.

[The phrase] "the images transformed by consciousness" below explains the latter three lines of the verse. In the text, first there is the summary of what preceded, followed by the introduction of what follows;
that is to say, although there are eight kinds of transforming consciousness, when categorized by type, there are only three.
The first [category] refers to the maturation (*vipāka*), which is the eighth consciousness. (Up to: The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that the six [consciousnesses] are grouped into one kind.
Regarding the phrase "The first refers to... and below: this is a brief explanation of the three names. First, regarding "maturation," there are three meanings: 1. Maturing at a different time.
"Different" (*vi-*) means distinct; it pertains to the cause. "Maturing" (*pāka*) means ripening; it is the result. The different cause resides in the present, while the result...
1. Maturation according to the future: because it matures in the future. 2. Maturation by way of different categories (*jāti*): "category" refers to the classes of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).

For example, when one performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds within the causal state, although the resulting retributions (*vipāka-phala*) are unequal in terms of suffering or pleasure, they are all collectively called "maturation fruits.

This is because while the causes encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome, the fruit is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). 3. Maturation through transformation: as when one performs an action and perfumes a seed, it must...

Through repeated irrigation, the seeds flourish; because the fruit matures only after the seed has undergone transformation, it possesses much *vipāka* (maturation), unlike the preceding six consciousnesses which possess only a single portion thereof.
Second, "constantly and thoroughly deliberating" means that it perpetually examines, reflects upon, and measures objects.
This distinguishes it from other consciousnesses: the eighth is constant but not thorough, while the sixth is thorough [but not constant].

[The first six] are not constant. The first five are neither constant nor investigative; only this seventh [consciousness] is both constant and investigative, because it constantly and investigatively evaluates the characteristics of self and non-self, whether [the state] has been transformed or not yet transformed. Third, regarding the coarseness of the mode of apprehending objects:

although the seventh and eighth consciousnesses both apprehend objects, their modes of seeing and perceiving are subtle; therefore, only these first six [consciousnesses] distinctly discern the six [objects].

Because the characteristics of the sensory objects are the coarsest and most manifest, the six sense-fields are unified. The word "and" (*ji*) indicates this unification; "and" carries the meaning of combining or joining.
These three are all called the "transforming consciousnesses" (up to: they cause the impure wholesome and unwholesome [seeds] to be perfumed and grow).

The following section, "These three," explains the meaning of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). It generally indicates two types of transformation. First, it explains "causal transformation" (*hetu-pariṇāma*).

Under the heading "First, cause," the name is stated. The first phrase, "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*), refers to the cause. "Outflow" (*niṣyanda*) means that among the [eight consciousnesses], the seeds of the three natures within the first seven [consciousnesses] are the direct causes;
because the subsequent fruit resembles its preceding cause—specifically, because it is a continuous flow of a similar kind—it is called "outflow."
Regarding "maturation" (vipāka): among the aforementioned six [consciousnesses], it refers to the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma that belong to the indeterminate nature (avyākṛta).

While the preceding causes encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome, the subsequent fruit is exclusively indeterminate. Because their natures are distinct and different, it is called "maturation. The first seven [consciousnesses] are capable of perfuming.

The eighth [consciousness] is that which is perfumed (*bhāvyam*). This is because the latencies of the two causes reside within the eighth. That which has not yet arisen is perfumed so as to cause it to arise; that which has already arisen is perfumed so as to cause it to grow.
This growth and arising is precisely the meaning of "capacity for transformation. Regarding the fact that the [first] six [consciousnesses] are not stated to be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):
it is because indeterminate karma lacks superior efficacy and thus does not perfume seeds. The seventh [consciousness], though indeterminate, serves as the perfumer (*bhāvaka*).
Because it is of a nature that is obscured (*nivṛta*).

Regarding the "resultant transformative consciousness" (*phala-pariṇāma*), this refers to the arising of the eight consciousnesses with their various manifested appearances due to the power of the two aforementioned types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Next, the "resultant transformative consciousness" is explained. The phrase "the two results" below serves as the title; the first clause cites the preceding cause, namely, the "causal transformative consciousness" (*hetu-pariṇāma*).
Because it is a fruit, both the direct and indirect types of irrigation have the power to bring it to maturity. There arise the eight consciousnesses;
this refers to the fruit manifesting various aspects, namely the image-part (*nimittabhāga*), the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), and so forth—this is the meaning of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).

Because the outflowing habitual tendencies (*niṣyanda-vāsanā*) serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), [it] is called the "outflowing fruit" (*niṣyanda-phala*); for the fruit resembles its cause. [The section on] "Outflowing" below provides a detailed analysis.

First, the outflowing fruit is explained. The first phrase cites the cause: the seeds of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) of the preceding seven [consciousnesses], which are subsumed under the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*), constitute the direct causal conditions.

As for the essence of the eight consciousnesses, it refers to their respective self-verifying portions (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*). As for their aspects (*nimitta*), they refer to their respective objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*).
The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is precisely this fruit; it arises through differentiation, which is the meaning of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
"Differentiation" refers to the distinctions among the various minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), such as the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) and the four parts (*catuṣ-kalāpa*).

It is called a "fruit of outflow" (*niṣyanda-phala*) because it is drawn forth by the cultivation of wholesome states and so forth, being either of the same kind or resembling prior karma, with subsequent results following accordingly.

The maturation habitual energy (*vipāka-vāsanā*) acts as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) [up to] being called the "maturation fruit" (*vipāka-phala*), because the fruit is different from its cause.
Next, the maturation fruit is explained. The first phrase cites the cause: the six preceding types of contaminated wholesome and unwholesome seeds are subsumed under the category of karmic seeds.
This is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). By means of the superior outflowing and immediate causal conditions, it directly brings about the fruit of the eight consciousnesses.

Now, the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma act as the dominant condition, assisting in the production of the consciousnesses. The six destinies and four modes of birth, along with their suffering and pleasure, are distinguished by this.
The eighth [consciousness] and the preceding six are the fruits; they are the retribution for the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), meaning that karma possesses the power to [project them].
It draws forth the eighth [consciousness], the master of the total retribution (*vipāka*). It is the master of the retribution for a single lifetime within the good or evil realms.
The karma of giving and morality leads to the retribution of the human and celestial realms; the karma of killing and stealing leads to the retribution of the three miserable states (*durgati*).

Because it continues uninterruptedly throughout a single lifetime without interval, it is called "true maturation" (*bhūtavi-pāka*). Regarding that which compensates for and fulfills the karma: this refers to karma that lacks power, which induces only one among the first six [consciousnesses].

The division of neutral [states] constitutes distinct retribution (*vipāka*). Due to differences in cause—such as the excellence or inferiority, superiority or inferiority, and loftiness or lowness of virtue, non-virtue, anger, or patience—the distinct retribution itself is unequal, lacking uniformity in terms of longevity versus premature death, nobility versus low status, and beauty versus ugliness.

That which arises from true maturation (*vipāka*) is not called "true maturation. Why? Because it is subject to interruption. As for the fruit being different from the cause, this means that they are of different natures.

Because it is matured, that which is capable of creating karma—namely, the sixth consciousness characterized by a wholesome or unwholesome nature—is able to create both projecting (*ākṣepa*) and completing (*paripūri*) karma.

A portion of the first five consciousnesses, when wholesome or unwholesome, can only create completing karma; the seventh and eighth consciousnesses do not create it, nor does the portion of the first five consciousnesses that is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding the fruit produced by the karma that has been summoned: the eighth consciousness is involved in its entirety, while a portion of the first six consciousnesses is involved.
That which is not summoned by karma consists of the entirety of the seventh consciousness and a portion of the first six consciousnesses that are of a wholesome or unwholesome nature.

The eighth consciousness is the sovereign of the collective retribution and is summoned by collective karma. A portion of the first six consciousnesses that is indeterminate constitutes individual retribution and is summoned by individual karma.
The indeterminate mind and so forth, as well as the faculties and the body, are also summoned by individual karma and are all termed "direct retribution" (*vipāka*).
The receptacle world is likewise summoned by individual karma, yet it is termed "dependent retribution."
In this context, it is said that the "appropriated by self-attachment" (ātmagrāhābhiniveśa-parigṛhīta) is called *vipāka* (maturation), but this does not refer to everything.
The phrase "in this context" serves to distinguish [the present case] from what was stated above: both "true maturation" (*bhūtavi-pāka*) and "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) were termed *vipāka*.
Therefore, the present statement excludes those and takes only the eighth consciousness. The designation "*vipāka*" in this verse refers to that which possesses all three meanings.
This is what is called "maturation" (*vipāka*); it does not mean that the preceding seven [consciousnesses] may properly bear this name.
Although the three names for the transformative [consciousnesses] have been briefly explained, what are the characteristics of the first transformative consciousness?

Although the preceding section has extensively explained the characteristics of the three transformations of consciousness, this passage concludes the former and introduces the latter by specifically interrogating the first transformation.
The verse says: "The first is the ālayavijñāna... constantly revolving like a violent torrent; it is abandoned at the stage of an Arhat."

The following verse provides the answer. The verse consists of ten lines, which are explained through twelve topical sections: (1) the section on the self-characteristic of the *ālaya*; (2) the section on the resultant characteristic of maturation (*vipāka*);

(3) the section on the causal characteristic of all seeds; (4) the section on the difficulty of knowing it as "unknowable"; (5) the section on the objective sphere of the appropriated basis; (6) the section on the objective sphere of the perceived object;
(7) the section on the aspect of the perceiving subject that cognizes; (8) the section on its constant association with [the afflictions] below; and (9) the section on [its nature as] exclusively...
