It is the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Regarding the gate of association with feeling, it is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Regarding the gate of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), contact (*sparśa*) and the others are likewise.

Regarding the gate of the mental factors following the pattern of the king [the mind], they perpetually flow like a violent torrent. Regarding the gate of the dharma and analogy of cause and effect, it is abandoned at the stage of the Arhat.
The Section on the Sequence of Abandoning and Subduing. The treatise states:

"Regarding the first transformative consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna [state that]... [omitted]. "...because its faults are the most grave at the beginning of the storehouse, it is explained specifically.

The treatise states: "Below, the explanation proceeds according to the gates. First, the gate of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is explained. The first phrase names the term, which applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna."

"Vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to the Abhidharma and so forth, as well as the Ekottarika Āgama and so forth. "Ālaya" is translated here as "storehouse" (*zàng*), because it possesses the three baskets (*piṭaka*).
This is the initial heading; what follows provides the detailed explanation. Regarding "defiled phenomena acting as mutual conditions":

all phenomena are stored within consciousness, and consciousness is likewise [stored] within phenomena; they thus serve as reciprocal causes and also constantly function as reciprocal effects. This...

This clarifies the meaning of that which can store and that which is stored. Sentient beings who grasp at this as a self do so because of the defiled *manas*, which clings to this aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) as its own internal self.
This clarifies the meaning of being "appropriated through the grasping of self-love" (*ātma-sneha-parigṛhīta*). This concludes the section below.

These three meanings of "storehouse" (*ālaya*) constitute the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of consciousness: it gathers and plants the causes of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and it maintains the results of manifest activity (*samudācāra*), thereby serving as the self.

This is because of its characteristics. To exclude confusion with what follows this consciousness, [the text specifies] that its own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) has many states, which comprise both the causal characteristic (hetulakṣaṇa) and the resultant characteristic (phalalakṣaṇa).
Now, it is specifically called "store" (ālaya) because it is the first to be relinquished and because its faults are grave; therefore, it is mentioned exclusively as such.
This is explained specifically because it is the actual, uncommon [result] that leads to birth within the various realms and destinies (*dhātu-gati-yoni*).
Next is the section explaining the characteristics of the fruit. The first phrase clarifies the meaning of its name: in Sanskrit it is called *vipāka*, which here means "maturation" (*yìshú*).
This term refers to the eighth consciousness. Wholesome and unwholesome karma are the projecting causes (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), while the various realms, destinies, and births are...
It is called "maturation" (*vipāka*) because it is the maturation fruit that is projected [by karma]. The phrase "apart from this" below serves as a counter-illustration;

it means that this [consciousness] is precisely the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth. The phrase "this very" below indicates its characteristic as a result. The phrase "this consciousness" below excludes confusion.

Regarding "various states," this refers to the differences between the virtuous and the non-virtuous, the ordinary person and the noble one, and so on. Regarding "of many kinds," it may be termed "mind" (*citta*), or distinguished by other names such as the "basis of the knowable" (*jñeyāśraya*).

Now, regarding the name "maturation fruit" (*vipākaphala*): in reality, it is not shared with others in terms of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) or causal-characteristic (*hetulakṣaṇa*), nor is it shared with the stage of a Tathāgata, because it exists within the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*). Therefore, it is mentioned specifically.
This [consciousness] is able to grasp and maintain the seeds of all phenomena... (up to) "because maintaining the seeds is its unique characteristic, it is specifically so described.
Third, the section explaining the characteristics of the cause. The first sentence clarifies the meaning of its name. In Sanskrit it is called *ādāna*;

here it is translated as "grasping and maintaining" (*zhíchí*). This expresses the name of the grasper by means of that which is grasped. The phrase "apart from this" below serves as a negative illustration (*paryudāsa*), while "this is then" below concludes the discussion on the cause.

Regarding the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*): the phrase "this consciousness" below serves to exclude confusion. As for the "multiple kinds of causal characteristics," these refer to the differences among seeds—such as those pertaining to the defiled and the pure, or to matter and mind, and so forth.

Although the seeds they support differ, the meaning of being the "supporting seed" is not shared with others; it is the specific characteristic and fruit-characteristic of itself. Therefore, it is mentioned specifically.
Although the substance and characteristics of the first transformative consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) are manifold, they are briefly explained as having only these three aspects.
The phrase "The first transformative... concludes [the section].
One should further distinguish all the seeds (*sarvabījaka*); this is because, according to the principle of substance, function, cause, and effect, it ought to be so.
"Below 'all'... [This] extensively clarifies all types. The first two phrases indicate and pose the question. "That which is the basis below" [refers to] the essence.
"Its own fruit" refers to the fruits produced, namely the resultant matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). "Functionality" refers to the generative activity, which is the very substance of the seed.
As for the distinctions, they refer to the various differences among matter, mind, defilement, and purity. This refers to the eighth consciousness’s self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).

The first part explains the capacity for manifestation. From the perspective of its ability to produce [phenomena], it is termed a "seed" (*bīja*). This section distinguishes between the essence and its function:
the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is the essence (*tattva*), while the seeds are the function (*vṛtti*). Because they consist of the holder and the held, they are not identical;

because the function is subsumed within the essence, they are not different. The seed is the cause and that which is produced is the fruit; because the seed and the manifest arise together, they are not...
First: Because cause and effect correspond, they are not different.
Although they are neither identical nor different, they are substantially existent as provisional phenomena; for that which does not exist is not a causal condition.

Although [the text says] "not inferior," this is a judgment based on the provisional and the real. An objection is raised: "If seeds are neither identical nor different, they are provisional and not real. First...
The first statement directly answers that [the self] is real because it is the immediate cause. The second statement establishes the opposite by means of conventional dharmas:
since this [self] is neither identical to nor different from these various dharmas, it must be conventional and not real, just like a jar or similar objects.
This and what follows establish the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) and address the objections as stated in the text.
If that were so, then True Suchness (*tathatā*) would have to be a conventional existence; if this were granted, there would be no true ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

"If that were so," and so forth, restates the objection and provides a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) as the answer: "True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the subject (*dharmin*); it must be conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*), this is the thesis (*pakṣa*; *pratijñā*);

because it is neither identical nor different [from phenomena], this is the reason (*hetu*); for example, like a seed. If one accepts its conventional existence, then there would be no ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Since that [seed] is not so, how could this [True Suchness] be otherwise? Although this objection is the same as the previous hypothetical question (*pūrvapakṣa*), the intent of the answer differs. The former [passage] revealed the seed...
This serves as the causal condition. This reveals that suchness (*tathatā*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
However, the various seeds are spoken of as being substantially different from suchness only by way of conventional designation (*saṃvṛti*).

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "However, all [seeds]... and below, the distinction is made between the ultimate and the conventional. The previous statement held that seeds are identical to suchness and both are real; now, it distinguishes the seeds [from suchness].
The "seed" exists as conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), while "suchness" (tathatā) exists as ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Although the seed depends upon the substance of the eighth consciousness, [it is nonetheless perceived], because the seeing portion (darśana-bhāga) constantly takes this as its object.
Regarding the seeds below, they are judged according to the fourfold classification as stated in the text.
All contaminated phenomena that are subsumed under the nature of maturation (vipāka-vijñāna), up to those subsumed under the nature of the wholesome, are designated solely as "wholesome."

Regarding the passage beginning with "All those that are inferior": this distinguishes the outflowing seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*) according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). First, from the perspective of their essential nature (*svabhāva-dvāra*), they are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Second, from the perspective of the differentiation of their functional capacity (*vṛtti-viśeṣa-dvāra*), they may pertain to all three natures; this is said in reference to the perfuming causes (*vāsana-hetu*) and the fruits they produce.
Unoutflowing seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are not subsumed under the indeterminate, because both in terms of their cause and their fruit, they are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*). As for their essence...

Because they are not mutually concordant; because their two natures are distinct categories; because they stand in the relationship of the antidote and that which is to be remedied; and because they are either with-outflow (*sāsrava*) or without-outflow (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, they are exclusively wholesome and are not subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
If that is so, why does the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* state that "all seeds of maturation are born of maturation"?
[The text] below addresses this objection: it restates the previous point that uncontaminated seeds are not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and raises a difficulty based on the treatise.

Regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), while the three faculties of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) are exclusively uncontaminated, and the five faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) pertain to both contaminated and uncontaminated states, it is said that...

All possess seeds of maturation (*vipāka*) and are all born of maturation. Examining this, it is also evident that they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Why, then, do you say they are exclusively of a wholesome nature?
Although they are called "maturation," they are not indeterminate; they are maturation that is not subsumed under the category of the indeterminate.

Although it is called "maturation" (*vipāka*), [the commentary] explains it as follows: The first phrase cites the treatise, stating that although it is named "maturation," the second phrase directly clarifies that it is not of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).

The section beginning with "depending on maturation" (*yīxì*) indicates that it receives its name based on its support (*āśraya*). The section beginning with "different nature" (*yìxìng*) illustrates this through a similar example. The untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are the subject (*dharmin*). Their thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they are not of an indeterminate nature.
The reason (*hetu*) is that they depend on a support of a different nature. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*), which depends on the eye.

The faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) pertain to all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). However, the faculties are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Alternatively, there is no [distinction] below this; they are designated as "maturation" (*vipāka*) in terms of transformation.
This is because the permeations (*vāsanā*) of hearing and reflection undergo transformation and reach maturity.
Regarding this, there is an interpretation that all seeds (up to) can only increase by the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*).

Herein, the passage beginning with "Among these" sets forth the views of the three schools concerning the original and the newly arisen. First, the passage beginning with "Originally existent" sets forth the meaning of the original existence.

"By means of perfuming... and so forth explains the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*). Question: Since seeds are themselves latencies (*vāsanā*), and "latency" refers to the act of perfuming, why say that [the seed] does not arise from perfuming?
The present explanation states: it is merely that the [seed] is perfumed so as to increase; it does not arise from perfuming.
As the sūtras state: "All sentient beings... and so forth; such textual evidence is manifold.

Regarding the phrase "as the sūtras state" below, two sūtras are cited as proof that [the seeds] exist inherently (*prakṛtistha*). This is according to the text. The term "akṣa-cluster" refers to the multiplicity of defiled and pure seeds.

A treatise is cited to prove that they are perfumed and thereby increased. Regarding the passage beginning with "all those who... below, it further proves [the existence of] both out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*) [seeds].
Although these seeds are all inherently present, those who attain parinirvāṇa possess both contaminated and uncontaminated seeds;
whereas those who do not attain parinirvāṇa possess only contaminated seeds, thereby lacking the uncontaminated seeds of the three vehicles’ dharmas. This concludes the section.

Furthermore, since it is said that all sentient beings "possess [these] from the beginning" (*prakṛtistha*), which refers to the nature abiding in its original state (*prakṛtisthagotra*) obtained through the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);

and furthermore, the lower section cites the treatise stating that there are five types of innate lineages (*gotra*). This proves that the seeds of both ordinary beings and sages are inherently possessed.
These five are: (1) śrāvaka, (2) pratyekabuddha, (3) tathāgata, (4) indefinite (*aniyata*), and (5) icchantika. Furthermore, it cites the treatise...
It refers to the realization of the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*): the "not-yet-known-to-be-known," the "knowing," and the "having known.

Furthermore, that which has been transmitted from beginningless time refers to the transmission of the characteristics of the *ālayavijñāna* among sentient beings since beginningless time, specifically the naturally pure seeds (*dharmatā-śukla-bīja*) that are dependent upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
By these proofs, it is established that while uncontaminated seeds exist, contaminated [seeds] must likewise exist by their very nature (*dharmatā*).
From this point downward, the analogy is drawn: "If the uncontaminated is thus, the contaminated is likewise."
By means of perfuming and growth, rather than through the production of distinct perfumings, the relationship between cause and effect is thus established without confusion.

Regarding the phrase "by means of perfuming" and below, the meaning of the causal relationship is concluded: the seeds originally present within the eighth consciousness are caused to grow by the perfuming of the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*);
they do not arise through separate, individual perfumings. Thus, the seeds and the manifest phenomena arise together, acting as mutual causes for one another.

The cause and effect are established in this manner; therefore, there is no confusion. If one were to allow for new perfuming (*navavāsanā*), then outflows and the non-outflowing, as well as the wholesome and the unwholesome, would likewise perfume one another, resulting in a confusion of cause and effect.
One interpretation holds that seeds all arise through perfuming (up to): "just as the fragrance of sesame arises because it is perfumed by flowers.
Another interpretation holds that [the first part] concerns the new perfuming; the initial phrase directly clarifies arising through perfuming.

As for the previously cited sūtra statement that "from beginningless time there are various realms," both the perfumable and the perfumer have existed from beginningless time; therefore, we know that perfuming has been established from beginningless time.
Regarding the section on seeds: below this, the generation of perfuming is clarified through the meaning of the characters, with both the doctrine and the analogy as they appear in the text.
As the Sūtra says: "The perfuming of external seeds by the minds of sentient beings may exist or may not exist."
As stated below, the sūtras and śāstras are cited as proof. "Internal seeds" refer to the specific functional capacities within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*);

these are non-common seeds. "External seeds" refer to the receptacle world, grains, barley, and so forth; these are common seeds. Those for one's own enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*) involve perfuming (*vāsanā*), whereas those for the enjoyment of others (*parasaṃbhoga*) do not involve perfuming.

Furthermore, regarding the three types of perfuming—namely, name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*) and so forth—up until [the end of the verse], it is shown that tainted seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*) must necessarily arise by depending on perfuming.

The phrase "and name" and below clarifies that tainted seeds arise through perfuming. The "three types," namely name-and-form, self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*), and the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), refer to the three kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
These three encompass all tainted phenomena of form and mind, including the sense faculties and their objects, as well as the basis and the supported.
Regarding this principle: those three [categories] below, when analyzed according to their meaning, establish that they are merely adventitious and not original.
Furthermore, the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) also arise through perfuming (*vāsanā*), because they possess the nature of being seeds for supramundane consciousness.
Regarding "the untainted" (*anāsrava*) below: this clarifies that untainted seeds are likewise produced through perfuming (*vāsanā*).

As for "that which flows equally from the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-niṣyanda*), it refers to *prajñā*, *nirvāṇa*, *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (perfect enlightenment), and so forth. This means that by hearing the untainted True Dharma, one perfumes and thereby produces untainted seeds;
these are called the "lineage of the supramundane mind. Since they arise from the perfuming of hearing, they are exclusively newly originated.
Regarding the statement that "the original distinctions in the spiritual lineages (*gotra*) of sentient beings... are established solely based on the presence or absence of obstructions":

the first phrase directly refutes the previous school, while the second phrase establishes one's own position by relying upon the nature of obstructions. The term "sentient beings" serves to reject the preceding [view]. The first clause is a direct refutation of the former school; the second clause establishes the author's own intent by means of the obstructions.

As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, regarding the object of suchness (*tathatā*)—down to the establishment [of seeds] based on hindrances—it is not the case that untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) do not exist.
As cited below from the *Yogācāra*: "Regarding suchness" means it is the basis for both delusion and awakening. "Ultimately" means it can never be destroyed.
"Not entering parinirvāṇa" refers to the icchantikas; first, because they lack leisure for even a single lifetime, and second, because of their negligence.
Because of the fault of transgression; because of the fault of three types of wrong practice; and because of the fault of having obstructions.

That which severs only the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) constitutes the nature of the two vehicles, which is divided into two based on the sharpness or dullness of their faculties. That which severs both hindrances constitutes the Buddha-lineage (*buddhagotra*). Thus, the following section concludes by establishing the basis of the obstructions.
The statement that one "possesses" untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) refers to their potential to arise in the future, not to their actual existence as a present entity.
The following passage refutes the previous claim that the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) exist as seeds within hell. The first phrase restates the preceding position;
the subsequent phrase explains its meaning: one is said to "possess" them based on the sense that they can arise in the future, rather than implying that they already exist within hell.
Regarding the essence of the seeds (*bīja*): there is one interpretation that each seed has two categories... this is precisely what is called the "seed abiding by nature" (*prakṛtistha-bīja*).

There is another interpretation [stated] below. The third school maintains that both the innate (*mūla*) and the adventitious (*āgantuka*) are present. First, the general heading: first, the innate; the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

Regarding the distinction of functional capacities: the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*) each possess their own distinct capacities that do not interfere with one another.

The term "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*) indicates that these are not produced by effort, but are spontaneously and inherently present. The remaining citations of evidence refer to the first school’s teaching on the "abiding in the original nature," thereby establishing that [the qualities] are innately existent.
The second [type] is that which begins to arise; this refers to what has come from beginningless time until the present, which is termed the "seed produced by habituation" (*vāsanā-niṣpanna-bīja*).

Next, regarding that which begins to arise as a manifesting activity, there are three qualifications: first, "manifesting" excludes that which is not a seed; second, "present" excludes that which is past or future;
third, "actually existing" excludes such things as empty flowers or the horns of a rabbit. "Produced by habituation" concludes the discussion on the newly perfumed (*navābhyasta*).
If the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) existed only as primordial [entities], they could not serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the ālayavijñāna.
If [the text says] "only the lower," this first refutes the first school. The phrase "only the primordial" restates the partial attachment of the first school;

the subsequent phrase "evolving consciousnesses" conversely clarifies that the evolving consciousnesses act as the direct causal condition for the ālayavijñāna, thereby correctly elucidating the evolving consciousnesses.
It acts as the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*). This proves that [the seeds] are newly perfumed;

how could they be solely innate? As the Sūtra says: "All dharmas reside within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)... they arise from one another in succession, serving as mutual causes and effects."

"According to the sūtra," and so forth, cites a verse as proof. In the first line, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the "container" (*ālaya*); all phenomena (*dharma*) are the cause, and consciousness is the result.

In the second line, consciousness is the "contained"; consciousness is the cause, and all phenomena are the result. Therefore, the latter two lines state that they are "mutually and eternally [so]," and so on.
Following this verse, the intended meaning of the verse is explained.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains the ālayavijñāna... (up to) "furthermore, like bundles of reeds, they abide in mutual dependence.
In the lower section of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the treatise is cited as proof, as in the text. Regarding the metaphor of the wick and flame producing and burning one another:

the wick producing the flame is a metaphor for the seed producing the manifest; the flame burning the wick is a metaphor for the manifest perfuming the seed. This is based on the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*); by analogy, it applies to the direct causal condition (*hetupratyaya*).

Next, the analogy of bundles of reeds leaning against one another illustrates the simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). This serves as a metaphor for how seeds and manifest phenomena act as mutual causes and effects;
it is solely based on these two that the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)—in relation to the ālayavijñāna—is established.
"Only based on the lower [level]" cites and confirms the intended meaning of the sutras and treatises being cited. "If all... cites the opponent's position and refutes it.

The preceding citations from sutras and treatises provide dual proof that the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) and the perfumed object (*vāsyamāna*) mutually serve as cause and effect. According to the introductory and concluding texts, the intent lies in the perfuming agent;
this is to refute the first school’s claim that there is no new perfuming (*navavāsanā*).

It is not the case that what is merely caused to grow through perfuming can be called a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); otherwise, wholesome and unwholesome karma would also constitute causal conditions for their ripened fruits (*vipāka-phala*).
[The phrase] "not by perfuming" below refutes the growth through perfuming. This is because the first school mentioned previously stated: "By the power of perfuming, there is only growth."

Now, to clarify the intended meaning: only that which perfumes and brings about production is called a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). The first phrase restates and refutes [the opponent's position].

The second phrase refutes it by analogy with the case of wholesome and unwholesome [actions], stating: "Wholesome and unwholesome karma can only serve as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); they are not direct causal conditions. This refutes their claim that perfuming and growth are also not direct causal conditions.

Furthermore, since various sacred teachings state that seeds exist [up to] "therefore," the position that there is only the fundamental consciousness contradicts both scripture and reasoning. The passage beginning with "Moreover, all...
generally refutes the contradiction with scripture; the passage beginning with "Therefore, only... concludes the refutation based on scripture and reasoning.

If only that which first arises were to exist as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), [then] wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth would have to be the seeds of unwholesome (*akuśala*) and so forth.
If [it is argued that it exists] only as inferior, this refutes the second school. The phrase "only that which first arises" restates the partial adherence of the second school.

From "conditioned" onwards, five phrases are used to reveal by contrast that [the untainted] must be inherently existent (*mūlataḥ san*). Regarding "conditioned and untainted," this refers to the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*catur-jñāna-bodhi*).
"Ti. Because one severs delusions and realizes principle, there is pure nirvāṇa, which is that which is realized by the *vijñapti-hetu* (the cause of comprehension);

and there is the bodhi of the four wisdoms, which is that which is produced by the *janana-hetu* (the cause of production). If there were no dharmatā-natured, inherently existing, direct seeds, these should not be able to arise. [The opponent] offers this defense:

It is argued that because one hears the True Dharma which flows equally from the Dharma-realm, and due to the perfuming of this hearing, it can serve as the seed for the untainted (*anāsrava*). To this, an objection is raised:
"The perfuming of hearing is a tainted (*sāsrava*) mind; it should not serve as the seed for the untainted. Conversely, if it were so, the untainted would instead produce the tainted."
The same applies to all the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena of the Buddhas, whether wholesome or unwholesome; they should all arise from one another.
Although the Vibhajyavādins make this claim [up to the point where it concludes], untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena do not arise without a cause.

[The section] "Distinguishing the Lower" refutes the position that the purity of mind (*cittaprakṛti*) serves as the seed [of awakening]. First, it cites the scriptural authority of the *Vibhajyavādins*—referring here to the masters who comment on the sūtras and śāstras.
In the passage beginning with "The nature of mind," the text presents the masters' own interpretation of the sūtra.

Therefore, in the passage beginning with "Thus, there is no...," the argument is finally established by citing this "purity of the nature of mind" as the untainted seed (*anāsravabīja*). Hence, it is said that untainted phenomena do not arise without a cause.
Although these phrases were spoken, the Master of the Treatise now refutes the words of those who first established [this system].
As for the statement regarding the "nature of mind," what meaning does that teaching convey? It is because its essence undergoes no transformation from beginning to end.
The two phrases beginning with "and the mind" serve as a summary. The phrase "if one speaks of the principle of emptiness" restates the opponent's position;

they take the principle of emptiness to be what is called "original purity. The phrase "emptiness is not... refutes this. "Mind" refers to the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*bodhi*); while the principle of emptiness is true and eternal, it is not the seed of wisdom.
The phrase "eternal dharmas... sets forth the reason why it cannot be a seed: the definition of a seed requires momentary cessation (*kṣaṇika-nirodha*). Therefore...
It is said that the permanent dharma is certainly not the seed, etc.
If one asserts that it is precisely the mind, then it would be identical to the Sāṃkhya [system] (up to the point where it says) lest good and evil, etc., act as causes for one another.

"If it is precisely... below refutes the identity with the mind. The first phrase restates the position; "it would be identical to... below refutes it by analogy with external systems. This concerns the characteristics of the mind.

Although there is arising and ceasing, the essence is fundamentally quiescent; thus, it would be identical to the *prakṛti* (self-nature) postulated by the Sāṃkhya school. [The text says] "evil is not inferior," which refutes [the view] by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

First, the two natures are refuted: since the mind permeates all three natures, if one were to claim that it is fundamentally pure, then evil and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) would both have to be wholesome (*kuśala*), and thus there would be no distinction between the two natures.
If one grants that the minds of these two natures are wholesome, they should then be associated with faith (*śraddhā*) and the other [wholesome mental factors].
[This is] associated. What is called "unwholesome-indeterminate"? It is not admitted to be wholesome; it is not even called wholesome, let alone being untainted (*anāsrava*).

[Regarding] the tainted (*sāsrava*) lower [category], one establishes a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to refute [the opponent]: "The nature of wholesomeness is not untainted. The tainted wholesome mind is the subject (*dharmin*).

The school that maintains that intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) is not untainted (*anāsrava*) designates it as the cause of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), just like an evil mind and so forth; therefore, it does not descend [to the level of the untainted].

To conclude: an outflowing mind (*sāsravacitta*) should not serve as the cause for what is untainted, lest even a single wholesome term be [misleadingly] applied by using good and evil as reciprocal analogies.
If there is a mind with outflows (sāsrava), its nature is without outflows (anāsrava), because no distinct causes or conditions can be found [to differentiate them].

Regarding the phrase "if there is a lower [level]," this explains the presence of outflows and the absence of outflows in relation to one another; as for the "distinct causes and conditions," they are the same mental factors (citta-dharma).

Furthermore, if the mind of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) were untainted (*anāsrava*), then—because the nature of their seeds and their manifest activity (*samudācāra*) would be identical—it would follow that they are not inferior to those below;

this constitutes the objection that an ordinary being should be called a noble one (*ārya*). If "if it were inferior" (*yadi hīnaḥ*) is taken as restating the opponent's defense, then "then the mind... (*tadā cittaṃ...*) [is the response].

[The opponent] refutes [this]. The intent of the defense is that although the nature of the mind in its active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is not called "untainted" because its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are defiled;
thus, there is no fault of having to designate it as "noble" (*ārya*). The intent of the refutation is that the seeds of the mind (*bīja*) would likewise not be untainted.
Why? Because the nature and characteristics of the seeds and the active manifestations are identical. If the seeds were also pure by nature...

If the marks (*nimitta*) were possessed of defilement (*sāsrava*), they could not be termed "outflow-free seeds" (*anāsrava-bīja*). Why, then, does your treatise state that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) possess only the accomplishment of outflow-free seeds?
Furthermore, when the sūtras speak of the "innate purity of the mind-nature," it is because its nature is outflow-free; therefore, it is called "primordially pure."

However, according to the general meaning of the scriptures following the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, that which is called "the nature of the mind" (*cittaprakṛti*) is precisely *tathatā* (suchness). This is because *tathatā* is the true nature of the mind.

Alternatively, because the essence of the mind is fundamentally free from afflictions, it is termed "nature-pure" (*prakṛtipariśuddha*). It is not that the nature of the tainted mind (*sāsravacitta*) is untainted;
rather, it is named "pure by nature" because [the mind's essence] is untainted. Furthermore, although the essence of *tathatā* is eternal, it is neither the cause of the mind nor a seed.
"Son, it is not so. [The Master] rebukes the erroneous citation below.
From this, one should believe that there exist various sentient beings (up to) the categories of tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena; this should be understood.

From "By this, below," the correct meaning is revealed. "By this" means that since the purity of nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) mentioned above is not the cause for the four untainted wisdoms (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one must believe in the existence of two types:
the innate (*sahaja*) and the newly perfumed (*navābhyāsa*). The first passage reveals the innate; from "untainted" (*anāsrava*) onwards, it reveals the newly perfumed.

Regarding "subsequent superior progress" (*viśeṣa-gati*): this refers to the stages of the provisions (*sambhāra*), the application (*prayoga*), the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and so forth—the progressive advancement.

This is because the term "pervasive" (tong) refers to both the shallow and the deep. As for "outflow-free dharmas" (anāsrava-dharma), they refer to the presently functioning wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). Regarding the phrase "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) below, by analogy, the category of outflowing [dharmas] should likewise possess both the fundamental and the initial [wisdom].
"Although in various holy teachings it is said that internal seeds... [down to] "...therefore it is said that internal seeds definitely possess perfuming.

The phrase "various holy [teachings]" below serves as a general reference to the preceding citations of scripture. By restating the previous citation that internal seeds definitely possess perfuming, it serves as proof for the theory of new perfuming (*navavāsanā*).

However, the following two phrases do not refute the existence of innate seeds (*sahaja*) according to the intent of the treatise. Nevertheless, the section beginning with "However, the original... provides a general commentary on the treatise.

Regarding the term "middle perfuming" (*madhyavāsanā*), it possesses both the meanings of "growth" (*utpatti*) and "manifestation" (*prakāśana*), thereby clarifying that [the seeds] are inherently present (*mūlataḥ sat*). Thus, the following section concludes:
these words indicate that the seeds of outflows (*sāsrava-bīja*) possess both the sense of being original (*mūla*) and the sense of being adventitious (*āgantuka*).
The perfuming of hearing is not merely impure (*sāsrava*); [it continues] until [the end of the passage], and for this reason it is also called the "perfuming of hearing.

Regarding the phrase "its hearing" and below: it penetrates the untainted (*anāsrava*), as it first arises through the perfuming of hearing. The first sentence restates and refutes [the objection]. "Above" refers to the impure mind hearing the True Dharma;
that which is perfumed—the untainted seed—arises for the first time. Regarding the phrase "hearing the True Dharma" and below: it clarifies that the perfuming is not [merely impure].
It is only through perfuming that [the seeds] first arise, yet they are also perfumed as being originally present. "Supramundane mind" refers to untainted correct gnosis;
thus, the following concludes the purport of the teaching: perfuming encompasses both the original and the emergent types.
Regarding the statement that "the permeation of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*) which is of a contaminated nature (*sāsrava-svabhāva*) [is] expediently taught as the seed of supramundane mind":

the passage beginning with "The permeation of hearing" below distinguishes between two categories. When one hears the True Dharma within a contaminated mind, the seeds thus perfumed are of a contaminated nature;
the originally existing uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), however, belong to the uncontaminated nature. The present judgment states: "That which is of a contaminated nature..."
Among the three types of abandonment, it is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Among the five fruits, it brings about the fruit of superior maturation (*viśiṣṭa-vipāka-phala*).

Among the four conditions, it serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). That which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is not subject to abandonment; it is the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Its resulting fruit should be the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), just as tainted morality and generosity, being of a tainted nature, bring about the retribution of being born as a noble human or deity.

This is called "superior maturation" (*viśiṣṭavipāka*). Regarding this, a doubt arises below [the text]: "In the scriptural teachings, it is said that tainted (*sāsrava*) generosity and morality are the seeds of the supramundane mind (*lokottaracitta*).
Why, then, is it now described as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*)? The intent of the explanation can be understood from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Asvabhāva, which states:
"Although this hearing-perfuming (*śrutavāsanā*) is a mundane, tainted state of mind, it is nonetheless supramundane."
Because it is the nature of the seeds of the mind.
Regarding the establishment of the distinctions among lineages based on hindrances (up to): there is the sense that hindrances are either capable of being severed or incapable of being severed.

Based on the hindrances below, this generally follows the *Yogācārabhūmi* in establishing the distinctions among lineages based on hindrances. The first two phrases provide the heading; they primarily concern the absence [of hindrances].

The seeds of outflows determine the distinction between genders (i.e., the nature of the afflictions). That is to say, the following section explains this distinction between genders; therefore, the conclusion is drawn from what follows below.
The untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are precisely the seeds of wisdom (*jñāna-bīja*). They are capable of manifesting active states that counteract and oppose the hindrances.
Consequently, by means of the presence or absence of untainted seeds, the meaning of whether hindrances can be severed or cannot be severed is elucidated.

However, the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are subtle and hidden, making them difficult to know... (omitted)... thus it is said that the distinctions between seed-natures (*gotra-viśeṣa*) are established based on obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).

"However, [they are] not... serves as a general rebuttal to an objection. The question asks: "Since the distinctions between natures are determined by reference to the untainted, why does the treatise determine them by reference to obstacles?
The explanation of the meaning is clear. "Not so... serves as a counter-clarification: if one did not determine them by reference to the untainted severance of obstacles, then...

What is the distinct cause for there being obstructions that can be destroyed and those that cannot? If you claim that it is due to the inherent nature (*dharmatā*) of the obstructions, we shall challenge this by analogy with the case of the untainted (*anāsrava*): why do you not admit that untainted seeds also exist by way of their inherent nature?

If [the opponent] fundamentally objects on the basis of the meaning [of the text], it is refuted by showing that the manifest noble path arises from untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) and is able to destroy the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*);
based upon this, the distinction of the five natures (*pañca-gotra*) is established.
Since that noble path (āryamārga) necessarily lacks the possibility of arising, the claim that it "can arise" is also certainly irrational.

The phrase "since that... below refutes the notion that the untainted faculties (anāsravendriya) can arise. In the text, following from the preceding, [it states]: "If there were no untainted seeds..."
It is also illogical to say that the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) will arise when the active manifestation of the Noble Path can never again occur;
for various sacred teachings state in many places that [the faculties] exist until [the end]. Thus, the principle of their initial arising alone contradicts both reason and scripture.

The section beginning with "However, as for all... generally refutes [the opposing view] by contradicting the scriptures. Thus, the section beginning with "Therefore, only... concludes by contradicting both scripture and reasoning.
From this, one should understand that the seeds of all phenomena are each of two types: those that are innate (*sahaja*) and those that are newly arisen (*āgantuka*).
From "By this, below" onwards is the summary.
However, the meaning of "seed" (*bīja*) briefly comprises six types (up to "...because it cannot be said that there is a capacity to produce").

From "However, seed, below," the meaning of the seed is clarified; first, it is generally indicated and listed, and below, it is explained individually. From "1. *Kṣaṇa*, below," the names are indicated.
This means that [the seed] arises at its very location and perishes at that same location; that is, its substance is "low" (momentary). To explain the meaning:

the substance of the seed must undergo arising and ceasing moment by moment before it can possess the superior capacity to produce [a sprout]. This is like worldly grains such as rice or wheat, which, depending on conditions such as water and soil, undergo successive transformations before they possess the capacity to produce a sprout.
It is not like the Sāṃkhya school’s reckoning that the substance of *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is eternal and yet possesses the capacity [to produce effects].
Since it serves as the basis for the functions of the great elements and so forth, this [text] refutes it by stating: "A permanent phenomenon is eternally without transformation;
it cannot be said to possess the function of production. This is because its nature is like that of space, which, though permanent, lacks the function of production."
"Both fruits are co-existent" means that [the cause] exists simultaneously with what it produces; therefore, one should simply say that it is "co-existent with the fruit.
"The two fruits" below is the designation of the name; it refers to the cause and effect being simultaneous and inseparable. "That is to say" below is the explanation of the meaning.
The causal seed and the manifest fruit are both simultaneous; both are present, and through their mutual conjunction, they constitute the meaning of "seed.

Below this, following the preceding section, the text clarifies the negation [of the seed-fruit relationship] by distinguishing cases that are not simultaneous and not present, as well as those that are spatially separated.

"Rejecting that they are not a synthesis" (*saṃnipāta*). From "the manifest and the seeds" (*vartamāna-bīja*) downwards, this further explains the first phrase. Because the seeds belong to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature while the manifest [dharmas] pertain to all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), they are called "of different kinds.

That they do not mutually contradict one another is precisely the meaning of "synthesis" (*saṃnipāta*). "In a single body" (*eka-kāya*) is the meaning of "manifest"; "simultaneously" (*saha*) is the meaning of "together.
Possessing the capacity to produce [an effect] is termed "coexistent with the fruit" (*phala-sahabhū*). "Not as below" further explains the preceding negation.

Seeds produce seeds; these are all of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) and are termed "of their own kind" (*svajāti*). There is no sense of simultaneity between the preceding and succeeding [moments].

Because they are mutually exclusive, there is no sense of conjunction. When a seed produces a manifest fruit, cause and effect are simultaneous; this is termed "coexistence with the fruit" (*phala-sahabhū*).

When a seed induces a subsequent seed, cause and effect are sequential; this is termed "necessarily not coexistent. Although the latter phrase [in the original text] cites the previous [point regarding] coexistence and non-coexistence...
Together. This appears below to clarify the meaning of "appropriating" and "not appropriating. In the first phrase, the seed-cause and the manifest fruit are both present simultaneously;
because the seed possesses the functional capacity to produce the manifest fruit, it is therefore appropriated. As for the second phrase, why is the seed that induces the seed not appropriated?

Because while the preceding cause remains in its state, the subsequent fruit has not yet arisen and thus lacks its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); at the time the subsequent fruit arises, [the inducing seed has already ceased].

Because the preceding causes have already ceased, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); therefore, they are not grasped. Regarding the phrase "arising based on" (*niśrityotpāda*), this clarifies the basis for establishing names.

The first clause clarifies that the seeds of manifest names arise based [on the seeds of the drawn-in], while the second clause clarifies that they do not arise based on the seeds of the projecting [causes].
Thus, the phrase "only" concludes [the argument].
"Third, it constantly evolves along with [the mind]" means that it necessarily persists for a long duration;

this reveals that seeds produce their own kind. "Third, it constantly... introduces the name. "Constantly" (*nitya*) means eternally. "Evolves along with" (*anuvartate*) has the meaning of being associated (*samprayukta*).

"Necessarily... explains the meaning. "For a long duration" refers to constancy; from the initial moment of perfuming until the time when the manifest activity (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) arises. "Of one kind" means exclusively...
It is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). As for "continuity" (*saṃtati*): it is uninterrupted and unceasing until its culmination, which refers to the stage of maturation.

This means that these seeds must evolve in immediate succession in association with the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Furthermore, seeds of their own kind follow one another from prior to subsequent moments until they reach the stage of maturation.
The phrase "this excludes the following" excludes the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), as they do not constantly follow [the seeds] in the same manner as the seeds do.
"Transforming" and "changing" mean that the three natures are not of a single category. "Interrupted" means that they do not continue for a long duration.
This constant transformation reveals the meaning of seeds inducing seeds.
The determination of the four natures means that, according to the power of causes, there is the sense of causal conditions for the arising of effects of different natures.
"The four natures" below is the heading of the name. "Natures" refers to the three natures. "Determination" excludes what is not fixed; this is explained by the phrase "according to" below.
Explanation of the terms: "The power of the cause" refers to past perfuming agents, whether unwholesome or wholesome causes. "Wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth" refers to that which is produced;

"and so forth" includes defiled and pure form and mind. "Function" refers to the seed—that is, the perfumed [basis]—which is capable of producing [results] equally throughout the preceding and succeeding moments, remaining unchanged as defiled or pure, and wherein cause and effect correspond. Therefore, it is called "determined. This excludes what follows.
This is to exclude the [theories of] other schools regarding matter and mind acting as mutual causes and conditions for defilement and purification.
Fifth, "depending on various conditions" means that this [seed] must depend on [conditions such as] reaching [the object]; therefore, seeds do not produce their fruits constantly or simultaneously.

"Five depend on the following": this indicates the name. "Dependence" means waiting for or relying upon. "Various conditions" refers to the sense organ (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), space, light, attention (*manasikāra*), and the immediate causal condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
"Discrimination," "defilement and purity," and "the fundamental" are explained below as follows: the visual consciousness, for example, depends on nine conditions, and so forth.

This section refutes [the opposing views]. First, by means of various conditions (*pratyaya*), it refutes spontaneous arising (*svabhāva-utpatti*). Next, by means of awaiting conditions, it refutes the notion that conditions are eternally present.
Therefore, regarding the seeds below, the conclusion is drawn:

citing the six characteristics of one's own fruit—namely, from "distinct" (*bhinna*) up to "possessing these six meanings"—it is established that only that which possesses these six meanings constitutes a seed, and nothing else.
"Six [factors] lead downward. This indicates the name [of the section], meaning that cause and effect arise in succession without any confusion. "That is to say, below," this explains the meaning:
each respective cause induces and produces its own distinct effect, such as form producing form, or mind producing mind, and so forth. "This excludes, below," [the possibility of cross-production].
First, it refutes the non-Buddhist view that a single cause, such as Īśvara, gives rise to all phenomena.

Next, it refutes the view of other schools that matter and mind act as mutual causes and conditions—specifically, that matter serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the mind, and the mind serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for matter.

This refers to the immediate cause (*samanantara-pratyaya*) that draws forth its own fruit; therefore, it is excluded [from the category of projecting causes]. Only the "fundamental" and "inferior" [causes] conclude the preceding six sections.
External grains, barley, and so forth, because they are transformations of consciousness, [function] until they cease, which is precisely what is called the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
Below, the external seeds are distinguished from [the internal]. Because the term "seed" is applied broadly, it is necessary to exclude any confusion.

That which is transformed by consciousness refers to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by the eighth consciousness; since it lacks the six characteristics [of a true seed], it is not a real seed.

However, because it is admitted to have a cause, it is metaphorically called a "seed. As for external seeds, in relation to the sprout, they are the direct productive cause (*janaka-hetu*); in relation to [the subsequent stages], they are the indirect cause.
The stalk and so forth serve as the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*). By analogy with this, internal seeds also possess two types of causes:

the ālayavijñāna, as an internal seed, serves as the producing cause (*janaka-hetu*) in relation to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) directly; it serves as the projecting cause in relation to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) through to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) indirectly.
Internal seeds necessarily arise through the growth of perfuming (*vāsanā*); [this is because] they are fruits produced from seeds of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding "internal seeds" below, this distinguishes between the presence or absence of perfuming in internal and external seeds, while simultaneously determining the two conditions of proximity and distance.

As for being a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), external seeds act as a dominant condition with respect to the fruit they produce, while internal seeds must necessarily serve as the immediate [condition].
What is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)? It is because [the fruit] is produced from seeds of common characteristics belonging to the eighth consciousness.

Regarding self-enjoyment [bodies], there is perfuming; regarding other-enjoyment [bodies], there is no perfuming. The above has clarified that seeds are the causal condition because they are capable of producing [their effects].
If one examines this in detail, there should be a fourfold analysis: namely, seeds producing manifest phenomena, and seeds inducing seeds.

The present [phenomenon] perfumes the seeds; the present induces the present. Of these four categories, the first three are direct causal conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*). The fourth category is a true outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Among these, those that are causal conditions and seeds are the first two; those that are neither causal conditions nor seeds are the fourth.
The third [type] is that which is a causal condition but not a seed. That which is neither a causal condition nor a seed is external grain such as rice or wheat.
Herein, in clarifying the meaning of "seed," both of the first two [of the four meanings] are taken together.

If one were to clarify the meaning of "all-seed" (*sarvabīja*) alone, one would take only the first type: the capacity within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to directly produce its own fruit, manifesting in the present.
Regarding the distinction:

on what basis is the term "perfuming" (*vāsanā*) established? [It is so called] because it causes seeds to grow and develop; this is why it is named "perfuming. The section beginning with "On what basis...
clarifies the meaning of perfuming. First, there is a general inquiry followed by a general response.
What are the four characteristics of that which is perfumable? (Up to: Because its nature is not stable, it is not perfumable. "What are they?
below introduces the specific inquiry regarding the perfumable; what follows is the detailed explanation. First, the characteristic of stability. Question:

Among all consciousnesses, mental factors (*caitta*), and material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), all are capable of receiving perfuming. Are they all equally termed "perfumable"? Now, by means of the characteristic of stability...

"Stability" (*sthira*) means being without change or transformation; this refers to being of a single type (*eka-jātīya*). "Abiding" (*sthitimat*) means being without interruption; this refers to continuity (*saṃtāna*).

Because of this stability and abiding, it is able to receive and implant habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); thus, it is that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*). This indicates that the eighth consciousness possesses these characteristics.

The phrase "this excludes the following" clarifies what is excluded: the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), namely the first seven. Among these, the first five follow conditions (*pratyaya-anuvartin*).

Regarding arising and ceasing: [the seeds] do not function during the sixth [consciousness] or the five states [of meditative absorption]. On the seventh stage and above, there is a transformation between the defiled and the pure.

Furthermore, material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) lack the capacity for cognitive reflection (*ālambana*). For these reasons, they are excluded. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are the subject (*dharmin*); they are not that which is perfumed (*anabhāvya*), this is the thesis (*pakṣa*).

The reason (*hetu*) is "because they are not stable" (*asthiratvāt*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like sound, wind, and so forth. This same reasoning may also be applied reciprocally to the evolving consciousnesses themselves.

Second, regarding the nature of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*): if a phenomenon is equal [to the alaya-vijñāna] (up to: it only carries old seeds and is not newly perfumed), it is of an indeterminate nature. Question:
The seventh and eighth consciousnesses serve as mutual simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*) and always function together;

since the seventh possesses the quality of being stable and enduring, it could be that which is perfumed. Why then is it distinguished by its being "indeterminate"? Regarding "indeterminate," this refers to that which is pure (*śuddha*).

It is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), equanimous, and thus unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Like plain white silk, it is therefore capable of receiving perfuming (*vāsanā*). This excludes the lower [realms]; this clarifies the exclusion.
The wholesome and the defiled are like blue or yellow; because they are mutually contradictory, they cannot accommodate one another, and thus they are not that which is perfumed.

The seventh [consciousness], being obscured, is likewise included within the defiled. From this point downward, it is shown that the Tathāgata’s pure consciousness is extremely wholesome and powerful;
it admits nothing and does not undergo new perfuming.

Third, the nature of being susceptible to perfuming (*vāsanā*). If a phenomenon is sovereign (up to: because it is not firm and dense), it is not that which is perfumed. Regarding the three natures of being susceptible to perfuming:
Question—The eighth consciousness possesses the two aforementioned meanings and could thus be that which is perfumed; why then is it excluded by the criterion of "being susceptible to perfuming"?

"Sovereign" refers to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), which has the characteristic of being the master of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). As for "its nature is not firm and dense": [it is not so].

"Simple" means not being solid and dense; that is to say, its essential nature is empty and porous. This negation [of "simple"] clarifies that the mind-associates (caitta), which depend upon others and lack sovereignty, as well as unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta)—which are as solid and dense as metal or stone—are all incapable of being perfumed (vāsanā).
Fourth, the nature of being in mutual conjunction with the perfuming agent (up to): it may be the perfumable, yet not a mental factor (*caitta*) and so forth.

Fourth, it is in conjunction with the perfuming agent. Question: For this person, the eighth consciousness, when compared to the seven [consciousnesses] of another, possesses the aforementioned three meanings and may thus be the perfumable;
now, it is distinguished by "being in mutual conjunction. This refers to being at the same moment and within the same body.
Because they consist of the subject and object, they are not identical; because they constitute a single body, they are not separate.

This [passage] "this excludes" clarifies the exclusion of other bodies, which do not occupy the same location, nor do they exist at the same time across preceding and succeeding moments. Since there is no conjunction, they are dissociated; therefore, they are not that which is perfumed.

The phrase "only different from" concludes [the argument]. The eighth consciousness possesses these four meanings, whereas the mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth do not. The term "and so forth" refers to what was previously excluded.
What are the four meanings of that which is called a "perfuming agent" (*bhāvanā*)? (Up to: Because it lacks the function of producing growth, it is not a perfuming agent.

Regarding the phrase "What are the [four] below," this specifically interrogates the perfuming agent; the following provides the specific explanation. First, the question regarding arising and ceasing: Are all phenomena capable of perfuming?
Could unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) also serve as perfuming agents? Now, this is distinguished by the fact that they possess arising and ceasing. There is an active [function].
Because it functions, it is impermanent. Because it possesses activity, it generates and nurtures habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). This [section] below clarifies the negation:
the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is immutable; therefore, it is truly eternal. It lacks activity and cannot generate [habitual tendencies].
Second, that which possesses superior efficacy: if there is arising and ceasing (up to) because its power is weak and inferior, it cannot be a perfuming agent.

Regarding "possessing superior efficacy": Question: The eighth consciousness and its mental factors constantly evolve like a flowing stream; this involves arising and ceasing, so they could serve as perfuming agents.

Now, by distinguishing them through the criterion of "possessing superior efficacy," even though they involve arising and ceasing, they must also possess the force of being either wholesome or defiled.
Only when the power [of a mind] is superior can it induce latencies (*vāsanā*). This excludes the following:

the resultant (*vipāka*) minds and mental factors, which are unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), are weak in their potency and therefore cannot be perfumers (*bhāvaka*). Furthermore, material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) lack objective cognition (*ālambana*), and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) lack substantial reality; thus, neither can they be perfumers.

If the three realms of existence (tridhātu) were subject to increase or decrease, and if they possessed a superior efficacy, then the fruits of Buddhahood attained at earlier and later stages would necessarily possess degrees of superiority or inferiority.

Thus, the three realms would be subject to increase and decrease. Question: If one takes up the perspective of superior efficacy, the wholesome dharmas of the fruit of Buddhahood are exceptionally sublime and beyond reproach;

they could therefore serve as the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*). Now, you distinguish them by means of their being subject to increase and decrease. If there were a superior efficacy, it too would necessarily be subject to increase and decrease. [This is] included.

This plants habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). This [passage] "prevents the lower" clarifies the prevention; because it is perfect, there is neither increase nor decrease. That [passage] "if the lower" is a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*);
those who possess superiority or inferiority [do so] because the former Buddhas have perfumed [the mind] more, while the latter Buddhas have perfumed it less.
Fourth, it evolves in conjunction with that which is perfumed (*bhāvyamāna*). To possess these four meanings is to be a perfuming agent (*vāsaka*).

Regarding "fourth, evolving in conjunction with that which is perfumed": Question: According to others, the first seven [consciousnesses] possess the aforementioned three meanings and can thus serve as my perfuming agents.

Now, by specifying "evolving in conjunction with that which is perfumed," this excludes the following [the eighth consciousness]. This clarifies the exclusion; the meaning is the same as [what was stated] previously.
Commentary on "Perfuming" (*vāsanā*). Only the seven [factors] below [are perfumers]. Conclusion:
Thus, the perfumer and the perfumed consciousness—[extending to] "like perfuming sesame seeds"—are therefore called "perfuming.

Thus, the section below provides a general explanation of the meaning of perfuming: first the principle (*dharma*), then the analogy. "Sesame seeds" (*tila*) refers to *hūmā* (Sanskrit for sesame). Sesame...
Originally there is no fragrance; it exists because of perfuming. Both [the fragrance and the perfumer] arise and perish together, and thus the meaning of perfuming is established.
When the perfuming consciousnesses and so forth arise from their seeds, the principle that cause and effect are simultaneous remains unshaken.

"Regarding 'the capacity to perfume' (nengxun) below: this clarifies that they mutually serve as cause and effect. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows: The three factors—the manifest, the seeds, and the dharmas—are the subject (*dharmin*).

Their simultaneous existence as cause and effect is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because they mutually produce and perfume one another. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like the wick and the flame, etc."

The capacity of the perfuming agent (*bhāvanā*) to produce various arising manifestations (up to) "even if termed 'causal condition' (*hetu-pratyaya'), it should be understood as a metaphorical designation.

Regarding "the capacity of the perfuming agent" and below: the first instance of cause and effect is analogous to the mutual production of seeds and manifestations; the second instance of cause and effect is analogous to the sequential production of seeds inducing seeds.

Regarding "these two" and below: this concludes the formation of the direct causal condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Regarding "apart from these" and below: this clarifies [the nature of the condition].

Exclusion. As for other phenomena that are not causal conditions, such as the present inducing the present, or form inducing form, these are called the brief explanation of all types of characteristics.
This concludes the summary of all types of characteristics from the preceding chapter. Furthermore, below this, there is the analysis of their essential nature.
Regarding the passages on the six meanings of the fundamental origin, perfuming, cause, effect, and so forth:
as for the mode of activity and the object of this consciousness, it is said that they are "the unknowable appropriation and the apprehension of the locus.
Below this [passage], two questions are posed together concerning the two gates of the subject (the appropriating consciousness) and the object. Below that, a verse is cited to answer both together.
"Apprehension" (*vijñapti*) means discernment (*vijñāna*), because consciousness has discernment as its mode of activity (*ākāra*).

Regarding "apprehension," the following provides a brief explanation in reverse order, beginning first with the subjective perceiver. "Discernment" (*vijñapti*) refers to clear and distinct differentiation.
"Mode of activity" (*ākāra*) refers to the mind, in its state of clarity, proceeding toward the characteristics of the object.
"Place" (*sthāna*) refers to the locus, namely the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), because it is the basis upon which all sentient beings depend.
"Place" also refers to the lower [realms]. Next, the object of perception (*ālambana*) is explained; first, the basis is clarified as in the text.

Appropriation (*upādāna*) is twofold, namely: the seeds and the root-body (*indriya-kāya*). [This continues] until: because they are subsumed as one's own essence and share the same security and peril.
Regarding the two types of appropriation: first, the seeds; second, the root-body. Each possesses two meanings. Within "appropriation" (*upādāna*), there are two meanings:
first, subsuming them as one's own essence; second, maintaining them so that they do not disperse. Within "sensation" (*vedanā*), there are two meanings: first, experiencing them as...

The objects (*viṣaya*). Second, that which causes the arising of sensation (*vedanā*): the seeds are the three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), namely those of names-and-words (*nāma-kāya*) and so forth;

the faculties (*indriya*) are the five sense-faculties and the pure *mahābhūtas*; the body (*kāya*) is the locus upon which the faculties depend, such as the grape-like [clusters of sensory organs] and so forth.

Below this, the two [categories] conclude the discussion on appropriation (*upādāna*). Although both are appropriated, the three types are not equal. The faculty-body (*indriya-kāya*) possesses four characteristics: first, it is gathered as one's own self-nature (*ātman*).

1. Because they are equally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). 2. They sustain [the body] so that it does not disperse; the eighth [consciousness] sustains it so that it does not decay. 3. They take [it] as an object of perception;
the eighth [consciousness] has it as its direct objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). 4. They cause the arising of sensation and awareness; because their security and peril are identical.

If it is the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), it can only be apprehended as an object (*ālambana*) and maintained so as not to disperse; thus, it is merely perceived (*ālambana*) but not grasped (*upātta*).

If it is a contaminated seed (*sāsravabīja*), it lacks one of the four meanings—that of producing sensation and awareness—and thus possesses only the function of maintaining [the continuity] but no grasping.
If it is an uncontaminated seed (*anāsravabīja*), among the four meanings, it only possesses the function of maintaining [the continuity] so as not to... [disperse].
The first meaning is dispersed; therefore, it is neither an object-condition (*ālambana*) nor appropriated (*upātta*). These are subsumed under the latter two phrases.
Within each of the two pairs of meanings, one is briefly cited, because each pair subsumes the other.
Appropriation (*upādāna*) and the bases (*āyatana*) are both objects of cognition (*ālambana*), because [the consciousness] arises in dependence upon their modes of activity (*ākāra*).
The phrase beginning with "appropriation" generally clarifies that these three types of objects are all the objects of the eighth [consciousness]. Below "ālaya" [the text continues].
The further explanation: Regarding the power of causal conditions, there are two: first, the power of the maturation of the eighth consciousness’s own seeds as the causal condition;

second, the power of the maturation of the seeds of the three types of objects as the immediate causal condition. Regarding the arising of the self-substance: this refers to the substance of the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the eighth consciousness manifesting from its own seeds.
The objective fields of the three types of image-divisions (*nimittabhāga*) arise through the transformation of the substance of the self-witnessing division.

As for the statement that "arising occurs because the aspect of the object of cognition can arise": internally, it relies on the transformation of the substance of self-cognition; externally, it depends on the objective part (*nimittabhāga*) as its condition.
Generally speaking, both the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) arise based upon self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*).

In this context, "apprehension" (*vijñapti*) refers to the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). [The passage] from "this apprehension" up to "[is] comprised by the seeing-part" explains its function of discernment.

Regarding the phrase "in this context" and so forth, the commentary provides a detailed explanation in reverse order. First, it explains the gate of the aspect (*ākāra*), which corresponds to the character "apprehension" (*vijñapti*) in the verse.
This initial passage briefly indicates the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) of the maturation-consciousness.

However, when the substance of a contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) arises, that which resembles the aspect of the subjective perceiver is designated as the "seeing part" (*darśana-bhāga*).

The phrase "However, there is... below serves to clarify the various parts of both the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) in general. The section beginning with "First, emerging from the two parts... first explains the two parts of all consciousnesses. The section beginning with "That aspect...
clarifies that mental factors, like the primary mind (*rāja*), likewise possess two parts. The section beginning with "Resembling the object... provides a reconciliation of the terminology.

[The] meaning [is as follows]: If mind and mental factors lacked the characteristic of an object (ālambana), they would not engage their respective objects, just as one thing does not engage another, or as one thing engages itself.

If the mind were [objectless], two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established below to provide counter-evidence for the existence of an object; together with the two means of valid cognition below, this clarifies the position of Sthiramati.

This merely establishes that the doctrine of "one mind" (cittamātra) is not exhaustive. The first formal argument (*prayoga*) states: **Thesis:** The mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) as the subject of the proposition (*dharmin*) cannot take their own objects of cognition (*ālambana*).
**Reason:** Because they lack an object of cognition. **Example:** Like their own [respective] objects, as in the case of others. Regarding "their own objects of cognition":

for instance, visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) takes visible form (*rūpa*) as its own object of cognition. Regarding "like their own objects, as in the case of others": this means the object of visible form is like the object of sound.

Fragrance and so forth are not the respective objects of visual consciousness. Next, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) must each be able to take all things as their objects.
This is because they possess the capacity to cognize even in the absence of a specific object. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like other cases, such as oneself;
for instance, just as a single visual consciousness lacks its own specific object—color—and yet possesses the capacity to cognize, so too should it be with all [minds and mental factors].
Sounds, odors, and so forth all serve as objects of perception just as one's own form does.
If mind and mental factors lacked the characteristic of being able to perceive, then even space and the like would be capable of perceiving.
If [it is argued that] the mind is inactive, one next establishes two formal arguments (*pramāṇa*) to prove by counter-evidence that there exists a capable cognizer (*ālambaka*).

The first argument states: "Mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are the subject (*dharmin*). They must be incapable of cognizing; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). Because they lack the characteristic of being a cognizer; this is the reason (*hetu*). Like space (*ākāśa*); this is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The second argument states: "Space is the subject. It is also a capable cognizer; this is the thesis. Because it lacks the capacity to cognize yet does cognize; this is the reason."

It is analogous to the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*). This statement that the mind lacks a "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) implies that since it is nonetheless able to take an object as its condition, one must prove that emptiness (*śūnyatā*), being without a seeing-part, should likewise be able to take an object as its condition—is this logically tenable?
By contrast, it is revealed that the mind is able to take an object as its condition precisely because it possesses a seeing-part.
Therefore, mind and mental factors must necessarily possess two aspects (up to): the divisions of the cognizer and the cognized each arise spontaneously. Thus, [the text] concludes with "mind below.
Based on the four aforementioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is conversely established that there exist the capable [cognizer] and the object of cognition (*ālambana*).

Using this as proof, it is therefore established that mind and mental factors must necessarily have two parts. As for the citation of the *Sūtra* below: the first phrase clarifies that there is only internal mind.

The second phrase clarifies that there are no external objects whatsoever. The final two phrases clarify that there are two parts. "Spontaneous transformation" means that the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) each arise from their own respective seeds.

Those who maintain that there exists an objective referent distinct from consciousness (until: "because this is the intrinsic nature of mind and mental factors")—the section beginning with "maintain that there exists" below—presents the three-part system.
First, it distinguishes between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; first, it clarifies the characteristics of the three parts according to the Hīnayāna.

Regarding "an object distinct from consciousness": the Hīnayāna maintains that phenomena exist externally to the mind and designate these as the objective referent (*ālambana*), because they are what is transformed.
