The image-part (nimittabhāga) serves as the aspect (ākāra) for the perceiving seeing-part (darśanabhāga), while the seeing-part serves as the entity that constitutes the self-witnessing (svasaṃvitti).
Mind and mental factors share the same basis and object; however, from the consciousness through feeling, perception, and so forth, their respective aspects are distinct.
The mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are determined below as being identical in three respects: their basis, their object, and their aspect. Regarding the identity of their basis:
just as the king-like eye-consciousness and its mental factors share the same basis in the eye-faculty. Regarding the identity of their object:

they both take the external, fundamental material form (*rūpa*) as their object, employing the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) as their mode of activity (*ākāra*), because each transforms its own image. Therefore, their aspects are identical.
"Similarity. Regarding the phrase "although the objects are numerous and so forth": "object" refers to the objective entity (*vastu*), while "number" refers to the mental factors (*caitta*).

Just as the sovereign [the primary consciousness] relies on the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), the mental factors likewise rely on the seeing-part; these two are equal and without difference. Nevertheless, their characteristics are distinct, because their functions—such as discerning (*vijñapti*) and experiencing (*anubhava*)—are each individually different.

"Realizing that there are no objects of perception apart from consciousness" (up to "...because one cannot remember an object never previously experienced")—the phrase "realizing that there are no" clarifies the three aspects of the Mahāyāna.
Because the Mahāyāna realizes *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), there are no objects apart from consciousness.

The image-part (*nimittabhāga*) is the object-condition (*ālambana*), and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) is the subjective perceiver. The basis for these two parts is termed the self-cognizing essence (*svasaṃvitti*).
This [passage] explains by way of reductio that there must be self-cognition; it clarifies that Nanda’s theory of the two parts is incomplete.
When the mind and mental factors perceive an object through their seeing-part, this is proven by the self-cognizing part, which subsequently enables memory. If this were not the case...
If self-cognition did not exist, one would not be able to remember at a later time, just as in the previous case. To illustrate this by analogy with the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*):

"furthermore" (*punar*) means "to experience again. Just as the seeing-part experiences an object, because of that prior seeing, one perceives it again at a later time and remembers it vividly, as if it had never been experienced before;
one could certainly not remember it otherwise. The seeing-part is like a measuring ruler, the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is like a cloth, and self-cognition is like the person.
If there were no one to know the number, even when measuring cloth with a ruler, one would certainly be unable to know the number oneself;
likewise, because the mind and its mental factors share the same supporting faculty (āśraya), yet their essential natures differ—such as consciousness, sensation (vedanā), and so forth.

The mind and its mental factors below [the first dhyāna] determine the similarities and differences among the three parts of the Mahāyāna King (the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*). They are similar because they rely upon the same sense organ (*indriya*).

Since the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) serves as the object of cognition (*ālambana*), each arises through its own transformation; thus, they are said to be "similar. Since the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) functions as the mode of activity (*ākāra*), [they are distinct].
Because the functions of the king (the mind) in terms of discernment, reception, and so forth differ, they are said to be distinct.

Although the king relies on self-cognition and the mental factors (caittas) likewise rely on self-cognition—such that they are equal to one another without distinction—their essential natures and characteristics, such as those of consciousness and sensation, are nonetheless different.
This object of cognition (*ālambana*) is not the same as the fundamental substance (*svabhāva*) that was the common object of the previous [consciousness] and the king.
This subjective cognizer (*ālambaka*) is not the same as the aspect of the image (*nimittabhāga*) which served as the mode of apprehension (*ākāra*) for the previous [consciousness].

This basis (*āśraya*) is not the same as the aspect of vision (*darśanabhāga*) which served as the supporting entity for the previous [consciousness]. Although the three parts—great, small, and medium—are identical, their underlying intent is fundamentally different.
However, when each mind and mental factor arises, it simultaneously functions as the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the result (*phala*); these three aspects are not distinct in their essence.

[The text] below, under "mind," continues from above: although the Great and Small Vehicles differ in their tenets, when examined through reasoning, whether it be the subject (*grāhaka*) or the object (*grāhya*), each possesses three parts.

Below, under "the object of cognition," the names and definitions of these three parts are set forth. The result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) refers to the essence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*). As for...

In the second section of the *Cheng weishi lun*, the scriptural citations are introduced. The first phrase establishes the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*); the second phrase simultaneously establishes both the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) and self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*).

The third phrase explains the preceding two phrases together; the final phrase concludes that there are no external objects, because both the objective and subjective aspects arise based upon self-cognition.
Furthermore, if one analyzes the mind and mental factors in detail, up to the point of realizing their own nature (*svasaṃvedana*), they must necessarily be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Below "Furthermore, the mind... [the text] presents the fourfold division; first it establishes these four parts, and then below "If this...

it provides a counter-proof that there is a fourth part, the *manas*, thereby clarifying that Dignāga’s threefold division was incomplete. First, regarding the divisions of the mind, it clarifies the existence of a fourth; next, regarding...
Regarding the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), it is clarified that there is a fourth [factor]; it should not be placed below [the third].

Fearing that the opponent might offer a defense by claiming that the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) itself constitutes the third fruit, the present text refutes this, stating "it should not be," and so forth. Below the term "seeing-portion," the reason why it should not be so is set forth:
because it is not subsumed under valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for that which realizes its own nature must necessarily be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Among these four aspects, the first two are external; thus, the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)—neither identical to nor separate from [the object]—is established.

Regarding the four below, there is a judgment. First, the internal and external are judged: the former two are functions, and are therefore judged to belong to the external; the latter two are the essence, and are therefore judged to belong to the internal.
This distinction of internal and external is made in terms of essence and function (*tattva* and *vṛtti*), and is not like an "internal" that is separate from the mind.

[The first part] is external; [the second] is initially only the lower [level]. This distinguishes between the subjective (ālambaka) and objective (ālambana) aspects. The first indicates that the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) is exclusively the object (*ālambana*); the latter three are both the subject and the object.

That is to say, the subsequent section provides a further explanation while also distinguishing the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The second [part], the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part), takes only the *nimitta-bhāga* as its object.

The seeing-part itself may correspond to all three types of valid cognition. Since the objects—the *nimitta-bhāga*—are already of three kinds, namely: substantial entities (*svabhāva*), purely projected images (*pratibimba*), and those accompanied by real objects (*sābhilāpa*).

Because it is substantial, it can serve as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and it also extends to both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). It is not [limited to] these three types alone.

The third, the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), can take as its objects the second, the seeing part (*darśana-bhāga*), as well as the fourth, the self-cognizing-of-the-self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-svasaṃvitti-bhāga*); thus, the second and fourth parts also become the objects of cognition.
The *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-cognizing aspect) takes only the third [aspect], the *svasaṃvitti*, as its object; thus, the third becomes an object (*ālambana*).

Why, then, does the fourth not take the second, the *darśanabhāga* (seeing aspect), as its object—that is, as the object of its own self-cognition? Therefore, it is said that [the fourth] would be useless.

Since the latter two are both subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they can mutually serve as the result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). Thus, [the author] concludes below that there is no fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
This means that since the third and fourth [moments] are both direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*), they can mutually validate one another, and thus there is no fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If it were otherwise, a fifth moment would be required to validate the fourth, and so on in succession, resulting in an infinite fault.
Because they are internal and external, and subject and object, they are not identical; yet because they are but a single mind, they are not separate.
Therefore, it is said in a verse of the *Sūtra*: [omission] ... because here, "seeing" refers to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*).
Thus, the following passage cites scriptural evidence; the subsequent commentary explains the meaning of that verse.
Thus, these four divisions may be subsumed into three (up to) or subsumed into a single entity because there is no distinction.
As stated below: "To bind the broad according to the concise. Above, from a single consciousness, two, three, and four different divisions were opened;

this was proceeding from the concise to the broad. Therefore, they are now bound together, proceeding from the broad to the concise. Regarding the four divisions, they are categorized according to the gate of the measure of the fruit (*phala*).

The three divisions are made according to the gate of essence and function; the two divisions are made according to the gate of mind and object; and the one mind is established according to the gate of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

This statement that "seeing" (*darśana*) has the meaning of being the subjective perceiver is intended to avoid confusion with the "seeing" mentioned within the aforementioned four divisions; therefore, this specific term is placed here.

Although the gates relied upon above are distinct, there are valid reasons for their respective inclusion or exclusion. Each *siddhānta* (doctrinal tenet) accords with reason as it serves its intended audience.
As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra-gāthā* (down to): "This expression 'one mind' also encompasses mental factors.
[The phrase] "as in the *Laṅkā*" below cites scriptural evidence for Mind-Only (*cittamātra*). [The phrase] "in this way" below points to the detailed exposition.
Therefore, the aspect of cognition (*vijñāna*) is precisely discernment (*vijñapti*), and discernment is precisely the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of cognition.
Thus, the text below [the verse] concludes by returning [to this point]. This refers to the "seeing-portion," which corresponds to the character "discern" (*liǎo*, *vijñapti*) in the verse.
That which is called "the bases" (*āyatana*) refers to the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) [up to] the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).

The word "below" (*adhas*) explains the gate of the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*). That is, the word "bases" in the verse is first cited and established; "referring to the maturation-consciousness" and so forth explain it.
The *vipāka* (maturation) is the transforming mind itself. The "common-characteristic seeds" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇabīja*) refer to the seeds of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).

While the transformations produced by each individual person are distinct—this being what is termed "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*)—sentient beings, through the mutual influence of their collective karma, experience the same locations without difference. Nevertheless, there is the sense of a shared common enjoyment;
because these [transformations] are identical to those of others, they perfume their own seeds, which are thus called "common-characteristic seeds. This occurs by virtue of the causal seed.
By the power of the maturation of conditions, [consciousness] transforms and appears as if it were form and so forth—“and so forth” referring to the other four sense objects.

The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are earth, water, fire, and wind; the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) consists of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility. Regarding the phrase “external,” this refers to what is external to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), as determined above.
"Although the transformations of sentient beings are each distinct... (down to) "...like the light of many lamps, which, though each is pervasive, appears as one.

The section beginning with "Although... explains away a potential doubt. The doubt is as follows: "If the transformations of sentient beings are indeed distinct, how is it that they are perceived as one?
Now, the text cites and explains this by stating: "Because their characteristics are similar; because their locations are not different. The section beginning with "Like many... provides an analogy.

To illustrate: it is like the light of many lamps; their substance is distinct, yet the light is one. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) transformed by all sentient beings is the subject (*dharmin*).
It is the thesis (*pakṣa*) that it appears as one. The reason (*hetu*) is: because its characteristics are similar and its location is not different.
It is like the light of many lamps.
"Who transforms the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) into this appearance?
"Who transforms it below? These questions clarify that the transformed appearances differ because the transforming seeds are distinct.

Due to these differing seeds, there are those that are common within the common, those that are uncommon within the common, those that are uncommon within the uncommon, and those that are common within the uncommon; therefore, the word "who" is used.
Regarding the inquiry as to who or what kind of being brings about this transformation:
one interpretation holds that it is brought about by all [beings]. Why is this so? Because it arises through the collective dominant influence (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of their karma.
There is one interpretation regarding the transformation of the seeds shared among the common [receptacle world]. There are three masters; here is the first.
He states that all sentient beings undergo this transformation, citing a sūtra as proof: "Because they are mutually induced by common karma."
There is an interpretation which says: "If that were so, what further use would there be for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to transform [other lands] into this land?

Next, the second school first refutes the previous position. From the words "If that were so" onwards, they cite the previous argument to refute it: "The transformed lands consist of four types of lands with differing degrees of purity and defilement;
likewise, the transformers also differ as noble ones or ordinary beings. Now, this term 'all' [in the previous argument] has no..."
If one were to fail to distinguish between them, there would be the error of confusing ordinary beings with noble ones (*ārya*).

It is appropriate for the Buddhas to truly transform impurity in order to subdue the stubborn and fierce through their provisional manifestations; it is also appropriate for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to temporarily behold a pure land as they are gathered by their karmic affinity.
However, the phrase "truly" (*yǐng shí*) is a term of censure. Furthermore, regarding the *anāgāmin* noble ones who feel weary of and seek liberation from the realm of form:
Having eliminated obstructions and entered emptiness, one will certainly not descend to be born [again]. What use would there be for transforming this?
Therefore, those who currently dwell [in that state] and those who are to be born there transform it together, as their karmic actions are identical.

"Therefore, below" [refers to] the correct explanation of what is transformed by one currently dwelling [in a realm] and by one about to be born [there]. Because of "currently dwelling," although the Buddha dwells in purity, he is born in an impure realm;

thus, there is no fault of a Buddha who has attained non-arising (anutpāda) undergoing mixed transformations. Because of "about to be born," there is no fault of one from the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) transforming into a lower land.
"The Sūtra, based on 'below,'" connects with the meaning of the preceding sūtra. "All" has two [meanings]: the partial and the whole. One [meaning is] the partial.
"Everything; everything and everything. This refers to "everything" in the sense of a partial totality based on common karma.
One interpretation holds: if that were so, when the receptacle world is about to be destroyed, what benefit would there be even if it were transformed into that [other state]?

The third school first refutes the preceding view. With the words "If that were so," it restates the previous position before refuting it: "The receptacle world undergoes formation, subsistence, destruction, and emptiness for twenty kalpas each;
however, that receptacle is not permanent, because it arises and perishes simultaneously with sentient beings. It requires seven fires and one water [to complete the cycle]."

Regarding the sequence of destruction by water, fire, and finally wind: since there are currently no beings dwelling there or destined to be born there at the time of destruction, who would perceive the transformation of this world-system as it is about to be destroyed?

Furthermore, [the text] below refutes the existence of those "destined to be born" (upapadya-parinirvāyin) by raising an objection: an Anāgāmin who has transcended [the lower realms] certainly does not descend to be born there;

yet when an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) passes away after falling [from a higher realm], how could there not be transformation? [The lifespan] of humans is fifty years; for the first heaven [of the Desire Realm], it is...

Day and night. Receiving this lifespan, it lasts five hundred years; above that, it increases fivefold at each successive stage. As for the gods of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), their lifespans extend through incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

Regarding the lower realms, what is the use of undergoing the various calamities? Even if one were to descend there, it would be difficult; furthermore, while those in the formless realm have no bodies, do those in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) who possess bodies not undergo transformation?
[The answer is: Generally speaking, the bodies in the higher form realm are subtle, whereas the lands of the lower realms are coarse; thus, the upper and lower realms are vastly different.
Since they do not support one another across a gap, what benefit would there be in transforming them?
However, the land that is transformed is fundamentally for the sake of the form-body (*rūpakāya*); thus, although there are no sentient beings [there], it nevertheless appears as if they exist.

However, regarding the formal explanation of "other realms and one's own stage": for example, the Realm of Mixed Dwellings in other directions is called "one's own stage" in relation to this Realm of Mixed Dwellings, because their karmic divisions and characteristics are identical; that consciousness likewise transforms this stage, and the same applies by analogy to other stages.
This explains that which is commonly experienced by all (up to) the fact that what is seen differs for ghosts, humans, gods, and so forth.

This section below explains the transformation of seeds within the common [realm] that are not-common. The first sentence concludes the preceding; "if distinct," etc., provides an illustrative explanation.

As the verse says: "For ghosts, animals, humans, and gods, each according to what is appropriate for them, because their minds differ regarding the same object, it is held that the object is not real.
"Each according to what is appropriate" means according to the power of one's own karma. "The same object" means that which is common [to all].

"Distinct minds" means they are not shared. This clarifies that each [mind] arises according to its own karma, because it is produced from the transformation of both shared and unshared seeds within the *vipākavijñāna*.
"All seeds" refers to the *vipākavijñāna* (up to) the nature of *tathatā*, which does not contradict *vijñaptimātra*.

"Among the various types below," [the text] explains the transformation of the unique seeds within the uncommon [consciousness]. The *vipākavijñāna* (maturation consciousness) is that which holds; the contaminated (*sāsrava*) seeds are that which are held.

Because they share the same neutral (*avyākṛta*) nature, they are the objects of cognition (*ālambana*). Uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) seeds, however, are exclusively wholesome in nature and are not subsumed under the neutral;
therefore, they are not objects of cognition. "Although not... [the text] addresses a potential objection. The objection states: "If it is not an object of cognition, then with..."

If the mental state (*citta*) is dissociated [from its seeds], does this not contradict the doctrine of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only)? To explain by means of a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*), it is said: The uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are the subject (*dharmin*). They do not contradict the tenet of consciousness-only.
This is because they are not objects of cognition (*ālambana*) yet are not dissociated from it; this is the reason (*hetu*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like true suchness (*tathatā*).
"Having faculties" refers to the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*)—up to [the point where it is said] "that is the internal primary elements and the derived matter.
Regarding "having faculties," the following explains the transformation of seeds that are both non-common and common. First, it is explained generally:

"That which resembles the material faculties" refers to the five faculties, such as the eye, which are the pure four great elements. "The bases of the faculties" refers to things such as the grape-like cluster or the newly curled leaf.

...and so forth. These are subsumed under the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). These two are formed by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as their creators and the four subtle particles (*paramāṇu*) as their derivatives.
The faculty is a transformation of the uncommon-uncommon seed; the body is a transformation of the uncommon-common seed.
Because there is the power of the maturation of common seeds, [it is so]; otherwise, there would be no experience of the objects of others.
Regarding "there are common [seeds]," this correctly explains the "common within the uncommon": the bodies and locations of other persons are transformations produced by my own common seeds.
"Not so," [the text] below explains by way of refutation. Regarding "experiencing others":

because all sentient beings are mutually conditioned by one another, there is a doctrinal interpretation (*yogācāra*) here that it also transforms into something resembling the sense organs (*indriya*). [This continues] until those other remains are still seen as a continuity.

Regarding the phrase "In this context, below": this refers generally to alternative interpretations. The first sentence clarifies the transformation of the faculties (*indriya*). Regarding the phrase "Discriminating the middle and below": this cites scriptural evidence;

for within what appears as one's own or another's body, the five faculties also manifest as transformed. Regarding the phrase "There is an interpretation, below": this reveals the correct meaning. The first sentence directly clarifies that only the body is transformed;
the second sentence clarifies that the faculties are not transformed. Regarding the phrase "Appearing as one's own, below": this reconciles the cited treatise, stating that within the treatise...

The phrasing is general, but the meaning is specific. It states that one's own consciousness transforms one's own sense-faculties and body, while the consciousnesses of others transform the sense-faculties and bodies of others;
thus, it is explained below. The citation of the actual phenomenon of a corpse’s continuity precisely demonstrates that it is what is transformed by the consciousnesses of various sentient beings.
If one were able to transform the sense-faculties of another person, then even after death, that person should still possess the capacity for seeing and hearing.
To begin with, let us discuss how that which is transformed by the power of karma (*karmabala*) arises through the impact of the power of present conditions.

Regarding the phrase "to begin with" (*qianlai*): this determines whether the aforementioned transformations are fixed or unfixed. The first sentence cites the preceding point that transformation caused by the causal condition of karma is fixed.

As for the phrase "if it is fixed" (*ruoding*) and so forth: the first two phrases indicate what is unfixed; the term "etc. (*deng*) includes the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñābala*), which also undergoes transformation.

Below, the indeterminate characteristics are clarified. As for those whose physical bodies and environments are mostly constant and continuous: because they benefit sentient beings throughout a single lifetime—sometimes through subduing and sometimes through gathering them—they manifest both impurity and purity, and thus are mostly continuous.
Only a small portion, or for a temporary duration, is otherwise. As for sounds and lights that are mostly temporary:

because they are bound by conditions for a time, such as the sounds and lights of forests and ponds, when the karmic trigger is forgotten, the response ceases; therefore, they are mostly temporary, with only a small portion being otherwise.
Or it may persist for a long time.
To briefly explain the objects transformed by this consciousness: [it includes] those that fall within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) as manifest forms (*rūpa*).

"Briefly explained below" summarizes the ten spheres of form (*daśa rūpāyatanāni*), namely the five sense organs and the five sensory objects; that is, the body composed of faculties and the external environment.
Together with seeds, these constitute the three types of objects. That which "falls into the sphere of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana*) refers to the residual shadows of the five sensory objects;

that is, the matter subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-saṃgṛhīta-rūpa*). Regarding the "matter manifested as reality," there are five kinds of matter within the sphere of phenomena:

namely, the extremely remote (*atyanta-dūra*), the extremely subtle (*atyanta-sūkṣma*), that which is conceptually imputed (*parikalpita*), that which is produced by what is derived from feeling (*vedanā-anvaya-ja*), and the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*). The first four are conventional (*prajñapti-sat*); the fruit of meditative concentration is...

The substantial [matter] is the matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), which is transformed by the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). The other four types of matter are provisional (*prajñapti-rūpa*), produced through the false discrimination of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Why is it that this [mental] consciousness cannot transform [matter] into something resembling [the sensory organs], such that at the beginning they necessarily have function, while later they serve merely as objects?
Why [is it said that] "below"? This generally clarifies that there are two kinds of transformation (*pariṇāma*) regarding all consciousnesses. First, a hypothetical question is posed:

since the preceding passage stated that the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth are transformations of maturation (*vipākavipariṇāma*), this now hypothetically takes the objects of non-transformed mental states as the starting point for inquiry, seeking to determine which of the two types of transformation these are.
Why are mental states not transformed? [The answer follows: "Because they are with outflows (*sāsrava*)," and so forth.

Answer: Generally, it is explained that all consciousnesses have two kinds of transformation (*pariṇāma*), which serves to show that the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is exclusively a transformation through causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Briefly, two types are indicated. Regarding the "transformation through causes and conditions" mentioned generally: this refers to the fifth [consciousness], the eighth, and a portion of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). These all arise from the influence of immediate and remote causes and conditions;

they are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because they spontaneously take objective realms (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) as their objects. Regarding the "transformation through discrimination" mentioned generally...
This refers to the seventh consciousness and a portion of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), both of which arise through constructive discernment (*vikalpa*).

They are not exclusively inferential cognition (*anumāna*), as they take as their objects both "objects with substance" (*sadravya*) and "mere images" (*pratibimba*). Because the former possesses actual substantiality and function, while the latter serves merely as an objective support (*ālambana*), the verse says:

The objective realm (svabhāva-viṣaya) does not follow the mind; the solitary reflection (pratibimba-mātra) arises solely from the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga). That which carries a substantial essence (sadravya-svabhāva) pertains to both the mental object and its basis; it corresponds accordingly to the nature-born seeds (prakṛti-stha-bīja) and so forth.

These are causal conditions (hetu-pratyaya), not conceptual constructions (vikalpa); this refers to the five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness. That which is not a causal condition is conceptual construction; this refers to the seventh consciousness.

It is both conditioned by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and conceptualized (*vikalpa*), namely, the sixth consciousness. It is neither conditioned by causes and conditions nor conceptualized, namely, the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The transformation of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) occurs solely in accordance with causes and conditions; were it otherwise, the Buddhas would not be omniscient.
Regarding "vipāka changes only [the material]," this separately clarifies that vipāka transforms solely through causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The first two phrases provide the answer: vipāka transforms only the material form (*rūpa*) because it possesses actual utility; therefore, it transforms only matter. Regarding "if it were to transform [the mind]," the answer is: because it lacks actual utility, it does not transform the mind.

The single phrase "the objective aspect" (*nimitta-bhāga*) provides the reason for its lack of utility: that which cannot serve as an object of cognition is like a magically conjured person (*nirmita-puruṣa*).
It is the mind (*citta*). The phrase "must be from that [mind]" below serves as a counter-illustration by citing what possesses a functional capacity.

If that mind and so forth possessed a real capacity for objective cognition (*ālambana*), they would necessarily arise from seeds distinct from this consciousness, rather than being transformations of consciousness. Since they are now shown to be transformations of consciousness, they lack real utility.
The subsequent phrase "unconditioned phenomena" (*asaṃskṛta*) follows the same principle: unconditioned phenomena appear within the meditative mind, yet they are not caused by it.

Because it undergoes transformation, it likewise lacks functional utility; thus, the subsequent phrase provides the concluding answer. Because it does not undergo transformation, it does not take [objects] as conditions.
From the section on "untainted" (*anāsrava*) downward, it clarifies that the untainted mind differs from the tainted (*sāsrava*): it both undergoes transformation and takes [objects] as conditions.
Therefore, in the state of being with outflows (*sāsrava*), this ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*)—[omitted]—that consciousness also takes this form as its object.

Thus, [the text says] "therefore there are below," summarizing the three types of objects. [The text says] "in the desire realm, below," judging that the objects of the various realms and stages differ, as in the text.
Regarding the *ālaya-vijñāna*, it should be said that within the desire realm, it takes a narrow and small appropriated object (*upātta-viṣaya*) as its object; in the form [realm],...

Within the realm [of form], it takes as its object a vast apprehended sphere. In the Formless Realm, in the Sphere of Infinite Space and the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, it takes as its object an immeasurable apprehended sphere. In the Sphere of Nothingness, it takes as its object a subtle apprehended sphere.
In the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, it takes as its object an extremely subtle apprehended sphere.
"Unknowable" (*ajñeya*) means that this mode of activity (*ākāra*)—extending up to its measure—is difficult to fathom; therefore, it is called "unknowable.
The section below clarifies the gate of the difficulty of knowing. First, it clarifies that the mode of activity of the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*) is unknowable;
next, it clarifies that the objective sphere (*ālambana*) is unknowable.
How is it that this consciousness perceives its object? (Up to: It should be understood that the same applies to states such as the attainment of non-conception.
Why? [The text] below re-examines the difficulty of knowing its mode of activity (*ākāra*). As for "like cessation," [the text] answers:

it means that the mode of activity of this consciousness is subtle and difficult to know, just like the consciousness within the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because it does not depart from the body and is extremely subtle. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows:
The mental aspect that takes an object as its condition is an existent phenomenon; one should believe it exists as a thesis, because it is subtle yet not separated from the body.

This is like consciousness within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). By means of this example—consciousness within the absorption of cessation—it is established that the subtle mental aspect exists.

Furthermore, how is it known that there is consciousness within the absorption of cessation? To prove this, another formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established: consciousness within the absorption of cessation...

This is an existent phenomenon (*dharma*). It should be accepted as the thesis that [it] exists. The reason (*hetu*) is "because it is comprised within sentient beings" (*sattva-saṃgṛhītatvāt*). The example (*udāharaṇa*) is: "just like a sentient being when possessing consciousness.

As for the cases of the non-conceptual attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth, they are analogous to the non-conceptual state; likewise, even in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), there is still consciousness.
Self-Examination of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Scroll Two;
Self-Examination of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Scroll Three.
Recorded by the disciple Da-hui of the Lianju [Hermitage] in Lin’an, Ming Dynasty.
With how many mental factors (*caitta*) is this consciousness associated? (Up to: Because it is subsumed under the universal (*sarvatraga*) mental factors.
Below this, the section explaining the associated mental factors begins. The first sentence poses the question; the second sentence provides the answer by citing the verse.
From "The ālaya... onwards, the meaning of constant association is explained: from the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) until the ālaya is no longer empty, [these factors] are all...

The names have not yet been transformed. The various states of the mundane and supramundane, the holy and the ordinary, including the stages of arising and sinking, concentration and distraction, transmigration and cessation, are called "all states.
Within these states, [these factors] are always associated with these five [mental factors].
This association is subsumed under the category of "universal" (sarvatraga) because it constantly functions in accompaniment at all times and across all minds. All...
Because consciousness is a composite, it pervades all natures and all stages, and it applies to both ordinary beings and sages.

Contact (sparśa) refers to the differentiation and transformation resulting from the conjunction of the three; its function is to serve as the basis for feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), and so forth.

"Contact" (*sparśa*) refers to what follows. This is a detailed explanation of the five objects. First, the essence, nature, and function of contact are indicated: "contact" (*sparśa*) means the act of contacting; "nature" (*svabhāva*) means its essential character;
"function" (*karman*) means its operational activity. All subsequent items are to be understood according to this pattern.

This refers to the state where the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) mutually accord with one another; hence it is called the stage of their "threefold conjunction" (*trikasamnipāta*).
First, regarding the faculties and so forth, the three—faculty, object, and consciousness—are termed "three" because their entities are distinct, yet they do not contradict one another.

Because they further accord with one another, it is called the "conjunction of the three. Contact arises depending on those three types [of phenomena], and it can also cause those three types to be conjoined;
therefore, contact is said to be the state of their conjunction. As for "state" (*avasthā*), it refers to the position established for their arising.

Just as positions are established in dependence upon persons, and persons in turn carry out administrative commands in dependence upon positions, so too, by relying on the three births, one brings about the harmony of the three; therefore, it is called a "position."

All possess the functional capacity to produce [subsequent] mental factors; thus they are called "transformative contact" (*vikāra-sparśa*). They are termed "discriminative" (*viniścaya*) because they arise resembling that [object].

Regarding the phrase "all possess," this explains "discriminative" and "transformative. "Transformative" means "producing"; that is, although things perish moment by moment, it is only when there is a superior power that they possess the function of producing [an effect].
This refers to the triad of the faculties and so forth, all of which possess the capacity to produce everything.

The functional capacity of the mental factors (*caitta*) is called "transformation" (*vikāra*). "Discrimination" (*viniścaya*) means resemblance, just as a son who resembles his father is said to "discriminate" his father.

That is to say, contact (*sparśa*) also possesses a functional capacity of the mental factors that arises resembling those [factors] such as the sense faculties; therefore, it is called "discrimination-transformation."
When the force of the transformation of the faculties induces contact (*sparśa*), [the treatise] speaks only of the discrimination of the transformation of the faculties.

Below, regarding the transformation of the faculties, it addresses an objection. Question: Since contact discriminates the transformations of all three [faculties, objects, and consciousness], why does the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* speak only of that which resembles the faculty (*indriya-sadṛśa*), and not mention the object (*viṣaya*) or consciousness (*vijñāna*)?
Explanation: The reason it mentions only the faculty is because it is spoken from the perspective of the predominant factor (*paramārtha*). First.
1. By way of being the primary [cause], because it possesses a superior capacity. 2. By way of proximity, because it can immediately give rise to the mind. 3.

By way of pervasiveness, because it not only gives rise to mental factors (*caitta*) but also to the mind itself. 4. By way of continuity, because it is constant and uninterrupted. The object and consciousness are not like this;
although the object can give rise to both the mind and its mental factors, it is not the primary cause, nor is it proximate, and thus it lacks these two [characteristics].
In meaning, it is not called "superior. Although the mind is the sovereign, because it arises immediately from the mental factors (caitta), it cannot produce the mind;

therefore, it is not pervasive. Because it lacks one of the two meanings [of being both pervasive and sovereign], it is not superior. Since neither the object nor consciousness is continuous, only the faculty is uniquely superior.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* speaks only of the transformation of the discerning faculty.
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of contact (*sparśa*) is that which brings together all minds (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), causing them to equally encounter their objects.

"Bringing together" (*saṃnipāta*) below explains its essential nature (*tattva*). Regarding the phrase "bringing together all minds and mental factors," the expression is general while the intended meaning is specific. [This is] the distinction.

This refers to the contact associated with visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna-saṃprayukta-sparśa*). Just as visual consciousness and its associated mental factors (*citta-caitta*) together contact the objective sphere of form, one should understand that the same applies to the contacts associated with all other consciousnesses. This constitutes the essence of contact (*sparśa*).
Since it resembles the functional capacity that accords with the arising of mental factors (*caitta*), its activity (*karma*) consists in serving as the basis for sensation (*vedanā*) and the others.

The phrase "since it resembles [the preceding]" explains this activity: because it possesses a resemblance to the threefold conjunction (*trikasamnipāta*) and the functional capacity that accords with the production of mental factors, it acts as the support (*āśraya*) for sensation and the rest; this is its function.
The *Udayavyaya Sūtra* states that the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*) arise from the conjunction of two, three, or four [factors].
In the section following "Arising and Ceasing," it cites evidence for the arising of mental factors (*caitta*) through contact (*sparśa*). Regarding the aggregate of formations:

among the fifty-one mental factors, with the exception of feeling and perception, the remaining forty-nine are all subsumed within the aggregate of formations. Therefore, it is said that "all [mental factors] have contact as their basis."

This is the condition for arising. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The conjunction of two produces consciousness; the conjunction of three produces contact; and the conjunction of four produces feeling and so forth.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks only of [feeling] because it is extremely proximate to sensation, perception, and volition, and because it is preeminent in its capacity to induce [subsequent states].

*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, lower section. Generalizing the *Yogācāra*. Question: In this context, the text speaks of "volition" (*cetanā*), yet the treatise says it applies to all mental factors (*caitta*).

Why is this? The explanation of the meaning is as stated in the text. *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, lower section. Generalizing the *Samuccaya*. The *Samuccaya* states only that [contact] is the basis for feeling (*vedanā*).
Why is this? Answer: Because contact gives rise to feeling; it is the most proximate and most predominant factor. This refers to the explanation following the passage on contact.

"Near to the ultimate reality" (*paramārtha-samnikṛṣṭa*). "Pleasant," etc., refers to [the categories of] unpleasant, neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant, beneficial, etc., referring to [the categories of] harmful, neither-beneficial-nor-harmful.
Since whatever is pleasant for ordinary beings is necessarily beneficial, it is said to be "extremely proximate.
The other two [categories] are to be understood accordingly. It is called "inducing" because it gives rise to feeling more powerfully than others.

However, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of contact (*sparśa*) is real and not provisional. [This continues] up to the point where it is stated that its nature is not identical to the threefold conjunction, just as with feeling (*vedanā*) and the others.
Now, below the section on contact, the provisional and the real are distinguished. The question asks: "Since contact arises from the conjunction of the three, it ought to be provisionally existent.

Yet, now a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is established to prove that it is real: 'The intrinsic nature of contact' is the subject (*dharmin*); 'it is real and not provisional' is the thesis (*pakṣa*). [This concludes the section on] mental factors (*caitta*).

Because it is their nature; because it is comprised within nutriment; and because it can act as a condition, it is the cause—just like feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.

Regarding the "six sixes," this refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling, perception, volition, and craving (*tṛṣṇā*). For example, from the contact of visual consciousness arises feeling, and so on, up to the feeling arising from the contact of mental consciousness;
thus, each of these categories possesses six members. This is because perception and the others are mental factors (*caitta*), and volition is...

It is subsumed within the four nutriments (*āhāra*). Feeling (*vedanā*) is the condition (*pratyaya*) among the twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*). These three are subsumed within the six sets of six phenomena (*ṣaṭ-ṣaṭka-dharma*);

each has its own distinct substantial entity (*svabhāva*). They are not nominal but real. This establishes that if contact (*sparśa*) is subsumed within the six sets of six phenomena, it is a real entity and not nominal;
it possesses its own distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and is not merely the conjunction of the three.
Mental attention (*manasikāra*) has the nature of being able to alert the mind. (Omitted) Because the mind is the sovereign, it is said only that it "draws forth" the mind.

Regarding "mental attention" below: first, the essence and function are indicated. All states of mind are collectively termed "mind" (*citta*); this [attention] is capable of producing movement, and is therefore called "mental attention.
Regarding "this" below: the explanation follows. First, it is the seeds of the mind that ought to arise but have not yet arisen; this [attention] is able to alert them and cause them to...
First, it arises; second, once arisen, it manifests as activity. Because it can lead [the mind] toward its object, it is called *manasikāra* (attention).
Although this [is so], the following [passage] explains away potential objections as in the text.

Some say that [if it were] causing the mind to turn toward a different object, it would not be a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*), as it would not differ from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Others say "below" [in the text], which is a refutation of this divergent interpretation. First, the statement "turning toward a different object" means that while the mind is currently focused on this particular object, it is further drawn toward another.
"Holding the mind so that it abides" means focusing intently without wavering. The phrase "both of them below" is a refutation; it refutes the former view.

Turning toward other objects, it would not be a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*). Excitement (*auddhatya*) causes the mind to be easily released, while distraction (*vikṣepa*) causes the mind to easily shift its object;
since these two are subsumed within the great derivative afflictions (*mahāpariṣkanda*), they exclude that which follows by holding the mind to abide without departing from meditative concentration.
This is because it is concentration (*samādhi*) among the object-specific mental states (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*).
"Feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to the experiencing of what is favorable, unfavorable, or neutral; its function is to give rise to desire for union, separation, or neither.

Regarding the phrase "feeling," first the essence and function are indicated: its essence is the experiencing of the three types of objects, and its function is to give rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Question:

Regarding "favorable objects are loved and unfavorable ones are hated," how is it that they can all give rise to craving? The subsequent line provides the explanation: when a favorable object has not yet arrived, one seeks its attainment;
once it has arrived, one hopes not to be separated from it. When an unfavorable object has not yet arrived, one hopes for its non-attainment;
once it has arrived, one wishes to be rid of it. Therefore, craving can arise toward all three types of objects.
Some say that feeling (*vedanā*) is of two kinds... [up to] ...because it shares its characteristics with objective feeling (*viṣaya-vedanā*).

Some provide the following refutation of alternative interpretations. First, they state: "That which experiences the object-condition" means experiencing the three types of objects, such as the favorable (*anukūla*), etc., as the object-condition (*ālambana*).
"That which experiences the concomitant contact" means that since contact gives rise to feeling, this feeling does not take the external [object] as its intake.

Regarding the object: it only receives the simultaneously arising contact (*sparśa*), taking that very contact as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); thus it is called "intrinsic-feeling" (*svabhāva-vedanā*).

Only contact is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of feeling's objective referent, because it does not share the same object as the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). Among these, feeling here refers only to the second type, intrinsic-feeling.
Why is the first type, objective-feeling (*viṣaya-vedanā*), not included? Because objective-feeling is common to both the mind-king and its mental factors (*caitta*).

Because of this condition, their statement is irrational. [The text says: "If it does not take [the object] as its condition, it should be called 'causal feeling' (hetu-vedanā); what then would be called 'intrinsic nature' (svabhāva)?

This is the refutation. The first phrase is a direct refutation. The section beginning with "If it resembles... is a refutation based on the meaning. The first phrase restates the opponent's position. Next...

[This is] refuted. Contact (*sparśa*) is the cause of feeling (*vedanā*), and feeling is the fruit of contact. If the fruit of feeling arises from the cause of contact, then the fruit must experience the cause;

all fruits that resemble their causes should likewise experience their causes and thus possess the nature of feeling (*vedanātva*). Since that is not the case for the former, how could it be so for the latter?
Furthermore, since contact is the cause of feeling and feeling experiences the cause, it should be called "feeling belonging to the cause. Contact, however, is not [so].
Regarding the intrinsic nature of sensation (*vedanā-svabhāva*): what is meant by its "intrinsic nature"?
If it is claimed that [sensation] is like a king consuming various kingdoms and cities, [this is untenable], because it contradicts one's own tenets and is not self-attested.

"If it is argued that... [and so on]. This cites the alternative position. The kingdom and city are metaphors for contact (*sparśa*); the king is a metaphor for feeling (*vedanā*); and the food is a metaphor for experiencing.
Just as a king is born from a kingdom and city, yet returns to consume the taxes of the kingdom and city—thereby consuming his own property—so too, feeling arises from contact;

when one experiences the feeling produced by contact, one is experiencing its own essence. This is called "feeling as self-nature" (*svabhāva-vedanā*). "The reasoning is also... [and so on]. This refutes it, because of that previous tenet.

Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of contact (*sparśa*) that arises simultaneously with experience, it does not perceive itself—just as a sword cannot cut itself or the eye cannot see itself.
If [feeling] were not to abandon its own nature, it would be called "feeling by way of its own nature" (*svabhāva-vedanā*). Therefore, what they have said is merely a deception for infants.

If [the opponent] does not concede, the argument is shifted by means of a counter-argument: namely, that which experiences without relinquishing its own nature is called "intrinsic experience" (*svabhāva-vedanā*).

This is refuted by the second statement: "All phenomena"—meaning that earth does not relinquish its own nature of solidity, water does not relinquish its own nature of moisture, and so forth—are they all likewise to be called "intrinsic experience"?
Therefore, the following section concludes with a reprimand.
However, the experience of objects (*viṣayavedanā*) does not share the same characteristics as others (up to: it is called the experience of objects because it is not shared with others).
Below the section on "objects," the commonality of the experience of objects with other [experiences] is refuted. The first sentence refutes it directly; the subsequent part explains:

this experience is called the experience of objects only when it exclusively undergoes (*anubhavati*) objects that are favorable, unfavorable, or neutral, and which are definitely one's own—just as a king [relates] to his domain.
The faculty of discernment (*vijñāna*) is capable of cognizing objects, yet it does not experience them. Contact (*sparśa*) merely brings about a confrontation; it too does not experience.

Perception (*saṃjñā*) merely grasps the mental image of an object. Attention (*manasikāra*) merely alerts the mind. Volition (*cetanā*) merely performs formative activities, and so forth. Regarding the characteristics of an object, none of these possess the quality of experiencing signs such as those that are disagreeable or agreeable.
It is this feeling (*vedanā*) alone that experiences them, for it is its unique function, unlike the others.
“Perception” (saṃjñā) has the nature of grasping the image of an object. [This continues until: “only then can one give rise to various names and expressions.

Regarding the phrase “perception,” first its essence and function are indicated; next, its scope and characteristics are explained. “Scope and characteristics” refers to shapes such as square, round, high, or low;
based on these forms and appearances, one gives rise to various names and expressions, such as “this is a vase” or “this is a garment.”
Volition (*cetanā*) has the nature of causing the mind to engage in activity (up to: driving and employing one’s own mind to perform what is wholesome and so forth).
Regarding "volition" below: first, the essence and function are indicated; next, they are explained. "Correct causes," etc., includes "false causes" and "neither false nor correct causes.
"Wholesome," etc., includes "unwholesome" and "neither wholesome nor unwholesome."

Since these five are subsumed under the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), they are termed "associated" (*samprayukta*) because they share the same object of cognition (*ālambana*) and other such characteristics.
Regarding the phrase "these five," it clarifies that which is associated with the King [the mind]. As for "subsumed under the universal mental factors," this means they pervade all minds;

because they are invariably obtainable within every state of mind, they are associated with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). The detailed explanation of the characteristics of the universal mental factors will follow later.

The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are contained within the three transformations. Regarding those whose modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ: it is asked, consciousness has discernment as its mode of activity;
contact has the act of touching as its mode of activity; attention has the alerting of the mind as its mode of activity; feeling has the experiencing of reception as its mode of activity;
perception has the forming of mental images as its mode of activity; and volition has purposeful construction as its mode of activity. Such are the modes of activity.
Since they are distinct, how can they be associated? To this, the text below answers by precisely clarifying their association.
"Identity of time" means they coexist within a single kṣaṇa, as there is no sequence between them. "Identity of basis" means that both take the manas as their simultaneous support (sahabhū-āśraya).

Regarding "having the same object" (*ālambana*) and so forth: "and so forth" refers to similarity, because each transforms its aspect into an object. "Entity" (*vastu*) refers to the substantial entity;
although their substances are distinct, they are called "associated" (*samprayukta*) because they are conjoined as if they were one, due to these two being identical in two respects.
The aspect (*ākāra*) of this consciousness is extremely indistinct; therefore, it is associated exclusively with neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Below this, the section on the association with feeling is explained. First, the association is clarified by means of the aspect of the consciousness.
"Neutral" (*upekṣā*) refers to being indifferent to both suffering and pleasure. One may know through five points that this consciousness is associated with neutral feeling: first...

1. They are extremely indistinct; for if they were feelings of suffering or pleasure, they would necessarily be distinct. 2. They cannot differentiate between favorable and adverse objects, whereas other feelings apprehend both adverse and favorable objects.
3. They are subtle; for the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of feelings of suffering and pleasure are necessarily coarse.
Fourth, it is of one kind; for if it were any other type of feeling, there would necessarily be change and detachment. Fifth, it proceeds as a continuous succession;

for if it were any other type of feeling, there would necessarily be interruptions. Consciousness possesses these five characteristics, and the characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is likewise; therefore, it is associated [with consciousness].
Furthermore, this associated feeling (*vedanā*) is exclusively maturation (*vipāka*). [The text continues: "Because it depends on present conditions, it is not associated with this.

Below this, the following section clarifies association by way of feeling being maturation. First, it correctly explains maturation: that is, true maturation is induced by prior wholesome or unwholesome karma;
it does not depend on present conditions that are either adverse or favorable, but rather proceeds according to prior karma. Therefore, it is maturation.

It is associated only with neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Suffering and pleasure are excluded; this is shown by contrast. Suffering and pleasure arise as retribution in a manner contrary to this [neutral feeling];

they belong to the first six consciousnesses and are not true retribution (*vipāka*). Because they cannot be sustained by prior karma alone but require present conditions to arise, they are not associated with this consciousness.
Furthermore, because this consciousness is constantly without transformation, it is associated only with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Moreover, as stated below, the three [lower realms] are explained in terms of being without transformation; thus, consciousness is accompanied by equanimity and remains eternally without transformation.
Therefore, there must be that which is appropriated (*upādāna*). If it were associated with both suffering and pleasure, it would undergo transformation; how then could it be appropriated?
Through this repeated demonstration, it is established that this consciousness is associated exclusively with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
If that is so, how can this consciousness also be the maturation (*vipāka*) of unwholesome karma?

[The text] below provides an explanation to resolve this objection. First, it asks: Since this consciousness is associated exclusively with neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*), it should be the maturation of human or celestial realms produced by wholesome karma;
how then can it also be the maturation produced by unwholesome karma? Unwholesome...

How could that which is summoned by karma not entail painful sensation? If there were no painful sensation, it would not be summoned by an unwholesome [karma]. This question is posed with reference to the maturation (*vipāka*) of the three miserable realms.

Since it is admitted that wholesome karma can summon neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*), just as neutral dharmas are summoned by both wholesome and unwholesome [karma], [the same logic applies here].
Having already granted [the premise], the commentary first provides an answer by analogy with the ripening (*vipāka*) of humans and devas.

Since it is granted that wholesome karma can induce equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) in humans and devas, one must likewise grant that unwholesome karma induces equanimity in the three miserable realms (*durgati*). Why is it that both wholesome and unwholesome [karma] are able to induce equanimity?

Next, he establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to explain this: "Equanimity" is the subject (*dharmin*); "it is induced by both wholesome and unwholesome [karma]" is the thesis (*pakṣa*). It does not...

The cause is so called because it contradicts the categories of suffering and pleasure, just as, for example, neutral phenomena do. Regarding the categories of suffering and pleasure: the two types of unwholesome [actions] belong to the category of suffering, while the wholesome [actions] of humans and devas belong to the category of pleasure.
How is it that this consciousness is not associated with the "object-specific" (viṣaya-viśeṣa) mental factors?
[The text continues: "...therefore, this is not associated with the object-specific. The section beginning with "How" below serves to exclude association with other factors;

the first phrase poses the inquiry, the first sentence provides a general explanation, the subsequent ten phrases provide a detailed explanation, and the final phrase provides a summary. Now, regarding the "object-specific" factors: they take their respective objects individually.
Because it is born [into existence], this consciousness is a single, homogeneous continuum; therefore, it does not associate with distinct objects, as explained in the text.
Since this consciousness is exclusively of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*), and because [other states] are subject to interruption, they are certainly not maturation.

Below this consciousness, it is clarified that it does not coexist with the wholesome, the defiled, and so forth; its nature is that of maturation (*vipāka*), meaning it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

"Wholesome and so forth" refers to the eleven factors such as faith; "defiled and so forth" refers to the twenty-six factors consisting of the root and secondary afflictions. This is because their categories are distinct.
Therefore, they are not associated. [The phrase] "remorse and so forth" includes sleep, vitarka, and vicāra; these all pertain to the three natures.
Since those that are neutral (avyākṛta) are intermittent, whereas this [state] is uninterrupted, they are not associated.
There are four kinds of phenomena, namely the wholesome, the unwholesome, [and so forth], up to what phenomena are subsumed within the ālayavijñāna?
Regarding "phenomena exist," this explains the section on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). First, the four phenomena are listed and presented, followed by the inquiry that initiates the discussion.
This consciousness is exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). [The text continues] "Therefore, this is exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate.
Below this, the verse is cited as a general response. Below "maturation" (*vipāka*), there are three specific explanations.

The first explains it in terms of its function as a support and basis. Within the text, this is illustrated through contrast: "evolution" (*pravṛtti*) refers to the defiled phenomena of afflictions, karma, and birth; "reversion" (*nivṛtti*) refers to *nirvāṇa*.
It functions as the support for the two [aspects] that accord with the pure dharma of the Path; this is because consciousness is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

If it were exclusively of a wholesome nature, it would not possess the function of the five destinies (*pañcagati*)—the rising and sinking of transmigration. If it were exclusively of a defiled nature, [it likewise could not perform this function].
There should be no function of alternating abandonment and acquisition or of returning to cessation; therefore, it is said that [the storehouse consciousness] could not be established.

Furthermore, from this point downward, the second section explains [the storehouse consciousness] by way of its sustaining of seeds. The first sentence provides a direct explanation: because it is neutral (*avyākṛta*), it sustains the seeds of both the wholesome and the defiled, serving as the basis for the wholesome and the defiled.
The following part provides a negative illustration: the wholesome is contrary to the defiled, and thus it should not serve as the basis for the defiled; likewise, the defiled is contrary to...
"Good. It should not serve as a basis for the wholesome. Furthermore, from here downward, three points are explained in terms of receiving perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it possesses the nature of being perfumable; thus, it receives the perfuming of both the wholesome and the defiled. Next, this is shown by way of contrast:

if the wholesome did not receive the perfuming of the defiled, or if the defiled did not receive the perfuming of the wholesome, they would be like fragrance and a foul odor, which do not perfume one another. Because there would be no perfuming, there would be [no continuity].
It is the seed. Without a seed, there is no cause; without a cause, there is also no fruit. Therefore it is said that both the causes and fruits of defilement and purity are not established.
Possessing these three meanings mentioned above, it is known through proof that this is subsumed under the category of the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

"Obscuration" (*nivṛti*) refers to defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), because they obstruct the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*). [This extends] until: "Because this is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, it is called 'indeterminate' (*avyākṛta*).
"Obscuration" is explained below as the meaning of "unobscured-indeterminate" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). In the text, this is explained through contrast: "Obscuration" has the sense of "concealing.

"Defiled phenomena" refers to afflictions (*kleśa*) such as greed (*rāga*). "The Noble Path" refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). "Pure mind" refers to the principle of purity. That is to say:
The afflictions (*kleśa*) that can obstruct the principle of wisdom are called "obscuration" (*nivṛti*). Since this consciousness is not defiled, it is termed "unobscured" (*anivṛta*).

"Predicted" (*vyākṛta*) means "to prophesy. "Wholesome" refers to white karma; "unwholesome" refers to black karma. The blissful fruits of ascending toward humans and devas are termed "desirable" (*iṣṭa*);

the bitter fruits of sinking into the three miserable realms are termed "undesirable" (*aniṣṭa*). Each of these possesses its own distinct substantial nature (*svabhāva*) characterized by either benefit or harm.
"Prediction" (vyākaraṇa) means "to predict. Since this [category] is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
Regarding the phrase "contact and so forth are also like this," this refers to the statement that contact and the other [mental factors] are likewise [indeterminate].

"Regarding 'contact and so forth' below": this explains the analogy of mental factors (caitta) to the sovereign mind (citta). The initial passage briefly clarifies that the sovereign and its factors must necessarily be of the same nature. Next, "furthermore, contact and so forth" below, extensively demonstrates that all five meanings are identical.

As for the "correspondence of the five dharmas": the ālayavijñāna corresponds with the five dharmas, such as contact; each of the five [mental factors] that serve as the analogies for the sovereign likewise corresponds with these five dharmas.

As it is said: ... [omitted] ... As for the "correspondence of the five dharmas": the ālayavijñāna corresponds with the five dharmas, such as contact; each of the five [mental factors] that serve as the analogies for the sovereign likewise corresponds with these five dharmas. Just as...

Contact (*sparśa*), in relation to the ālayavijñāna and the four beginning with attention (*manasikāra*), consists of these five factors. Attention, in relation to the ālayavijñāna and the four beginning with contact, likewise consists of these five factors.
The remaining three [mental factors] should be understood by analogy. The meanings of the four [remaining factors] are as stated in the text.

One interpretation holds that because the statement "and so forth" (*tathā ca*) contains no qualification, the mental factors such as contact (*sparśa*) and the rest should be treated like the *ālayavijñāna*.
Another interpretation follows below to refute this divergent view. First, it sets forth the argument: "In this context, contact and the others are used as examples for the sovereign [mind].

Since 'and so forth' contains no qualification, everything should be treated as an example for everything. This interpretation should not be accepted as using contact and the others as examples [for the sovereign mind].
The king is named Sarvabījaka. His explanation is irrational; why is this? [From here until: "How could a single consciousness maintain seeds?

His explanation is refuted below. The first sentence is a general censure; the next establishes a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to refute it. Contact and so forth are the *dharmin* (the subject); they cannot...
Regarding the school that maintains [the ālayavijñāna] receives perfuming and sustains seeds: because it lacks sovereignty, it serves as the cause, just like craving, faith, and so forth.

Only that which receives perfuming and sustains seeds is designated "all-seeded" (sarvabījaka). Since [the defiled mind] lacks the meaning of receiving perfuming and sustaining seeds, how can it be analogized to the king and called "all-seeded"?

Furthermore, if it is argued that contact (*sparśa*) and so forth can also receive perfuming (*vāsanā*)—up to the point where they arise simultaneously with the six visual consciousnesses (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and so on—and if, as stated below, the first phrase restates the opponent's position by saying, "If one claims that contact and so forth can also receive perfuming, and are therefore also called 'possessors of all seeds' (*sarvabījaka*)," then [the response] is as follows: "It should be... and so on.
This refutation consists of two parts: (1) a refutation based on the formation of the six [consciousnesses] through a single perfuming; and (2) a refutation based on multiple types [of perfuming].
1. Refutation by means of the single sprout; 3. Refutation by means of the five kinds of uselessness; 4. Refutation by means of the sequential production of fruits; 5.
Refutation by means of the simultaneous production of six fruits—all as explained in the text.
"Who says that contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors] can also receive perfuming? ... "It is also like fire, which lacks the function of burning.
Who says this? The following section refutes the attempted defense. The first sentence provides a direct defense. "Not so," etc., is the Master's further interrogation.

"As for contact," etc., presents the defensive argument. Regarding "resembling the characteristics of a seed": when contact and the others perceive objects, they must rely upon the eighth consciousness as their objective support (*ālambana*).

Taking the three categories of objects as the objective basis (*ālambana-pratibimba*), consciousness itself transforms into an aspect (*ākāra*) which serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*). This very transformed aspect that resembles the seeds is termed "all-seeds" (*sarvabījaka*);
this indicates that it receives its name based on its object-condition. It does not mean that the capacity to receive perfuming and maintain seeds is called "all-seeds.
Furthermore, below, three reasons are established to prove that there must necessarily be an aspect resembling seeds, for consciousness takes the three categories of objects as its conditions.
If contact and the other factors did not manifest as resembling seeds, they would not be equivalent to the objects of consciousness.

Since contact and the others are indeed equivalent to the objects of consciousness, they must therefore manifest as resembling seeds. Furthermore, if it is argued that contact and the others merely take as their objects that which resembles the sense organs, the body, and so forth; [then...]

It does not take as its object that which resembles the seed. If one were born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there would be no form (*rūpa*) upon which to rely; thus, there would be no objective support (*ālambana*).

Yet, since that which is formless must have an objective support, this [support] is precisely what resembles the seed. Furthermore, when the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) takes the seed as its object, although contact (*sparśa*) and other factors rely upon it as a substantial basis (*pratibimba*), they are merely called "remote objective conditions" (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*).
Since a "direct objective condition" (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*) must necessarily exist, this [condition] is precisely what resembles the seed. This resemblance...
The single phrase, "the various characteristics do not arise as causes for the manifest consciousnesses," is intended to avoid the five previous faults.
That is to say, "all seeds" is designated in terms of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); it does not mean that they receive perfuming or maintain the seeds.

How then can one raise the objection: "Seeds must necessarily produce fruits—whether one or many, and whether simultaneously or gradually"? This is like the section on "contact" (*sparśa*) below, which cites [the case of] what resembles a sense organ (*indriya*) but is not one.
The support of consciousness is like a seed that is merely similar [to the actual cause] and does not function as a direct causal condition (*pratyaya*). This is also as explained below:
citing something that resembles fire but lacks the capacity to burn serves as a metaphor for how a semblance of a seed does not function as a direct causal condition.
That defense—that the objects of contact and so forth are not [the seeds]—is incorrect; otherwise, there would be the fault of redundancy in the root verse.

That defense is refuted below. Regarding the objects of contact and so forth, which possess characteristics resembling seeds and resembling sense-faculties, in the third line of the subsequent verse, it says "appropriation" (*upādāna*).
Just as the King takes the three types of objects as his domain, contact and the others follow the example of the King and likewise take them as their objects.
It transforms into three types of similar images and takes them as its object. This phrase serves as an analogy for the characteristics of a king.
Because of the term "all modes" (*sarvākāra*) in this second sentence, it must refer to the meaning of being perfumed and maintaining seeds;
otherwise, if one were to claim that the preceding term "all modes" also refers to the object appearing as the image of a seed, then the treatise would incur the fault of redundant repetition.
Furthermore, what they have stated is likewise [intended] as follows (up to): "it is said according to what is appropriate, not with reference to everything.

Furthermore, below that, [the text] refutes the lack of distinction. The initial passage cites the position and refutes it in general. The section beginning with "lest there be contact... refutes it specifically.

If one were to claim there is no distinction, such that contact and so forth, like consciousness, are also capable of discernment—the word "lest" (*mā*) is a term of refutation—[referring to] contact and so forth.

Regarding the statement that [the mind] is also associated with contact (*sparśa*) and so forth: the phrasing is general, but the intended meaning is specific; thus, each case should be explained individually.

If one were to claim there is no distinction made, then contact itself would have to be associated with contact, just as it is associated with the "king" (the mind). However, contact can be discussed as being associated with the other four [mental factors], because it is not associated with itself;
association occurs with what is of another nature, not with its own nature. The same principle applies to the remaining four. This also applies to the mind (*citta*).
Regarding that which is associated with the five factors: it is like the contact being associated with the "one king" and the "four attendants.
