In a single moment within the mother’s womb, one undergoes birth and becomes bound to that [new existence]; therefore, it is called the 'defiled consciousness of linking birth' (*pratisandhi-saṃkleśika-vijñāna*). If this eighth consciousness did not exist, then...

To say that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) has volitional formations (saṃskāra) as its condition is a reversal of the proper sequence of terms; because there is a vast temporal gap, the sense of "condition" would not apply.
Since this case of volitional formations having consciousness (vijñāna) as their condition cannot be established, all subsequent factors likewise fail to be established.
All pure dharmas (*viśuddha-dharma*) also have three types, distinguished by the mundane and supramundane paths and their fruits of abandonment.
[The phrase] "All pure... and below next explains the pure dharmas. The initial passage lists the three types:

the mundane path of purity refers to the four dhyānas, the eight concentrations (*samāpatti*), the twelve gates of dhyāna (*dvāra-dhyāna*), and so forth. The supramundane path of purity refers to the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*) and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
The ten spheres of totality (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*) and so forth are both mundane and supramundane meditations;

these include the six subtle gates (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā-mukha*), the sixteen stages of special excellence (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), the nine penetrations (*navābhijñā*), and the clear knowledges (*vidyā*). As for the fruits of abandonment, they refer to *pariniṣpanna-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of intrinsic purity).
Because the categories differ, the pure paths each permeate their own respective seeds.
Answer: This consciousness does not exist, because if it did not, the support for both mundane and supramundane [attainments] would likewise have to arise without a cause.

The phrase "If there were none" below indicates that this eighth consciousness exists, capable of sustaining the seeds of the two types of pure paths; the text expresses this through a negative implication (*paryudāsa*).

Regarding "different categories" (*visabhāga*): from the perspective of the three miserable realms in relation to humans and devas, they are called different categories because there is no mundane path of purity therein.
From the perspective of the six classes of ordinary beings in relation to the four types of noble ones, they are called different categories because there is no supramundane path of purity therein.

Since both types of seeds of purity are absent, that which arises subsequently would lack a cause. As for other causes: defilement would be the cause of purity, and the outflowing (*sāsrava*) would be the cause of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). [This concerns] the basis (*āśraya*).

"Those" refers to the body and mind. For one who has entered *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), because what was to be done has been accomplished and both body and mind have ceased, it is said that the pure path must arise from body and wisdom. Since they lack body and wisdom, how could [the path] arise again?
Therefore, it is said that the basis (*āśraya*) would likewise have to arise without a cause.
Furthermore, the supramundane path should not initially arise; [if it did,] there would consequently be no fruits of the three vehicles.
The section "Furthermore, transcending the lower" specifically clarifies the supramundane path. The first two phrases directly state that because the seeds do not exist, [the path] does not arise.

The section beginning with "With outflows" cites and refutes a counter-argument. The counter-argument states: "Pure seeds exist by virtue of the permeation of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*). Therefore, [the text] rebuts this, saying: "If they existed..."

The category of the outflows (*āsrava*) and the category of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) are distinct natures; [the latter] is not the cause for those [outflows]. "Not produced from seeds of consciousness" means it is not produced from seeds within consciousness.
"Not produced initially" means there is no originally existing seed (*prakṛtistha-bīja*). "Not produced subsequently" means there is no newly perfumed seed (*navasaṃskṛta-bīja*).
Alternatively, it may be that because there is no seed initially, it is not produced; by analogy with the latter case, it is likewise not produced in the former. Since...
Without the cause of purification, it is difficult to expect the fruit of sainthood—the fruit of the Path, meaning the fruit realized through the Path, which is the Bodhi of the Three Vehicles.
If this consciousness did not exist to maintain the seeds of affliction, upon what would [the fruit] depend, and by means of what would the fruit of abandonment be established?
If one includes the lower [stages], the intent is to clarify that there exists this eighth [consciousness] capable of sustaining the seeds of afflictions;
it is only by means of the path that severs these seeds that one can realize the two fruits of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). The text expresses this through contraposition:

it explains that only by severing the afflictions does one realize the fruit of severance. "Path" refers to untainted contemplative wisdom (*anāsrava-bhāvanā-jñāna*). "Both seeds and manifestations are absent" refers to the antidote.

Because it is contrary to the characteristics of hindrances (*āvaraṇa*). The phrase "defiled and pure" [in the verse] explains that the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) does not exist, because light arises and darkness ceases.

The phrase "the characteristic of the path" [in the verse] explains that the seeds (*bīja*) do not exist, because the public does not harbor private [seeds]. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The mind associated with the path is the subject (*dharmin*);
it does not possess those seeds, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is "because of contradiction with its own nature" (*svabhāvaviruddha*). It is like water and fire.

Because they share the same vessel, it is like *nirvāṇa*. "Going and coming" refers to the consciousnesses of the past and future. "Attainment and so forth" refers to the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

Since there is nothing below [the present], it concludes that there is no consciousness to maintain the seeds. "That which is abandoned" refers to the afflictions; "that which abandons" refers to the wisdom of contemplation.
Since both are unobtainable, the two instances of the word "who" (or "which")—one pointing to that which is abandoned and one pointing to that which abandons—[demonstrate this].

Both [the arising and non-arising of afflictions] are due to being sustained by the eighth [consciousness]. If it is argued that subsequent afflictions do not arise through the power of the Path—[this is because] only this [eighth consciousness] can sustain the seeds of both the defiled and the pure—if one were to rely on the lower [view], one would be restating the opponent’s defense and refuting it.
The first passage restates the defense, namely: "Because when the Path arises, the afflictions do not arise. This establishes [the position].

Regarding the fruit of abandonment: it is first and then subsequently destroyed. As for the arising of the initial path, this refers to the time when one practices the five objects of mental abiding (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana*) through both general and specific mindfulness;

at that moment, one becomes an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*). However, because the seeds of the present afflictions have not yet been severed—despite the power of the currently active path acting as an antidote—one has not yet become an Arhat.

If one were not to take the seeds into account, one ought to become an Arhat immediately. Why? Because [the seeds of] the views to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya-dṛṣṭi*) remain.
Because the volitions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) are never again produced, without requiring further effort. Why are they never again produced?
Because there is no consciousness that sustains the seeds of those various afflictions (*kleśa*). This concludes the section; the eighth [chapter] of the main text follows.
The proof that this consciousness exists possesses boundless principles and rationales (up to the point where it says): "All wise persons should believe and accept this with deep conviction.

From "The proof that this... onwards, the ten principles are summarized. From "Furthermore... onwards, there is the exhortation to believe. The above concludes the explanation of the first transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Having thus explained the characteristics of the first transformation, what are the characteristics of the second transformation?
The verse says: "Next, the second transformation... [omitted] ...is absent in Arhats, in the meditative attainment of cessation, and on the supramundane path."
The following explains the second transformative consciousness (*dvitīya-pariṇāma-vijñāna*). Within the text, the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent topic is introduced.

The verse below consists of twelve lines in response, divided into ten sections: 1. The first two lines explain the *nāman-mukha* (the section on the name). 2. The three characters "depending on that and transforming" (*tad-āśritya vartate*) constitute the *āśraya-mukha* (the section on the basis). 3.

The two characters "taking that as its object" (*tad-ālambana*) constitute the *ālambana-viṣaya-mukha* (the section on the objective sphere). 4. "Having reflection as its nature" (*mananātmaka*) constitutes the *svabhāva-mukha* (the section on the essential nature). 5. [The character] "reflection" (*manana*)... [continues].

The first phrase defines the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). The four phrases beginning with "able to perceive" (*ālambana*) concern the gate of the aspect of the object (*ākāra*). The three phrases beginning with "the four afflictions" concern the gate of associated mental factors (*caitta-samprayukta*).

The remaining one phrase concerns the gate of other associated factors. The one phrase concerning "obscured" (*nivṛta*) concerns the gate of the three natures (*tri-dhātu*). The one phrase beginning with "according to" concerns the gate of the realms of existence (*dhātu-bandhana*).
The two phrases beginning with "Arhat" concern the gate of the stages of abandonment and suppression (*prahāṇa-vinodana-krama*).

The Commentary says: Following the first *vipāka-vijñāna* that undergoes transformation, [it is established] because it constantly and thoroughly deliberates (*manana*), being superior to other consciousnesses.

The Commentary says: Below, the explanation proceeds by way of gates. The first two phrases conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one. Regarding the phrase "This consciousness," this first clarifies the gate of explaining the name;
the name is established based on the teachings. In the Sanskrit language, *manas* is fully called *kḷiṣṭa-ya*.

*Manas* (the seventh consciousness) is here translated as "defiled mind" (*kliṣṭa-manas*). The second phrase explains its meaning: it is both "constant" (*nitya*) and "thoroughly investigative" (*santīraṇa*). It is superior to the first six [consciousnesses] and the last one [the ālayavijñāna].
The detailed analysis is as before. In both the state with outflows (*sāsrava*) and the state without outflows (*anāsrava*), it constantly and thoroughly examines self and non-self.
"What is the difference between this [name] and the sixth consciousness? (up to) "Just as the visual consciousness and other cognitions differ from the mind (*manas*).

Regarding "this name," the question and answer distinguish it [from others]. This uses the identity of the name to inquire into the difference in its meaning. Regarding "this sustains," the answer explains it by way of separation and combination.

The character "this" (*ci*) refers to the seventh [consciousness]. "Sustaining activity" (*dhāraṇa-karman*): consciousness is the essence (*svabhāva*), while the mind (*manas*) is the activity (*karman*).

Regarding "function": the essence of consciousness (vijñāna) possesses the function of deliberation (manana). The essence is revealed by means of its function, because the essence is able to sustain the function.
As with the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the essence of consciousness possesses the function of the three stores, because the essence is able to sustain those functions.

Therefore, this is cited as an illustration. The formal argument is: the manas and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) are *dharmadhāraya* compounds, because consciousness is itself the mind (*manas*), just like the storehouse consciousness.
Regarding those characters: "sixth" refers to the sixth [consciousness]. As for "dependent on the master" (*adhipatīya*), consciousness is that which depends, and the mind (*manas*) is its support;
the mind is the seventh, being the master upon whom it depends. Because it is named by depending on this master, it is called "dependent on the master.

As in the case of "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and so forth: consciousness is that which depends, and the eye is the master upon whom it depends; thus, the consciousness is indicated by citing the master, the eye.

This name is also established based on the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound; therefore, an example is cited. The same applies to the other four [consciousnesses]. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
The sixth mental consciousness is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, because "consciousness" is distinct from "mind," just like visual consciousness and the others.
However, in the various sacred teachings, fearing that this [term] might be confused with that, [it is designated as such] because it serves as the proximate basis;

thus it is simply called "mind" (*manas*). The phrase "However, all... below serves to distinguish it. First, regarding the distinction between the single and the dual: this is the single name "mind," while that is the dual name "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*).

Furthermore, the section beginning with "Moreover, marking... secondly distinguishes their functions by way of superiority and inferiority: the eighth [consciousness] is named "mind" (*citta*) because its function of accumulation is predominant.

The first six are called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because their function of discerning (*vijñapti*) is predominant. The seventh has both functions in a subordinate manner; therefore, it is designated simply as "mind" (*manas*).

Alternatively, the following three [categories] distinguish the supports (*āśraya*) by way of distance and proximity. Consciousness (*manovijñāna*), when compared to the eighth consciousness, has a distant support;

this [seventh consciousness], however, serves as its simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), and is thus called the proximate support. This is just as visual consciousness has four supports, yet only the eye is its specific support.

The sense-faculties (*indriya*) are the co-existent supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*), because they are the immediate supports; therefore, they are simply called "eye" [and so forth]. This [mental faculty] serves as the immediate support for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); therefore, it is simply called "mind" (*manas*).

The phrase "that upon which it turns" (*tad-āśrita*) reveals this basis (*āśraya*). Because the Noble One stated that this consciousness depends upon the *ālayavijñāna*, the section beginning with "that upon which" (*tad-āśrita*) explains the gate of the basis.
First, the two characters "depending on that" (*tad-āśrita*) are explained; the word "this" (*idam*) at the beginning of the passage provides the general heading.
"Refers to the seventh" indicates the basis (*āśraya*). "Refers to the eighth" means that [the former] depends on the latter; the subsequent explanation follows the text.
According to one interpretation, this meaning is that because those seeds of consciousness must have [the eighth consciousness] as their simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) in order to arise.

There is an interpretation [stating] that the two schools differ regarding their basis. The first school clarifies that this seventh consciousness relies solely upon the seeds of the eighth consciousness and does not depend on the manifest consciousness.

This is because, as previously stated, the eighth consciousness possesses the quality of "evolving" (*pravṛtti*); it arises and perishes moment by moment, undergoing transformation from one instant to the next.
There is an interpretation that this intention [is] because that consciousness-seed (*vijñāna-bīja*) only arises when it has the [seventh consciousness] as its co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).

Next, the second school clarifies that this co-existent support consists of both the seed and the manifest (*bīja-vijñapti*). Although there is no [explicit statement] below, it explains the meaning of relying on the manifest:
because this [seventh] consciousness undergoes transformation between defilement and purity from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, it may rely upon the manifest.
"Transformation" (*pravṛtti*) refers to the process of flowing forth; it indicates that this consciousness always depends upon that [eighth] consciousness to apprehend its objects.

Regarding the phrase "transformation refers to below," this is an etymological explanation of the term *pravṛtti*. "Flowing" (*pravāha*) has the meaning of continuity, while "transformation" (*vṛtti*) has the meaning of change.

Regarding the phrase "it indicates below," this is a general explanation of the three characters: it indicates that this seventh consciousness always depends upon that eighth consciousness to take it as its object.

Because they depend on me, and because the supported and the support arise in uninterrupted succession, all minds and mental factors possess a support (āśraya); thus they are said to "possess a support," whereas other phenomena do not.

Below the section on "The Various Minds," there is a general clarification of the three bases for all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). The initial passage provides a general enumeration of these three types.

First is the brief explanation: regarding the phrase "first, the causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*), the first clause states the name, while the subsequent clause reveals its essential nature (*svabhāva*); here, the cause is itself the condition.
The name is derived from the fruit. A "cause" (hetu) has the sense of being the direct capacity for production; a "condition" (pratyaya) has the sense of stimulating functional activity.

If one speaks only of "causes and conditions," it is general, as it encompasses both manifest phenomena and seeds. If one speaks of the "basis of causes and conditions," it is specific, as it refers specifically to one's own seeds.
The subsequent phrase, "all conditioned phenomena, etc.," explains this; it refers to form, mind, faculties, objects, and defilements.

Because pure and other such phenomena all arise by depending upon this basis, the next phrase provides a counter-illustration; these are stated in detail through alternating perspectives to distinguish the general from the specific.
Regarding the "predominant conditions" (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and so forth: the first phrase indicates the name, and the second phrase reveals its essential nature (*tattva*).

This refers to having superior power, because it assists in the arising [of the mind]. If one speaks only of "predominant" (*adhipati*), then it is universal, as it applies to all internal and external factors, whether favorable or adverse, proximate or remote, and powerful or powerless.
To speak of the "basis of the predominant condition" (*adhipatipratyaya-āśraya*), however, is restrictive, as it is limited to the locations of the six internal sense faculties.
The final phrase of each section concerning the various minds explains that the eight mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) and the five classes of mental factors (*caitta*) are all...

Because it functions in dependence upon the co-existent faculty (*sahabhū-indriya*), the next phrase provides a counter-illustration. These points are stated repeatedly and in detail to distinguish the general from the specific and to adopt the restricted meaning.
Regarding "the three equalities" (*samanantara*, etc.): the first phrase indicates the name, while the second phrase reveals its essential nature; their functional power is equal.

Because there is no mind of the same category intervening within it. If one speaks of the "equal and immediate" (samanantara), then it is universal; it applies to all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

That which draws forth each subsequent moment from its preceding moment is called "equal and immediate. However, when speaking of the "equal and immediate condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*), it is restricted;
it is restricted to the primary mind (*cittarāja*) because it possesses the sense of "sovereignty," because it can "open the way" (*avakāśa-dāna*), and because it has ceased previously.

The meaning is as follows: this refers to the basis in relation to the [mental] syllables (*akṣara*). It concerns only the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), because all mental states and mental factors (*caitta-caitasika*) rely upon this very basis;
for when one opens the way, the others likewise open the way. By setting aside the following [explanation], it serves as a counter-illustration (*pratikūla-darśana*);

it is stated in detail through repetition to distinguish the general from the specific. Now, regarding these three bases, what are the distinct characteristics of "arising" (*jāti*), "transforming" (*pravṛtti*), and "originating" (*utpāda*)? Arising...
"Arising" (*utpāda*) refers to the production of the essence based on its seeds; "evolving" (*vartana*) refers to the conformity and the application of power that cause it to evolve;

and "occurring" (*pravṛtti*) refers to the opening of a path by the preceding [moment] that allows the subsequent [moment] to arise. These are the distinct characteristics of these three. The phrase "only mind" (*cittamātra*) concludes [the section].

Only in the two states do the mental factors (*caitta*) universally possess all three bases (*āśraya*); they do not belong to other phenomena. This excludes matter (*rūpa*), non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and non-existence (*abhāva*).
This constitutes the three stages. Regarding the first, the basis of the seed (*bīja-āśraya*), some state: (up to) "because the seed and the sprout, etc., do not coexist.

Below the section on the initial seed, there is an extensive explanation. First, the basis of the seed is explained. The meaning of "seed" lies in its function of producing the manifest (*vartamāna*). It does not [function]...

The merit lies in leading toward what follows. Regarding the explanations of these two schools: the first citation from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* is partial rather than correct, while the subsequent citation from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* is correct rather than partial.
First, the partial interpretation is presented; this concerns the meaning of seeds inducing seeds, and thus it states that "the seed perishes and the fruit arises.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* is cited as proof. Next, the analogy of the seed perishing and the sprout arising is cited.
One interpretation holds that the proof cited by that [opponent] is unestablished, because the flame and the wick are simultaneous and do not act as causes for one another.

Another interpretation holds that the following section first refutes the previous partial citation: the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that "the seed has already arisen," which is said in reference to the seed inducing a subsequent seed of its own kind.
Furthermore, the section beginning with "the seed produces the sprout" refutes the previous analogy; the production of a sprout from a seed is not a case of [mutual causality].

"Meaning" refers to what is spoken in terms of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), not in terms of ultimate principle (*tattva*). As for the claim that "the cessation of the seed and the arising of the sprout are not universally established," this is because there are cases where the seed and the sprout exist simultaneously;
therefore, it is not universally established. Below the section on the "flame and the wick," the correct meaning is revealed; by means of this analogy, the Dharma is elucidated.
This analogy illustrates how the seed and the manifestation arise together, mutually serving as cause and effect.
However, while seeds of the same category do not coexist as cause and effect, the arising of seeds from manifest phenomena is necessarily simultaneous.
Now, the following section generally clarifies that all three types [of phenomena] act together as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). In the first phrase, seeds of the same category do not coexist;

this clarifies that seeds induce seeds as causal conditions. In the second phrase, seeds and manifest phenomena arise together; this clarifies that seeds produce manifest phenomena, and manifest phenomena perfume seeds.
These two distinct categories arise together and both serve as causes and conditions. Only the seeds produce the manifest; this is the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) support.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains that impermanent phenomena [from seeds] to [manifestations]—that is, the relationship between seeds and active manifestations—serve as mutual causes for one another.
Therefore, Yu [the commentator] descends to cite evidence from three categories of direct causes and conditions. First, regarding impermanent phenomena (*anitya-dharma*):

these consist of seeds (*bīja*) and manifest activities (*samudācāra*), because they perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇika-nirodha*). Second, regarding self-nature (*svabhāva*): this refers to seeds of their own kind, as they are all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Third, regarding other-nature (*parabhāva*): this points to manifest results, as they encompass all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*); thus, in contrast to the indeterminate nature of the seeds, they are called "other. Manifest activities, when viewed in relation to seeds, are likewise...
It is called "other-nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* also states this (up to): "it is certain that there is a distinct basis for seeds.

The lower section of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* cites both [seed and manifestation] together as mutual causes and conditions, as in the text. Furthermore, the subsequent section provides a singular proof.

The seed serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the support (*āśraya*); thus, the first phrase concerning the seed establishes this. Because the support of the seed must necessarily be simultaneous with it, the subsequent passage beginning with "Even if...
addresses objections from other quarters, as the text explains. The section beginning with "In this way... provides the summary.
Next, regarding the simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), some say: [this extends] up to the point that the five faculties, such as the eye, are themselves the seeds.
Next, the simultaneous support is explained; because the supported (*āśrita*) and the support (*āśraya*) must necessarily exist at the same time, it is called "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*).
Within this, there are differences in the interpretations of the four schools. The first is erroneous and not correct, while the fourth is correct and not erroneous. The second...
The second [section] refutes errors and leads to the correct understanding; the third, while appropriate, is not exhaustive. First, the divergent interpretations of the initial school are presented.
The first phrase establishes the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as the basis; the subsequent phrase explains that there must necessarily be a simultaneous mental consciousness.

The phrase "there is no separate... excludes the sense organs (*indriya*) from being the basis. The following phrase establishes his own position: because the sense organ is itself the seed of consciousness.
In the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is stated: "Therefore, the sense organs such as the eye are the seeds of the five consciousnesses.
[Below this, the proof is cited. First, the verse is cited; below that, the meaning of the verse is explained. Regarding the first line, the text says:
"The Blessed One, in order to establish the ten dharmas—the two categories of internal and external bases—and specifically to establish the five internal bases, spoke of the five consciousnesses."

The seeds constitute the five faculties, such as the eye; in order to establish the five external bases, it is taught that the objective aspects (nimittabhāga) transformed by the five consciousnesses constitute the five objects, such as visible form.
Therefore, the single phrase following "the eye" serves to conclude the author's own position.
The *Ālambanaparīkṣā* also states this (up to): "Because the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) and the seeds (*bīja*) act as causes for one another.

[The text] below the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* further cites scriptural evidence. First, it cites the verse; following that verse, it explains its meaning. Regarding the phrase "visual consciousness and so forth":

that which depends on the sense organ is called "visual consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*), while that which depends on the object is called "consciousness of form" (*rūpavijñāna*). Therefore, they are combined and named thus. That [interpretation] is erroneous.
That which is called the seed of consciousness is termed "efficacy" (*śakti*) and is designated as the five sense-faculties (*indriya*).

There are no separate faculties such as the eye and so forth. This explains the latter two phrases regarding seeds: seeds and objective forms (*rūpa*) constantly serve as mutual causes for one another.

As for the term "form-consciousness," form is the objective sphere (*ālambana*) that constitutes the "image-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) of consciousness. The primary meaning is that the faculty and its object serve as mutual causes; it is an error to claim that the objective form alone [is the cause].

The "consciousness of form" refers to the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). This is because this perfuming manifest consciousness and the seeds of consciousness serve as causes for one another.
The seventh and eighth consciousnesses do not have a separate basis other than this; they must depend upon the *manas* (the seventh consciousness) in order to arise.
The seventh section below clarifies the latter three consciousnesses as stated in the text.
There is an interpretation that their explanation contradicts both principle and scripture, because it is stated in various places throughout the holy teachings.

The section beginning with "There is another interpretation" (有義下) presents the second school’s explanation. First, it generally refutes the preceding [position] for its contradiction of both scripture and logic.

From the passage beginning "If the five... (若五下), it proceeds to refute it through nine points; in each instance, the contradictions of scripture and logic are evident from the text. The first sentence restates the opponent's tenet. The first point refutes it by showing the confusion of elements and seeds:

the three—sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—each have their own distinct seeds. The five faculties belong to the category of form (*rūpa*); the five consciousnesses...

This concerns the mind. If the sense-faculties (*indriya*) were themselves the seeds of consciousness, and the seeds of form (*rūpa*) were themselves the seeds of mind, then conversely, the seeds of mind would be the seeds of form;
thus, there would be no distinction between matter and mind, and their seeds would become confused. However, as explained below, scriptural authority is cited to prove that they cannot be conflated.

Furthermore, the seeds of the five consciousnesses each have the capacity to produce [their respective results], and all are subsumed within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Regarding the "five below" [in the verse], the second part analyzes by means of the two divisions of the aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing (*darśanabhāga*). The first phrase establishes these two divisions based on principle;

the second phrase simultaneously interrogates what constitutes the root. As for the section beginning with "If the seeing... [it] analyzes [the position]: if one takes the seeds of the seeing-division as the root, then the seeing...

If they were assigned to the mind, they would have to be subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), which would contradict the sacred teaching that all five sense organs (*indriya*) are subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

If one were to take the seeds of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) as the sense organs, then since the objective aspect belongs to form, it would—according to the previous judgment—be subsumed under the external [aggregates] and thus belong to the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
This would contradict the holy teaching that the five faculties are subsumed under the internal bases (*āyatana*).

Furthermore, if the five faculties were identical to the seeds of the five consciousnesses, it should not be said that they are subsumed under the category of dominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*).

Furthermore, from "If [the sense organs] are... onwards, the third section refutes [the opponent's view] by examining the distinction between proximate and remote conditions. The first sentence restates the position:

the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) are the co-existent supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*) of the five consciousnesses and are subsumed under the category of dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*); the seeds of the five consciousnesses are the direct causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) of the five consciousnesses.

If the five sense organs were identical to the seeds of the five consciousnesses, then one would be taking a dominant condition as a direct causal condition, thereby conflating the two categories of proximate and remote conditions.
[This] is a fault.
Furthermore, the objection that the nose and tongue faculties are the seeds of the two consciousnesses [and thus belong to] two stages or five stages is likewise invalid.

Moreover, regarding the nose and below, there is a refutation based on the distinction of realms and stages: the two faculties of nose and tongue pertain to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), whereas the two consciousnesses pertain only to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): this is analyzed by breaking down the manifestation of consciousness from its seeds. If the sense organ (*indriya*) were identical to consciousness, then the organ would follow consciousness and thus belong exclusively to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
If consciousness were identical to the organ, then consciousness would follow the organ and should therefore extend through the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The eye, ear, and body organs extend across five stages (*bhūmi*), whereas the three consciousnesses extend across only two. If the organ were identical to consciousness, then the organ would follow consciousness and would exist only in those two [stages].

If consciousness were identical to the sense faculty, then since consciousness conforms to the faculty, it would necessarily pertain to all five levels (*bhūmi*). Yet the treatise states that the three faculties of eye, ear, and body reside in two levels.
By analogy, the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue reside only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
If there were no distinction between the faculty and the consciousness, it would be difficult to clarify their respective realms and levels; therefore, they are said to be "contradictory."
Furthermore, since the seeds of the five consciousnesses pertain to both the wholesome and the unwholesome, the five sense organs (*indriya*) should not be exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Moreover, [the text] refutes [the opponent's view] regarding the five [consciousnesses] by means of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*): while the consciousnesses pertain to all three natures, the organs are held to be exclusively indeterminate.
If the five organs were identical to the seeds of the five consciousnesses, then the organs would not be exclusively indeterminate, but would likewise pertain to all three natures.
Furthermore, since the seeds of the five consciousnesses are not comprised within "appropriated" (upātta), the five sense faculties would also have to be non-appropriated.
Moreover, [the text] refutes [the position] by examining the six [faculties] in terms of appropriation. Regarding the statement that the seeds of consciousness are non-appropriated:

because seeds lie latent, they lack the capacity to produce the experience of feeling (vedanā) within the category of sensation; they merely function as "maintaining" (dhāraṇa). If the sense faculties were identical to the seeds of consciousness, they too would necessarily be non-appropriated.
Appropriation (*upātta*).

Furthermore, regarding the five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) and the seeds of the five consciousnesses: [the argument] applies because they share the same nature as the five faculties.
Furthermore, from "the five below" to "seven," the refutation is based on their shared nature. Consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) is the subject (*dharmin*); it has the manas as its co-existent [basis].

This is the fundamental principle. Since it is subsumed under the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*), it is the cause; this is illustrated by the way the five consciousnesses depend upon the five sense organs.

If the five sense organs were themselves the seeds of the five consciousnesses, then the manas would likewise have to be the seed of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Why? Because they [the proponents of that view] treat the five sense organs as being of the same nature (the *sapakṣa*).
Since the manas is not the seed of the mental consciousness, how could the five sense organs be the seeds of the five consciousnesses?
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that from the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) up to the [other] five consciousnesses, there should be only two bases for their seeds.
Moreover, the lower section of the *Yogācāra* refutes [the theory] by means of three bases: the seeds of consciousness are the immediate causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) basis;

the sense organs (*indriya*) are the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) basis; and the immediately preceding ceased mind (*manas*) is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) basis. If the sense organ were itself the consciousness...

This would mean that the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) serves as the immediate cause (*samanantara-pratyaya*). This contradicts the two [conditions] that should apply according to the *Abhidharmakośa* and the three conditions upon which it relies.

Furthermore, it contradicts all the holy teachings (*āgama*) which state that the eye and other faculties [function] up to [the point where they produce consciousness]. Thus, it would contradict all the holy teachings.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover, the various lower [stages]" refers to the nine [faculties] in terms of both their manifest and seed states. According to the sacred teachings, the five manifest sense-faculties serve as the simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*) for the five consciousnesses;
therefore, to maintain that the faculties exist only as seeds is contradictory, because seeds remain latent and cannot serve as supports for consciousness.
Thus, the two positions are in conflict.
There is an avoidance of the aforementioned faults (up to the point where it) "exquisitely accords with" the two verses, thereby well conforming to the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Below, there is an avoidance that brings forth a partisan defense: "The seeds of predominant karma" refers to the retributive karma (*pūrṇakarma*) produced by the five consciousnesses, which perfumes the ripening habitual tendencies (*vipākavāsanā*) and in turn induces the indeterminate five consciousnesses; these very seeds of karma are called the "five faculties" (*pañcendriya*). They function as...

The eye-consciousness and other consciousnesses arise based on their respective predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Since they take the seeds of predominant karma as their root, it is logical that the twenty types of consciousness arise from their own seeds.
Furthermore, it is logical that the functional capacity described in the treatises is designated as the five faculties (*indriya*).

These do not act as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the arising of the seeds of the five consciousnesses; rather, these seeds serve only as predominant conditions and not as causal conditions. Moreover, this is in full accord with the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Third, regarding the basis: previously, it was held that the seeds of consciousness are the five sense-faculties (*indriya*). Now, it is stated that the seeds of karma are called faculties because the seeds of karma within consciousness are designated as the "consciousness link" (*vijñāna-aṅga*).
Thus, while the former refers to the seeds of consciousness and the latter refers to the seeds of karma, both are termed "consciousness.
Nevertheless, one still maintains that the seeds of consciousness are named the five material sense-faculties.
That [position] contains empty words and lacks any real meaning (up to the point where it is said that the eyes and so forth should not be understood as comprising both the manifest and the seeds).

Regarding the phrase "That [position] contains... and below, there are likewise nine refutations. Six points are identical to those previously mentioned; three points differ slightly from the previous ones.

Here, the confusion between the elements (*dhātu*) and the seeds (*bīja*), as well as the mixing of the direct and the indirect, has been omitted. Regarding the three bases (*āśraya*) discussed in the treatise, the latter three are sufficient for the preceding [analysis].

This can be seen from the text. The first phrase critiques the sense-faculty (*indriya*) by asserting that it must pertain to all three moral natures (*trividha*). The second phrase critiques the sense-faculty by asserting that it must not be appropriated (*anupātta*).
The character "not" (*fei*) extends through the following two phrases: if the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) were the sense-faculty, it would not be subsumed under form (*rūpa*);

if the "image-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) were the sense-faculty, it would not be subsumed under the internal (*ādhyātmika*). For the section on the nose and tongue, one phrase must be supplemented: consciousness follows the sense-faculty.
It should also pertain to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the phrase "the three faculties," one sentence should be added below it. Consciousness follows the faculties;

it should not be restricted to only two stages. As for the statement that the karma which brings about the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) should be [associated with] the manas, this is because those [five faculties] share the same nature as the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*).
To illustrate this clearly: the karma that induces the five consciousnesses should correspond to the five sense organs. The word "should" (*ying*) here is used ironically.
If the karma that induces the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) were not the manas, then how could the karma that induces the five consciousnesses be the five sense organs?
If the eyes and other organs were merely seeds, they would be unable to serve as the support for consciousness, which would contradict the scriptures.
Furthermore, [the opponent's position] must entail that the eyes and so forth are not material faculties (*rūpendriya*). Thus, what they have said does not constitute a sound defense.

Regarding the point that "the eyes and so forth are not material faculties," this refutes [their position] by pointing out the confusion between the characteristics of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

If the seeds of karma are designated as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and one insists on regarding them as faculties, then those faculties would not be subsumed under the category of matter. Furthermore, the phrase "if [it were] below" reiterates that all consciousness is produced by the influence of karma; this refutes [the opponent's view] by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The five consciousnesses pertain to all three natures. That which is produced by karma is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

If they were all produced by karma, they would necessarily be restricted to the indeterminate alone and could not pertain to the wholesome or the defiled. Below, [the author] refutes [the opponent's position] regarding their basis (*āśraya*).

Building upon the preceding point that the indeterminate five consciousnesses are produced by karma and possess the eyes and so forth as their dominant and co-existent bases (*adhipati-sahabhū-āśraya*), [the author] applies this by analogy to the wholesome and defiled five [consciousnesses].
Since consciousness is not produced by karma, it would follow that it lacks the eye and other faculties as its dominant and co-existent supports (*adhipati-sahabhū-āśraya*).
Therefore, the latter phrase serves as a concluding rebuke. To claim that karmic seeds serve as its root is not a sound defense.
Furthermore, throughout various sacred teachings it is stated [down to] that such delusions and errors deeply contradict the scriptural principles and logic.

The phrase "Moreover, all... concludes by refuting the contradiction of scriptural principles. First, the scripture is cited: the teaching states that the *ālayavijñāna* transforms into the sense organs, the body, and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
If one claims that there are no distinct eyes and so forth serving as simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*), this is a denial of reality. This...
This deeply contradicts the teachings. Allowance is granted for the five objects (*viṣaya*) under the eyes; next, the reasoning is cited. The first sentence presents an example:

since the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are allowed to manifest as the five objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) as their objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*), why is it not allowed that the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) manifests the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) as its objective parts? This deeply contradicts reason.
The second line concludes the reprimand.

However, the *gāthā* explains the functional capacity of seeds (up to the point where it says) that it does not mean the physical sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) are themselves the karmic seeds of consciousness.
"However, in the *gāthā*" below refutes errors by citing a verse; the first line of that verse cites both lines of the verse text. "In order to refute" below presents both [arguments].
The meaning of the two verses is as the text states. It does not refer to a single sentence; rather, they jointly conclude and rebuke the first and the last schools.
"That the faculty is itself the seed of consciousness" rebukes the first school. "That the faculty is itself the seed of karma" rebukes the school that offers a defense.

Furthermore, regarding the clear mental consciousness that takes the five objects as its conditions—up to the point where they mutually rely on one another due to the equality of their power—it also takes what is below it as its condition.
This refers to the coexistent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) of the clear mental consciousness; that is, the mental consciousness takes the five sensory consciousnesses as its coexistent support.

This is because the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the five [sensory] consciousnesses share the same object of perception. As for the phrase "If that... and so forth, it reiterates and mutually clarifies the co-existent supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*).
The first sentence means: if the visual and other consciousnesses do not serve as the co-existent support for that mental consciousness.
The second phrase means that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) should likewise not serve as the simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) for the five sensory consciousnesses.

Why? The subsequent phrase, "because they are mutually [related]," explains the meaning of their mutual dependence. Regarding "their powers being equal": the mental consciousness takes the five sensory consciousnesses as its gate of clarity, while the five sensory consciousnesses take the mental consciousness as their basis of discrimination.
Furthermore, although the seventh consciousness is uninterrupted [until], it is subsumed within the eighth consciousness as it manifests.
Furthermore, below this, the co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) of the seventh consciousness is explained.

According to the first school’s judgment, there is no distinct support for the seventh and eighth consciousnesses because they function in constant continuity, and the seventh possesses superior autonomous power. Now, this text generally states that although the seventh [consciousness] is uninterrupted...

"Abandonment and so forth" refers to the stages from the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) up to the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), because outflows (*āsrava*) and outflow-free states arise in alternation. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The seventh consciousness is the subject (*dharmin*);

it possesses a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), this is the thesis (*pakṣa*); because it is included within the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), this is the reason (*hetu*); the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like the six consciousnesses.

If it were not so—that is, if the seventh [consciousness] lacked a simultaneous support (sahabhū-āśraya)—then that seventh consciousness would not be subsumed under the category of evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna).
If one holds the position that there is no simultaneous support, this reason commits the fallacy of the thesis being unestablished (asiddha-sādhya-dharma). This would contradict reason.

If it were not subsumed under the *pravṛtti-vijñānas* as a cause, it would further incur the fault of contradicting the sacred teachings; therefore, one must conclude that the eighth consciousness is taken as its simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), thereby avoiding contradiction with both scripture and reasoning.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, because the ālayavijñāna exists (up to) "thereby their [arguments] contradict both reason and scripture.

In the passage beginning with "As in the *Yoga*," the proof is cited according to the text. In the section beginning with "That treatise," the intended meaning of the treatise is set forth: namely, that it previously relied upon that [ālayavijñāna] for its operation.
Otherwise—that is, if the seventh consciousness did not take the eighth as its co-existent support (*sahabhv-āśraya*)—the seventh would not [function].

[The opponent replies: "The treatise should state that because the ālayavijñāna exists, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) can undergo transformation. This single phrase serves as a concluding rebuke;
however, it still retains the aforementioned faults of contradicting both reason and scripture."

Therefore, it should be said that the first five *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (up to the point of their own establishment) lack simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*) because they are established by themselves.
Thus, below, the simultaneous supports of all consciousnesses are summarized and determined; their number, presence, and absence are as stated in the text.
One interpretation holds that this explanation has not yet exhausted the principle (up to the point where it asks): "What fault is there in their being mutually dependent?

Another interpretation follows below; this is the third school’s explanation. The first sentence refutes the preceding [view]. It establishes the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "The eighth consciousness is the *dharmin* (subject)."

There is a school that maintains the doctrine of simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*). Because it is subsumed under the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*), it serves as the reason; the example is like other forms of consciousness. The seventh [consciousness] below explains that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses serve as mutual supports.
It is accepted that manifesting consciousness takes seeds as its support, because the seeds of consciousness do not grow, develop, or abide apart from them.
This permits the present [discussion]. It clarifies the eighth type: the mutual dependence of the manifest and the seeds.

The first phrase cites and clarifies that the manifest consciousness depends on seeds, because if its own seeds did not exist, the manifest consciousness would not arise. The second phrase illustrates by analogy that the seeds must depend on the manifest;

this is because the manifest consciousness is able to grasp and maintain them, causing the seeds to abide. "The perfuming [consciousness]" and so forth explain in turn and establish that the seeds depend on the manifest consciousness, as follows:
The first seven manifest consciousnesses act as the perfumers (*vāsaka*), causing the seeds within the eighth consciousness to grow, develop, and abide. As the subsequent text states:
"In the initial stage of perfuming, the eighth consciousness is also the perfumed (*vāsya*) based upon the perfumers; it is therefore called the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*)."

Regarding the term "basis" (*āśraya*): it specifically refers to the perfuming consciousness (*vāsaka-vijñāna*) as the basis, because the seeds depend upon it for their arising, growth, and persistence.
The subsequent phrase provides a counter-explanation.

Furthermore, within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the maturation consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*)—[up to]—or the reason established [for its existence] may suffer from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, [the text] differs from what follows below. It clarifies that the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness) also relies upon the material sense-faculties (*rūpindriya*). The initial passage concerning "the mind" (*manas*) cites a sūtra to provide scriptural support for the fact that the maturation-consciousness universally relies upon all sense-faculties.
The section beginning with "The *Yogācārabhūmi*" cites a treatise to provide a counter-proof that the visual consciousness and other cognitions each rely upon their respective distinct bases.

The passage beginning with "If it were otherwise" restates the intent of the treatise to clarify that if the maturation-consciousness did not universally rely upon all sense-faculties, it would have to be like...

The six consciousnesses are not the appropriating subject. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The subject (*dharmin*) is the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth;

the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they cannot appropriate the body possessing material sense-faculties; the reason (*hetu*) is "because they have distinct bases"; the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). Furthermore, the subject is the ripening consciousness;
the thesis is that it also cannot appropriate the body possessing material sense-faculties; the reason is "because it has a distinct base"; the example is like [the six consciousnesses].
The six consciousnesses are not like this regarding their maturation (*vipāka*). [If it were so,] they would be able to grasp and maintain the sense organs and the body.

If they were able to grasp and maintain them, then because the reason—"because they each have a distinct basis"—would apply to the established [six consciousnesses], there would be the fallacy of being "inconclusive due to commonality" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The subject (*dharmin*) is the maturation-consciousness;

the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is capable of grasping and maintaining [the body]; the reason (*hetu*) is "because it has a distinct basis"; the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like the six consciousnesses. Thus, this "distinct basis" is one [common factor].

[The reason] is that it would follow that the six consciousnesses could not perform the function of appropriation (*upādāna*), and it would follow that the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) alone could perform the function of appropriation;

thus, there is the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). To avoid this inconclusive fallacy, one must establish a separate reason: "because [it] must universally rely upon all the sense faculties (*indriya*).
By virtue of this scriptural authority and reasoning, it is proven that the ripening consciousness must universally rely upon all the sense faculties.
Therefore, when the ālayavijñāna manifests (up to) it also relies on the perfuming agents; the rest is as previously explained.

"Therefore" below concludes the determination that all consciousnesses have simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*). The manifest ālayavijñāna relies on the seventh [consciousness]; this is the aforementioned mutual reliance between the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses].
Furthermore, it relies on the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*); this is the aforementioned reliance on the material sense organs in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
The transformation of the seeds of the *ālayavijñāna* depends upon the manifest maturation (*vipāka*). This is the same as the aforementioned seeds depending upon the manifest consciousness;

it also depends upon the perfuming agents (*vāsana*). This refers to the aforementioned perfuming agents taking the maturation as their basis for growth, development, and maintenance. As for the remaining five, six, and seven consciousnesses, they are to be determined according to the previous analysis.
There is one interpretation that all the preceding explanations are unreasonable (up to the point where it says "like a king and his ministers mutually depending on one another," etc.).

There is another interpretation [found] below, which is the explanation of the fourth school. The first phrase is a general refutation of the various previous schools; the second phrase sets forth the intent of that refutation.

Because the "basis" (āśraya) and the "based upon" (āśrita) have not yet been distinguished, the term "basis" is general while the "based upon" is specific. The former school spoke of them as a confused "basis," failing to distinguish between the general and the specific.
Now, these two are presented with the intention of setting aside the general and adopting the specific. First, the "basis" is explained:

that which possesses the nature of arising and ceasing refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), whether form (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*), which are all subject to the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Because of their transmigration, these phenomena arise and abide by relying upon causes and depending upon conditions. The causes relied upon are direct, as they are the specific seeds of the phenomena themselves;
the conditions depended upon are indirect, as they provide auxiliary assistance. Although there is a direct cause, [the conditions are necessary].
If there is no auxiliary support, then production cannot occur. Although auxiliary conditions may be present, if there is no primary seed, production likewise cannot occur.
Therefore, the cause must rely upon conditions, and conditions must rely upon the cause; only through this mutual dependence of these two can phenomena be produced.

This makes no distinction between those who are close or distant; all are termed "reliances" (*āśraya*). To establish the formal argument (*prayoga*): "All things that arise and perish, which serve as supports and dependencies, are the subject (*dharmin*).
They are all asserted to be 'reliances,' this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). Because they depend upon one another, this is the reason (*hetu*). It is like a king and his ministers:
the king relies on the ministers' assistance for governance, and the ministers rely on the monarch for their commands to be executed; therefore, it is said they are mutually dependent."
If a phenomenon is determinate, possesses an object, and acts as a sovereign—like a king rather than a minister—then [it is a primary condition].
Next, the basis is explained. In the initial passage, four meanings of the "basis" are first established. "Determinate" means definitely existing;
it excludes that which is not determinate, such as things that may or may not exist. "Possessing an object" means having the sense of illuminating an object.
Therefore, that which acts as the sovereign is so because it operates with mastery, independent of other forces.

That which causes the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) to apprehend their objects is so because it possesses the functional capacity to initiate the mind and mental factors, causing each to perceive its respective domain. Possessing these four meanings, that alone is the support;
namely, the six internal bases (*ādhyātmika-ṣaḍāyatana*). This phrase defines the essence, referring to the six sense faculties (*indriya*), which uniquely manifest their own [respective] spheres.
The term "basis for the superior arising of the locus of names" excludes everything else that is not inferior. The word "else" (餘) indicates the things being excluded:

namely, the five sense objects such as form (*rūpa*), seeds, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), mental factors (*caitta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). These are not "possessors of an object" (*saviṣaya*).

This excludes the five sensory objects such as form and their seeds. Sensory objects are the *ālambana* (objects of cognition); they lack the capacity to cognize. Seeds are excluded because they remain latent.
"Not fixed" (*aniyata*) excludes the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), the primary minds (*citta-rāja*), because these are intermittent and not constantly present.

"Not being the master" (*asvāmika*) excludes mental factors (*caitta*), because they depend upon the primary mind and lack autonomy. Non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are incapable of...
Because it causes the mind and mental factors to apprehend their respective objects, an analogy is given: this "letter" refers to the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
It is like a king who serves only as a basis and is not the dependent; he is not like a minister, who is both the dependent and the basis.

Therefore, in the various holy teachings, it is said that "only mind and mental factors" (up to) "or taking their support as their support," all of which are provisional designations made according to the occasion.

The phrase "therefore, in the various... below cites the scriptures to establish this proof. The first sentence, "only mind and mental factors are called 'having a support' (*sāśraya*)," proves the six internal bases;
that is to say, mind and mental factors all arise in dependence upon the faculties. The phrase "not matter... and so forth proves the distinction of meaning.

"Form and so forth"—the "and so forth" includes other objects (*viṣaya*) as well as seeds. The phrase "that which has no object" serves as a counter-illustration to show that there is no corresponding subject (*ālambaka*).

The words "only [the mind] below" prove that the mind is the support (*āśraya*), thereby distinguishing it from mental factors (*caitta*), which are not supports because they lack the nature of being a sovereign.

While the previous establishment of the support took only the six sense organs (*indriya*), why is the "sovereign mind" (*cittarāja*) included here among the supporting proofs? This is because... [the previous section].

Because it refers to the immediate, non-common basis (*asādhāraṇa-upastambha*), it takes only the sense-faculties (*indriya*). Because this refers to its remote basis, it includes the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as well.

Furthermore, while the first five rely on material faculties (*rūpīndriya*), the latter three rely on the mind; thus, there is a lower [level] that universally addresses these objections, which may be understood accordingly.
Because these five consciousnesses possess a simultaneous support (upastambha-āśraya), and because they must necessarily share the same object and be closely concordant.

From the phrase "by this" onwards, the supports of the various consciousnesses are summarized and determined. First, the supports of the first five [consciousnesses] are explained. Regarding "sharing the same object":

it means that the sense organ and the consciousness have the same object. Regarding "non-discriminative": it means that the first five [consciousnesses], when perceiving objects, do not engage in distinct analytical discrimination; this is due to the sixth [consciousness].

"Pointing with a finger": because it clearly distinguishes [objects]. "Defiled and pure": because the seventh consciousness, through its grasping or non-grasping, causes the defilement or purity of the preceding six to follow accordingly; thus, the six are called the "basis of defilement and purity. "Root":
because the seeds of all consciousnesses are gathered and stored by the eighth, just as a tree has a root. Below, the sacred teachings reconcile these differences.
Regarding "exclusive" (*asādhāraṇa*): for example, the eye-faculty is the exclusive support (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*) of visual consciousness because it is not shared with other consciousnesses;

the same applies to all other consciousnesses by analogy. Regarding "proximate" (*āsanna*): the latter three supports [the mind-faculty] are considered distant, whereas the faculties are proximate. Regarding "conformable" (*anukūla*): the faculty and consciousness are conformable because they share the same object;
the remaining three [supports] each rely on a different meaning when termed "support," and therefore "conformable" is not mentioned.
The sixth consciousness has a simultaneous support (sahabhū-āśraya) [which extends to] being subsumed under the same category of evolving consciousnesses, because they are closely concordant.

Regarding "the sixth" below: this clarifies the supports of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The seventh [consciousness] is its simultaneous faculty (*indriya*), and it is also the support for both defilement and purification.
The eighth fundamental basis: although the five lower [senses] are mentioned, this clarifies that the five consciousnesses are not taken as the basis for the mind (*manas*).

If it is a simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it may require the five consciousnesses; if it is a mental consciousness that arises sequentially, it does not require the five consciousnesses, being either present or absent.
Therefore, it is said to be indeterminate. Regarding the "inferior scriptural teachings" below, the reconciliation of differences follows the text.
As for the seventh consciousness, its co-existent support (from [text] until... is the mind and the mental faculty (*manas*); upon these, the other evolving consciousnesses arise.
Section Seven: The Lower Part. This clarifies the support (*āśraya*) of the *manas*. The first passage clarifies that the eighth consciousness serves as its support;
the subsequent phrase provides a negative illustration. The treatise states: "Because the *ālayavijñāna* always functions simultaneously with one consciousness.

As in the verse below, this cites evidence that the eighth consciousness is the support for the seventh. The section beginning with "Depending on" provides general proof that the six evolving consciousnesses depend upon both the seventh and the eighth.
The *ālayavijñāna* has a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*)... [omitted] ...it is not that there is no eighth consciousness; this case should also be understood in the same way.
From "The *ālaya*" below, it clarifies the support of the eighth consciousness. The first section clarifies the seventh consciousness as its support. From "That consciousness" below...

This serves as a counter-illustration. To cite the treatise for proof, it says "and below," which addresses potential objections. Question: It was previously stated that the manas does not exist in three states;
in what then does the eighth consciousness rely? Answer: As the text explains, the meaning is as follows.

The "three states" refer to the stage of an Arhat, the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), and the supramundane path. "Defiled" refers to the afflicted manas (kliṣṭa-manas). The "four states" refer to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
From the eighth stage of the bodhisattva upward, as well as at the stage of the Tathāgata,
although they possess the form realm and likewise rely upon the five sense faculties, while the sense of "relying" may exist, there is no actual basis upon which to rely.

Although there are lower [positions], they are refuted by the preceding alternative interpretation. As for the five sense faculties not being necessarily present: they do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

As for the seeds of consciousness being unable to apprehend present objects: they remain latent within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Therefore, none of these are the support (*āśraya*).

Regarding the basis (*āśraya*) of mental factors (*caitta*), it should be explained according to consciousness (*vijñāna*). [The text continues] up to: "If one explains it in this way, it perfectly accords with both reason and scripture.

Below the section on "mental factors," it clarifies that mental factors follow the primary mind (*citta-rāja*) in stating their basis; furthermore, the primary mind itself is added. Below the section beginning with "If one explains... is the conclusion.

Regarding the subsequent explanation of the *āśraya-pravartaka* (the inducing basis), there are three interpretations concerning the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) having only their own kind as their inducing basis.
First, the explanation of the initial school: the first phrase clarifies that the five consciousnesses are all incapable of serving as an inducing basis.
Regarding "self and other": visual consciousness is "self" in relation to visual consciousness, but it is "other" in relation to auditory consciousness.

Next, the following two lines clarify that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) must necessarily serve as the "opening-and-guiding support" (*āśraya*). Below this, the sixth section clarifies the opening-and-guiding support of the sixth [consciousness].
The first line clarifies that the independent mental consciousness (*nirūpakālambana-manovijñāna*) arises from its own continuity;

the second line clarifies that the simultaneous mental consciousness is induced by the preceding five [sensory consciousnesses]. The final line below summarizes that the mental consciousness is preceded by these six.
This serves as the basis for the opening and guiding [of consciousness]. Next, it clarifies that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses each open and guide their own respective classes.

One interpretation holds that the previous explanation has not yet fully investigated the principle; [it applies] until one encounters a non-superior object, at which point it may be as previously stated.

There is an interpretation according to the *Xià* (下) school, which explains the passage in sequence. The first phrase is a general refutation. The section beginning with "Furthermore, as for the preceding... provides a concession (*yǒng*).

"Those not in the state of mastery" refers to the stage of outflows (*sāsrava*). "Not being a superior object" refers to a subtle and inferior object. Based on these two meanings, it can be said that the five consciousnesses do not continue in succession.
If one is in a state of mastery, such as that of the Buddhas and others, why not allow for a continuity of many moments?

If [the argument is] from a lower perspective, first, regarding the state of mastery: "The various sense faculties function interchangeably" refutes the lack of continuity between the five consciousnesses and other [faculties].
"Spontaneously and determinately" refutes the lack of continuity within the five consciousnesses themselves. "Seeking" refers to the mental faculty (*manas*).
Regarding "dharmas associated with consciousness," the term "not dependent" clarifies that in the untainted (anāsrava) state, the five consciousnesses are not induced by the mental consciousness;

rather, those five consciousness-bodies are able to continue in a stream of their own accord. The following section on "equal outflow" (niṣyanda), however, still explains this in reference to the tainted (sāsrava) state.

Within the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there are five stages of mind: first, sudden encounter (*ābhoga*); second, seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*); third, determination (*niścaya*); fourth, defilement or purity (*kliṣṭa-viśuddha*); and fifth, equal outflow (*niṣyanda*).
The flow [of consciousness] is as follows: when the visual consciousness first encounters an object, it is termed "sudden" (*sa-er*) and belongs to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Subsequently, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) seeks out the object; having sought it, it then determines whether the object is beautiful or ugly, good or evil, and so forth. Having made this determination, [the process continues].
Immediately, a defiled or pure mind arises. Subsequently, the visual consciousness becomes defiled if it follows a defiled [mind], or pure if it follows a pure one;
this is called "equal outflow" (*niṣyanda*). The first and last moments are visual consciousness, while the three intermediate moments are mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Since the visual consciousness of equal outflow has been induced by these three moments of mental consciousness, as long as it remains focused on its object and has not yet relinquished it—this passage clarifies that although the five consciousnesses arise from...
It is induced by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and does not shift toward other objects; it can also continue through its own power. How so?
One sentence [from the text] refutes the preceding five consciousnesses because they do not continue from self to other or from prior to subsequent moments.

This section still explains this in terms of the state with outflows (*sāsrava*), because there is no defilement in the state of mastery (*vaśitā-avasthā*), whereas in the state with outflows, there is a provisional seeking.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that after a determinative mind (*niścaya-citta*), [the subsequent moment arises]; thus, it is not the case that two consciousnesses arise in mutual succession.
Consequently, the *Yogācāra* text below cites scriptural evidence: "When the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is defiled, the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) functions unwholesomely;

when the mental consciousness is pure, the visual consciousness functions wholesomely. This explains that the visual consciousness takes the mental consciousness as its basis for conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

"Producing [the subsequent moment] and not proceeding toward other objects" clarifies that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises in the same manner as the eye-consciousness in relation to visible forms, rather than proceeding toward other objects such as sounds or odors.
"Whether wholesome or defiled" clarifies that these two consciousnesses function with the same nature, as explained below.

The same applies to the remaining consciousnesses as well. In the passage beginning with "That mind... [the author] judges that the two consciousnesses—the mental consciousness and the visual consciousness—arise simultaneously.

The mental consciousness arises from its own continuum, and the visual consciousness likewise arises from its own continuum. Since the phrase "following the eye" cites the simultaneity of these two aforementioned consciousnesses, it is not a single [independent] statement.
It refutes the previous view that the sixth and the five [sensory] consciousnesses mutually induce one another's arising.
If an intense object-continuum manifests before one—as in the case of the hot hells or the *krīḍāpramoṣaka* gods—and so forth;
or if it is less intense: next, the intense object is explained. In the hot hells, the object of suffering is intense; among the *krīḍāpramoṣaka* gods, the object of pleasure is intense.
Since the object is thus intense and continuous, the five consciousnesses directed toward it also continue in succession.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "If these six consciousnesses... (up to "...therefore we know that the five consciousnesses possess the meaning of continuity").

Thus, the *Yogācāra* [text] below cites scriptural evidence. Here, "this" refers to the preceding moment; "that" refers to the succeeding moment. Because it possesses the sense of inducing the production of the subsequent [moment] through immediate contiguity (*samanantara*), it is called the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
If the five [consciousnesses], etc., reiterates the first school's view that the five and the sixth mutually serve as the opening and guiding conditions. That...

In the commentary below, he cites treatises to refute [the opponent]. The first phrase refutes the claim that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) induces the five sensory consciousnesses; the second phrase refutes the claim that the five sensory consciousnesses induce the mental consciousness.
Since this is not the case, it is concluded that the five sensory consciousnesses constitute their own independent continuity.

When the five consciousnesses arise, they must necessarily have the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) [as their antecedent condition]... [it] should also serve as their "opening and guiding" support (*kṣaṇika-āśraya*).

Below the section on the five consciousnesses, it clarifies that the mental consciousness opens and guides [the five] by being induced by a simultaneous mental consciousness of its own kind. Why rely on the following phrase?

It refutes the previous view that the mental consciousness is opened and guided by the five [sensory consciousnesses]. During the five states of non-mindfulness (*acittaka*), [the mental consciousness] is induced by the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses].
If that [consciousness] employs its own preceding class to open the way [for the subsequent], this [case] is not so;

how then could that be? From "If that" onwards, the two schools mutually challenge one another. The first school, conceding the challenge, says: "In the state of no-mind (*acittaka*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is induced by its own preceding class;
