why then rely on the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] to induce it? The second school cites that challenging statement and counters with a refutation:
The five consciousnesses should likewise be admitted to [arise] from their own kind; why then rely on the mental consciousness to induce them?
Since this is not the case, this statement [of yours]—even if those five consciousnesses do not require their own kind—is refuted by the following:
how can it be that the mental consciousness alone must require its own kind?
The manas associated with the wisdom of equality first arises (up to: it should also take that [wisdom] as its leading support (*āśraya*).

"Equality" and below clarify the leading support of the seventh [consciousness]. When the manas first undergoes transformation at the stage of reliance, it achieves the transformation from defilement to purity through the cultivation of the contemplation of the two emptinesses by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); therefore, it takes the mental consciousness as its leading support.

The eighth pure consciousness, which is co-existent with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna), [is discussed] from here up to the point where it says: "Because of this, those words do not at all investigate the principle.

Below the section on the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, it clarifies that the eighth [consciousness] provides the guidance for the initial arising of the stainless consciousness (amala-vijñāna). This occurs because, through the sixth consciousness, one cultivates the contemplation of self-emptiness;

consequently, the seventh consciousness no longer functions as the grasping of a self, the afflictive hindrances (kleśāvaraṇa) are extinguished, and for the first time, the name "storehouse" (ālaya) is abandoned. This is due to the cultivation by the sixth consciousness...

Through the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), the seventh [consciousness]—the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*)—no longer functions; the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) are extinguished, and subsequently, the maturation (*vipāka*) of emptiness arises.

Therefore, it is said that "the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] are induced by skillful means. Furthermore, the contaminated maturation (*sāsrava-vipāka*) evolves with the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) as its co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).

Moreover, it relies upon a virtuous mind associated with compassion and the vow (*karuṇā-praṇidhāna*); this compassion and vow are dharmas associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is...

Because it functions in accordance with the sixth consciousness’s projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), it is said that the sixth and seventh consciousnesses serve as the "opening and guiding supports" (*āśraya*). By this statement, [the opponent's position] is generally refuted.
One should explain that among the six consciousnesses, the five consciousnesses [precede the sixth]; [this] does not contradict the reason previously stated.
It should be stated below. This concludes the determination of the opening and guiding supports (*āśraya*) for the various consciousnesses. The *Kaimeiyun* (Opening the Ignorant) states:

"Regarding the five consciousnesses, whichever among the first six they employ, one knows that the first five have six layers of support. Regarding the sixth consciousness, it employs its own kind as well as the seventh and eighth;
thus one knows it has three layers of support. Regarding the seventh consciousness, it employs its own kind as well as the sixth; thus one knows it has two [layers of support]."
It is based on a triple support (*tri-āśraya*). The eighth [consciousness] employs its own kind as well as the sixth and seventh; thus, it is known that there is a triple support.

One interpretation holds that this statement is also unreasonable, because [the nature of the storehouse consciousness] belongs solely to the mind (*citta*) and not to mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth.

The section beginning with "There is another interpretation" (*yǒu yì xià*) presents the third school’s explanation. The first phrase refutes the preceding view. Regarding the term "opening and guiding" (*kāidǎo*), it requires that [the seeds] be of the same class (*zǒnglèi*) and not simultaneous.
This excludes the simultaneous arising of different classes. According to the first school, the five consciousnesses do not continue from themselves or others; thus, they rely entirely on others.

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) continues from itself, yet also depends on the preceding five; thus, it utilizes both self and other. The seventh and eighth consciousnesses continue from their own respective classes; thus, they rely entirely [on themselves].

The first [position] holds that [the mind] uses only itself; thus, the former is incorrect and the latter is correct. The second school maintains that the various consciousnesses open and guide one another, using both themselves and others;

this [position] contains both what is correct and what is incorrect. The third school maintains that cognitions of the same kind do not arise simultaneously and all exclusively use themselves; this is solely correct and not incorrect.

Deeply conforming to the principles of the teachings, he refutes the preceding view by stating: "That too is not reasonable. Regarding the phrase "opening and guiding" (*ānudharmya*), he first establishes the correct definition of the essence of the "opening and guiding" factor:

(1) because it possesses an object of cognition (*ālambana*); (2) because it is sovereign and capable of acting as a master; and (3) because it functions as an immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
If that which is an immediately antecedent condition were not an "opening and guiding" factor, then this name would be overly broad (*atiprasaṅga*), extending even to the [primary] king.
For this reason, if these were not "opening and guiding" (āvakāśa-pradāna), the designation would be too narrow, as it would apply only to the primary mind (*citta-rāja*).

This term refers to the preceding moment of the primary mind which possesses the power to open and guide, thereby causing the subsequent moments of the primary mind and its mental factors (*caitta*) to arise.
Since this "opening and guiding" dependence belongs exclusively to the primary mind, it does not apply to mental factors or, by extension, to material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*). [This avoids...]
[The character] "zi" (字) should be read as "pi" (闢).

If this [consciousness] and that [consciousness] lack the sense of arising together—up to the point where it would be identical to the schools that maintain minds do not arise simultaneously—then, from "If this...
onwards, the correct principle of "opening and guiding" (*kaidō*) is presented to refute the erroneous view. "This and that" refers to those of the same category (*svajāti*).
This refers to the preceding and succeeding moments of thought. "There is no simultaneous arising" excludes those that are not contemporaneous;

it means that for there to be the two meanings of being of the same kind and not arising together, there must be the power of opening and guiding. Regarding "in a single body" below, this refutes the previous point. If the eight consciousnesses are viewed in relation to one another, they lack the meaning of being of the same kind.
If they arise together within a single body, they lack the meaning of not arising together. This [passage] concedes their simultaneous arising; how then can [the term] "below" be applied?

[This] sentence negates their being of different types, refuting the fault that the preceding consciousnesses would mutually act as one another’s equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

If it were granted that [the ālayavijñāna] serves as the support, then even if they were of different types, they should not arise simultaneously; thus, [this statement] negates their simultaneous arising. If they do not arise simultaneously...

Consequently, minds do not arise simultaneously; thus, it is refuted [by the opponent] by saying that this is equivalent to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), because the Lesser Vehicle allows only for a single consciousness to possess the functions of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing.
Furthermore, among the various consciousnesses arising simultaneously within a single body, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) applies only to mind and mental factors.
Moreover, even if the various consciousnesses are of different types—whether numerous or few—they may serve as equal-and-immediate conditions for one another.
Next, an example is raised to refute [this position]: Form and so forth are of a different category from the mind; they too should function as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*).
If form and so forth could serve as such conditions, it would further contradict the sacred teachings.
However, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that even matter (*rūpa*) can potentially serve as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for consciousnesses of a different category.

The word "however" (*ran*) at the beginning of the passage from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* introduces an objection raised by the treatise; it expresses a concessive refutation, which conveys the intent of the treatise. The phrase "it is said that...
(*jiǎ xià*) articulates the meaning of this concessive refutation. The Hīnayāna school maintains that matter and mind can mutually serve as direct causes for one another.
Regarding the condition (*pratyaya*): the treatise permits it as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) while denying it as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Otherwise, one might attempt to defend it, claiming that the wording does not permit it, but that it is in fact an equal-and-immediate condition. The word "equal" (*sama*) in the following phrase serves as a refutation. It is "equal" for three reasons: first, because their functional power (*vṛtti-bala*) is identical;

second, to exclude any inequality in quantity; and third, to indicate that they belong to the same category (*jāti*). If one were to say that matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) act as mutual opening and guiding conditions, [it would be untenable].

All three meanings are absent; therefore, it is said that [the argument] is useless. As for the phrase "if one says... and below, this restates the opponent's defense, which is not a refutation of the quantity [of consciousnesses].
Because one intends to establish multiple consciousnesses by citing a single consciousness, it merely expresses a similarity of kind; thus, among the three meanings, only one meaning is obtained.

Because the field is deficient in two respects. His statement that "homogeneous" refers to mind in relation to mind as being homogeneous—though he speaks of homogeneity, it actually results in heterogeneity.
Therefore, one refutes him by using "heterogeneous" as the equivalent immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). This uses his own words to state the refutation of his intended position.
Therefore, since each of the eight consciousnesses is exclusively of its own kind (up to the point where it is said that) the mental factors (caitta) must follow the consciousness in their basis.
Thus, the conclusion below follows the text. The mental factors also take the mind-king (cittarāja) as their opening and guiding cause; hence it is said they "follow the consciousness."
Although mind and mental factors arise simultaneously as distinct categories, [the case of] the various consciousnesses is not like this, and thus should not be used as an analogy.

Although the preceding section on "mind" generally addressed these objections, the objection here states: "The previous statement said that members of the same category do not arise together; now you say that mental factors follow the consciousness."
Is this not a case of different categories? Furthermore, since it arises simultaneously with the subsequent moment of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), is this not a case of co-arising?

The first phrase restates the objection; the following explains it by means of six points: because the king and its retinue correspond through mutual interaction—this "mutual" (*zhuǎnzhuǎn*) refers to their reciprocity, like the light of many lamps;

because they are blended together such that they are difficult to distinguish; because they arise and cease together with the king; and because the objective basis (*āśraya*) and the sensory faculty (*indriya*) are identical.
Therefore, because their objective conditions, spheres, and karmic functions are identical, when one [consciousness] opens the way, the others also open the way. That is to say:
one induces one aggregate, one aggregate recompenses one; one aggregate induces one, one recompenses one aggregate; one induces one, one recompenses one.
One aggregate induces one aggregate; one aggregate repays one aggregate. Therefore, the following phrase is expanded to conclude [the point]:

the preceding moment of the mind-king (citta-rāja) induces the subsequent moment of the king’s objective field (viṣaya), and this objective field, in turn, induces that [subsequent] objective field; hence it is called "successive" (*krama*). Regarding the passage beginning with "the various consciousnesses" (*sarva-vijñāna*):...
Question: Since the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is already able to induce mental factors (*caitta*) of a different category, it should likewise induce other mind-kings.
Answer: It is said that the various consciousnesses are not like this; when comparing one mind to another, all six criteria are absent, so they should not be taken as an analogy.
However, the mental factors (*caitta*) are not the "opening-and-leading" support (*āvedhaka-āśraya*). [This continues until: all minds and mental factors arise from four conditions.

Regarding the phrase "However, etc.": [this is] a question. As for the term "successive" (*krama*) mentioned above: just as a king acts as the opening-and-leading guide who leads [his subjects] to arise, do the subjects also successively act as the opening-and-leading guides for the king?

Regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that they are either six or ten, this difference is taught based on distinct meanings;

specifically, it is explained according to different perspectives. That is to say, "aspect" (*ākāra*) refers to the mode of activity, while "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) refers to what is associated with the sixth consciousness.

The coarse [defilements] are those associated with the seventh consciousness; the innate ones are called subtle. They are neutral, specifically "obscured-neutral" (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*). Regarding the twenty-two:
these consist of the twenty [secondary defilements] plus wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*) and wrong resolve (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*). The six and the ten specific meanings are as stated in the text.
This does not contradict the five universal [mental factors].

However, the fifteen mental factors associated with this [volition] consist of the aforementioned nine dharmas, the five secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the discernment (*prajñā*) among the object-specific factors (*viṣayaviśeṣa*).
From "However, below this" onwards, the author formally presents his own interpretation as follows:

Although the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is subsumed under the category of wisdom (*prajñā*) among the object-specific mental states (*viśeṣālambana*), it is divided into two because there is a distinction in their meaning.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "The view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence. As previously stated, there cannot be two instances of wisdom within a single moment of mind;

why, then, is it now said separately that [the view of self] is wisdom? Answer: The view of self is exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*), whereas wisdom permeates all three moral natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*).
Because their meanings are distinct. This is not the case for the various views (*dṛṣṭi*), as they are exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
For what reason does this *manas* lack other mental factors? [The reason] that it lacks other mental factors is as previously explained.

For what reason are they categorized as "lower"? This interrogative phrase serves to distinguish their specific meanings. "Anger" (*krodha*) and so forth are distinguished from the ten minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*) by way of their coarseness or subtlety.

"Lack of shame" (*āhrīkya*) and so forth are distinguished from the two intermediate [afflictions] by way of their dual natures. "Distraction" (*vikṣepa*) and so forth are distinguished from the three major derivative afflictions by way of being internal or external.

Within the text, "loss of mindfulness" (*muṣitasmṛti*) and "improper conduct" (*asamprajanya*) are omitted by ellipsis; these refer to the discipline of the five categories and seven groups of offenses. Because one knows what is improper, it causes the body and speech [to act accordingly].
Because one has committed many transgressions and the three karmas are impure, it is said that they have "violated" [the precepts]. Regarding the phrase "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*) and below:
this distinguishes the four categories of objects, the six root [offenses], the wholesome, and the indeterminate, as explained previously.
There is one interpretation that states there are six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) [and so forth], [concluding that] not all defiled minds are capable of giving rise to them universally.

There is another interpretation which explains this in the following section. First, it clarifies the association with the six secondary afflictions. Next, it cites the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* to list their names.

Finally, it clarifies the intention behind selecting three specific secondary afflictions; within this text, the terms "forgetfulness" (*muṣitasmṛti*) and "distraction" (*vikṣepa*) are explained through their contrapositives.

Dull wisdom (*dauṣprajña*) necessarily takes what is inferior as its object. To explain these three meanings in sequence: regarding "the category of previously experienced objects," one forgets the actual substance of the previously experienced object and takes a similar type of object as being real;
therefore, it is called "forgetfulness" (*muṣitasmṛtitā*). Dull wisdom is erroneous discernment, which is precisely "lack of clear comprehension" (*asaṃprajanya*).
Lethargy (*styāna*) and mental excitement (*auddhatya*) are distinguished from the two [preceding factors] by their lack of clarity and their being contrary to the mind's composure, respectively.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "five factors pervade the defiled mind" (up to the point where it says "ten [factors] pervade"), the meaning of the term "pervade" is as previously explained.

The passage in the *Śāstra* stating "below" refers collectively to the five pervasive factors of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. The passage stating "ten below" refers collectively to the ten pervasive factors of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
However, these nineteen mental factors associated with this mind— [from] "up to" (至) "and including mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom," as well as adding torpor—
will now be formally presented according to my own interpretation, as the text [proceeds].

This separate explanation of mindfulness (*smṛti*) should be understood according to the previous explanation of wisdom (*prajñā*). [The passage] up to "the remaining mental factors" should be understood as above.

Regarding this separate [explanation] below, an objection is raised: "In the preceding [section], forgetfulness was explained as having mindfulness as its essence; why then is mindfulness mentioned separately here?"

Answer: According to the interpretation of the *Zhunhui* (Commentary on the Meaning), among the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*), there are distinctions in their meaning. Forgetting (*muṣitasmṛti*) is exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*), whereas mindfulness (*smṛti*) pervades all three natures (*trividha*).
Furthermore, the phrase "and including the lower" explains the inclusion of concentration (*samādhi*); "including torpor and the lower" explains the inclusion of lethargy (*styāna*);

and "no restlessness and the lower" excludes restlessness (*auddhatya*). All of these follow the text. There are no other mental factors; [this includes] desire (*chanda*) and understanding (*adhimokṣa*) from among the object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*). And...
"Good. The [categories of] indeterminate and so forth are also explained as above.
According to another interpretation, it is further stated that the ten secondary afflictions (upakleśa) [extend] throughout all locations because they are bound to all three realms (*dhātu*).

There is an interpretation [stating] that the following three schools provide an explanation. First, the text clarifies the ten pervasive [afflictions]. Below, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* is cited to list their names:
"Because when there is no wrong desire or wrong resolve, the various afflictions such as greed do not arise. (up to this point).

If there were no "lower" [afflictions], this would clarify the addition of wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*) and wrong resolve (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*). The first passage explains by way of contrast; the section beginning with "at the object... explains in a direct manner.
Regarding "those who delight in union and separation": this wrong desire involves taking pleasure in the union of desirable objects and taking pleasure in the separation of undesirable objects.
Through wrong resolve, one determines a desirable object and gives rise to craving, and determines an undesirable object... [and gives rise to aversion].
[He] gives rise to anger.
Regarding those who doubt the principle [of the self], the meaning of the mutual presence and absence of entities such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth is as previously explained.

Regarding those who doubt what is inferior, it is said by way of objection: "The aforementioned statement that 'false understanding pervades all defiled minds' [applies here]; yet, as for the affliction of doubt (*vicikitsā*), regarding its object..."

[Question: "Anticipation" (*prekṣā*) is a distorted understanding (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*) that is determined with respect to its object. Why, then, is it said that distorted understanding pervades and defiles the mind? [Answer: It is replied: There are two kinds of doubt (*vicikitsā*):

doubt regarding principles (*tattva-vicikitsā*) and doubt regarding phenomena (*vastu-vicikitsā*). One gives rise to the affliction of doubt when there is indecision regarding a principle; one gives rise to distorted understanding when there is determination regarding a phenomenon.

Therefore, they can be associated [with the mind]. [Objection: Regarding the passage below, another objection is raised: "If one gives rise to doubt regarding a phenomenon, then as for the understanding..."
It does not exist. How are they associated? The answer says: to give rise to doubt regarding a principle (*nyāya*) is the affliction of doubt (*kleśa-vicikitsā*);
to be hesitant regarding a particular object (*vastu*) does not belong to the afflictions. To cite an example: it is like doubting whether something is a person or a tree stump;

because this is not an affliction, there is no contradiction with other treatises regarding the two types of non-pervasiveness mentioned below. The term "elsewhere" refers to the characteristic of doubt as the absence of desire when taking an unpleasant object as its condition.
Regarding the statement that "the mind has no resolve": this is said to be "non-existent" only in reference to coarse and superior forms of resolve; it does not mean they are entirely absent.
Even subtle and faint desires for resolution may be said to exist. This is like when one contemplates an unattractive object and wishes for non-attachment, or when one deliberates amidst doubt.

There are also determinate [factors]. Regarding "the others being mutually present or absent," this refers to the aforementioned five universal and six particular mental factors, discussing their mutual presence or absence.
This implies that there are twenty-four mental concomitants (caitta); as for those that are not universal, they should be understood as explained above.
From this point downward, the author formally presents his own interpretation as follows.
According to one interpretation, what was stated previously does not fully capture the underlying principle (extending to: "How can it cause afflictions to manifest?").
There is an interpretation [which states]: "The following four schools provide their exegesis. The first sentence generally refutes the various preceding schools.

Furthermore, "doubting the following" refutes the third school for adding "desire and resolve" (*chanda-adhimokṣa*). "Afflictions... refutes the second school for lacking "sloth and restlessness" (*styāna-auddhatya*). "If defiled... [refutes the first school].

Refuting the first position [which holds that there is no distraction, loss of mindfulness, or lack of clear comprehension], the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: Excitement (*auddhatya*) is the subject (*dharmin*);

it is not a state of defilement (*kliṣṭāvasthā*), this is the thesis (*pakṣa*); because it lacks agitation (*cañcalatva*), this is the reason (*hetu*); just like states such as the wholesome (*kuśalādi*), this is the example (*udāharaṇa*).
Therefore, defiled minds are invariably associated with [the universal mental factors] up to the pervasive defilements (*paryavasthāna*), as previously explained.

Thus, "defiled" and below, the correct doctrine is set forth, listing the eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) by name. Regarding "forgetfulness" (*muṣitasmṛti*) and below, the meaning of whether forgetfulness and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) are pervasive or non-pervasive is analyzed.
Forgetfulness is subsumed under one part of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and also subsumed under one part of delusion (*moha*). Lack of clear comprehension...

It is subsumed under a portion of wisdom (*prajñā*) and also subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*). If its essence were mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom, it would not pervade all defiled minds;
thus, it could not be established by the single phrase [of the definition]. If, however, its essence is ignorance (*avidyā*), then it pervades all defiled minds.
However, these eighteen mental factors associated with the mind (citta-samprayukta-caitta) [from "to" (至)]: if one explains it in this way, it does not contradict reason or scripture.

Now, from "however, these below," the number is concluded. Regarding the three treatises: the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* has five occurrences; the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* has six occurrences; and the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* has ten occurrences.
"According to the former [explanation]" means that the interpretation encompasses the distinct meanings of the coarse, the subtle, and so forth.
*Investigation of the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Four;
*Investigation of the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Five.
Recorded by Da-hui, disciple of Lianju in Lin-an. Regarding the phrase "What is the feeling associated with this defiled [manas]?"—this clarifies the associated feeling (*saṃprayukta-vedanā*).
This manas, like the aforementioned first transformative consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), is associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Therefore...
This was not set forth in the verse because there were two schools with differing interpretations; therefore, it is now presented in this treatise to refute errors and reveal the correct meaning.
The first phrase poses the inquiry.

One interpretation holds that this co-existent [mental factor] is associated only with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*), because it constantly grasps at an internal self, giving rise to joy and attachment.
Another interpretation holds that [the text] below presents the first explanation; the first sentence clarifies that among the five feelings, *manas* is associated only with joy.

The following verse provides the explanation and proof: This attachment takes the eighth [consciousness] as its internal self because it constantly gives rise to joy and affection. One interpretation holds that this is not so;
for if it were, one would have to admit that the sensation of joy exists even up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), which would contradict the sacred teachings.

There is an interpretation that the following passage provides a subsequent explanation. First, the two characters "not so" (不然) provide a general refutation. Next, it refutes [the opponent's view] by appealing to contradiction with scripture:

the noble teachings state that the experience of joy (*saumanasya*) extends only up to the second dhyāna, whereas the manas is pervasive throughout all three realms, including the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), which refers to the stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
If one were to claim that the manas is accompanied by the experience of joy, then that experience should follow the nature of consciousness and likewise extend to the Peak of Existence.
Therefore, it is rejected by stating: "Because it contradicts the words of the Sage.

One should explain that this intention is associated with the four feelings (up to the point where it says): "because it is the fruit of wholesome karma belonging solely to the stage of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

The word "should" indicates that the following is an application of one's own explanation. The first phrase generally clarifies association with the four feelings; among these five, the remainder refers to suffering (*duḥkha*). That is to say:

Having explained [the preceding], the four types of feeling (*vedanā*) are now elucidated. This means that because the retributive fruits of wholesome and unwholesome [actions] differ according to their respective objects (*ālambana*), realms (*dhātu*), and stages (*bhūmi*), there are four distinct categories of associated feeling:
sorrow (*daurmanasya*), joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

There is an interpretation that their [previous] explanation is also unreasonable (up to the point where it says) "therefore, this [manas] is associated only with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

There is another interpretation which presents the third solution. The first phrase [“此無... generally refutes the two previous schools. The passage beginning with “此無... explains the meaning of why [the previous views] are untenable.

The word “this” (*ci*) refers to the manas. “Spontaneously” (*ran-gyur*) excludes [its arising] in dependence on conditions. “Of one type” (*gcig-tu*) means it is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
"Conditioned by the internal" excludes external conditions. "Grasping at a self" means there is no separate grasping; therefore, it is said to be "permanently without change.
"Variable feelings" refer to sorrow, joy, and pleasure. Since consciousness here is without change, it is refuted by saying it "should not be associated with variable feelings.
Furthermore, from this point downward, the present verse is contrasted with the previously mentioned storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) to explain [the distinction].

The explanation proceeds by distinguishing similarities and differences. First, regarding the general point that the two types of consciousness differ in their nature (*artha*), the verses treat them separately.

By analogy, if the nature of "feeling" (*vedanā*) were different here, the verses should have treated it separately. However, next, regarding the feeling of the present [consciousness], there is no separate statement in the verses;

it is determined to be the same as the feeling of the *ālayavijñāna*. Therefore, the concluding judgment states: "This consciousness should be associated with only the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). The word "only" (*kevala*) indicates that it is not associated with [other feelings].
Associated with sorrow, joy, and pleasure.

In the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), because [the mental factors] previously mentioned (up to... always operate with equanimity toward their objects, they are not transformed.

The phrase "prior to transformation" concludes and judges the preceding text, first clarifying the breadth and narrowness of the mental factors in the stages of transformation and non-transformation. Prior to transformation...

Regarding the state [of transformation]: it is associated with the eighteen mental factors previously mentioned. This phrase concludes the preceding section. Transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) arises together with twenty-one mental factors;
their names are cited and their number is enumerated as in the text. "As in the case of the eighth consciousness in its state of transformed basis" is an illustration used to clarify.
This phrase serves as an analogy both for what precedes and for what follows. As an analogy for what precedes, it refers to the seventh consciousness in its state of transformed basis.

There are also twenty-one mental factors; as in the following cases, even in the state where the basis has been transformed (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), they are associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
The final two phrases of the verse establish that it is associated solely with equanimity. It constantly takes the ten kinds of *tathatā* (suchness) as its cognitive object (*ālambana-viṣaya*).
Because it functions with equanimity, the mental factors (*caitta*) of the *manas* are subsumed under which nature? They are subsumed under the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and not others.

Below the section on the *manas*, this explains the gate of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). The first sentence poses the question; there are four types of nature, and now [the text] examines among those four.
What does it include? What word serves as the interrogative particle? The second line of the verse presents the answer by citing the summary.
"Not others" excludes other wholesome, unwholesome, and non-obscured [states].
Regarding these four afflictions associated with this manas (up to the point where), once the basis has been transformed (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), they are exclusively of a virtuous nature.

The following section explains this. First, it clarifies the state prior to transformation. Initially, it explains the "obscured" (*nivṛta*); the term "etc. includes the eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

The "Noble Path" refers to the path for entering the state of a noble one; it is precisely right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). "One's own mind" refers to the intrinsically present pure nature, which is ultimate truth (*tattva*).

Because these [two] are both defiled phenomena capable of obscuring wisdom and reality, they are called "obscured" (*nivṛta*). The meaning of "obscuration" (*nivṛti*) consists of hindering and concealing.
Next, the "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) is explained as in the text. As above and below, this generally addresses potential objections. An anticipated question states: "The faculties..."

The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) pertain to both the defiled and the two natures [of the non-defiled]. Why, then, is it said that they are subsumed only under the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)?

In the response, examples are first cited: in the two upper realms—namely, the form and formless realms—the various afflictions and so forth are subdued and concealed by the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Because their defiled activity is not predominant, because they are extremely subtle, and because they function spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*), they are therefore unspecified. This is the analogy.
This basis for the defiled dharmas is subtle and spontaneous; by revealing that the defiled dharmas which depend upon it are likewise so, it is also indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Next, regarding the stage of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it is associated with the eleven wholesome dharmas; therefore, it is exclusively of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*) and is distinguished from the other three natures.
To which stage (*bhūmi*) are the mental factors (*caitta*) of the *manas* bound? They are bound to the stage in which they arise.
Below, the section on the binding by stages (*dhātu-bhūmi-bandhana*) is explained. The first sentence poses the question: "Stages" refers to the nine stages within the three realms.

The text here simultaneously inquires as to which stage the sovereign (*rājā*, i.e., the *manas*) and its associated factors belong to. Next, the verse is cited in response; the initial word "that" (*tat*) refers to the eighth consciousness.
Next, regarding the term "that" (*tat*): it refers to the realm and stage. That is to say, whichever stage the eighth consciousness is born into, the manas is bound to that same stage.
Specifically, when the active manas arises in the desire realm, it is said to be "bound by that" because it is bound by the [afflictions] belonging to that [realm].

This refers to those born below. This is a further explanation. First, it clarifies the state before the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). First, it explains the bondage to realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi-bandhana*).

That is to say, when sentient beings are born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the manas and its associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta*) that manifest—excluding the seeds—are bound to the desire realm.
The phrase "and so forth" (*yāvat*) is an abbreviation of the text; that is, for those born in other realms and stages, it is likewise bound to those respective stages. How is this known?

It arises and is bound according to the level [of rebirth]. The mental factors of the *manas* constantly take the *ālayavijñāna* of its own level as the self, because it does not take the *ālayavijñāna* of another level as the self.
If it arises in a lower level, this next explains the binding by maturation (*vipākasaṃbandha*).

Both names are mentioned together because it is the fruit drawn forth by karma and because the *manas* clings to it as a storehouse. If it arises in that level to repay the previously drawn-in karma...
When the ripening store-consciousness (*vipākālayavijñāna*) manifests, it is said that one is "born" in that realm.

The afflicted *manas* takes that store-consciousness as its object and clings to it as an internal self. This afflicted manas is bound to that ripening store-consciousness and is thus called "bound to it.
The first two instances of the word "it" (*tat*) refer to the realm and the stage; the latter three instances of "it" refer to the ripening [consciousness], or alternatively, to the lower [stages].

Third, the explanation of the bondage of afflictions: if one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the mental factors associated with the manifest *manas* are bound by the various afflictions of the desire realm;
this should be understood to apply likewise up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). This is termed "being bound by those [afflictions]."
If one has already undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), one is no longer bound.

From "if one has already [transformed]" onwards, the text next clarifies that for one who has undergone the transformation of the basis, being "not bound" means that the transformed basis is untainted (*anāsrava*);
it is not bound by the realms (*dhātu*), not bound by maturation (*vipāka*), and not bound by afflictions (*kleśa*).

This defiled manas has been in continuous succession since beginningless time; it ceases to exist for an Arhat, during the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and on the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*).

Regarding the phrase "this defilement," etc., this explains the sequence of stages for abandoning and suppressing [the afflictions]. First, there is a question: the first clause asks about abandonment, and the second clause asks about suppression.
"A-ra-han" (Arhat): This verse provides a general response. Whether it be "subduing" or "abandoning," both are collectively termed "non-existence.
An Arhat generally manifests the three vehicles; because [the afflictions] are all temporarily subdued and extinguished, they are said to be non-existent.

*Arhat* (A-luo-xià). First, a brief explanation: those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the three vehicles are all called *arhats*. This is because they have reached the ultimate truth and exhausted their delusions;

thus, in this stage, the seeds and manifestations [of afflictions] are eternally severed, which is termed "non-existence" (*wu*). To investigate the truth and sever delusions is termed "with-learning" (*youxue*).

Alternatively, whether one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) or cultivates the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), in these two states, the active manifestations [of afflictions] do not function; they are merely suppressed for a time, which is termed [the state of non-functioning].
It is not [absent]. Because it arises again after emerging from meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) or contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), it is said to be "temporarily suppressed.
This means that the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*), which has existed since beginningless time, is called the "supramundane path" because it is accompanied by the untainted (*anāsrava*).
This refers to the defilements of the lower realms. Next, the detailed explanation follows. To explain in reverse order first: regarding the temporary suppression by the Noble Path. Question:

In the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*), this consciousness is permanently severed, so one may say it does not exist. However, in the stage of Learning (*śaikṣa*), both [the defilements and the consciousness] are temporarily suppressed and extinguished;

how can it also be said that [the consciousness] does not exist? Answer: The various contaminated paths—namely, the four dhyānas and the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)—are only able to suppress [the defilements] within the six consciousnesses.

It is defiled. It cannot subdue or extinguish the seventh consciousness, which is defiled, subtle, and constantly active. Next, it clarifies that the noble path of the two vehicles has the capacity to subdue [the afflictions].

"Understanding of selflessness" refers to the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Regarding the term "true," it refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the emptiness of persons;

because it is diametrically opposed to the obstacles it treats, the grasping at a self does not function. Subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is the equalization of that fundamental wisdom.
The outflowing class likewise contradicts the grasping at a self; therefore, it is said that [the self] does not exist. "Truly non-existent" below concludes and correlates with the verse text.
Both the fundamental and the subsequently attained [wisdoms] are termed the supramundane path.
Since the attainment of cessation is an outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the Noble Path and is characterized by extreme tranquility, it likewise does not exist [in the form realm].
Below this, the attainment of cessation is explained; following the same principle as the Noble Path, it is also truly untainted (*anāsrava*), and is therefore called an "outflow."
Therefore, this defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) is likewise not [absolutely] non-existent.
Because its seeds have not been permanently severed, it manifests again until it is extinguished.

The phrase "because they have not been severed" explains the sense of "temporary," clarifying that it manifests once more. Anticipating an objection, [the text states]: "Since both the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and the Noble Path..."
The untainted [path] (*anāsrava*) can oppose the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*). Why, then, do you say it merely suppresses it temporarily? Our explanation is as follows:

although the defiled mind is absent during the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and the noble path (*ārya-mārga*), because its seeds have not been permanently severed, these various defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) manifest once one has arisen from that state.
Furthermore, until they are naturally extinguished, they continue to evolve in constant succession; therefore, it is said that [the path] merely suppresses them temporarily.
However, because these afflictions associated with the defiled manas [have been abandoned] up to that point, they never arise again in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
From "However, this below," it next clarifies the permanent abandonment in the stage of no-more-learning. First, it clarifies the characteristics of abandonment:

discriminative afflictions are generally abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*), whereas untainted wholesome dharmas are not to be abandoned. Now, because this defiled dharma is innate (*sahaja*), it is...
Because it is defiled, this indicates that it is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Regarding "the subtle atom" (*paramāṇu*) below, this clarifies the limit of abandonment:

these seeds of defilement are simultaneously and instantaneously severed along with the inferior-inferior grade (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) of active afflictions within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Why is this so? Because the seed and its power are equal, both being extremely subtle. "The Peak of Existence" refers to the Stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
"The lowest-of-the-low afflictions" refers to the very lowest grade among the nine grades; that is, the eighty-first grade of the delusions of thought (*vitarka*).
"Below the diamond" clarifies the sequence of the stages of abandonment. As for the "diamond-like concentration," it is the third...
The "vehicle" refers to the final moment of mind of an Anāgāmin; the "bodhisattva who awakens through shame" refers to the period after the Far-Going Ground (Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi);

[The text below] generally addresses potential objections. Regarding this, there is an interpretation [of the text] from "In this regard" up to "Furthermore, it is called the defiled basis of consciousness.

Fourth, because it is subsumed under the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), and because "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*) carries the meaning of "affliction," the manas is associated with them;
the first six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) become defiled accordingly. Therefore, it serves as the basis for the defilement of all consciousnesses.
Based on this evidence, there is only the defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*).

According to one interpretation, that [opposing] explanation contradicts both scripture and reason, because [the defiled mind] must necessarily have a co-nascent and specific support (*sahaja-asādhāraṇa-āśraya*).

"Co-arising" (*jusheng*) means that the sixth and seventh consciousnesses evolve simultaneously. "Non-common support" (*bujuyi*) means that the sixth consciousness takes the seventh as its non-common support.

Regarding the common root (*sādhāraṇendriya*): The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows. The uncontaminated mental consciousness (*anāsrava-manovijñāna*) is the subject (*dharmin*). It necessarily possesses a co-arising, non-common support (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*), this is the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Because it is subsumed under the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), this is the reason (*hetu*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like the contaminated mental consciousness. To maintain that there is no pure mind (*viśuddha-manas*) would it not be a violation of reason?
The treatise states that the *ālayavijñāna* is definitely and always [accompanied by others]... at that time, the *ālayavijñāna* definitely functions as two together.

The section following "the treatise states" extensively refutes contradictions with the scriptures. First, it contradicts the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Initially, it cites the text: "If one abides... and so forth.

Regarding the state of abiding in the Noble Path—meaning when the sixth consciousness is practicing contemplation—if the seventh consciousness were absent, then at that time the ālayavijñāna would be conjoined with only one consciousness and not two; yet at that time, the ālayavijñāna is certainly functioning in conjunction with two.
This passage would then become a mere empty formulation.
Since the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that the manas is "constantly associated with" [the afflictions], we know that this manas encompasses both the defiled and the non-defiled.

[The text from] the latter part of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* next contradicts the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*: the first phrase refers to the defiled manas, while the second phrase refers to the non-defiled manas.

To take pride in one's own elevation as a practice is the *manas* associated with the conceit of "I-am-ness" (*asmimāna*). To reverse that and establish it as a practice of equanimity is the *manas* associated with purity.
Thus, we know that a single phrase establishes both the defiled and the pure states; alternatively, it should perhaps read "should be established," for I fear the current text may be erroneous.

The purified *manas* merely abandons its defilements but does not abandon its essence. The following two lines clarify this by means of reciprocal analogy.

"Equalizing Wisdom (*samatājñāna*) is the subject (*dharmin*); it necessarily has a supporting, associated pure consciousness (*viśuddhavijñāna*) as its basis, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*)."
Because it is subsumed by wisdom, it is the cause; this is like other forms of wisdom, namely the three wisdoms such as the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

Next, by using "perpetual functioning" as the reason (*hetu*) and the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) as the corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is established that the perpetually functioning Wisdom of Equality does not rely upon the evolving consciousnesses;
this clarifies the existence of the pure *manas*. The formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows: The Wisdom of Equality is...

First, the constant operation of the clinging to a self (*ātman-grāha*) among those in training (*śaikṣa*) is cited as an analogy for the constant operation of the clinging to phenomena among those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) in the two vehicles.

[The text] proceeds. That which serves as the basis for the clinging to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) is precisely the seventh [consciousness]. Below this, the text uses a counter-argument to establish that it relies upon the seventh.
Clinging to dharmas is itself wisdom (*prajñā*); it does not rely upon the eighth [consciousness], because the eighth lacks wisdom and does not coexist with it.

For this reason, one should believe that the noble paths of the two vehicles [do not eliminate the seventh consciousness], because they have not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
From "for this reason" onwards, there is an exhortation to believe that their grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) coexists only with the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

When the sacred teachings state that it is absent in the three stages, they mean only that the grasping at a self is absent. "For this reason" refers back to the manas associated with the grasping at phenomena; one should...
We maintain that the pure manas is not non-existent in these three stages. This is because they have not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*);

because the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) takes the seventh consciousness as its support; and because although the grasping at phenomena does not obstruct their wisdom, it is nonetheless designated as "pure."

Furthermore, in various treatises, regarding the "five similar dharmas" (up to the point where it says) "the five always have a support," the sixth [consciousness] should also be understood in this way.

The passage beginning with "Furthermore, all... clarifies that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has a support, thereby revealing the existence of a seventh [consciousness]. Regarding the "five similar dharmas":

the treatise uses the first five consciousnesses as the *dṛṣṭānta* (example) for the sixth consciousness. The formal inference (*pramāṇa*) states: "The sixth mental consciousness necessarily possesses a co-nascent support."

It does not have a non-common basis, because it is subsumed under one or another of the six well-established consciousnesses, just like the visual consciousness and the others. If there is a fault in the thesis or the reason:

if the seventh [consciousness] did not exist, the thesis would suffer from the fault of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) being unestablished (*asiddha*), and the reason would suffer from the fallacy of being inconclusive due to commonality (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*).

If you grant that the first five [consciousnesses] likewise lack a support, then in order to establish that the sixth lacks a support and thereby avoid the fallacy of the "uncertainty" (*anaikāntika*) reason within the *hetu*, there remains the fallacy of the "unestablished predicate" (*asiddha-viśeṣaṇa*) in the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Now, since these five share the same nature as having a constant support—because they do not function apart from their simultaneous roots—it must necessarily be admitted that this support for the sixth is also constantly present. This...
The support (*āśraya*) is precisely the pure seventh [consciousness].
Therefore, there must certainly be an undefiled manas; it is not the case that an eighth [consciousness] does not exist. This [eighth consciousness] should also be understood in this way.

Thus, the concluding summary provides the correct explanation. The two characters "therefore" (*shìgù*) are words that承接 (*chéngshèng*) what precedes, according to the aforementioned teaching and reasoning.

Inference: One must certainly admit the existence of a seventh pure mind (*anāsrava-manas*), which constantly arises and manifests within the cessation-attainment of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-nirodha-samāpatti*) and during the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*).
Regarding the phrase "that [mind] below," this concludes and correlates the meaning of the two characters "non-existent" (*na asti*) in the verse.

As for the statement "just as below," this provides an example to establish the proof; it should be understood that this case is likewise so—for just as the eighth pure mind is not non-existent, it should also be so.
There is a pure seventh [consciousness].

Second, it clarifies that for those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it arises intermittently. This pertains to the stage of the mind associated with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*).

Next, "pervading the lower [stages]" clarifies the mental state associated with the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmanairātmya-dṛṣṭi*).

Regarding "maturation" (*vipāka*): because it persists into subsequent states, its presence conversely reveals that the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*) has become manifest, whereby [the maturation] no longer arises.
Subsequently, it pervades the mental continuums of all Tathāgatas, reaching as far as the maturation consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and giving rise to the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).
The subsequent passage "penetrates downward" clarifies the mental state associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).

Because the Tathāgata is eternally continuous, has forever severed the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), has reached the ultimate realization of the two kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and persists until the end of time; whereas for Bodhisattvas, as indicated by the following section, it arises intermittently.

The text explains that because their functions are distinct while their substance is identical, they do not contradict one another. This is because they are both a single wisdom (*prajñā*).
This refers to their being of the same substance (*ekadravya*). Next, the visual consciousness and so forth are cited as analogies.

Thesis: Although their functions differ, they are not mutually contradictory; therefore, it is the reason (*hetu*). For example, like the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth.

First, it generally explains how the three vehicles suppress the clinging to a self and give rise only to the clinging to phenomena.

Arising. It counteracts the obstacles through their incompatibility, for ego-clinging has already been subdued. Regarding the Bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment who speaks of "cultivating the path" (*bhāvanāmārga*):

it refers to the aspiration to sever [defilements] all at once; because ego-clinging has already been subdued, the coarse impurities fall away first at the initial moment of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

This is because from the eighth stage upward, all bodhisattvas—even up to the highest level—still give rise to the grasping at phenomena, which is therefore not contradictory [to this statement].

Apart from the eye and the other [faculties], there exists a seventh [consciousness]. This is the general answer provided in the Holy Teachings (*āgama*).
That is to say, in various sūtras, the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) states that "discernment" (*vijñapti*) is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); these are three distinct meanings.

This refers to the "thinning of the lower [fetters]. First, I shall cite the scriptures to provide a specific explanation. First, I will generally cite the three—*citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*—from various sūtras; these are three distinct names.
"Collecting and arising," "deliberating," and "discerning" are their three distinct meanings. Since the names and meanings are distinct, they must possess distinct entities.
Although the texts are cited generally, the intent points specifically to the *manas*. By this, it is proven that a seventh consciousness exists.
