"Neither" (ubhaya-viparīta) refers to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), which is called "neither" because it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
To briefly explain the two characters "neither":
it is capable of bringing about benefit and advantage for this life and the next; however, because it does not [bring such benefit] to future lives, it is not called wholesome.
This section explains the three natures in detail, beginning with the definition of the virtuous (*kuśala*). "This world" refers to the present; "other worlds" refers to the future.
Virtuous actions performed here can induce what is desired by the mind in both worlds, leading to great abundance. By mentioning "humans and devas," the result is distinguished from its cause.
A question is raised: since the pleasant fruits of humans and devas involve upward progression and are conducive to benefit, they may indeed be called virtuous.

No. The present answer states: "The fruit of pleasure follows the transformation of prior karma; although it may provide benefit and support in this life, its retribution will not last once that karma is exhausted.
Only when the grasping of karmic causes extends through both lifetimes can it be termed 'wholesome'."
It is able to cause harm and loss in this world and the next; it is not [non-unwholesome] because it does not do so in the next world alone.
Next, the characteristic of the unwholesome (*akuśala*) is explained: the evil karma one performs causes what is sought in both worlds to fail, and it agitates and afflicts the body and mind.
[The phrase] "in the evil destinies" distinguishes the fruit from its cause. It is asked: the fruit of suffering in the evil destinies is a state of sinking, falling, and being harmed.

It may be called unwholesome. The answer says: "The fruit of suffering follows the transformation of prior karma; although it can be countered and diminished in this life, it ceases only once the retribution is fully paid.
Only that which takes up karmic causes spanning two lifetimes is termed unwholesome."
It is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) because it cannot be designated in terms of being wholesome or unwholesome, beneficial or harmful.

There are three explanations for the characteristics of the indeterminate: first, it does not accord with the sense of benefit, as there is no goodness to be designated; second, it does not contradict the sense of harm, as there is no unwholesomeness to be designated.
If these six evolving consciousnesses are associated with faith and so forth [up to] and are not otherwise associated, they are subsumed under the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Below this, the essential nature is set forth to clarify their mutual inclusion; above, only the two natures of wholesome (*kuśala*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*) were presented.

Herein, the essential nature is set forth: faith, shame (*hrī*), dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), non-attachment (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), non-delusion (*amoha*), diligence (*vīrya*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and non-... [omitted].

Harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*). Those associated with these [six consciousnesses] are comprised within the category of the wholesome. Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāśa*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), harmfulness, and hatred (*vyāpāda*):
those associated with these are comprised within the category of the unwholesome. Those that are associated with neither are comprised within the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

One interpretation holds that the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) of the six consciousnesses do not coexist; [this is because] it would contradict correct reasoning, and thus they certainly do not coexist.

Another interpretation below explains whether the three natures coexist or not. First, the explanation of non-coexistence: it means that the three natures of the six consciousnesses definitely do not arise simultaneously.
The next two lines explain the meaning of this non-coexistence: because they take the same external objects as their objective conditions (*ālambana*), the three natures are mutually contradictory.

Therefore, below the section on the five consciousnesses, the difficulty regarding the simultaneous arising of the three natures is addressed. The first two lines establish that the six consciousnesses necessarily arise together;

their nature as wholesome or defiled is identical. That is to say, when the five consciousnesses arise, they must do so with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) acting as their discerning support (*viniścaya-āśraya*), being induced by it and arising simultaneously, sharing the same objects of the five sensory domains, and being equally wholesome or defiled. The following section presents the formal objection. Five.

The [other] consciousnesses function simultaneously with the three natures; the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), following them, should accordingly be understood as pervading all three natures. The final phrase concludes that they do not coexist [in the same moment].

The *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts state that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) arises and ceases at one time; thus, there is no contradiction in its arising and ceasing not occurring simultaneously [with the other consciousnesses].

In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, a general objection is raised: "The *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts state that the ālayavijñāna arises simultaneously with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

How can you say they do not arise together? Although the commentary cites a single sentence from the full text of the treatise, its intent is solely to use the fact that the evolving consciousnesses arise with the three natures to provide an explanation.
It states: "That which it calls 'simultaneously' is spoken of in terms of multiple moments (*kṣaṇa*), as for example..."
It speaks of "one mind," not of a single moment of arising and ceasing. Since it relies here upon a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), multiple [minds] cannot coexist;
thus, there is no fault of contradiction with that treatise.
According to another interpretation, the six consciousnesses and the three natures may coexist; [therefore,] the objections previously raised are rendered futile in this case.

There is an interpretation [stating] "below. Next, the simultaneous arising is explained: the six consciousnesses and the three natures may arise together. "Sudden" (*sūtra*) refers to the initial moment of mind;

"or many" means five arise together; "or few" means two, three, or four. "Below" explains the meaning of simultaneity. "Sudden" means the very first thought; "or many" means those arising with the five [sensory consciousnesses]; "or few" means two, three, or four.

Just as visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is necessarily indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) when it arises abruptly, auditory, olfactory, and other consciousnesses become wholesome or defiled when they arise in a continuous flow (*nisyanda*).
Since the five consciousnesses can arise simultaneously, their three moral natures must necessarily coexist. Below this, the preceding objection is refuted:

although the five consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (*manas*) definitely arise together, their moral natures—wholesome and so forth—are not necessarily identical; therefore, the previous objection that the five consciousnesses must always function with all three natures simultaneously is rejected.

At that time, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) should be understood as encompassing all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). Now, to argue that the nature of the mental consciousness must necessarily be the same as that of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) is a futile objection.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If one encounters the condition of sound... [omitted] ...or if there is an expectation, it emerges only at a later time."
Therefore, Yu cites scriptural evidence below. First, he clarifies that the two consciousnesses arise simultaneously; second, he determines their respective natures.

When various yoga practitioners enter meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samāpatti*) and encounter an auditory object such that they emerge from concentration, this is merely the arising of the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) associated with the remaining wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that is concomitant with the meditative state, which perceives the sound; only after this does one subsequently emerge from concentration. It is not [the case] alone...

Below, it is clarified that the two consciousnesses must necessarily depend upon one another. First, it is shown that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) requires the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*).
It is not only the mental consciousness associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that can apprehend this sound; there is no other auditory consciousness [that could do so].

If there were only mental consciousness and no auditory consciousness, the mental consciousness within meditative concentration would be unable to hear sounds, because it would not perceive these vocal sounds. This should not be the case.

[Objection: One emerges from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*). It is not the case that [the ear-consciousness] does not arise because it is not grasping [the object]. This clarifies that the ear-consciousness must necessarily be accompanied by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

If one were to argue that one emerges from absorption at the very moment the ear-consciousness perceives a sound, and therefore it does not function simultaneously with the mental consciousness associated with absorption—this reasoning is also incorrect.
One does not emerge from absorption at the time of perceiving the sound; rather, it is after having perceived the sound, if there is a desire or expectation [to remain absorbed], that one emerges.

Since one emerges from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) only later, when the sound is heard, the mind is still within concentration. Consequently, two consciousnesses must simultaneously apprehend this sound.

This is because the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) that suddenly hears the sound while in concentration is a sudden, falling [into object] mind (*sūtrala-patita-citta*), which is by nature ethically neutral (*avyākṛta*).

In the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are determined to belong to two natures. The first phrase establishes that the *saṃtīraṇa* (investigative) ear-consciousness is not wholesome.

The second phrase explains its status as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). It follows logically that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within concentration should be wholesome. This clarifies that while these two consciousnesses arise simultaneously, their natures differ;
this serves to demonstrate that the three natures can coexist.

By this clear proof, it is established that the five-sense-accompanying mental consciousness (*pañcaka-manovijñāna*) also takes the five objects as its domain, even though it is not said to be of the same nature [as the sensory consciousnesses].

From "by this" downwards, the conclusion establishes that their natures are different: an indeterminate ear-consciousness may arise simultaneously with a wholesome mind associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

From "in all places" downwards, the text again cites passages concerning the same object having different natures, concluding that the three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate) can coexist.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states that the claim that the five consciousnesses are absent during the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) is based on what is generally the case.
In the lower section of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it addresses this objection: "The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that there are no five consciousnesses in the state of meditative equipoise;

why then is it said that the mental consciousness associated with concentration arises simultaneously with other ear-consciousnesses hearing sounds? The commentary explains that this [statement] relies upon...
"For the most part" refers here to a small portion. Regarding "equipoise" (*samāhita*): this applies to both meditative absorptions with mind and those without mind.

That which is free from lethargy and agitation is called "equilibrium" (*sama*). That which draws forth (*ākarṣati*) virtuous qualities is called "drawing forth" (*āhita*). Since this applies to absorptions with mind as well, [it is not limited to the formless realm].
That [statement] refers to the majority of cases, so it may be said that [the seeds] do not exist; this [present statement] refers to a minority of cases, so it may be said that they do exist.
Therefore, these two passages do not contradict one another.
As for the simultaneous occurrence of the three natures within the five consciousnesses, [this continues until] the seeds of conceptual proliferation have been permanently extinguished.
If the five [sensory consciousnesses] arise together with the lower fetters (*paryavasthāna*), a question arises:

since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises simultaneously with the five cannot be of the same nature as those five, why did the preceding text state that the three natures (*tridhātu*) of the six consciousnesses may also arise together? The text answers this by distinguishing between the "exclusive" and the "non-exclusive.

"Exclusive" refers to being one-pointed; for example, if the visual consciousness belongs to the wholesome (*kuśala*) category, and the mental consciousness is exclusively and one-pointedly focused upon it.
It is also established as wholesome. Alternatively, when other consciousnesses are unwholesome and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is intensely focused upon them, it is also unwholesome;

if it is not so focused, the mind is then indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Therefore, from "the six [consciousnesses] below" up to "established as co-arising," the point is made that they arise together. From "attaining mastery below" on, it clarifies that in the stage of Buddhahood, [the mind] is comprised solely of a wholesome nature.
The final two phrases exclude the other two natures, because being subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), it is not unwholesome. It is cessation.
Because it is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding how many mental factors (*caitta*) the six consciousnesses are associated with, the verse says: [omitted] "they are associated with the three feelings.
Below the section on the six consciousnesses, this is the section clarifying the associated mental factors. The first line poses the question; the verse below provides the answer.
The Commentary says: These six evolving consciousnesses collectively [relate to] six states... (as far as) "just as things belonging to a self are designated by the name 'mine'.
The Commentary says: Below, the six states are generally indicated. "Constantly relying on... first explains the general name for mental factors (*caitta*).
Because they can only manifest when taking the mind (*citta*) as their support, and because they are mutually associated and harmonized as if they were one, they are bound and subsumed [under it].

Because they belong to the sovereign mind itself, they are called "mental factors" (caitta). To clarify this by means of an analogy: just as things belonging to oneself are designated as "one's own" (ātmīya), those phenomena that belong to the mind are termed "mental factors."

The mind apprehends only the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of its object (up to the point where it says): "like a master painter and his apprentice making a model and filling it with colors.
Regarding the phrase "the mind [acts] below," this explains the mental aspect (*ākāra*). "The mind apprehends only the general characteristics of its object":

the word "only" clarifies that it does not apprehend specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). While the mental factors (*caitta*) toward their objects do not only apprehend general characteristics but also apprehend specific characteristics, the word "also" clarifies that they apprehend both.

Regarding the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and the "object" (*artha*) and "mind" (*citta*): the activity of cognizing an object is called the "object. Next, an analogy is given: the mind is like a master painter, and the mental factors (*caitta*) are like his disciples.
Grasping the general characteristic is like creating a model; grasping the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is like applying the colors.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is able to discern [objects]... (up to this point). This indicates that mental factors (*caitta*) also take general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) as their objects.
Thus, the subsequent section of the *Yogācāra* text cites evidence for the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

The first sentence clarifies that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) only discerns the general characteristic of the object, while the subsequent sentences beginning with "attention" (*manasikāra*) clarify that mental factors additionally discern both general and specific characteristics; that is, the various mental factors apprehend specific characteristics.

"Signs" (nimitta): this term applies throughout the preceding and following sections. "Not yet understood" means not clearly comprehended; now, through mental attention (*manasikāra*), one is able to comprehend them clearly.
"Agreeable and so forth" refers to that which is agreeable, disagreeable, and that which is neither, and their apprehension—meaning that which is conducive and beneficial.
"Such as" refers to the characteristics of harm and contradiction. Regarding "the cause of verbal expression":

it is by means of the conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) that establishes the boundaries of objects that various names and expressions can arise. "Correct causes," etc., includes "incorrect causes" and "neither.

Therefore, the final phrase is composed to conclude by naming them "mental factors" (*caitasika*). The fact that all phrases refer to "this" indicates their general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

In another passage, it is further stated that desire (*chanda*) is also able to cognize [objects] (up to the point where it says): "all [mental factors] take both the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) with respect to their objects.

In the subsequent section, which cites evidence for the distinct objects of the various mental states, the word "also" (*api*) in each sentence includes the mention of the general characteristic. From the phrase "By this...
onwards, the four remaining positions are illustrated as taking both general and specific characteristics; the two characters "by this" (*tataḥ*) here refer back to the two preceding positions.

The mind (*manas*) is capable of alerting the [primary] mind, whereby mental factors (*caitta*) arise. Contact (*sparśa*) enables the mind to confront its objects; both possess the functional capacity to give rise to mental factors.

Feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) arise together: feeling gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and craving produces the various types of grasping (*upādāna*). Volition (*cetanā*) is the master of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Desire (*chanda*) is able to aspire; resolve (*adhimokṣa*) is able to determine; mindfulness (*smṛti*) is able to remember; and concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are able to discern gain and loss.
It is through these two pairs that take objects as their conditions that the various mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) of the four categories—wholesome, defiled, and so forth—can be induced.
The final phrase explains the establishment of these categories, while also encompassing both their general and specific characteristics.
Although the names and meanings of the various mental factors (*caitta*) do not differ, there are six stages (*ṣaḍ-avasthā*) of categorical distinctions.

[The commentary] states: "Although... and so forth, classifying them according to their designations. Question: Since they are collectively termed "mental factors" and collectively possess the meanings of being constant, dependent, and so forth, their names and meanings do not differ;
why then are they divided into six distinct stages? Answer: In the response, the first phrase restates the question, and the subsequent phrase relies upon...
They are divided into six categories based on the distinctions between their types, such as wholesome, defiled, and so forth.
That is to say, there are five universal mental factors and five object-specific factors; [the remaining ones] are indeterminate with respect to being wholesome, defiled, and so forth.

This refers to the "comprehensive downward" [classification], which enumerates the categories based on their types. The "all-inclusive downward" provides a brief explanation of the specific meanings of the six stages, as found in the text.
However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* combines these six into five; this is because of the distinctions among the various types within these five stages.

However, below [this], Yu cites evidence to harmonize with his own intent: that both the root afflictions and the secondary afflictions (*anuvyañjana-kleśa*), when defiled, together constitute a single category. Furthermore, below [this], based on the four [categories], he distinguishes five [points].

First, he indicates the four "all-inclusives" (*sarvatraga*): first, "all natures" (*sarvabhāva*), which refers to the three natures such as the wholesome and so forth; second, "all stages" (*sarvabhūmi*).
This refers to the three realms and nine stages; to all times, meaning the three periods of past, future, and present;

and to all [mental states], meaning they are associated with all eight consciousnesses. Next, to correctly distinguish their differences: it should be understood that the universal mental factors possess all four "all-inclusives" (sarvatraga).

The five object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-viniyata*) exist only in the first two [mental applications], because they pervade all three natures and all nine stages. The wholesome factors exist only in one [the third application], because the wholesome pervades all nine stages.
The four defiled factors are entirely absent [in the third application], because they do not pervade the wholesome or the pure, nor do they pervade the higher stages.
Because there is no such thing as "wholesome time. Because the eighth [category] is non-associated (*viprayukta*). Regarding "the indeterminate is only one":

this is because it is indeterminate with respect to both the wholesome, the defiled, and so forth. The next phrase concludes [this section]. The word "this" refers to the four "all-inclusives" (*sarvatraga*).

These six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are easily detached and unstable; that which is neither oppressive nor pleasant is called the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*). [The text continues:

"These six," etc., explains the fourth line of the verse regarding the gate of association with sensation (*vedanā-samprayoga*). First, it generally indicates the association with the three types of sensation.

Because the six consciousnesses are easily detached, they are associated with the sensation of change (*vipariṇāma-vedanā*). "Experiencing what is favorable," etc., specifically explains the characteristics of sensation. It is not... [text ends].
That which is oppressive but not pleasant is an object of neutral indifference (*upekṣā*). That which is neither painful nor pleasant is the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
These three sensations may each be divided into two; [this is because] even the sensation of suffering can arise from the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Thus, below, the numerical divisions are established. First, the division is indicated as twofold. In the explanation, the first part concerns body and mind; the second concerns the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The final phrase explains that the untainted also includes painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*). A question is raised: "The untainted is subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*)."
[This leads to] the eternal exhaustion of all suffering. How, then, is it connected to painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*)? The commentary explains:
Those who cultivate the untainted (*anāsrava*) must labor their minds and exert their will before they finally attain it; therefore, painful sensation also arises from the untainted.

Alternatively, each is divided into three: namely, those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), up to [those abandoned by cultivation], and furthermore, those of training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those that are neither.

Alternatively, each is divided into three as follows: first, the heading indicates the division into three; in the explanation, the first is categorized according to the three types of abandonment, the second according to the three types of training (*śikṣā*), and the third refers to that which is not to be abandoned—namely, untainted sensation (*anāsrava-vedanā*).
"Neither of training nor beyond training" refers to the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Alternatively, they may be categorized collectively into four: wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and non-obscured-neutral feelings.
Or, as stated below, first the four are collectively indicated; in the explanation, the initial section categorizes them collectively according to the four natures:
pleasant feeling is wholesome, painful feeling is unwholesome, and neutral feeling is both types of neutral.

One interpretation holds that each of the three feelings (*vedanā*) can be further divided into four [categories], and that all of these are capable of being associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).

Another interpretation holds that, following the previous [classification], one should divide each individual feeling into four: namely, the wholesome (*kuśala*) is associated with all three feelings;

the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the two types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) are likewise all associated with the three feelings. The section beginning with "The five consciousnesses" (*pañca-vijñāna*) explains those associated with the five consciousnesses.
Spontaneous afflictions (*svarasakleśa*) and spontaneous afflictions within the realms of pure suffering—these two types of afflictions do not give rise to unwholesome karma;
they are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). Therefore, they are associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).

Since the treatises state that the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not unspecified, this explanation—that obscured-unspecified states can be associated with the feeling of suffering—is extended by analogy to mean they are also associated with pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*). There is [this].

It has been restated that [the neutral] pervades the three types of sensation; by analogy, the non-obscured-neutral, as well as the wholesome and the unwholesome, should likewise pervade the three types of sensation.
Therefore, each of the three types of sensation can be divided into four categories.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that if [afflictions] arise spontaneously (*svarasena*), they are associated with all faculties up to the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*).

The lower section of the *Yogācārabhūmi* cites scriptural evidence to prove that all spontaneously arising afflictions are subsumed under the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) category and are found to manifest in association with all three types of feeling (*vedanā*).
If these were unspecified [afflictions] common to the first six consciousnesses, they would be universally associated with all those consciousnesses.

Regarding the statement that "the middle three are associated with feeling, but do not pervade all consciousness-bodies": this means they are associated only with the three feelings of the mental level (*manobhūmi*).

Since this proof shows that the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) states already pervade the three feelings, by analogy, the wholesome (*kuśala*), the unwholesome (*akuśala*), and the non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states likewise pervade the three feelings.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that because [the afflictions] are bound to the desire realm... [omitted] ...it is known that each of the three feelings can accommodate four [types of affliction].
In the lower section of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it is proven that the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) pertain to all three feelings.

The former [discussion] was based on the premise that those obscured-unspecified [afflictions] which do not incite unwholesome conduct by way of spontaneous (*svarasa*) activity are subsumed under the obscured-unspecified; the present [discussion], however, concerns those which, although spontaneous, do incite unwholesome conduct, and these are likewise [subsumed under the obscured-unspecified].
"Unwholesome" (akuśala) refers to those [afflictions] that are spontaneous (svarasavāhin), which indicates they pertain to both natures.
"The remainder" refers to other afflictions bound to the desire realm that do not manifest as evil, as well as the spontaneous afflictions of the two higher realms;

all these are subsumed under the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta). This proves that the unwholesome and the obscured pertain to all three types of sensation. By analogy, the wholesome and the non-obscured likewise pertain to all three.

[The section on] Feeling. Therefore, know that [the following] is the conclusion. Based on the introductory statement and the concluding text, as well as the explanations and cited proofs, all should be treated accordingly.
Each of the three feelings may contain four [aspects].

Alternatively, they may be categorized generally as five: namely, suffering (*duḥkha*), pleasure (*sukha*), grief (*daurmanasya*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). [This continues] up to: "because they are without conceptual differentiation and because they function with impartiality.
Alternatively, [the text] below categorizes them generally into five. First, there is the general heading; second, the enumeration of names; third, the explanation of the meaning of these divisions.

That which afflicts the body is called suffering; that which delights the body is called pleasure; that which afflicts the mind is called grief; that which delights the mind is called joy. As for "without conceptual differentiation," it applies to all.
The first five consciousnesses are termed suffering and pleasure; those involving discrimination exist only in the sixth [consciousness] and are termed grief and joy.

Those that are particularly intense are suffering and pleasure; those that are slight are grief and joy. As for equanimity (*upekṣā*), which does not differentiate, it is neither oppressive nor gratifying;
it lacks distinct characteristics in either body or mind. Being purely non-discriminative and devoid of intensity or mildness, it is not divided into two.
All pleasant feelings associated with the five consciousnesses (up to) being tranquil and especially profound because they are non-conceptual. Regarding "all pleasant" below:

this distinguishes pleasure (*sukha*) and joy (*prīti*) according to their association with the various consciousnesses. Pleasant feeling (*sātā vedanā*) is so called because it experiences favorable and beneficial objects.

That which is associated with the five consciousnesses is always termed "pleasure. That which is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is divided into three types according to realm (*dhātu*) and level (*bhūmi*).

Regarding their classifications: in the desire realm, as well as in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the first and second dhyānas, it is called joy (*prīti*). In the fundamental stages (*maula*) of the first and second dhyānas, it is called both bliss (*sukha*) and joy.
In the preparatory stage and the fundamental stage of the third dhyāna, it is called bliss; [in the case of] the preparatory stage [of the fourth dhyāna], it is not so named.
This refers to the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*).
Because all oppressive feelings associated with the five consciousnesses and the mental ground (*manobhūmi*)—namely, the dejected feeling—are designated as the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

To explain this in detail: by the power of mindfulness, one repeatedly recalls objects previously experienced, causing the mind to remember them clearly without loss, thereby inducing the arising of concentration;
thus, it serves as the basis for that concentration.
Regarding objects whose nature has never before been experienced (up to the point stated), mindfulness is necessarily not subsumed under the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).

The phrase "regarding what has [previously] been experienced" serves to exclude those that are not universal. If there is no object previously experienced and it is not clearly remembered, then there is an absolute absence of mindfulness.

Therefore, it is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*). Its substance (*tattva*) refers to the self-body (*ātman*) that has been experienced. Its category (*jāti*) refers to objects that are similar to those previously experienced.
Some say that the arising of the mind must be accompanied by mindfulness (*smṛti*), as it can serve as the cause for recollection at a later time.
Some say that this excludes the interpretation [of mindfulness] as being distinct. To state it first: when the mind arises, it must necessarily be accompanied by mindfulness (*smṛti*).

Why? Because mindfulness clearly and precisely attends to and retains its object, thereby serving as the cause for recollection at a later time; thus, mindfulness is established as a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*).
That explanation is irrational; lest it later [become] a cause for recollection at a subsequent time.
That statement is refuted below. The first phrase is a brief censure; the following provides a refutation by analogy. If it is claimed that there is recollection at a subsequent time...

There must necessarily be mindfulness (*smṛti*) preceding [the state of confusion or faith] to serve as its cause; it is not possible for confusion, faith, and so forth to exist at a later time without such a cause.
Although this mindfulness also exists previously, the power of the preceding thought or perception (*saṃjñā*) is sufficient to serve as the cause for the subsequent recollection.
Therefore, one cannot maintain that mindfulness definitely exists prior to the mind.
"What is concentration regarding the object of observation...? (up to) "...by relying on this, there arises the wisdom of decisive discernment.

How is it "inferior"? This explains concentration. First, it raises the question to bring forth its essence and function: that is, binding the mind to the object of observation, with single-minded and diligent application.
Not allowing distraction to become its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it takes as its functional activity (*karma*) being the basis for wisdom.
This refers to the subsequent explanation: namely, observing objects that are *yoniśas* (in accordance with reason), *ayoniśas* (not in accordance with reason), or neither.

By the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it causes the mind to be focused and not dissipated; based upon this, there arises the wisdom of discernment (*viniścaya-jñāna*), because concentration is able to give rise to wisdom.

The phrase "the mind is focused" (*cittaikāgratā*) indicates the object in which one wishes to abide. [If it were otherwise,] there would be no meditative concentration (*samādhi*) regarding distinct objects before and after.
"The mind is focused on the lower" explains "focused. The phrase "the mind is focused" expresses the object in which this mind wishes to abide;

this concentration enables the mind to abide therein immediately. It is not that the mind remains fixed upon a single object without ever shifting. "Otherwise... [and so forth], the following provides the counter-argument.

[The opponent] objects: "In the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one contemplates the eight truths (*satya*) across the upper and lower realms; since the preceding and succeeding objects differ, they are not one and the same.

If there were no focused attention (*ekāgratā*), there would be no meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore, the term 'focused attention' does not imply a single object. Although the objects shift, the mind remains focused upon them.
If a distracted mind takes an object as its focus, it is dragged away by that object; if a concentrated mind takes an object as its focus, it is not [dragged away]."
Because it draws the mind [toward its object], it is called concentration (*samādhi*).
If the mind were not bound and focused upon the state of the object, concentration would not arise; therefore, it is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*).
By stating "if not" (*yadi na*), it distinguishes it from those that are not universal.
Some say that at that time, concentration (*samādhi*) also arises, but its characteristics are subtle and hidden.

Others say it is "inferior" (*hīna*), distinguishing it from the [higher] liberation previously described. It is established that even in a state where the mind is not bound to a specific object but remains focused, concentration arises;

however, its characteristics are subtle and hidden rather than manifest. This does not mean it is entirely absent, for the concentration of mental formation (*manomaya-samādhi*) is a universal factor (*sarvatraga*).

One should state the true words: [if it is claimed that] concentration can certainly cause the mental application (*manasikāra*) to cause the mind to grasp the object, this should be stated as follows.

[The first phrase] is a warning; the second phrase sets up a hypothetical position and then interrogates it. "The principle also... and so forth refutes [the claim]. Because the state of the threefold conjunction is the function of contact (*sparśa*).

If one says... and so forth, this again sets up a hypothetical position and interrogates it. "Nor is it... and so forth refutes it. In a single moment... (Note: This is a technical commentary on a Buddhist Abhidharma argument concerning the relationship between concentration, mental application, contact, and the grasping of objects.)
That mind is extremely brief in duration because it is not stable by nature. If one were to immediately set up a further argument to challenge this, that too would be refuted;
for the mind’s grasping of an object occurs through the power of attention (*manasikāra*), and neither is fixed.

Some say that the essence of this meditative absorption (samādhi) is precisely the mind (*citta*), because the Sūtra describes it as "mental training" (*citta-śikṣā*) and "one-pointedness of mind" (*citta-ekāgratā*).

Others say [the following] to distinguish it from other interpretations: First, the essence of the absorption is stated to be the mind; next, a scriptural passage is cited to provide an explanatory gloss. Regarding "mental training":

among the three trainings, concentration (*samādhi*) is the mental training, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is the bodily training, and wisdom (*prajñā*) is the verbal training. Wisdom resides in speech.
Therefore, the phrase "one-pointedness of mind" (cittaikāgratā) further explains the training of the mind (citta-śikṣā). This is because this concentration constitutes one-pointedness of mind.

That [concentration] is not a definitive proof [that it is the training of the mind], because the mind is gathered by relying on concentration—just as mindfulness, wisdom, and so forth are not themselves the mind.

That [position] is not inferior; it is refuted. First, the citation of scripture is refuted. Based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the mind is collected; since concentration can cause the mind to be one-pointed toward its object, it is said that concentration is the training of the mind.

Regarding the passage "the faculties and powers are not the mind," a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute the claim that concentration is identical to the mind: concentration is not identical to the mind.
Because the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path are subsumed under the categories of the path-factors (mārga-pakṣya), just as mindfulness and wisdom are;
and because mindfulness and wisdom are subsumed under the categories of the path-factors, they are not identical with the mind. How is this so?
What is wisdom (*prajñā*)? Regarding the objects of observation... [omitted] ...because one attains certainty through the investigation and seeking of wisdom.

What follows below explains wisdom. First, it raises the question to establish its essence and function: its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the analytical discernment and decisive resolution regarding the objects of observation;

its activity (*karman*) consists of the elimination of hesitation. "That is to say, observing... and so forth provides a further explanation, meaning that one observes and thereby attains [certainty].
Regarding objects that are neither [perceived nor non-perceived], one attains certainty through the investigation of wisdom; based on this, all doubts are permanently severed.

However, because there is no discernment within a mind that is ignorant regarding objects not currently under observation, these [mental factors] are not included among the universal mental concomitants (*sarvatraga*).

Regarding "not in the lower [realms]," this excludes those that are not universal (sarvatraga). Because there is no discerning wisdom (viniścaya-jñāna) in states that are not objects of observation, nor in minds characterized by delusion and darkness, they are not universal.
Some say that at that time wisdom (*prajñā*) also arises; this is because the *Abhidharma* explains it as being among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).

Others say "below" [in the text] is intended to distinguish it from understanding (*vijñāna*). First, the phrase "at that time" refers to the aforementioned non-contemplative objects and the deluded mind;

it means that while the characteristics of wisdom are subtle and hidden, it nevertheless arises, rather than wisdom being entirely absent. The phrase "great receptivity" (*mahāvedanā-pada*) provides an illustrative example.

Just as a minute object, when covered by a large object, remains hidden and is not known; so too, according to the *Abhidharmapada*, the citation of the universal [mental factors] (*sarvatraga*) is established because they exist within the minds of both the foolish and the wise.
Thus, the wisdom that constitutes mental formation (*manasikāra*) is a universal factor.
The various Abhidharma schools contradict one another; (up to: the claim that ten [points] are not based on the sūtras should not be dogmatically adhered to.

[The text] below refutes this: the first two phrases refute the mutual contradictions among the treatises and do not accept them as authoritative; the subsequent two phrases refute erroneous attachments that contradict the sūtras.

However, because the five factors beginning with desire (*chanda*) are not contact (*sparśa*) and so forth, they are certainly not universal (*sarvatraga*), just like faith (*śraddhā*), greed (*lobha*), and so on.

Thus, the following formal argument (*prayoga*) is established as a summary: The five factors beginning with desire are certainly not universal, because they are not contact and so forth, just like faith, greed, and so on.
There is one interpretation that these five are necessarily mutually supportive, such that whenever one arises, the other four must also be present.

There is another interpretation that explains the stages of their actual manifestation; first, according to the initial explanation, these five—desire and so forth—are not contradictory in their modes of activity (*ākāra*).
They mutually support and benefit one another, and wherever one is present, they are always together. Whenever one arises, the other four must necessarily be present.
There is an interpretation that this is not fixed; the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the object (*ālambana*) and the subject (*ālambaka*) are not necessarily simultaneous.
There is an interpretation [which states]: below, the following is explained. First, it is generally clarified that these five, beginning with desire (*chanda*), arise in an indeterminate manner.
Next, the *Yogācārabhūmi* is cited as proof. Regarding the four "all-inclusives" (*sarvatraga*), the latter two are absent because they do not pervade all times and do not pervade all minds;

thus, the objects of perception (*ālambana*) are not fixed and do not necessarily arise together. This serves to contrast them with the five stages of the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*), which are not constant.
They are associated because they may arise together or not. When one to four arise, it is called "not together"; when five arise, it is called "together.
It should be explained that these five may sometimes arise as one—namely, when there is no focused attention and the mind is distracted and searching.

It should be stated below: a separate clarification of the characteristics of the indeterminate. First, "arising as one" refers to that which arises solely as a single [state], where the subject and object are distinct, acting alone, and possessing a solitary object and a single mind;
this is called "arising as one. That which is desired to arise is "desire"; that which arises with certainty is "understanding"; and that which arises from prior habituation is "mindfulness."

Regarding the arising of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) through what is observed: this refers to the "foolish and inferior. This section provides a detailed analysis to resolve potential objections.

The intent of the analysis clarifies that while there is focused concentration (*ekāgratā*), there is no discernment (*pravicaya*). The objection states: "If within a state of ignorance there is no discernment, why is it said that such a mind takes the object of observation as its condition? The explanation states:

"Because during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) prior to meditative absorption, there has been some degree of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*). Alternatively, it may be based on the "inferior" [level], which shifts [the argument].

[Objection: This is difficult. Since it is said that there is "a small amount of hearing and reflection," this may also include wisdom (*prajñā*). Why then do you say that what is understood consists solely of meditative concentration (*samādhi*)?

[Response: The explanation says: This is based on the majority of cases and does not refer to a small portion; therefore, it is said to consist solely of concentration. As in the passage following "like play," he cites actual instances to establish the proof.
Alternatively, when wisdom arises regarding a lower object of observation, because it is not focused, there is no concentration; because it wanders and seeks, there is only wisdom.
Or at times both arise—namely, concentration and wisdom arising regarding an object of interest (up to the point mentioned)—which together total twelve.
At times, they descend and give rise to two [factors]. If the objects are each different, the minds are likewise distinct in pairs;

thus, there are ten sets of two. This applies even up to two characters, skipping over the text; subsequent passages follow this same pattern. Regarding what is desired: it gives rise to desire and resolve (*chanda-adhimokṣa*).

Regarding what was previously practiced: it gives rise to desire and mindfulness (*smṛti*). Regarding what is desired and being observed: it gives rise to desire and concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding what is desired and being observed... [the text continues].

Desire, wisdom, determination, prior cultivation, and the arising of understanding; mindfulness, determination, the object of observation, the arising of understanding, concentration, determination regarding the object of observation, the arising of understanding, wisdom, prior cultivation, the object of observation, the arising of mindfulness, concentration, prior cultivation, the object of observation, the arising of mindfulness, and wisdom.
Regarding the object of observation, concentration (samādhi), wisdom (prajñā), and mindfulness (smṛti) arise;
at times, all three arise—namely, regarding the desired [object] up to [the neutral], there arise mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, totaling thirteen.
At other times, the three [lower ones] arise. Since the objects are three and these three arise together, the mind also arises as three sets of three; thus, they total [thirteen].
Ten sets of three: 1. Desired, determined, and previously practiced; 2. Aroused desire, understanding, and mindfulness; 3. Desired, determined, and observed; 4.
Aroused desire, understanding, and concentration; 5. Desired, determined, and observed; 6. Aroused desire, understanding, and wisdom; 7.

Desired, previously practiced, and observed; 8. Aroused desire, mindfulness, and concentration; 9. Desired, previously practiced, and observed; 10. Aroused desire, mindfulness, and wisdom; 11. Desired and observed.

Arouse desire, concentration, wisdom, decisiveness, what has been previously practiced, the object of observation, understanding, mindfulness, concentration, decisiveness, what has been previously practiced,

the object of observation, understanding, mindfulness, wisdom, decisiveness, the object of observation, understanding, concentration, wisdom, what has been previously practiced, the object of observation, and arouse mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
At times, four [mental applications] arise; that is, regarding what is desired (*iṣṭa*) up to [what is observed], the latter four types arise, making five in total when combined.

At other times, four arise from the lower [levels]. If the objects change sequentially or inversely, the mind then eliminates one [application] in reverse order; thus, there are five sets of four in total. These are:

desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), or [the application] arising toward what is desired, what is determined, what has been practiced, or what is being observed. Or, in this regard...

The four: the arousal of desire, understanding, mindfulness, and wisdom; that which is delighted in, that which is determined, that which is observed; and the arousal of desire, understanding, concentration, and wisdom; that which is delighted in.

Previously practiced; that which is observed; the arising of desire; mindfulness; concentration; wisdom; decisiveness; previously practiced; that which is observed; the arising of understanding; mindfulness; concentration.
Wisdom (*prajñā*).
At times, five [mental factors] arise together; that is to say, when one focuses upon an object of observation that is pleasing, determined, and previously familiar, all five arise in full.

At other times, five arise in a lower degree. Since the objects of focus are simultaneous, the minds are likewise concurrent; because the objects are collective and the minds are equal, they are termed "the arising of five."
Thus, regarding the four [foundations], there are thirty-one phrases in total, comprising the five [mental states] such as desire, both collectively and individually.
The following section provides a summary. The first phrase marks the conclusion; while the wording is general, the meaning is specific.

Although there are various combinations and separations—single, paired, triple, or quadruple—all are termed "arousing the five upon the four. The second phrase concludes the enumeration; "arousing the five" is the general term, while "arousing... [is the specific].

From the first to the fourth, there are four distinct categories, totaling thirty-one propositions. In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), each arises individually to form five single [propositions]. When the realm of desire is contrasted with the latter four [realms], they form four propositions.

Regarding the three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the two meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), there is only one. This is what is called the "two [categories] of ten propositions."

When desire (*chanda*) and resolve (*adhimokṣa*) are paired with concentration (*samādhi*), three [factors] are established. When desire and mindfulness (*smṛti*) are paired, two [factors] are established; when desire and concentration are paired, one [factor] is established. When resolve and mindfulness are paired, two [factors] are established;
when resolve and concentration are paired, one [factor] is established. When mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom (*prajñā*) are combined, one [factor] is established.

Thus, ten [factors] are formed. By successively excluding the five factors beginning with desire, five [groups] are formed. When desire and the others arise together, one [group] is formed. These are called the thirty-one [combinations] of general and specific [factors].

There are instances where none of the five [consciousnesses] arise within the state of mind (citta-bhūmi), including those associated with the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna); such cases are numerous.

Regarding the phrase "or there are lower," this next section clarifies non-arising. As for the phrase "not being the four objects," this refers to the four types of objects, such as those that are not desired and so forth.
The "casual mind" refers to the initial momentary consciousness. That which "accompanies the storehouse consciousness" is the eighth [consciousness] with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Within such categories, none of these five arise.

Regarding the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, these five specific mental factors (pañca-viśeṣa-ālambana-citta-dharmāḥ)—from [the first] to [the fifth]—are not excluded whether the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) has occurred or not.

In the section on the seventh consciousness below, it clarifies the association of the various consciousnesses and their presence or absence according to the respective stages: in the stage where the basis has not yet been transformed, the seventh consciousness possesses only wisdom (*mati*);
the eighth consciousness possesses none at all. If the basis has already been transformed, both consciousnesses possess all five. In the section on the sixth consciousness below...
First, the heading: All [consciousnesses] are associated with these five factors. Second, the explanation: Because neither the transformed nor the non-transformed states are excluded.
One interpretation holds that the five sensory consciousnesses (pañcavijñāna) lack all five of these; because they cannot engage in inferential deliberation and lack discernment (vīkṣaṇa).

There is one interpretation [stating] that below this, the presence or absence of these five [mental factors] in the five consciousnesses is explained by two masters. The first master explains that they are all absent, as the text states.
There is another interpretation that the five consciousnesses may possess these five; (up to: the remaining three are to be understood accordingly; there is no fault in having wisdom (*prajñā*).

Next, the Master clarifies that [concentration] may indeed exist, though its characteristics are subtle and weak rather than predominant; all this is as stated in the text. Regarding the section beginning with "Obstructing, etc.," it addresses an objection.

The question asks: "The nature of the five consciousnesses is distracted; how can they possess concentration? The explanation states that "equipoise" (*samāhita*)—the Sanskrit term for which is *samāhita*—applies to both states with mind and without mind.
It is called "equipoise" (*sama*) because it is free from dullness and agitation, and it is called "inducing" (*āhita*) because it performs the function of inducing [virtuous states].

"Virtue is called 'inducing. As for 'equipoise' (samādhi), the Sanskrit term is *samāpatti*, which applies exclusively to states with mental consciousness (*sacittaka*) and distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*).

The treatises exclude 'equipoised induction' (*samāhita-samāpatti*) because the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) do not exist [in those states], stating that their nature is distracted and mobile; however, this does not exclude the meditative concentration of equipoise (*samādhi*)."

Therefore, it is permissible that the five consciousnesses possess concentration (*samādhi*). From this point downward, he cites evidence for their possessing wisdom (*prajñā*): the two supernormal powers of the eye and ear are both designated by the nature of wisdom;
by analogy with these, all five [consciousnesses] possess wisdom.
In the stage prior to mastery, these five may be absent; (up to: because all five consciousnesses possess the wisdom of accomplishing activities.

"Prior to [mastery]" below clarifies that they may be absent before transformation, but are definitely present once transformed. They universally take both the ultimate and conventional as objects, because they constitute thorough and universal knowledge.

Their apprehension of objects is direct and clear, because they are free from hesitation. As for the cause, it exhausts the long-term cultivation of reality; as for the fruit, it exhausts the long-term...

Because he has realized the ultimate truth; because he possesses the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives throughout the three periods of time; because the Nāga is always in meditative concentration;
and because all five [faculties] are endowed with wisdom—he is supremely predominant and not at all inferior.

With which sensations (*vedanā*) are these five object-specific mental states (*viṣaya-niyata*) associated? (Up to: Because the five sensory consciousnesses lack the functions of investigation and determination.
"These five... and below explains their association with sensation. The first phrase poses the question. Regarding "There is one interpretation... and below, the first explanation is given:

desire is associated with joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). This single phrase excludes the mental faculty (*manas*), because the two objects of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*) are not what is desired.

Therefore, the analysis of mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and [the feelings of] sorrow, joy, pleasure, and equanimity excludes suffering. By examining a single phrase, one explains the intent of excluding suffering.

"Examining and deciding" refers to the analysis of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; these are associated with the sixth consciousness (manovijñāna) and not with the five sensory consciousnesses.
The five sensory consciousnesses possess suffering, whereas the mental consciousness does not. Since these four [mental factors] are not associated with the five sensory consciousnesses, this is...
Therefore, suffering is excluded. This is the interpretation of Master Wu-ku (無苦師) regarding the preceding section on the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
According to another view, all [mental factors] are associated with the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*); thus, desire and the others are associated with these five feelings.
There is an interpretation that follows. Next, "all" refers to the five dharmas; this generally clarifies that all five dharmas are associated with the five feelings (*vedanā*).

The passage beginning with "The treatise says... provides specific proof that the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) possesses sorrow and suffering. The first phrase proves that the realm of desire possesses sorrow; "grief and distress" is the characteristic of sorrow.

The second phrase explains the presence of suffering; "longing" is desire (*chanda*). Regarding the phrase "the mind possesses the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and so forth," this refers to what precedes it.

The *Yi-di* (Mental Stage) contains the commentary by Master Shi. The passage beginning with "The treatise says, below" cites the treatise to provide general proof that there is sorrow and suffering within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Craving" refers to the factors associated with desire. Regarding the passage "The faculty of suffering, below," it explains that the four factors possess suffering.

Since the mental consciousness already possesses the faculty of suffering, [the passage] clarifies mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; these are factors associated with the mental consciousness. By means of this, one knows with certainty [that the aforementioned factors exist].

Fourth: there must be painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*). Furthermore, because the five [sensory] consciousnesses possess suffering, it is proven that the four mental factors [associated with them] also pertain to suffering.

These four—*nimitta*, *ālambana*, etc.—are precisely the previously mentioned subtle aspects of understanding, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. From this point downward, the various object-specific mental factors (*viṣayaviśeṣa-viniyata*) are summarized as being associated with the five types of sensation.

These five should further be reflected upon according to reason through various categories such as nature (*svabhāva*), realm (*dhātu*), and training (*śikṣā*). Regarding these five: "nature" refers to the three natures;

"realm" refers to those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth. This concludes the section by applying the same pattern to the analysis of other categories. Nature means the three natures. Realm means being bound to the desire realm and so on.

"Training" refers to the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*). Since these five [factors] already possess the first two of the four "all-inclusives," one knows that the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) and the three realms (*tri-dhātu*) all pertain to them.
As for the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna*), since it is not obstructed whether its basis is transformed or untransformed, one knows that the trainings and so forth likewise apply.
All such categories should likewise be present. One may infer this by applying the same principle to similar cases.
