This refers to doubt and the three views, which directly delude one regarding the principle of suffering (up to) the unshared ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*), which directly deludes one regarding the principle of suffering.

"Doubt and below" [refers to the subsequent section]. Next, the eight [afflictions] that generally delude all four [truths] are explained; first, it clarifies that ten [afflictions] delude the truth of suffering. Among the headings, eight are indicated.

Regarding the ten [factors] explained within the section on the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*): because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are instruments of suffering;

and because doubt (*vicikitsā*), the view of a self-identity, and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are intimately deluded regarding the principle of suffering. Briefly stated, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are collectively termed "suffering.

Within these five aggregates of clinging, the foolish give rise to twenty modes of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): five modes perceive a "self," while the remaining [fifteen] perceive "what belongs to a self" (*ātmīya*). This is called being deluded regarding suffering.
The view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) takes this very view as its basis;

because it perceives a self—either as annihilated or eternal—within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is likewise deluded regarding suffering.

Furthermore, various false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), such as the denial of giving and so forth, up to the denial of the results and maturation of wholesome and unwholesome actions, are false views deluded regarding suffering. If, with respect to the truth of suffering...

To harbor hesitation is doubt regarding suffering. Regarding the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*): one grasps those three views, the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and their associated aggregates as being supreme and capable of purification.

If there is grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), one falsely grasps all views that are deluded regarding suffering as being foremost, capable of attaining purification, liberation, and transcendence. This is called grasping at views that is deluded regarding suffering. If...

There is false grasping that accords with this view; this view regards the precepts and observances undertaken in accordance with its doctrine as supreme, believing they can bring about purification, liberation, and transcendence.
This is called the "clinging to precepts and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa) regarding suffering.
Toward one's own views and those of others, as well as their respective adherents, one accordingly gives rise to greed, hatred, and pride. If, regarding such [views] of one's own...
To give rise to views regarding what is precious and cherished, and to be firmly attached to them, is delusion regarding suffering that is craving.

To harbor thoughts of hostility and harm toward others who hold different views is delusion regarding suffering that is anger. To rely on such views and give rise to arrogance toward their followers is [delusion regarding suffering that is pride].

This is the ignorance associated with the pride of being deluded regarding suffering (*duḥkha-māna*). The common ignorance (*sāmānya-avidyā*) is distantly deluded along with the nine [afflictions], whereas the specific ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) is intimately deluded regarding the principle of suffering.

If there is a lack of wisdom that is associated with these various views, doubt, craving, and so forth, or if there is a lack of wisdom that functions independently regarding suffering alone—both of these are termed the ignorance that is deluded regarding suffering. These ten afflictions are all delusions.
The Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). That which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

Doubt (*vicikitsā*) and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) directly delude [the practitioner] regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudaya*) and so forth. Such is the coarse characteristic of the direct and indirect delusions regarding the Truths.

Regarding doubt and the subsequent [afflictions], the following explains how eight [afflictions] generally delude [the practitioner] with respect to all three [Truths]. Doubt and false view directly delude [the practitioner] regarding the Truth of Origination and so forth. The two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*)...

Greed and the other [afflictions] should be understood by analogy with suffering. That is to say, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, holding the false view that denies causes, reckon that Īśvara and others are the progenitor, the transformer, and the creator of all things; they hold that there is no giving, no receiving, and no sacrificial offerings;
and that there are neither sublime deeds nor evil deeds. This is the false view arising from delusion regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

If there is the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), wherein one takes those various views to be supreme, capable of attaining purity, liberation, and transcendence—this is the grasping of views arising from delusion regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).

If, with respect to those phenomena that accord with such views, one takes the observance of precepts and prohibitions (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) to be supreme and capable of attaining purity—this is the grasping of precepts and prohibitions arising from delusion regarding the Truth of Origination. As for the remaining [defilements] such as doubt and craving, they are likewise included.

This should be understood as previously explained. These eight kinds of afflictive latent tendencies (anuśaya) are delusions regarding the Truth of Origination and are to be abandoned by the vision of origination.

Furthermore, they include a portion of the views of certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold to the extremes of finitude or infinity, those who resort to evasive equivocation regarding death, and those who propound a theory of nirvāṇa in the present life; these individuals deny the quality of abandonment possessed by arhats and disparage it.
To slander the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and recklessly imagine it to be liberation is the false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) arising from delusion regarding the Truth of Cessation.

If one holds to those various views with the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), considering them to be supreme and capable of attaining purification, this is the grasping of views arising from delusion regarding the Truth of Cessation.
If, regarding those dharmas that accord with such views, one holds the observance of precepts and prohibitions (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*) to be supreme and capable of [attaining purification]...

Purity. This refers to the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arising from delusion regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). The remaining [afflictions], such as craving (*rāga*) and so forth, should be understood as previously explained.
Thus, these eight types of latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) are delusions regarding the Truth of Cessation and are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*).

If one denies the existence of the true Arhat in the world who is led by the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*), or who possesses conditioned outflows-free states (*asaṃskṛta-anāsrava*) and the "undying" evasion (*amarāvikṣepa*), [these are also abandoned through the vision of cessation].

A portion [of this] consists of slandering the Truth of the Path, claiming it is not true liberation, and falsely imagining what is not the path to be the right path, asserting that it can exhaust and transcend all suffering;
such is called the wrong view of being deluded regarding the path. If there is the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), [it is as follows].
To take that wrong view as supreme, thinking it can bring about purity, liberation, and deliverance—
this is called the "clinging to views regarding the path. If one takes those precepts and observances associated with such a view as supreme,
thinking they can bring about purity, liberation, and deliverance— this is called the "clinging to precepts and observances arising from delusion regarding the path."

The remaining [afflictions], such as greed and so forth, should be understood as previously explained. Thus, these eight kinds of latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) are deluded regarding the Truth of the Path and are abandoned through the vision of the Path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
However, hatred (*dveṣa*) can also directly delude one regarding Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path; this is because, through fear of them, it gives rise to aversion and envy.
That is to say, being deluded regarding Cessation and the Path, one gives rise to a mind of fear, a mind of harm, and a mind of resentment and vexation. Thus it is.
Hatred is deluded regarding cessation and the path; this concludes the lower fetters. Such is the coarse aspect of being deluded regarding the truths in terms of their proximity and distance.
To explain in detail: greed, hatred, and pride are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they do not contradict the contemplation of the truths.
[The section] "In Detail" follows. Next, it clarifies that the subtle aspects [of the afflictions] are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

If greed, hatred, pride, doubt, false views, and the two types of grasping arise in association with [speculative] discrimination (*vikalpa*), they are abandoned according to their respective categories as [afflictions] abandoned through seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*).

However, as for the innate (*sahaja*) views of self and extremes (*satkāya-antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), along with the craving, pride, and ignorance associated with them—these five, although they are delusions regarding the principle of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), are subtle.

They are difficult to sever; they are severed only through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*). Furthermore, anger and other forms of craving arise from being specifically deluded regarding particular objects (*vastu*), and thus do not contradict the contemplation of the truths (*satyadarśana*);
therefore, they are abandoned through cultivation.
Although all afflictions (*kleśa*) possess objective aspects (*nimittabhāga*), they are designated as "afflictions that take existent or non-existent things as their objects."

The passage beginning with "Although all [objects]... clarifies the distinctions among objects of cognition (*ālambana*). First, it clarifies those that have a real substrate (*sapratigha*) and those that lack one (*apratigha*), noting that both possess objective aspects (*nimittabhāga*).

As stated previously: "Within one's own mind, all internal aggregates (*skandha*) exist; their original substrates (*mūlabhāva*) are not fixed. Regarding external aggregates outside of one's own mind..."

There are cases where [the object] exists and cases where it does not. If one takes a present object as a condition, the substance relied upon exists; this is called "conditioning an existent thing" (sadravyālambana).
If one takes a past or future object as a condition, the substance relied upon does not exist; this is called "conditioning a non-existent thing" (adravyālambana).
Although those direct objects of perception (*ālambana*) are all with-outflows (*sāsrava*), they are termed "afflictions that take both the out-flowing and the out-flow-free as objects.

Regarding the phrase "those direct [objects] below," this clarifies that [the afflictions] take both the out-flowing and the out-flow-free as objects. As for the direct objects being with-outflows, it is because the mind that undergoes transformation consists solely of afflictions.
As for the fact that the primary substance (*bhāva*) extends to the out-flow-free, it is because the Path (*mārga*) and Cessation (*nirodha*) belong to the out-flow-free category.

Regarding those that take their own level as an object, the aspect (nimitta-bhāga) resembles the substance (dravya). [This continues] through the other gates of analysis; one should reflect upon them according to reason.

Regarding those that take their own or lower levels as objects, there are two types: the objective field of names (*nāma-viṣaya*) and the objective field of things (*vastu-viṣaya*). Those that take their own level as an object have an aspect that resembles the substance, and are therefore called the objective field of things.

Those belonging to other levels or the cessation (*nirodha*) [of suffering] have an aspect that does not resemble the substance, and are therefore called the objective field of names. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The afflictions..."
There are, in brief, five kinds of objects of focus (*ālambana*): first, objects that arise from false conceptualization; second, objects of views;
third, objects of rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); fourth, objects named by one's own conceptualization; and fifth, objects that are spontaneously and firmly established.
This concludes the indication under the subsequent section.
The characteristics of the six root afflictions have already been explained; what are the characteristics of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)?
The phrase "already explained below" introduces the explanation of the secondary afflictions. The initial passage concludes the preceding section and poses the subsequent question.

The verse says: "The secondary afflictions (upakleśa) are said to be anger (*krodha*)... up to... negligence (*pramāda*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*).
The verse says: "Below. Next, the verse is cited as the answer.

The treatise says: They are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) because they are of the nature of an outflow (*niṣyanda*) from specific states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the primary afflictions (*kleśa*).
The treatise says: Below is the explanation. First, it explains the general name. "Affliction" refers to the aforementioned root afflictions.

"State" means that they lack independent substance and are specific stages or positions within those [root] branches. "Specific difference" means that among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), they are comprised within the defiled portion. Etc.
"Outflows" (anuśaya) refers to those that possess a self-nature and are of the same category as the aforementioned outflows;

they all arise following the root [afflictions], conforming to and disturbing the mind, causing it not to be free from defilement, not to attain liberation, and not to sever the obstructions; therefore, they are called "secondary afflictions" (upakleśa).
These twenty types are divided into three categories; because they universally defile the mind, they are called "great secondary afflictions" (*mahā-kleśa-mahābhūmika*).
Regarding the phrase "these two [categories] below," they are classified according to their meaning. As for those such as anger (*krodha*) that arise individually:

because their nature is fierce and sharp, each acts as its own sovereign, they do not coexist with their own kind, they do not pervade both moral natures, and they do not pervade all defiled minds; therefore, they are called "minor secondary afflictions" (*parīttakleśabhūmika*).

Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) arise together with their own kind; they are exclusively pervasive among the unwholesome (*akuśala*), but not pervasive among the obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), nor pervasive among all defiled minds.

Therefore, they are called "intermediate universal" (*madhya-anuśaya*). The eight [afflictions] beginning with restlessness (*auddhatya*) arise together with their own kind; they are pervasive within both categories of the defiled and are present in all defiled minds.
Therefore, they are called "great universal" (*mahā-anuśaya*).
What is anger (*krodha*)? It is that which, based on an object present before one, [arises]... because there is no distinct characteristic or function of anger apart from hatred (*dveṣa*).

"What is it? and so forth, explains it according to its categories. First, regarding the minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*): first, the inquiry and explanation of the essence and function of anger.

Relying upon contact with a presently manifest object of great harm, its nature is that of a violent outburst. "That is to say, harboring... and so forth, further explains that its activity is the grasping of weapons; [it manifests] in the body.

Regarding the "manifest karma" (*vijñapti-karman*): the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that if one is bound by the obsession of hatred (*pratigha-anuśaya*), it can cause the facial expression to become fierce and agitated;
if one is bound by the obsessions of the afflictions (*kleśa*), it can cause one to grasp weapons and engage in combat, litigation, and conflict.
Because this is a portion of hatred, it serves as a repeated explanation below to establish that hatred constitutes its essential nature.
What is resentment (*upanāha*)? It is preceded by anger (*krodha*). [This is because] apart from anger, there is no distinct characteristic or function of resentment.

"What is it? and so forth: this interrogates and explains the essence and function of resentment. Its nature is to harbor anger and accumulate malice, thereby binding oneself in enmity. First, one encounters an object that is harmful;
subsequently, one maintains this bound resentment in every thought-moment without relinquishing it. "Binding" and so forth: this further explains its heat (*tāpa*).
"Affliction" (*nirbandha*) means harboring resentment and being unable to endure it; the mind becomes heated and ignites like fire, forging its vital energy (*prāṇa*) into metal.
Because it is constantly afflicted by heat, this also—by way of repeated explanation—establishes that hatred (*dveṣa*) constitutes its essence.
What is *mrakṣa* (concealment)? It is the act of hiding one’s own committed transgressions because, in the end, they will inevitably lead to regret, distress, and a lack of peace.

What does "below" mean? It interrogates and explains the essential nature and function of concealment. One commits a transgression oneself and, fearing the loss of material gain and reputation, conceals and hides it;

this constitutes its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The phrase "regret and distress" below provides a further explanation: while a transgression is extinguished through confession, concealment [perpetuates it].
One will inevitably fall into suffering; later, one will feel regret because of constant anxiety and distress.

According to another interpretation, this concealment (*mrakṣa*) is subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*), because one conceals one's own transgressions out of a lack of fear regarding future suffering.
There is an interpretation that the following clarifies the stages [of the factors]. First, it explains that [this factor] is subsumed under delusion (*moha*); second, it cites a treatise as proof:
because one is shrouded by the darkness of delusion, one does not fear future suffering.

One interpretation holds that this *mrakṣa* (concealment) is subsumed under a portion of both greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*), and thus it cannot be maintained as being exclusively a portion of greed.

Another interpretation states that it is subsequently explained as being subsumed under a portion of each—greed and delusion—because the fear of losing material gain and reputation constitutes a portion of greed.

Next, the meaning of its being exclusively delusion is discussed in general; as stated below, the example of *auddhatya* (restlessness) is raised for clarification. *Auddhatya* is [subsumed under] greed...
Furthermore, this is based on its coarse and manifest aspects rather than its actual nature as a derivative of greed.

Why is it called *pradāśa* (malice)? Because it is preceded by anger and resentment (*krodha* and *upanāha*); for apart from hatred (*dveṣa*), there is no separate characteristic or function for malice.

"What is it that is inferior? This interrogates and explains the essence and function of affliction (*nigha*). "Preceded by anger and resentment" means to pursue past transgressions and encounter present adverse conditions;

its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is one of stubbornness and perversity. "To pursue [the past]" and so forth provides a further explanation. "Stinging insects" refers to creatures that move with venom. "This also...
and so forth repeatedly explains that hatred (*dveṣa*) constitutes the essence.
"What is envy (*īrṣyā*)? It is the pursuit of one's own fame and profit. [The text continues] "...because there is no separate characteristic or function of envy apart from hatred (*dveṣa*).

"What is it? [This] interrogates the essence and function of envy. "To pursue" (*xùn*) means to follow after objects for the sake of the self. "That is to say, envy... [This] provides a further explanation.
"This also" (below) is a repeated explanation of the essence [of stinginess].
"What is stinginess? refers to being attached to wealth and the Dharma; [it continues] until: "because there is no separate characteristic or function of stinginess apart from greed.

"What is it that... (below) interrogates and explains the essence and function of stinginess. "That is to say, stinginess... (below) provides a further explanation. "This also" (below) is a repeated explanation.

What is deception? It is for the sake of gaining profit and reputation (up to the point where it is said that there is no distinction between the two, because their deceptive characteristics and functions are non-different).
What follows below interrogates and explains the essence and function of deception:

for the sake of gaining profit and reputation, one falsely manifests dignified deportment to appear extraordinary and delude the masses, displaying oneself as possessing virtue; through guile and fraud, one may manifest acts of intimacy or employ defiled speech; therefore, it is called deception.

"Deceit" (*kuhana*) refers to feigning inferiority. To explain further: "wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*) consists of the four wrongs, namely: *tiryagmukha* (horizontal mouth), *ūrdhvamukha* (upward mouth), *adhomukha* (downward mouth), and *vaihāryamukha* (mouth of ostentation).
The five wrongs are: first, falsely manifesting wonders; second, speaking of one's own virtues; third, divining omens and signs of good or ill fortune;

fourth, raising one's voice and assuming a formal demeanor; and fifth, preaching the Dharma for others' sake. These constitute the "downward" [category], which explains that their essence is greed and delusion.
"What is flattery (*śāṭhya*)? It is for the purpose of deceiving others. [The text continues] "...because there is no distinct characteristic or function of flattery apart from these two.

"What is it below? This interrogates and explains the essence and function of flattery. "That is to say, flattery... and so forth, provides a further explanation. It means to crookedly conform to the requirements of the occasion;

that is, to adjust one's status high or low according to the object, to advance or retreat as is appropriate, to meet with joy or sorrow in a welcoming manner, to read the intentions through facial expressions and gestures, and the like. This also...
[The text] below repeatedly explains that greed and delusion constitute its essence.
As for what constitutes harm toward sentient beings (up to the point where it says): "The specific characteristics of hatred and harming should be explained by analogy with the wholesome [factors]."
"What is it? introduces the inquiry into the essence and function of harm (*vihiṃsā*). "That is to say" (*yad uta*) introduces the further explanation of affliction (*bādhanā*).

"This too" (*iyam api*) provides a reciprocal explanation of its essence. Regarding the distinct characteristics of hatred (*dveṣa*) and harm: hatred severs the life-force of beings, while harm injures and afflicts others.
Hatred obstructs great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), and harm obstructs great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); these are their respective distinct characteristics.
What is *mada* (haughtiness) regarding one's own flourishing prosperity? [From "to" ... because there is no distinct characteristic or function of *mada* apart from the absence of greed (*rāga*).

What follows [the phrase] "what is" interrogates and explains the essence and function of *mada*. "One's own flourishing prosperity" refers to: physical vigor, noble lineage, wealth, sovereignty, longevity, intelligence, virtuous conduct, and physical complexion.
These eight are correlated with the eight birds: the owl, the screech-owl, the eagle, the vulture, the hawk, the falcon, the partridge, and the pheasant.
Crows, magpies, pigeons, and doves—those who are intoxicated with arrogance do not feel humble respect toward their elders and fields of merit;
this refers to "pride" (*māna*). This further explains the basis of defilement. Furthermore, "this too" refers back to explain that greed (*lobha*) constitutes its essence.
What is the lack of shame (*āhrīkya*)? It is that which disregards one’s own Dharma... [and so forth] because it obstructs the growth of shame and gives rise to various unwholesome conducts.
What follows below is the detailed explanation; following the sequence, it first interrogates and explains the essence and function of the lack of shame:

it is the sudden abandonment of the noble and the good, being without reverence or veneration toward all meritorious qualities and those who possess virtue, having no sense of restraint or difficulty, and being without any sense of subordination or dependence.
This is called *āhrīkya* (lack of shame). To explain this further: what is *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread)?
It is the failure to take account of the world [and so forth], because it obstructs the growth of *apatrāpya* (dread of blame) and causes the proliferation of various unwholesome actions.
"How is it that... [The text] interrogates and explains the essence and function of *anapatrāpya* (lack of shame). "That is to say, regarding... [The text] provides a further explanation:

not feeling shame for one's transgressions and evils is the common characteristic of both [lack of shame and lack of dread]. [This continues] until: "furthermore, this contradicts the treatise’s statement that both [lack of shame and lack of dread] pervade all unwholesome minds."

One does not feel shame before those below. Regarding the discernment [of the two roots], one first determines their common and specific aspects. Shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) each have both common and specific characteristics.

The sacred teachings rely on the common aspect and provisionally designate it as their essence. If one adheres to the latter phrase, it restates that the common characteristic is taken as the essence.

Then it should be refuted by the "lower" [position]. It is not a refutation by way of non-acceptance; rather, it is a refutation by way of analogy. If one awaits the "lower," this is the restatement of the defense. It should be a non-"lower"; this is the restatement of the refutation.
If the "lower" is conceded, this is again the restatement of the defense and its refutation. All of these are explained by reversing the sequence of shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*).
At the time of an unwholesome mind, regardless of what object it encounters—up to the point where the object of cognition does not differ—there is no fault of [the mind] arising separately.
Below this, an objection is raised: "Since wholesome and unwholesome objects are distinct, their respective objects of cognition must be different;

therefore, they should not arise simultaneously. They do not arise together; they arise separately. Since these two points are identical, why is the criticism directed only at one? If one arises and not two, then...

It is not the case that unwholesome minds are not universal. Therefore, the answer now states: all unwholesome minds arise in accordance with their respective objects and possess the quality of rejecting the wholesome and exalting the unwholesome.
Thus, the following section concludes the answer: unwholesome minds that are universal have no difference in their objective referents.
However, the various holy teachings state that those who disregard both self and others (up to) are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of that [lack of shame], not its very nature (*svabhāva*).

The passage beginning with "However, all... provides a general rebuttal to objections; the preceding section constitutes the explanation of the meaning, both of which are stated as the opposites of *hrī* (shame). The passage beginning with "The treatise... poses a question.
Since these two each possess their own substantial entity, why does the treatise describe them as divisions of greed? The general meaning is as stated in the text.
Why is restlessness said to cause the mind to [distract] toward objects, having the function of obstructing equanimity (*upekṣā*) and calm abiding (*śamatha*)?

Regarding the section "What is the lower [level]": this is a separate explanation of the great secondary affliction (*mahābhūmika-kleśa*). First, it interrogates and explains the essence and function of *auddhatya* (restlessness):

it is a state of agitation and levity that causes the mind to be non-quiescent with respect to its objects; thus, the body is like one who has fallen alone, the mouth is like a spring frog, and the mind is like a lamp in the wind.

The practice of equanimity has the function of abiding in tranquility. Śamatha—here translated as "stopping"—is the cessation of delusion and the realization of the true essence. This [equanimity] makes [the mind] easy to understand;
however, because it causes the cognitive faculty (ālambaka) to lack stillness, it obstructs both [śamatha and vipaśyanā].
One interpretation holds that restlessness (*auddhatya*) is subsumed under a portion of greed (*rāga*), because it arises from recollecting past pleasurable experiences.

Another interpretation [proceeds] below to clarify its states (*avasthā*). First, the initial explanation subsumes it under greed, citing scriptural evidence and providing a formal proof, as the text itself explains.

One interpretation holds that restlessness (*auddhatya*) is not subsumed solely under greed (*lobha*); rather, because it increases during the state of greed, it is described as a derivative of greed.

Another interpretation [proceeds] below. The second explanation [consists of]: the first phrase refutes the former view; the second phrase cites the treatise [to show that restlessness] pervades all defiled minds, and therefore it is not a derivative of greed.
Furthermore, the section beginning with "Moreover, restlessness" clarifies its inclusion within the universal [mental factors], for all afflictions (*kleśa*) are by nature non-quiescent.

The next phrase explains by way of contrast. Since restlessness (*auddhatya*) is nothing other than this lack of tranquility, it has no separate characteristic. Although it relies on the lower [realms], it serves as a general counter-objection. One might ask:
"If it is subsumed within the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), why does the treatise describe it as a division of greed (*rāga*"? The explanation for this is as stated in the text.
One interpretation holds that *auddhatya* (restlessness) has a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that pervades all defiled minds, just like *āśraddhya* (lack of faith) and other such factors.

Another interpretation [the third solution] establishes through formal inference (*pramāṇa*) that it possesses a separate entity: "Restlessness has a distinct intrinsic nature because it pervades all defiled minds;
for example, like lack of faith and so forth. Among the eight great secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), lack of faith and laziness (*kausīdya*) pervade all [defiled minds].

Because the defiled mind has a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is not the case that its substance is unreal simply because it is described as belonging to another category—just as sleep and so forth are described according to their dependent characteristics.

The phrase "it is not said" below refutes the first interpretation; for according to that first interpretation, greed subsumes it and it lacks a separate intrinsic nature, and thus it would not be substantially real. Now...

The specific characteristic of *styāna* (sloth) is that it is a state of dullness and heaviness which renders the co-arising factors incapable of being sustained.

This explains the hindrance to meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*). Since there is a distinct hindrance to observation, it must necessarily have a distinct characteristic; therefore, the final phrase [of the verse] does not apply as a concluding censure.
This differs from the characteristic of delusion (*moha*) in that it directly hinders pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) rather than being characterized by confusion and darkness.

That is to say, through laziness (*kausīdya*) as well as greed, hatred, and delusion—up to this point—it is collectively termed "heedlessness" (*pramāda*), and it does not possess a separate substantial entity.

That is to say, by way of the states of the lower [levels] and the lack of illumination (*aloka*), this is established based on the four factors of laziness, greed, hatred, and delusion; it has no separate substantial entity.

Because all [of these] belong to the defiled.

"What is it that is inferior? This interrogates and explains the essence and function of improper awareness (*asamprajanya*). Because one knows incorrectly, one has a distorted understanding regarding the objects of observation:
taking the impermanent to be permanent, and taking the non-self to be self; these are the four inversions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Because they are pervasive taints.

Regarding the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) taught by the Blessed One within the *Kṣudrakavastu*, ranging extensively from sorrow, lamentation, grief, and despair, to joy, delight, and affection: Question:

If it is as stated in the *Kṣudrakavastu*, should the suffering, pleasure, grief, and joy among the [five] feelings (*vedanā*) also be subsumed under the afflictions? Answer: They arise [from them], yet they are not [themselves] included therein.
This is what is subsumed under the "afflictions" (*kleśa*). When one's conduct deviates from the proper measure, this belongs to the afflictions.
Regarding the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) explained in the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*: they are the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion;
as well as anger, resentment, and so forth, including all such various defiled matters. Furthermore, these secondary afflictions also subsume the primary afflictions.
Because these are of the nature of the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the aforementioned afflictions (*kleśa*), they are both termed "outflows" when viewed in relation to one another.

Regarding "afflictions of the same class and other defiled phenomena," this refers to those within the categories of the specific objects (*viśeṣālambana*), the indeterminate (*aniyata*), and the defiled portions among the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).

These are called only "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*), as they are not subsumed under the category of root afflictions. Question: Since they possess the remaining three classes of defiled phenomena, [the verse states...]

Regarding the statement that there are "only twenty" [mental factors] in the middle [section]: why is this? The answer is that first they are excluded and then subsumed. Although other categories exist, only twenty are mentioned;

that is to say, those which are not afflictions (*kleśa*) are excluded, thereby removing the root [afflictions]. The character "not" (*fei*) runs through the following: it is not only the defiled ones [that are excluded].
Excluding those that are defiled within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the word "only" (*kevala*) also governs what follows. It is not merely the coarse;

by excluding greed and other various factors that pertain to both the coarse and the subtle, these three categories are excluded, leaving only twenty. These remaining defiled dharmas comprise the defilements within the three natures;
this "state" (*avasthā*) comprises the many varieties within the "mixed matters" (*vyavakīrṇa-vastu*); and this "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) comprises the fundamental [defilements].
These three are all subsumed within these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). The second phrase establishes the meaning of this subsumption:
according to their respective categories and distinctions, each is subsumed by its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, they likewise number only twenty.
Regarding these twenty secondary afflictions (upakleśa), the principles and scriptural citations adduced therein should be understood as previously explained.

Thus, below, the classification according to different categories first distinguishes between the provisional and the real. The first phrase provides a general heading for the three types; next, they are distinguished.

The ten minor afflictions, such as anger (*krodha*), and the three major ones—heedlessness (*pramāda*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*)—are definitely nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*), because they are established based on the states of the fundamental [afflictions].
The two intermediate [major] ones and the two major ones—restlessness (*auddhatya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and distraction (*vikṣepa*)—are definitely substantially existent (*dravyasat*).

These [three] apply to both the provisional and the real. Each of these three has three interpretations. Those that are categorized as part of greed, part of delusion, or as common characteristics that pervasively defile are provisional.
Those whose essence consists of agitation, dullness/heaviness, and restless disturbance are real.
The twenty [types of afflictions] all pertain to both the innate (*sahaja*) and the conceptual (*vikalpita*), as they arise through the power of either of these two afflictions.
The first line indicates that they pertain to both; the second line explains their meaning.
Among these twenty [mental factors], the ten minor ones may arise together with one another; that is, they may all arise simultaneously both among themselves and with the intermediate ones.

Regarding the phrase "these two [intermediate ones] below," they are associated with their own respective categories. The ten minor ones do not arise simultaneously with one another. The next two lines explain the meaning of their non-simultaneity.

The two intermediate unwholesome minds arise together with the minor ones as appropriate: namely, anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāsa*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).

These are unwholesome. Eight of the great [mental factors] and one part of the others are common to the unwholesome. The two intermediate [factors] arise together with these; therefore, it is said they "accord accordingly.

because they pervade both [wholesome and unwholesome] natures.

"From this [point] below," refers to those associated with all feelings (*vedanā*). regarding the first explanation of anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), vexation (*pradāsa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*): these are associated only with the three feelings of joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and sorrow (*daurmanasya*), because they are subsumed under the category of hatred (*dveṣa*).

Regarding the three—hatred, delusion, and their concomitants—both innate (*sahaja*) and discursive (*vikalpita*), all are capable of arising together with the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*).

If one follows the coarse characteristics, [the afflictions] from anger (*krodha*) through enmity (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāsa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*)—up to the intermediate and great [degrees]—are also according to their actual meaning.

If one follows the subtle characteristics, it is clear that they are associated with both feeling (*vedanā*). The five minor [afflictions], such as anger and so forth, are associated with both sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), because they are divisions of hatred (*dveṣa*).
They are not associated with pleasure (*sukha*) or joy (*saumanasya*); they exist only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). They are not associated with suffering (*duḥkha*).

Concealment (*mrakṣa*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the three—flattery (*śāṭhya*), deceit (*māyā*), and arrogance (*mada*)—are associated with pleasure, joy, and equanimity, as they are all part of greed (*lobha*). According to the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, they arise together with the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*).
Thus, these twenty [mental factors] and the five object-specific ones (up to the point where it says) "therefore, there is no fault in their association with distraction and concentration.
Thus, below, they arise together with the object-specific ones. First, it clarifies that the twenty arise together with the five.

Regarding "defiled mindfulness" and so on, this addresses an objection. The question asks: Defiled mindfulness refers to forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), and defiled wisdom refers to lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*). These should not be associated with mindfulness and wisdom [respectively].
They arise together. Answer: Furthermore, that which is a portion of delusion (*moha*) can also be associated with them. Again, it is asked:

Memory (*smṛti*) takes as its object what was previously practiced, while anger (*krodha*) confronts a present contradiction; how can they be associated? Answer: Memory also takes as its object a present object of a type previously practiced, and anger can also take a momentary past object as its object.
Alternatively, memory may recede toward the later [moment], or anger may advance toward the earlier; therefore, anger and memory [can be associated].
It is also possible for them to be associated. Furthermore, it was asked: "How can distraction and agitation be compatible with meditative concentration? The answer was:
"When defiled concentration arises, the mind is likewise agitated; therefore, there is no fault in distraction being associated with concentration."

The two intermediate [unwholesome roots] are associated with eighty great afflictions (up to the point of) having no contradiction in their modes of activity (*ākāra*), because they are categorized as greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*).
The two intermediate [roots] are associated with the lower [afflictions]. The two intermediate [roots] are associated with eighty great afflictions.

The ten minor [afflictions] certainly do not arise together with views (*dṛṣṭi*) or doubt (*vicikitsā*), because there is a difference between them in terms of coarseness and subtlety. Anger (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāśa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), and arrogance (*mada*) may be associated with delusion (*moha*).

Regarding "concomitant with both": because the objects of what is detested and what is despised can be the same, and because delusion (*moha*) pervades all defiled states of mind; it is not concomitant with greed or hatred, as these belong to different categories.

Regarding its being subsumed under the category of hatred: because although the objects differ, the type [of mental affliction] is the same. Regarding its concomitance with stinginess (*mātsarya*), delusion, and pride (*māna*): delusion pervades the defiled mind.

Because greed and self-reliance are similar; it is not that greed and hatred coexist. That which is subsumed under the category of greed is so because their nature is similar while their objects differ.
That conceit (*mada*) is associated only with delusion (*moha*) indicates that it does not coexist with greed, hatred, or pride (*māna*). Greed, hatred, and pride are as described above.

Because their nature is similar while their objects differ, it is distinct from pride. That it is a subdivision of greed is because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) consists of passionate attachment and disdain.

Because they are distinct: concealment (*mrakṣa*), deceit (*māyā*), and guile (*śāṭhya*) are compatible with greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), and pride (*māna*). There is no contradiction in their modes of activity (*ākāra*).

Because they are parts of greed and delusion: that which is a part of greed is associated with delusion, and that which is a part of delusion is associated with greed. Since the object of defiled self-conceit is the same, it can be associated with pride.

The seven minor [afflictions] and two intermediate [afflictions] are subsumed exclusively under the unwholesome; the three major [afflictions] and eight intermediate [afflictions] also pertain to the neutral.

Regarding the seven minor [afflictions], the three lower [categories]—anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāsa*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*)—as well as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), are subsumed exclusively under the unwholesome.
The three major [afflictions] and eight intermediate [afflictions] pertain to both natures (wholesome and unwholesome).

The seven minor [unwholesome mental factors] and two middle ones are comprised solely within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); deceit (*māyā*) and guile (*śāṭhya*) belong to both the desire and form realms (*rūpadhātu*);

the remainder are common to all three realms. The seven minor [factors] are comprised within the lower three realms; the two middle ones belong solely to the desire realm and do not extend to the two higher realms, as they are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Deceit and guile belong to the desire and form realms; pride (*mada*) and the eight major [unwholesome factors] are common to all three realms.
One born in a lower stage may give rise to the eleven [afflictions] of a higher stage (up to the point of not being the actual moisture for rebirth and not slandering cessation).

"Born in a lower [stage]" clarifies the state of manifest activity; first, one gives rise to afflictions of a higher stage from a lower stage. In a lower stage, it is possible to give rise to the eleven [afflictions] of a higher stage.

This refers to the three—flattery (*śāṭhya*), deception (*māyā*), and pride (*mada*)—as well as the eight great [afflictions]. Being attached to the indeterminate, one gives rise to flattery, deception, and pride toward sentient beings in higher realms.

If born in a lower realm, one clearly gives rise to the lower afflictions; in the higher realms, one gives rise to the latter ten [afflictions], namely the two intermediate ones and the eight great ones.
This is because wrong view slanders liberation, and the craving for rebirth (*upapatti-tṛṣṇā*) born in a lower realm can give rise to the latter ten.

The minor [afflictions] of the ten stages cannot arise from a higher stage to moisten a lower one, because they do not properly moisten rebirth nor do they involve the denial of cessation (*nirodha*).

While wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) denies cessation and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) moistens rebirth, the two intermediate [categories] and the eight major [categories] of the lower stages also take the higher as their object. This extends up to pride (*māna*), which does not take the lower as its object because it is not something upon which one relies.

The middle two [levels] and the lower [level] take the upper as their object. First, regarding the lower afflictions taking the upper as their object: the middle two [levels] and the eight great [afflictions] of the lower [level] also take the upper as their object.

This is because they arise in association with greed and so forth directed toward the upper [levels], namely, the greed for the *āsvādana-samādhi* (tasting concentration), hatred toward the separation from desire (*vairāgya*), and the views of self, extremes, and pride which take all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as their general object.

Regarding the twelve minor [afflictions], according to the first interpretation, the ten minor [afflictions] of the lower [level] do not take the upper as their object; according to the second interpretation, they do.

Envy and the other [afflictions] can also take higher levels as their objects. The eight great [defilements] take lower levels as their objects; the higher afflictions take lower levels as their objects.

The eight great [defilements], namely flattery (*māyā*) and deceit (*śāṭhya*), also take lower levels as their objects because they arise in association with pride (*māna*) and so forth that take lower levels as their objects. For instance, Brahmā gives rise to flattery and deceit toward the Śākya sons;
just as the Great Brahmā King, within his own assembly, concealed his true state and manifested deceptive signs to mislead the bhikṣu Aśvajit.

In order to avoid being questioned by Aśvajit, he thus indulges in self-conceit and self-praise; for conceit does not take lower levels as its object, since the dharmas of those lower stages are not objects of reliance for him.

All twenty [types of pride] are neither included within the state of training (*śaikṣa*) nor beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because these [types of pride] are exclusively defiled, whereas those [two states] are exclusively pure.
The first twenty are subsumed within the three trainings; this can be understood accordingly.
The latter ten are exclusively abandoned through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, because envy and other such afflictions arise toward the cessation, the path, and so forth.

The latter ten are subsumed under the three types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*). The latter ten pertain exclusively to both the abandonment by insight (*darśana-prahāṇa*) and the abandonment by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*);

they are not non-abandonable (*aprahātavya*). The subsequent phrase provides the proof: because they arise in association with both conceptualized (*vikalpa*) and innate (*sahaja*) afflictions (*kleśa*). Regarding the section on "abandonment by insight" below, it specifically explains the distinctions among the latter ten as being abandoned by insight.
Their fundamental delusion regarding the truths is either general or specific, as previously stated; the latter ten follow accordingly.

Those fundamental [afflictions], whether general or specific, arise simultaneously and all equally involve delusion regarding the Four Truths; the degree of intimacy or remoteness of this delusion regarding the Truths is also explained according to the fundamental afflictions.
Regarding the first ten [categories] below, there is a separate explanation of the distinctions among the ten types of abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

There are two interpretations: the first interpretation holds that they are abandoned solely through cultivation, as stated in the text; the second interpretation holds that they pertain to both types of abandonment. The first phrase indicates the two types of abandonment, and the subsequent phrase provides the explanation.

Second, the characteristic of abandonment (*prahāṇa-lakṣaṇa*). Because they arise based on both the conceptual (*vikalpita*) and the innate (*sahaja*), the next phrase explains the characteristic of abandonment through views (*dṛṣṭi-prahāṇa-lakṣaṇa*):

because they arise by taking other views and so forth as their objects. Among those abandoned by views, the first ten [categories] follow their respective fundamental objects; while they take the truths (*satya*) as their objects, they are distinguished by being delusions regarding specific aspects.

Furthermore, all of them equally involve delusion regarding the four truths. Below this, the characteristics of direct and indirect delusion are clarified. There are two interpretations: the first explains indirect delusion, and the second explains...
Envy and the others apply universally to both those who are close and those who are distant; all are as stated in the text.

However, the ten [afflictions] such as anger take only existent things as their objects (緣有事); it should be understood that taking contaminated things (*sāsrava*) as objects follows the same principle as above.

However, from "but anger" (*krodha*) onwards, it clarifies that [anger] occurs whether there is an object or not, and whether it is with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), as explained in the section on the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Having already explained the characteristics of the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), there are four that are indeterminate (*aniyata*); what are their characteristics?
The phrase "Having already explained" below explains the indeterminate factors. First, it concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent inquiry.
The verse says: "The indeterminate [mental factors] are regret, sleep, vitarka, and vicāra; each of these two pairs is twofold.
The verse provides the answer by citing the preceding summary.

The commentary states: Because regret, sleep, vitarka, and vicāra occur across wholesome, defiled, and other states, and pervade all levels of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are designated as "indeterminate" (*aniyata*).

The *Śāstra* says, "Below," [the author] explains the general name. Regarding the statement, "These four are called 'indeterminate' (*aniyata*)," faith and the others are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*), while greed and the others are exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*);
each is restricted solely to one category. These [four mental factors] are not like those; they are both wholesome and defiled, and are therefore called "indeterminate.

The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). This reveals that these four categories pervade all three natures (*tridhātu*). The final two phrases provide an example to illustrate this.

The term "definite" (niyata) serves to distinguish these from the "indefinite" (aniyata). While contact (*sparśa*) and the others are universal to the mind (*citta*), and desire (*chanda*) and the others are universal to the stages (*bhūmi*), each of those is definitely universal.
These [four] are not like them; they are restricted solely to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and do not pervade the other seven consciousnesses.

Furthermore, the first two exist only in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the latter two cease at the First Dhyāna; thus, they cannot definitely pervade the stages and are therefore called "indefinite. The first phrase refers to their commonality with both [realms].
It is said to be indeterminate (*aniyata*). The latter two phrases contrast with the determinate (*niyata*) and universal (*sarvatraga*) to exemplify the indeterminate.
"Regret" (*kaukṛtya*) refers to remorse regarding an action performed poorly; it is the thought: "Such an undertaking was a regrettable act of mine."
"Remorse" (*kaukṛtya*) refers to the lower [mental state]. Next, the specific characteristics are explained. First, remorse is explained. Initially, its specific name is presented;
next, its essence and function are presented. "Badly done" (*akṛta*) means that the action performed was evil. Its nature is to follow with regret after having committed an evil deed.
Its function is to obstruct tranquility (*śamatha*). The essence of tranquility is stillness; remorse, together with restlessness (*auddhatya*), is agitated and obstructs it. This is...
Below, [the text] further explains that "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*) is named "evil-doing" (*akṛtya*). "Evil-doing" is the name for the cause; "regret" (*vipratisāra*) is the designation for the effect.
Now, when it is called "evil-doing" at the stage of remorse, this is a case of metaphorically applying the name of the cause to the effect; it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound (possessive compound).
The second phrase explains the intention behind applying the name "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*) to its result: because one first performs an evil act and only later feels regret.
Thus, regretting a prior inferior act is subsumed under "remorse" even when it refers to what was not previously done. Next, the text cites examples to explain the characteristics:
regretting that one did not do what should have been done is "my remorse. Both doing and not doing are termed "remorse," as in the case of not having previously performed a virtuous deed.
If one subsequently gives rise to a mind of regret after having previously committed evil, this regret is also wholesome.

If one gives rise to a mind of regret after not having previously committed evil, this regret is unwholesome. If one gives rise to a mind of regret after having previously performed a wholesome deed, this regret is unwholesome.
One should apply this same principle to cases of neither-wholesome-nor-unwholesome (avyākṛta) actions and non-actions; therefore, this [regret] pervades all three natures.

* middha* (torpor) refers to sleep, which renders the body unresponsive; [it continues] up to "because it is associated with the mind like other hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).

*Middha* refers to the lower state. This explains *middha*. The dulling and darkening of the six sense faculties is called *svapna* (sleep); the relaxation and release of the four limbs is called *middha* (torpor). The first two phrases define its essence and function.

When observing the essence, one finds it is characterized by clarity and discernment, yet it is obscured by dullness and inferiority—this is what is meant by "the lower state of *svapna*. This further explains that the body is no longer... [responsive].

Regarding "mastery": the body possesses the four modes of deportment, whereas sleep is restricted solely to the reclining posture; thus, the mind is extremely dark and inferior. This explains the obscurity [of sleep]. During the waking state, the six consciousnesses are luminous and clearly discerning;

in the state of sleep, the mental faculty is dark, dull, and narrow. Regarding "transforming through a single gate": *Note: The term "six consciousnesses" (ṣaḍ-vijñāna) refers to the five sensory consciousnesses and the mental consciousness. The term "mental faculty" (citta) here refers to the underlying substrate consciousness (ālayavijñāna).*

This is a brief explanation. When the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes objects as its conditions, it extends to both the internal and external. In dreams, when it functions independently, it tends primarily toward the internal gate.

This is similar in outward appearance to the state of meditative concentration and the waking state; however, they differ in their clarity and scope. In the state of meditative absorption, one is alert and lucid; in the waking state, one’s awareness is comprehensive and all-encompassing.
The two characters together reveal the essence and function of sleep. Regarding the phrase "whether it exists or not," this distinguishes its differences.

Question: In a mindless state of sleep, this essence does not exist; why then is this name still applied? Answer: Because it resembles that [awake state], this name is provisionally established for it.

Regarding the phrase "as with others," this establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) with a metaphor: sleep is not without essence and function, because it is associated with the mind, just like [other mental states].

The remaining hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and fetters (*paryavasthāna*) refer to the five hindrances and ten fetters. Sleep (*middha*) is subsumed under both the hindrances and the fetters; the others belong to the same category.
According to one interpretation, these two have delusion (*moha*) alone as their essence, because they are described as secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and as parts of delusion.

There is an interpretation [which holds that] the following clarifies the stages (*avasthā*) of two dharmas, with four different explanations. The first explanation takes delusion (*moha*) as its essence, citing a treatise to prove it.

Another interpretation says this is not so, because it also extends to the wholesome (*kuśala*); thus, it is said to be subsumed under the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and a portion of delusion.

There is an interpretation that [the passage] "below" refers to the subsequent explanation of how [the two types of mindfulness] pervade both the defiled and the pure. The two characters "not so" (*bù rán*) refute the preceding view. The following phrase establishes that they pervade both natures.

The words "it should be said" (*yīng shuō*) below explain this in detail. The two defiled [types of mindfulness] take delusion (*moha*) as their essence; the two pure [types] have non-delusion (*amoha*) as their essence.
The words "the treatise relies on" (*lùn yī*) below reconcile this with what was previously cited.
There is one interpretation that this explanation is also illogical (up to the point where it says): "Just as lack of faith and so forth are said to be divisions of delusion (*moha*).

There is another interpretation [stated] below, which provides three explanations. The first two lines generally refute the preceding [view]: the indeterminate factors of regret (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) do not belong to either the wholesome or the defiled categories.

"Should they not be without substance? [The author] says "should be explained" (*vaktavyam*) below to state his own position: remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is subsumed under delusion (*moha*), and torpor (*middha*) is subsumed under vitarka and vicāra;

both are indicated by the first phrase and explained by the second. Next, he cites a treatise (*śāstra*) stating that they exist conventionally (*saṃvṛti-sat*) to prove their inclusion within the category of others.

Regarding "those defiled... and below, he establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to encompass the preceding citation from the treatise: "Defiled remorse and torpor are said to be parts of delusion; they are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of delusion."

Therefore, just as with lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) and so forth, there is an interpretation that their stated reasoning is also incorrect. [This continues until: "it is designated as conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*) according to the characteristics of delusion (*moha*).

There is another interpretation below; the first two phrases generally refute [the opponent's view], while the next phrase identifies conceptualization (*vitarka*) as the essence of deliberative wisdom (*cintāmayī prajñā*). The subsequent phrase...

Regarding the establishment of the thesis: the fetters of regret (*kaukṛtya*) and the fetters of torpor (*middha*) constitute two distinct essential natures (*svabhāva*). One should state that they possess individual entities;

by means of one phrase clarifying their distinctness from others, and another phrase showing the distinction in their functions, it is demonstrated that their essential natures are distinct. This is because these two differ in their modes of activity (*ākāra*) from the other five categories of mental factors (*caitasika*).

Regarding the phrase "following delusion" (*moha-anuśaya*): according to the general principle, when something is designated as existing conventionally (*saṃvṛti-sat*) based on its dependence upon the characteristics of another, it is called "conventionally existent."
It is not that they lack distinct entities.
"Vitarka" (applied thought) refers to seeking and searching, which causes the mind to be hurried and urgent. [This continues] until: because no distinction in their essential nature can be found.

Regarding the phrase "Vitarka refers to... and below, this is a combined explanation of vitarka and vicāra (sustained thought). First, the essence of vitarka is set forth: vitarka is the act of pursuing and seeking, which causes the mind to be occupied with its tasks.

*Vitarka* (initial inquiry) has the nature of coarse and rough mental activity directed toward an object of mental discourse (*manojalpa*). Next, the essence of *vicāra* (sustained investigation) is explained:
it has the nature of subtle and refined mental activity directed toward an object of mental discourse, causing the mind to be occupied with urgent and immediate application.

As for the "object of mental discourse," it refers to the objects apprehended by the mind, as they mostly rely on the names and phrases of the mental level (*manobhūmi*). Below this, the two are explained together.
When it functions with a subtle transition toward the objects of mental discourse, it serves as the basis for a settled body and mind;

when it functions with a coarse transition toward the objects of mental discourse, it serves as the basis for an unsettled body and mind. Although they differ in being coarse or subtle, both take a portion of *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom born of reflection) as their essence.
That which causes the mind to be settled is the aspect of *cintā* (reflection); that which causes the mind to be unsettled is the aspect of *prajñā* (wisdom).

As for "vitality" (*vitarka*), it is slow and subtle; as for "discernment" (*vicāra*), it is rapid and coarse. Regarding their simultaneous application, there is both a primary and an auxiliary function.

If vitality is used primarily, rapid discernment follows it, which can cause the mind to become unsettled. If discernment is used primarily, slow vitality follows it, which likewise causes instability.
Therefore, one should primarily employ discernment while employing a portion of vitality as an auxiliary. As for "investigation" (*vicāra*)...

It employs volition (*cetanā*) correctly and a portion of wisdom (*prajñā*) concurrently; therefore, it is said that its essence consists of both a portion of volition and a portion of wisdom combined.

Regarding the section below on "the mental faculty" (*manas*), this addresses a potential objection: "If the essence of both is volition and wisdom, by what meaning are they distinguished? The answer is: although the two essences are the same...

When *vitarka* (applied thought) operates coarsely, it involves shallow investigation; when *vicāra* (sustained thought) operates subtly, it involves deep investigation. Their meanings and categories are distinct according to their coarseness and subtlety, and their shallowness and depth.

If one excludes the lower [levels], they are revealed by contrast; furthermore, apart from the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), the essential nature of *vitarka* and *vicāra* cannot be found, nor can their distinctions in meaning and category be established.

Regarding the phrase "each of the two has two," there is an interpretation that *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) each have two distinct categories: the defiled and the pure.
The section beginning with "Each of the two" explains this "each of the two has two. There are three different interpretations. In the first interpretation, *vitarka* and *vicāra* are the two;
since each of these has the two distinctions of being defiled or pure, they are called "each of the two has two."
One interpretation holds that this explanation does not accord with correct principle (until): "Alternatively, each has its own envelopment (*paryavasthāna*) and latent disposition (*anuśaya*).

Another interpretation holds that the following section provides the solution. The first phrase refutes the preceding view; the second phrase cites remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) as counter-examples.

This master also regards vitarka and vicāra as the two [factors], but states that they should not apply to the pure (*anāsrava*) states and should exist only in the defiled (*sāsrava*). Therefore, he refutes them by calling them "remorse."
Since sleep (*middha*) also possesses both defiled and pure aspects, it is not appropriate to designate it by two distinct names, "defiled" and "pure.
If one were to name it thus, it would redundantly overlap with the preceding two [categories], which is illogical. It should be stated as follows:

To provide a formal explanation by citing an example, just as the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) belonging to a defiled mind differ in their natures, so too do vitarka and vicāra each possess [their own distinct characteristics].
The wholesome and the obscured-unspecified each possess two natures; alternatively, each has both envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), which is termed "two for each.
Envelopments refer to active manifestations, while latent dispositions refer to seeds.
There is an interpretation that his [previous] explanation is also unreasonable (up to the point where it says: "Therefore, placing this statement is profoundly useful.

There is another interpretation [beginning with] "The following three explanations": the first two lines refute the preceding [view], because this statement occurs after the four indeterminate [factors].

How could it be restricted solely to vitarka and vicāra? Therefore, it is unreasonable. It should be stated that [the following] next presents the correct meaning; it should be stated that there are two.
The word "these" (*ime*) cites the two characters from the verse. The second line enumerates them. These first two characters manifest two kinds of pairs:
one kind of pair refers to regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*); the second kind of pair refers to vitarka and vicāra. Regarding the phrase "these two," this explains their meaning.

The expression "these two" refers to the two kinds mentioned above—regret, sleep, vitarka, and vicāra—because each possesses its own distinct nature and category; hence the use of the singular and plural terms.
This reveals two pairs. "Each of these has... and below explains that each has two. The word "this" refers to regret (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), vitarka, and vicāra;

since each of these pertains to both [categories], it is said that "each has two. That is to say, they are either defiled (*kliṣṭa*) or non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*). This is not like the single phrase [previously cited], which serves as an example to contrast and reveal the characteristics of each pair:

those associated with the wholesome (*kuśala*) are exclusively wholesome, while those associated with the defiled are exclusively defiled, each being strictly one [of the two]. This case is not like that.

Therefore, it is said that "each has two. Or, to distinguish them from those that are exclusively defiled, the phrase "each has two" is stated. The subsequent sentence explains the intent of this distinction:

because some [factors] are also described as secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), this demonstrates that these four apply to both the defiled and the non-defiled, and do not possess a single uniform characteristic.

Therefore, it is said that each of the two has two aspects. That which is "profoundly useful" refers to those types mentioned above which are distinct from one another, yet pervade both the defiled and the pure, thereby excluding those that are exclusively defiled. Because they possess these many meanings, they are said to be "useful."
Among the four [dhyānas], vitarka and vicāra are definitely nominally existent (prajñaptisat). This is because the treatise also states that they are conventionally existent (saṃvṛtisat).

Regarding the phrase "among the four," this is a classification by way of different categories; first, it distinguishes between the nominal and the real, establishing that vitarka and vicāra are nominally existent by citing the treatise as proof.

There are two interpretations regarding remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*). The first interpretation holds that they exist as designations (*prajñapti-sat*); the second, the correct interpretation, holds that they are substantial entities (*dravya-sat*).

Only the final phrase of the latter section cites the existence of vitarka and vicāra as being nominal, thereby contrasting them to reveal that remorse and sleep are indeed substantial. The three subsequent phrases concerning the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) apply generally to the preceding citation from the treatise.
Regarding the discussion of conventional terminology (*saṃvṛti-vyavahāra*), it serves only to reveal the latter two [categories] and not the former two.

Furthermore, as will be shown below when establishing formal arguments (*pramāṇa*) to reveal the ultimate (*paramārtha*), although the entities of regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) are indeed real, the treatise also states that they exist conventionally (*saṃvṛti-sat*), just like internal seeds.
Among the four [types of wisdom], vitarka and vicāra are definitely not associated [with one another]... (up to)... the first two also have the sense of being mutually associated.

Among the four, those of the same category are associated with themselves; however, the two dharmas of vitarka and vicāra are definitely not associated. The next phrase explains the meaning of non-association:
because their essence is the same as reflection (cintā) and wisdom (prajñā), yet their functions differ as coarse and subtle. "Based on the following" refers to the removal of objections.

Question: If vitarka and vicāra do not arise together—such as when vicāra arises in the first dhyāna while vitarka does not—would this not then be confused with the stage of the preparatory level (sāmantaka), which is "without vitarka and with only vicāra"?
Answer: The distinction between the three stages is established based on whether vitarka and vicāra are defiled or free from defilement.

In the first dhyāna, both vitarka and vicāra are defiled; therefore, it is established as the stage "with vitarka and with vicāra. In the preparatory stage, one has already become free from the defilement of vitarka.
The stage of "without vitarka and with vicāra only" is established [when] both defilements of the second dhyāna are abandoned. The stage of "without vitarka and without vicāra" is established.

These names are not established based on whether the seeds give rise to active manifestations; therefore, there is no fault of confusion among these three stages, and this should not be raised as an objection.
[The phrase] "both with the lower" clarifies that vitarka and vicāra can be associated with remorse (kaukṛtya) and torpor (middha), and that remorse and torpor are likewise mutually associated.
Correspondence.
All four do not coexist with the seventh or eighth [consciousnesses] (up to: because they do not coexist with the sixth consciousness, as they are not among the five factors).
Regarding "All four," etc.: the correspondence of all consciousnesses—how all four do not coexist with the seventh and eighth—is as explained previously.
Regarding this, the eighth [section] distinguishes by stating: "The four [mental factors] beginning with regret (*kaukṛtya*) are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*);

because they are subject to interruption, they are certainly not maturation (*vipāka*). The seventh [section] distinguishes by stating: "Regret (*kaukṛtya*) is the remorse for prior actions; this takes a present object as its condition.

Sleep (*middha*) is a state of heavy dullness that arises momentarily due to external conditions; this is solely an internal grasping. Vitarka and vicāra operate by way of the external door; these depend on the internal."

Therefore, they do not coexist with those [five consciousnesses]. Regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) arise only in conjunction with the sixth [consciousness], for they are not associated mental factors of the first five.

According to another interpretation, vitarka and vicāra also coexist with the five consciousnesses, because the five consciousnesses are said to possess spontaneous conceptualization (*svatantra-vikalpa*).

There are two interpretations regarding vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought). According to the first interpretation, vitarka and vicāra are also present simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). Next, he cites a treatise as proof.
He further cites the *Yogācārabhūmi*, which states that vitarka and vicāra are the seven types of discrimination (*vikalpa*), and that discrimination is precisely vitarka and vicāra.

He further cites the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, which identifies spontaneous discrimination (*svarasa-vikalpa*) as the five sensory consciousnesses. He now synthesizes these views from the *Yogācārabhūmi* concerning seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*), examining (*pratyavekṣaṇā*), and spontaneous discrimination. Now, this...
Since the analysis in both treatises is identical, it serves as proof that the five consciousnesses also possess vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought).

As for the seven types of discrimination, they are: discrimination with signs, discrimination without signs, spontaneous discrimination, investigative discrimination, analytical discrimination, defiled discrimination, and non-defiled discrimination.

One interpretation holds that vitarka and vicāra are associated exclusively with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is because [the treatises] never state that they are associated with pleasure or pain.

Next, it explains that vitarka and vicāra are associated exclusively with the mental consciousness; next, it cites a treatise to prove that these are unique characteristics (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of the mental consciousness.
Furthermore, it cites a treatise stating that vitarka and vicāra are associated with sorrow and joy, but does not state that vitarka and vicāra are associated with pain and pleasure.

The five consciousnesses possess suffering and pleasure; yet, suffering and pleasure are not mentioned [in that context] because it is proven that vitarka and vicāra do not associate with the five consciousnesses.
Since the sensation of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā) is omnipresent, it need not be mentioned; however, because it resembles sorrow (daurmanasya), it is generally described as sorrow.
[The opponent] objects from below regarding equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), stating: "Investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) coexist with both suffering (*duḥkha*) and pleasure (*sukha*);

however, that treatise omits this mention. For example, although equanimity necessarily exists [in these stages], it too is not mentioned. The explanation states: "Because equanimity is universal (*sarvatraga*), it need not be mentioned.
Suffering and pleasure are not universal; for what reason are they not mentioned? Furthermore, the objection continues: "The five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) possess suffering and pleasure."

Vitarka and vicāra are devoid of suffering and pleasure.
