If one says that vitarka and vicāra are devoid of suffering and pleasure, yet claims that vitarka and vicāra do not coexist with the five consciousnesses, this contradicts the previous statement that the first dhyāna possesses mental-sphere pleasure (*manobhūmika-sukha*), and that if there were mental-sphere suffering (*manobhūmika-duḥkha*) in that state, it would be purely [unpleasant].
If it is said that vitarka and vicāra are devoid of suffering and pleasure, then would vitarka and vicāra also not coexist with the mental consciousness? The commentary states:
The pleasure of the first dhyāna is collectively termed *prīti* (joy); when one is situated purely in suffering, it is collectively termed *daurmanasya* (grief).
Since it has been stated that vitarka and vicāra are associated with grief and joy, therefore vitarka and vicāra coexist only with the mental consciousness.
Furthermore, it is said that vitarka and vicāra take the "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth—and indeed the meanings of the name-body and so forth—as their objects.

It is further stated below that, with respect to their focal objects (*ālambana*), they are associated with the mind (*manas*). The treatise states that vitarka and vicāra take the meanings of the name-body, phrase-body (*padakāya*), and syllable-body (*vyañjanakāya*) as their focal objects;

these are exclusively the objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and are not the objects of the five sensory consciousnesses. Therefore, vitarka and vicāra are associated only with the mind.
Therefore, it is definitely not associated with the five consciousnesses.
However, when it is said that the five consciousnesses possess vitarka and vicāra, this indicates that they mostly arise from them; it does not mean that they are associated with them.
However, the subsequent explanation applies generally to the preceding *yoga*. The first phrase restates [the position], while the second phrase provides the explanation.

Regarding the statement that "the five consciousnesses possess vitarka and vicāra," this indicates that the five consciousnesses are for the most part induced by vitarka and vicāra; it does not mean that they are associated with those vitarka and vicāra.

Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* concerning "spontaneous conceptualization" (*svarasa-vikalpa*) [up to] "by this, the five consciousnesses definitely lack vitarka and vicāra":
the first two phrases of the preceding section from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* first judge that the doctrines of the two treatises differ.

The phrase "what the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* says differs from the *Yogācārabhūmi*" indicates that the latter explains the difference in meaning. The phrase "the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that spontaneity is... [indicates that] spontaneous conceptualization is precisely...

Regarding the five consciousnesses and the seven types of discrimination taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, these are the *vitarka* and *vicāra* associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises simultaneously with the five consciousnesses.

Therefore, that single phrase [from the *Yogācārabhūmi*] refutes the citation as being unestablished; by means of this same phrase, it is concluded that the five consciousnesses definitely lack *vitarka* and *vicāra*.

One interpretation holds that remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is associated with mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), because in the realms of pure suffering, the mind is accompanied by mental pain.

Another interpretation holds that it is associated with all [five] feelings (*vedanā*). The former explanation is correct: remorse is associated with both mental distress and equanimity; its association with mental distress is explained by its nature of being dejected (*dīna-gati*).

The indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is explained as being associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*). Sleep (*middha*) is associated with joy (*saumanasya*), sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity; this explains how it pervades all three [mental factors] based on the distinctions of elation, dejection, and neutrality.
Vitarka and vicāra are associated with sorrow, joy, pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity. Next, the association with pleasure is explained: because there is mental pleasure within the first dhyāna.
According to one interpretation, [the lower stages] each add suffering (*duḥkha*). Next, the association with suffering is explained: in the realms of pure suffering, the mind...
Because suffering exists.

All four [universal mental factors] are compatible with the five object-specific factors (*viṣayālambana*), as their modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects of perception (*ālambana*) do not conflict.
Thus, all four are associated with the object-specific factors; all four coexist with the five. This refers to the modes of activity and the objects of perception of the perceiving subject.

Because they do not contradict one another, remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) can coexist with the ten wholesome [mental factors] up to the first dhyāna, as they coexist with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) therein.

Below that, remorse and torpor are associated with the wholesome; however, remorse and torpor exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), where they coexist only with the ten [wholesome factors] and do not extend further.
Because the higher stages lack pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), whereas vitarka and vicāra are fully present throughout the first dhyāna, pliancy is indeed present there.
Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) can only be associated with ignorance (*avidyā*), because these two do not contradict one another in their mutual occurrence.

Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is associated only with the affliction of delusion (*moha*). This is because the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of remorse is coarse, whereas the nine factors such as greed (*rāga*) are subtle.

Regarding the next point, the explanation that [remorse] does not coexist with the nine [other afflictions]: it is because the remaining three [mental factors] fully coexist with all ten afflictions, as there is no mutual contradiction between them.
Remorse may coexist with the intermediate and great secondary afflictions, because it arises during all states such as sleep and so forth.

Remorse is associated with the lower secondary afflictions; the second phrase clarifies the reason why it does not coexist [with them], because anger (*krodha*) and the others each function as primary [afflictions].
The remaining three [secondary afflictions] coexist entirely with the twenty [mental factors]; the next phrase clarifies the meaning of this coexistence. During the state of sleep...
Because all [of these] can arise.
These four are all common to the three natures—wholesome and so forth—since remorse also occurs regarding neutral (*avyākṛta*) karma.

Regarding the phrase "These four," below, this clarifies their inclusion within the three natures. The first sentence provides a general clarification that the four are common to the three natures; the subsequent sentence provides a specific clarification.

Regret (*kaukṛtya*) is pervasive across the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Question: Regarding the remorse for wholesome or unwholesome karma, how can it also be pervasive across the indeterminate? Explanation:

As stated in the text. According to one interpretation, the first two [mental factors] are exclusively innate wholesome (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*), because remorse and torpor (*middha*) exist within the stages of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*).

There is an interpretation that the following section provides a detailed explanation of the nature of wholesomeness (*kuśalatva*). Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) are exclusively innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*);

they do not extend to the applied wholesome state (*prāyogika*). The second phrase explains the reason for this non-extension: the characteristic of remorse is coarse and vulgar, while the characteristic of sleep is obscure and brief;

therefore, they do not apply to the subtle and comprehensive applied wholesome state. Vitarka and vicāra extend to both the innate wholesome state and the applied wholesome state. The subsequent phrase explains their extension to the applied wholesome state, such as that produced by hearing (*śrutamaya*), etc.—the "etc. including those produced by reflection (*cintāmaya*).

Cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Since all three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) possess vitarka and vicāra, there is one interpretation that the subsequent section explains that remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) also pertain to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).

The following sentence explains their pervasion of the preparatory stage: hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*) are themselves the preparatory stage, because there is also wholesome remorse and wholesome sleep therein.
The latter three are all common to both the defiled and the pure-unspecified (*avyākṛta*). (Up to: because they are unable to investigate the meaning of names and so forth.
"The latter three" and below is the specific explanation of the unspecified. The latter three are all common to the two types of unspecified:

"defiled" refers to the obscured (*nivṛta*), and "pure" refers to the unobscured (*anivṛta*). Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is not obscured; the characteristic of remorse is coarse and violent, whereas that [obscured state] is subtle and refined. There are four types of the unspecified.

Regarding the five types of action—ripening (*vipāka*), deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), supernormal power (*abhijñā*), and regret (*kaukṛtya*)—only the middle two, namely deportment and craftsmanship, are [associated with the intermediate state] when they are not the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

This is because [regret] excludes the mind [of the intermediate state], as it is not born of dhyāna; it excludes supernormal power, as it is not a karmic maturation (*vipāka*); and it excludes ripening, [as these two are not the result of karma].

"Sleep excludes the fourth" means that it does not induce meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), thus excluding the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). "The mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) can also possess sleep" explains that there is maturation;

this refers to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) sixth consciousness. "Investigation and analysis exclude the maturation-born" means that among the three types of indeterminate states, those [lacking investigation and analysis] are excluded.
The phrase "their understanding is subtle and weak" explains the exclusion of the mental faculty (*manas*).
Regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); [this continues] until: "the factors of the other realms and stages are all sublime and tranquil.
Regarding "regret is lower," this clarifies their realm-affiliation (*dhātuparyāpanna*). First, it determines their inclusion within the realms as per the text.

As for "the factors of the other realms and stages are all sublime and tranquil," this clarifies that vitarka and vicāra are coarse and mobile; they do not pervade the seven higher stages, because the factors of those higher stages are all sublime and tranquil.

When remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) arise in a higher stage, they certainly do not manifest; whereas applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) may arise in both higher and lower stages.

Remorse and torpor belong to the lower stages. As for the fact that remorse and torpor do not manifest among sentient beings of the higher realms, it is because they exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The vitarka and vicāra of a higher stage arise with respect to a lower stage; the vitarka and vicāra of a lower stage arise with respect to a higher stage.

This is because the vitarka and vicāra of both lower and higher stages can take both the lower and higher as objects (up to the point where), and even in dreams, they can universally take all experienced objects as their objects.

Regarding "lower and upper" and "the lower can take the upper as its object": this clarifies that the two factors of *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) function such that the lower can take the upper as an object and the upper can take the lower as an object.
Regarding the two interpretations of *kaukṛtya* (remorse) and *middha* (drowsiness): according to the first interpretation, remorse and drowsiness cannot take the upper [levels] as objects.

The second sentence explains why they do not take them as objects: because remorse is coarse and proximate, while drowsiness is dull and abbreviated. According to the subsequent interpretation, remorse and drowsiness can also take upper objects. The following two sentences provide the explanation for this.

It can take [such objects] as its cognitive object because of wrong view, regret, and the cultivation of meditative concentration; because dreams arise by taking as their objects previously experienced states;
because regret is not the equanimity of one beyond training who has abandoned desire; and because all conditioned wholesome dharmas belong to those beyond training.
"Regret is not [the state of] one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). This clarifies that it is subsumed within the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*). Regret does not belong to those beyond training;

it exists only in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), because those who have attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) have already abandoned the defilements of the desire realm. The latter three [mental factors] all pertain to both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training.

As for these three being subsumed under the nature of the wholesome (*kuśala-svabhāva*), they are termed "conditioned wholesome" (*saṃskṛta-kuśala*). Those seeking liberation are in the stage of training; the wholesome dharmas practiced by them are likewise [conditioned wholesome].

All are not included [within the category of] training (*śaikṣa*). The wholesome dharmas practiced by one who has reached the ultimate state of training are likewise all included within that which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Regret (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) pertain exclusively to what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); therefore, they are included in both what is abandoned through seeing and cultivation, and are not included in what is not to be abandoned (*aheya*).

Regarding "remorse and sleep" (*kaukṛtya-middha*), it clarifies their inclusion within the three types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*). Remorse and sleep are exclusively abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);

this indicates they do not extend to that which is not to be abandoned (*aheya*). Furthermore, the phrase "also [arising] from the false" (*mithyādṛṣṭi-vaśotthita*) establishes their abandonment through these two paths. That which arises by the power of false views is included in what is abandoned by seeing;

"and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to those included among tainted wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*), which are abandoned through cultivation. The phrase "not non-" (*na nāsti*) [refers to the following].

That which is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*) is that which is led by the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). It is "not to be abandoned. Now, the initial character "non-" (*a-*) serves to exclude it.

It is not "not non-to-be-abandoned," nor is it merely a single phrase; rather, it is cited as an example to explain what is "not to be abandoned. The feeling of sorrow (*daurmanasya-vedanā*) that seeks liberation deeply is "not to be abandoned.
This is not like that [other type], therefore it is "not non-to-be-abandoned. That which is tainted (*sāsrava*) has already been abandoned.

Regarding those that arise subsequently and are untainted (*anāsrava*): they are not subject to abandonment. Thus, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are included among those not subject to abandonment.

Vitarka and vicāra pertain to all three types of abandonment. In the passage below, "pertain to all three" explains this meaning. Although vitarka and vicāra themselves are not untainted, those that can induce the untainted pertain to what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Those untainted factors that are induced [by them] pertain to what is not subject to abandonment.
There is an interpretation that *vitarka* and *vicāra* are not to be abandoned, because the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that they are conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

There is another interpretation that [they belong to] the lower two [dhyānas]. These are the two schools' determinations regarding what is subsumed under *vitarka* and *vicāra*. The first explanation determines that *vitarka* and *vicāra* are not to be abandoned.
Among the five dharmas, it is subsumed solely within the third, conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Next, a treatise is cited to prove that this is indeed conceptualization.
The five dharmas are: first, name (*nāman*); second, appearance (*nimitta*); third, conceptualization (*vikalpa*); fourth, correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*); and fifth, suchness (*tathatā*).
One interpretation holds that these two are also subsumed under correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*), because it is further stated that they are the causes of verbal expression.

Another interpretation holds that, as explained below, they are not merely conceptualization (*vikalpa*); since among the five dharmas, conceptualization belongs to the outflowing (*āsrava*) category, they also extend to being subsumed under correct cognition.
The passage beginning with "It is said that... explains their inclusion within correct cognition; specifically, they correspond to right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) within the Eightfold Noble Path.

Because it is untainted (*anāsrava*). Since volition (*cetanā*) enables the mind to seek and examine, and since it is said that reflection (*manasikāra*) is the cause of verbal expression while volition is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for speech, this explains that reflection is untainted. Since volition induces applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), these are also untainted;
therefore, they are subsumed under right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "because [it applies] from the stage of non-finality to the medicine, the disease, and so forth," these two types also pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*).

The phrase "not yet having reached the final stage" provides a further explanation: while a Bodhisattva remains in the stage of non-finality, they are unable to fully and accurately comprehend all dharma-gates and the mental activities of sentient beings;
it is within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that they teach them to others.
The Dharma necessarily requires the investigation and analysis of the medicine and the illness; only then does one preach the sublime Dharma according to the capacities of beings.
This is not like the effortless preaching of the Buddha-stage. Therefore, these two types [of speech] also pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Although it is said that *vitarka* and *vicāra* must be conceptualization (*vikalpa*), this is because conceptualization also exists within subsequently attained correct cognition (*prsthalabdha-samyagjñāna*).
Although it is said "below," this is a general discussion refuting the preceding [view].

The treatise states that *vitarka* and *vicāra* must be conceptualization, yet it does not definitively state that they are the third among the five dharmas, because conceptualization also exists within subsequently attained cognition. What the treatise describes is precisely [this].
The discrimination within wisdom belongs to the untainted (*anāsrava*), whereas the third type of discrimination belongs to the tainted (*sāsrava*).
This refutation is made by pointing out that while the names are identical, their meanings differ.
The remaining sections should be considered according to reason as above.
At the bottom of the other sections, the conclusion is shown:
"Thus, regarding the mental factors (*caitta*) across these six stages... [up to] 'even if that were so, what fault would there be? Both positions have faults.'"

Thus, below, the text clarifies the "place" (*sthāna*) of the King. First, it presents a general inquiry. The first three phrases of the answer respond to the question of whether the King's place is distinct (*pṛthak*) or identical (*tādātmya*).
The next phrase responds by asking: even if it were either identical or distinct, what fault would there be? Finally, there is a general objection.
Whether they are identical to or distinct from [the mind], both positions entail faults.

If they were distinct from the essence of the mind and possessed a separate intrinsic nature, then—just as with faith and so forth—there would be no defiled or wholesome dharmas that are not distinct [from the mind].

If one departs from the lower [position], first the faults of departing from the mind are explained. The first phrase cites the meditative state that departs from the mind; the section beginning with "How so?

cites scriptural authority to demonstrate the fault. As it is said in the Sūtra: "The three realms are mind-only," and it is further said that "the object of cognition is what is manifested by consciousness."
The *Saṃgrahaṇīkārikā* states: "The mind travels far and wanders alone; Bodiless, it lies within the cave. One who can subdue this mind, so difficult to subdue— I call him a brahmin.
In this verse, that which is called "mind" (*citta*) is also termed "intellect" (*manas*) and also termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
It is called "traveling far" because it ranges over all objects of cognition. It is called "wandering alone" because it has no [second]...
Secondly, "bodiless" means lacking physical form or substance. "Sleeping in a cave" means dwelling within [the body]. "Difficult to subdue" means its nature is stubborn and unruly.
Regarding the citation of the first line of the verse, the intent is to demonstrate that there are no separate mental factors (*caitta*);

that defilement and purity depend on the mind, as stated in the Sūtra: "Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is purified, [sentient beings are purified]. There...

Regarding the purity of feeling and the six elements of the person (*ṣaḍdhātu-puruṣa*): as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the four great elements, space, and consciousness constitute sentient beings.
Among these, matter, motion, and mind are the most excellent bases: matter depends on the four great elements; motion depends on space; and mind depends on consciousness.
Nowhere is it said that mental factors (*caitta*) depend [on them]. Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states that the mind appears as two: it appears as faith and so forth.
It resembles greed; it does not exist as a distinct entity apart from the mind, whether defiled or wholesome.
If it were merely a specific state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the mind itself, then because its causal conditions would be no different [from those of the mind], it would contradict the sacred teachings.
If [it were] identical [to the mind], next follows the refutation of that identity with the mind. The first phrase identifies the specific state of being identical to the mind.
The section beginning with "How" cites scriptural authority to expose the error. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks: "With what are all phenomena associated?

For what purpose is association established? It answers: "They are associated with other-nature (*parabhāva*), not with self-nature (*svabhāva*), for the sake of thoroughly understanding that which depends upon self-nature."
The nature of the mind is pure, yet there are phenomena of defilement and purity that either increase or decrease; therefore, their association is established.
Furthermore, it is said that the mind and mental factors arise simultaneously, like the sun and its light.

If the light were identical to the sun, how could one see the orb of the sun separately in the sky? By this analogy, it is clarified that [the mental factors] are not identical to the mind. A verse from the *Yogācārabhūmi* says: "Five..."

The categories of lineage (*gotra*) are not established. Suppose there were a certain śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who wished to maintain that, among names, only the mind is substantially real, while the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) are not.
This is unreasonable. Why? Because, first of all, it is taught that the five aggregates (*skandha*) do not possess five distinct lineages.
Furthermore, if he were to reckon that there are five lineages because of differences in states (*avasthā*), then as for those states—

To calculate them separately also entails faults. Why? Because whether these various states are considered to have distinct functional activities relative to one another or to lack them, both positions result in errors.
If one says they exist, then because their characteristics are different, there would necessarily be distinct real entities with separate natures.
If one says they do not exist, then the postulation of distinct states becomes a futile waste of effort.
Furthermore, one should not say that it is like the distinctions in the states of the six groups of consciousness.
This is because those states are found in a single location, whereas the six groups of consciousness possess distinctions in their bases and objects; therefore, [the former position] is illogical.
If it is argued that there is transformation, this too is illogical. Why? Because transformation is possible only for material things, and [in this case] such [transformation] is obtained.
The distinction between preceding and succeeding states does not exist in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) in the way that there are differences such as milk, curd, and clarified butter.
Furthermore, because there is no differentiation in the causes and conditions of the mind, it is illogical for there to be distinct states of formations (saṃskāra) within a single moment.
It is impossible to find any causal conditions that could produce distinctions among those states;
therefore, your assertion of distinctions between states is unreasonable. Furthermore, it contradicts the scriptures.
Thus, the claim that "mind alone truly exists" is unreasonable, as a sūtra states: "Greed, hatred, and delusion afflict and defile the mind, preventing its liberation. If...
If it were the case that only mind exists and two [mental factors] do not coexist, then greed and the like would not depend upon consciousness.
Furthermore, if you claim that consciousness precedes them, this is also unreasonable, because the fault of there being no distinction has already been stated previously.
Moreover, a sutra says: "The triad of contact arises simultaneously with feeling, perception, volition, and so forth. And another sutra states: "In this way, these various..."
Phenomena are eternally in a state of mutual conjunction; it cannot be said that these phenomena can be analyzed and rendered distinct or separate from one another.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, wishing to establish this meaning of conjunction, spoke the analogy of a lamp and its light.
Therefore, conjunction cannot be described apart from their co-arising; thus, they are called the four formless aggregates included within [the aggregate of consciousness].
The principle that the mind and mental factors are mutually associated is established;
therefore, it must be stated that they possess a distinct intrinsic nature apart from the mind.
[This point] shall now be explained below to set forth the correct doctrine: thus, these six categories of mental factors exist apart from the eight sovereign minds.
Regarding the "real intrinsic nature": previously, the error of [asserting] a mind that is dissociated was refuted;

now, the establishment of something else existing apart from the mind serves as a thematic preface for the subsequent text’s integration and discernment of the two truths, thereby proving that [the relationship between them] is neither identical nor dissociated.

Because the mind is predominant, it is said that there is "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) and so forth; [this applies] up to the point where things appear as such, and there is no fault in this.

From the phrase "because the mind is predominant" onwards, this connects with the preceding citation of scripture. Question: The scriptures state "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) and "mind-only" (*cittamātra*).

Now, you claim that there exists something distinct from the mind; how can this be reconciled? Answer: When the scriptures speak of "consciousness-only" and so forth, they do so because the mind is predominant while its objects are subordinate.

This is said in terms of preeminence. First, it can act as a sovereign; second, it can act as a support; third, its modes of activity (*ākāra*) are comprehensive; and fourth, it is always determinate. The mental factors (*caitta*) are not so;

therefore, the mind (*citta*) is preeminent. Next, regarding the statement that the mind appears as two: because the mental factors arise through being drawn forth by the power of the mind upon which they depend, they are said to appear like it.
This does not mean that those mental factors are identical to the mind. Furthermore, it is called "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

"Mind-only" (cittamātra) also includes mental factors (caitta), because they are always associated [with the mind]. "Consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) concludes by demonstrating the absence of faults.
Regarding the word "etc. (ādi): it refers to [the verses] such as "wandering far, traveling alone," "defilement and purity depend on the mind," and "the six elements of the person" (ṣaḍdhātu).
This is based on the conventional truth; if based on the ultimate truth (up to the point where it says), this is called the sublime principle of the conventional and ultimate truths of the Mahāyāna.

"This is based on the lower [truth]" below concludes and demonstrates the principles of the truths. Thus, based on the conventional truth, the existence of an essence is explained separately; if based on the ultimate truth...

Neither identical nor separate. Regarding the passage "the various consciousnesses" and below, the same principle applies to the [ālaya-]vijñāna. From the conventional perspective, there are eight aspects;
from the ultimate perspective, there are no aspects. This refers to the following phrase, which establishes the two truths.

The correspondence of the six consciousnesses with mental factors has already been explained (up to the point where it was stated), as well as [the states of] the two mindless attainments, sleep, and fainting.
Having finished the preceding explanation, the following clarifies the stages in which consciousness arises. The initial passage concludes the previous section and introduces the subsequent one.

Next, two lines of verse are cited in response. The first line concerns the gate of the common support of the six consciousnesses; the next four lines concern the gate of the simultaneous operation of the six consciousnesses; and the final three...
Section: The Gate of Non-Functioning in the Five Stages.
The treatise states: "The fundamental consciousness" refers to the *ādāna-vijñāna* (up to: "...taking the fundamental consciousness as the common, immediate support").
The Commentary states: Below, first is the explanation of the first phrase, the "Gate of Common Basis. *Ādāna* is translated here as "grasping and maintaining.
It is called the "fundamental" because it is the basis for the manifestation and arising of all defiled and pure consciousnesses, whether the basis has been transformed or not yet transformed.
The common support refers to the manifest fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), which serves as the sovereign condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for all consciousnesses.
The immediate support refers to the seed-consciousness, which constitutes the respective individual seeds of all consciousnesses and serves as their immediate causal condition (*hetupratyaya*).
The "five consciousnesses" refer to the first five *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (up to the point where they arise only when various conditions harmonize).

Following the section on the five consciousnesses, the second phrase, the "simultaneous arising gate," is explained. Following the section on the five consciousnesses, the general meaning of the five consciousnesses is clarified.
Regarding their similarity in type: first, they both rely on the same physical sense-faculties; second, they both take external objects as their objective conditions;
third, both take the present as their object; fourth, both are direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*); and fifth, both are characterized by interruption. Therefore, they are explained together.

The phrase "appearing according to conditions" indicates that [cognition] arises through the conjunction of conditions; it does not arise when they do not conjoin, nor does it arise constantly. Regarding these "conditions," the verse states:

Eye-consciousness arises from nine conditions; Ear-consciousness arises from only eight; Nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses arise from seven; The last three (mental consciousness) arise from five, three, and four respectively.

If the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is added, one is added to each starting from the beginning. As for the "nine conditions": the sense organ (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), space (*ākāśa*), and light (*āloka*).

Mental attention (*manasikāra*), seeds (*bīja*), the root (*mūla*), defilement and purity (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna*), discrimination (*vikalpa*), the eight factors excluding the light of emptiness (*śūnyatā-āloka*), the seven factors excluding the light of emptiness, and the five factors excluding the light of emptiness—namely, defilement and purity, discrimination, and discrimination itself. Defilement and purity constitute the root; three are merely mental attention.

Furthermore, its own seeds, the sense organ, and the object constitute a single basis, as their support and conditions are identical. For the four [mental factors], there are only the sense organ, the object, the seed, and attention, each further augmented by one equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Now, it is said that the five consciousnesses arise only when they are internally supported by the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), externally accompanied by attention, and brought into manifestation through the harmonious conjunction of various conditions such as the five sense organs, objects, and so forth.
"By this, they either arise together or do not arise together" (up to) "these dharmas and their metaphors are explained at length as in the Sūtra.
From "by this" onwards, the third four-line verse is explained. Depending on conditions, they may arise together or not; the next line explains both arising together and not arising together:
when the various conditions converge simultaneously, the five consciousnesses arise together; when they converge gradually, from four up to... [the sixth].

First: Just as waves on water arise according to conditions such as the wind, being more or less frequent as explained at length in the sūtras, so too, because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the five evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are coarse and agitated, there are no obstructing conditions that can cause them all to cease functioning simultaneously.
The first line of the subsequent verse is explained by means of the five lower [stages]. First, the various consciousnesses are explained in general:

the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of these consciousnesses are either coarse or subtle, and the multitude of conditions (*pratyaya*) upon which they rely are either many or few; this is why, when they manifest, some arise while others do not.
Furthermore, the five groups of consciousness (pañca-vijñāna-kāya) lack the capacity for deliberation; for this reason, it is not said that they manifest according to conditions.

[The text says] "Furthermore, the five" and so forth, next explaining the six consciousnesses individually. Question: Regarding the statement that the first five [consciousnesses] "follow conditions," is there a time when they do not manifest?

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) also arises in accordance with conditions; why, then, does it arise constantly? This explanation clarifies that while the first five consciousnesses have intervals, the mental consciousness arises continuously.

This distinction is based on the capacity or incapacity for deliberation; therefore, the spheres of activity differ between the internal and external gates, which causes the arising of the sixth and fifth consciousnesses to be distinct.

Regarding the "five states": what are they? They are [the states] from the birth in the *asaṃjñika* heaven up to [the attainment of cessation]. Thus, the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are all suspended in those states.

Below this, the explanation of the latter three phrases concerns the "gate of the non-functioning of the five states. First, there is a general inquiry, a heading, and a listing. Second, there is a specific explanation of the *asaṃjñisattva* heaven:
having practiced meditative concentration during the causal stage, one seeks to escape coarse conceptualization; by virtue of that concentration, one is born in that heaven.
In the intermediate state, it contradicts the six evolving consciousnesses; it is named after its primary characteristic, which is the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā*).

Although the lifespan of the "Fruit of Vastness" (*bṛhatphala*) and the "Unconscious Body" (*asaṃjñisattva*) are the same, the former takes the absence of vitarka and vicāra as its cause and effect, whereas the latter takes the absence of mind (*acittaka*) as its cause and effect.
One interpretation holds that those gods always lack the six consciousnesses (up to the point where it says), because they are further described as being "without a mind-ground" (*acittabhūmi*).

Another interpretation distinguishes between the presence or absence of the six consciousnesses in the lower realms. First, regarding the initial explanation: the first phrase establishes the definitive position that the six consciousnesses are constantly absent;

the subsequent three phrases cite scriptural authority to prove this. As for the phrase "only possessing the member of form" (*rūpāṅga-mātra*): among the twelve members [of dependent origination], this refers to...
It consists of one branch, namely form (*rūpa*), because there is form but no name (*nāman*).

There is an interpretation that this refers to the state of those gods when they are about to die; it is spoken of in terms of their long duration [of life], not to say that [form] is entirely absent.

There is an interpretation [which states]: "Below" refers to the subsequent explanation. The first phrase establishes that for those beings in the heavens, at the end of their life-span, it is necessary for the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) to arise.

The second phrase provides the proof: because the craving that moistens rebirth (*upapatti-bhava-tṛṣṇā*) coexists with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). "The *Yogācārabhūmi*... below cites scriptural evidence. However, the passage beginning with "But as for the statement... reconciles this with the previously cited teachings.

There is one interpretation that at the time of birth there are also evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). [The text continues: "...because, as in other cases of initial existence, there must be evolving consciousnesses.

There is another interpretation below; this is the third explanation. The first phrase establishes the certainty that at the time of birth there are also evolving consciousnesses. The second phrase provides the proof:

because in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) one necessarily gives rise to the afflictions that moisten rebirth. The phrase "as in other cases" cites an example to clarify the presence of evolving consciousnesses. "Other" refers to...

This refers to the other dhyāna heavens. Regarding "the original existence" (*pūrvakālabhava*) and "the initial": the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The original existence is that which precedes death and follows the moment of rebirth.

The "original existence" is this present body, so called because it has not yet reached its future state of existence. As for the term "initial," it refers to the very moment the original existence first arises. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
At the precise moment of taking birth, there is a subject (*dharmin*) which must possess evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) as its predicate (*sādhya*).

Because that intermediate state (*antarābhava*) necessarily gives rise to craving for rebirth (*upapattirāga*), it serves as the cause, just like the beginning of any other existence (*pūrvakālabhava*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If one is born there, [the transition] from prior existence to subsequent non-existence is called 'entry' (*praveśa*)."

Regarding "Entering [the meditative attainments]" (*yoga-praveśa*): this introduces the proof of the meaning that, at the initial arising [of these states], there must be evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). As for "arising therein," it refers only to entering [the state] and not to the non-arising [of consciousness].

Regarding "that fundamental [state]" (*tad-mūla*): this explains the establishment [of the point]. The first phrase is an explanation by way of contraposition; the second phrase is an explanation by way of direct affirmation.

Since the initial moment of that fundamental state must necessarily possess evolving consciousnesses, and because one subsequently ceases these [consciousnesses] and abides in a mindless state, it is therefore designated as "entering."

Regarding the phrase "the section on definitive analysis" (*viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*): because all that is acquired at birth [continues] until [death], in that initial stage, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) temporarily arise.

Below this, the meaning of cessation is cited as proof that the evolving consciousnesses exist at the moment of initial birth. "Acquired at birth" (*upapatti-lābhika*) refers to the cessation of the mind and mental factors born of maturation (*vipākaja*) obtained through retribution;
this is termed the "state of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). The following passage provides a further explanation according to the intent of the treatise.

This demonstrates that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) initially possesses the transformation-consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) born of maturation (*vipākaja*), which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Due to the power of having previously habituated oneself to this meditative absorption (*samādhi*), it opposes the aforementioned transformation-consciousness, causing it not to manifest.

Consequently, it gives rise to a specific state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the true maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which is designated as "non-conception" (*asaṃjñin*). This is illustrated by the analogy of wholesome states, such as the wholesome roots of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśalamūla*).

Just as that which is induced by meditative concentration is called "wholesome concentration," this case should likewise be so. Furthermore, that which is produced by the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi*) is called the "maturation of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*).

Otherwise—this below refutes the preceding view by demonstrating it through logical inquiry—if there were no evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) from the very beginning until the end, how could one say that [the state] consists solely of the cessation obtained at birth? Since it is stated that it is the cessation obtained at birth, therefore, in that initial stage...
The evolving consciousnesses arise momentarily;
those gods exist only in the fourth dhyāna because it alone can induce the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of that celestial realm.

Regarding the lower realms of those gods, this clarifies the level of the world-sphere (*dhātu-bhūmi*) they inhabit: the first phrase determines their location within the four dhyānas. The four dhyānas possess...
The Nine Heavens: this corresponds to the fourth [category]. The next two phrases explain the reason why [the *asaṃjñisattvas*] do not reside in the lower or upper stages.

In the lower stages, the perceptions and mind are coarse and active, making them difficult to sever; in the upper stages, there is no place for the maturation (*vipāka*) of non-perception (*asaṃjñi*).

As for "having no place": in the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), matter is extinguished while the mind remains; in the state of non-perception, the mind is extinguished while matter remains. Since they lack matter, there is no place for the maturation of matter to persist.

It can thus be established. To explain the fruit by means of the cause: volition (*cetanā*) is mental action (*manas-karman*); this serves as the projector (*ākṣepaka*), while meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is that which is projected (*ākṣipta*).

Volition is the agent that brings about the result (*vedaka*), and the result is that which is brought about (*vedya*). Since the cause is without ideation (*asaṃjñika*), the fruit must necessarily correspond to its cause.

"And the two mindless attainments" refers to the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); because both are devoid of the six consciousnesses, they are called "mindless.
Regarding the phrase "and the two [attainments]" below: first, the initial two lines cite the verse to provide a general heading and list the two names individually;
the subsequent line first explains the common name "mindless."

The "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) refers to a state of ordinary beings (up to the point where it) causes the body to be peaceful and harmonious; thus, it is also called an "attainment.

Below this, the text provides a detailed explanation of the attainment of non-perception, first clarifying the efficacy of its cultivation. "Universal Purity" (*śubhakṛtsna*) refers to the third heaven within the third dhyāna.
One has suppressed the craving for this heaven, but has not yet suppressed that which lies above it. One comes to loathe perception as being like a sore, like an abscess, or like...
Sickness is like an arrow piercing the body. With the mental application of renunciation as the precursor, one causes the six evolving consciousnesses and their associated mental factors to cease.
Below this, the meaning of the name is established. Question: Since all mental factors cease together, why is it specifically called "non-perception" (*asaṃjñā*)?

Answer: Because the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā*) is primary, it is given the name "non-perception. Question: Since it is called "non-perception," why is it further called a "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*)? Answer: As the text states.
The cultivation of this meditative absorption (samādhi) is divided into three categories; [it continues] until, at the end of a lifespan as long as a *puṣpa*, one finally passes away.

The section on "Cultivation of the Lower" clarifies the distinctions among types of concentration. Due to the presence of either diligence or indolence, there is a difference between falling back and not falling back from it in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*).
Regarding the fruits, there are differences in physical form and lifespan, which are categorized into the distinctions of lower, middling, and superior types. [It continues] until the end.
As for Bhadraśaṃsa, he exhausts five hundred kalpas.

This meditative concentration belongs exclusively to the fourth dhyāna; as for the four types of karma, they pertain to all three [time periods], with the exception of karma to be experienced in the present life.

This section below clarifies the inclusion [of these karmas] within the realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*). The first sentence determines that they belong to the fourth *dhyāna*. Because they are induced by the wholesome, they are exclusively wholesome;
they do not exist in the lower or higher stages, as previously stated. Regarding the four types of karma: first, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dr̥ṣṭadharmavedanīya*).

This refers to extremely superior wholesome or unwholesome karma, which is experienced in the very body in which it was performed. Second, karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*).

1. Karma of medium strength, which is slightly inferior to the superior type, is experienced in the very next life; thus, it is called "karma to be experienced in the subsequent life" (*upapadyavedanīya*). 2.

Karma that is somewhat weaker than the medium type is experienced from two lifetimes onwards, even extending through many lifetimes; thus, it is called "karma to be experienced later" (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*). 3. Karma that is not fixed as to when it will be experienced is called "karma to be experienced at an indefinite time" (*aniyatavedanīya*).

The most feeble and inferior grade of karma is set aside for last because its timing is indefinite. Regarding the fourfold classification of *yoga*, there are: (1) definite time but indefinite retribution;
(2) definite retribution but indefinite time; (3) both time and retribution definite; and (4) both time and retribution indefinite.

Those with both time and retribution definite belong to the first three categories; the remaining three phrases belong to the fourth. This excludes [karma] that ripens in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
Regarding "receiving [the result]": this is because one does not receive the retribution of that heavenly realm in the present life. Regarding "indeterminate in both [time and species]":
there may be non-Buddhists who, by slandering liberation, are reborn in hell; or those who subsequently cultivate correct karma and transcend the realms.
This refers to the category of cases where both time and species are indeterminate.

There is one interpretation that this meditative absorption arises only in the desire realm; because it is [associated with] [the defilements], it is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) and is not produced by noble ones (*ārya*).

There is another interpretation regarding the lower [realms], clarifying the place where it is cultivated and produced. The first explanation clarifies its cultivation and production in the desire realm; the subsequent explanation clarifies its cultivation and production in the form realm.

By excluding the "absence of lower [states]" (*an-avara-bhūmi*), it is clarified that this absorption is contaminated and is not inhabited by noble ones. By excluding the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), it extends [to the limit].

As for "the ultimate," this refers to the nine heavens of the four dhyānas: Anabhraka (Cloudless), Puṇyaprasava (Merit-born), Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit), Asaṃjñisattva (Non-percipient), Avṛha (Without Affliction), Atapa (Without Heat), Sudṛśa (Good Vision), Sudarśana (Good Appearance), and Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form).
This refers to those who have attained the fruit of a Non-returner (Anāgāmin) and follow the "upward-stream" path (*ūrdhvasrotas*);

having passed through all [lower realms], they bypass the Heaven of Non-perception and are born in Akaniṣṭha. The following explains the meaning of "bypassing": this heaven is [avoided] by non-Buddhists due to their aversion [to it].
Because one enters this state with the thought of aspiring for its fruit, it is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) and is not produced by noble ones (*ārya*);

therefore, it is excluded [from the category of the supramundane]. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "This attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is neither entered by those in training (*śaikṣa*) nor by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Why? Because within this state, wisdom (*prajñā*) does not manifest; furthermore, because there exists a superior, peaceful dwelling and rebirth above this level. Moreover, this...
One will certainly be unable to realize those superior wholesome dharmas not yet realized, because one remains lingering in a state of deceptive illusion.

As for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*): it refers to those who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) [up to] those who, through a partial revulsion toward sensation and perception, are also said to have "extinguished" them; this is called the attainment of cessation.
"Extinction below. This is a separate explanation of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). First, the function of its cultivation as a cause is clarified:

the noble ones, whether in training (*śaikṣa*) or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), have already suppressed or abandoned the defilements of the eighth stage; [the abandonment of] the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is not fixed.

Preceded by the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the notion of seeking temporary rest, they cause the non-perpetually active mind and mental factors, as well as the defiled portion of the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*), and that mind...
All [mental factors] are completely extinguished. The term "cessation" (*nirodha*) is established below based on the preceding meaning; thus, it is given the name "cessation.
Because it causes the body to abide peacefully, becoming harmonious and supple, it is also called "concentration" (*samādhi*). The subsequent phrase provides an alternative name:

because this preparatory application (*prayoga*) involves a specific aversion toward feeling and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*), it is also termed the "attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception" (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*).
The cultivation of this meditative concentration is divided into three grades: (up to) those who cultivate it at the superior level never regress.

The cultivation at the inferior level clarifies the distinctions among types of concentration; depending on whether there is diligence or indolence, one may regress or not regress in the present life.
Thus, the distinctions between the three grades—inferior, middling, and superior—are established.

This concentration, when first cultivated, must necessarily rely on the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), because it is not included within the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and resembles *nirvāṇa*.
This section below clarifies the place of cultivation. When first cultivated, it must necessarily rely on the Stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*);

contemplating the Four Noble Truths serves as the expedient means for entering this concentration. This is because wisdom supports concentration, and because concentration and wisdom are cultivated in equal measure. Next, the question is asked: Why?
Therefore, it relies solely on the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Answer: Starting from the First Dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence, one enters them in immediate succession;

because this is the final [stage] of the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), there is no other distinct stage above it. Thus, the attainment belongs to that [Peak]. Although it belongs to the lower [stages], Question:

This state at the Peak of Existence still belongs to the realm of attachment (*dhātubandhana*); is it therefore outflowing (*sāsrava*)? Answer: It is the fundamental dhyāna of relishing (*āsvādanasamprayukta*).
Because it is obscured (*nivṛta*), defiled (*sāsrava*), and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is with-outflows (*sāsrava*). This [state] relies upon the fundamental pure dhyāna;

because it is unobscured (*anivṛta*), undefiled (*anāsrava*), and determinate (*vyākṛta*), and because it observes, refines, perfumes, and cultivates [the mind], thereby shaking the mountain of the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), it is without-outflows (*anāsrava*). Question:
It must necessarily rely on the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). May it also extend to other stages? Answer: The dharmas of meditative concentration become increasingly profound;

through the "exertion" (*vispanda*) and "leap-over" (*vyutkrāntaka*), one enters and emerges with mastery. Without requiring further effort from the first dhyāna, one enters the cessation attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in successive order.

Then, from the cessation attainment, one proceeds from the upper stages downward in reverse order until returning to the first dhyāna. Therefore, it is said that it may also be attained in other stages.

[The state of] presence. Question: Since concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) belong to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), under which [of the three categories of practitioners] are "those in training" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth subsumed? Answer: They are not subsumed under either.

Because they are tranquil, subtle, and resemble *nirvāṇa*, they are not subsumed under those in training; yet, because they are not true *nirvāṇa*, they are also not subsumed under those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This meditative absorption first arises only among human beings (up to the point where it is known that the *ālayavijñāna* exists and is not interrupted).
This section below clarifies the place of its arising. The first sentence clarifies that this absorption first arises only among humans within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The next two lines explain that [the meditative attainments] also arise in the higher realms. If one attains mastery, they can also manifest when born in the form or formless realms.
Question: It is possible for them to arise in the form realm; however, since those in the formless realm lack a body, how can they arise there? Answer:

Among the proofs cited, the reference to those in the formless realm as "mind-made gods" (manomayā devāḥ) indicates that although those gods lack the physical results of karma, they are not devoid of what is subsumed under the name "non-form" (arūpa).

The four aggregates arise from this; thus, one also gives rise to this meditative absorption. Form within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is the domain of the Buddha and is not known by the followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Although it arises in the formless realm, there are two differences: those who do not believe in the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) do not give rise to it when born there, for they fear it would result in annihilationism.
Those who have already believed in the storehouse consciousness can also bring it before them, for they know it does not undergo annihilation.
It is necessary to sever the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms (up to the point of being induced by the subsequently attained wisdom as appropriate).

"It is necessary to sever the lower [afflictions]" clarifies the distinction between suppressing and severing manifest [afflictions]. First, regarding the initial interpretation, it is explained in terms of severing the afflictions:

one must first sever the afflictions of seeing (*darśana-heya*) before being able to initially give rise to the severance of seeing and enter the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*). This refers to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) at the first fruit (*prathamaphala*).

Regarding the mind: when a bodhisattva is at the initial moment of the first stage (*bhūmi*), they are still an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*). This is explained by way of contrapositive definition: if one has not yet abandoned [the afflictions of] the view, that is the nature of an ordinary being.
This is because an ordinary being cannot suppress or extinguish the mind and mental factors of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

This is certain. Next, the explanation is given in terms of realizing the principle: one must realize the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), as these are subsequently induced by the post-meditative wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) corresponding to their respective [realizations]; first, the fundamental [wisdom].

Having realized the two kinds of emptiness through primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), one subsequently enters into the emptiness of persons and phenomena by means of the application of effort (*prayoga*) within subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
Whether for the followers of the Two Vehicles or for Bodhisattvas, this may be practiced either singly or in combination; as it is not fixed, it is said to be "according to what is appropriate."

One interpretation holds that among the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the lower eight stages, one may give rise to subsequent [afflictions] upon reaching the upper eight stages.

Another interpretation explains this as follows: this explanation does not apply solely to the abandonment of the afflictions of view (*darśana-heya*), but also requires the abandonment of the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Within the three realms, this applies exclusively to the stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); regarding the afflictions of cultivation in the lower stages, one must completely abandon all nine grades of desire before the others can be merely suppressed and removed.
Only then can one first initiate this meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The first phrase of the verse from the *Kāmadhātu* explains the reason for abandoning desire.

Regarding the two natures—namely, the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)—these two natures are complex and their obstruction of absorption is powerful; therefore, they must be abandoned.
The verse mentions only the latter phrase to cite human testimony: the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) has already completely severed the nine grades of afflictions of the *Kāmadhātu*.
They come to take birth in the desire realm; the same applies to those who have attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

According to what is appropriate, as in the two types of emptiness—whether single or combined—they may practice "complete leaping" (*atyantātyaya*), "half-leaping" (*ardhapluta*), or "universal dissolution" (*sarvasthānacyuta*); in whichever of the eight stages they are born, they all attain the subsequent arising [of the fruit].

Regarding the meaning of "must sever the four lower stages" [and] "arising in the five upper stages all obtain subsequent arising," there are three interpretations of the phrase "the meaning has 'lower'.
Within the eight lower stages, one must sever the four lower stages—namely, from the desire realm up to the third dhyāna;

the remainder are merely suppressed and eliminated. The phrase "transformation of the lower" explains the reason for severing the lower stages: it refers to the transformation of sensation (*vedanā*).

This refers to suffering, pleasure, grief, and joy. Because these are the seeds of afflictions associated with them, they are coarse, unstable, and subject to rapid change; thus, they strongly obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Following the subsequent phrase, one should apply the same logic as before regarding their single or combined occurrences.

If one can give rise to this meditative absorption by suppressing the afflictions of the lower realms—because it severs the innate afflictions associated with the *manas* of those lower levels—then [one must consider] the case where, having suppressed the lower afflictions, one later regresses and the previously unsuppressed afflictions manifest.
This constitutes a general objection that anticipates the initial difficulty. The first phrase restates the preceding position; the following two phrases present the formal objection.
If one can give rise to this absorption by suppressing the lower afflictions, then at a later time when those suppressed but not yet severed afflictions regress and manifest...

How could one who has already been born in a higher realm return to sever the afflictions of a lower realm? If one suppresses the lower [afflictions] while being born in the upper, it would follow that the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) must also be severed from below.

First, the question and answer proceed in accordance with this; the first phrase provides a direct answer, and the subsequent phrases are answered by analogy with the case of being born in a lower realm.

For example, just as one born in a higher realm who has attained the state of a Non-Learner (*aśaikṣa*) severs the innate afflictions associated with the *manas* of the lower realms, so too should this be understood here.
However, because the power of the antidote for one who is a Non-returner (anāgāmin) is so strong, [the seeds of defilement] merely moisten the seeds of birth in the higher realms;

they do not descend [to lower realms]. An objection is raised: "If the suppression of other defilements enables the arising of this meditative absorption, and once suppressed those defilements do not regress or manifest, then for one born in another realm, would it not be the case that there are no defilements to moisten birth there? [The response] explains: ...

It is said: Non-returners (anāgāmin) reside in the fourth dhyāna. When they are born into the four higher stages, they do not require the actual manifestation (samudācāra) of afflictions; rather, birth is moistened solely by the seeds of affliction.

Although there may be cases where the afflicted states previously suppressed undergo regression or do not, there is no loss of having severed lower-stage afflictions upon being reborn in a higher stage.

Although what was set forth below subsequently contradicts the question-and-answer, there is a regression; thus, "regression" refers to restating the preceding [point] to manifest the difficulty, while "non-regression" refers to restating the subsequent [point] to suppress the difficulty.

There is no case of suppressing what is below to produce what is above; the intent of this principle lies in severing what is below to produce what is above, and therefore there is no fault of reversing the severance.
The previous section provided a compliant answer, yet regarding the seeds of the co-emergent afflictions of the seven consciousnesses, the three vehicles...
When one is about to attain the fruit of *aśaikṣa*, the afflictions of the three realms are abandoned instantaneously within a single moment.

Therefore, for one who has been born in a higher plane (*ūrdhvabhūmi*) and attains the state of *aśaikṣa*, there is the principle that they abandon the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of the lower planes. This statement regarding "instantaneous abandonment" refers to the fact that these afflictions arise spontaneously from within without distinction between coarse and subtle.
The following passage provides a response that contradicts this [position]. This concerns the seeds of the innate afflictions associated with the six consciousnesses. Three.
The nine grades of each of the nine stages within the realms are abandoned gradually and individually; alternatively, they may be abandoned as a single aggregate through their nine distinct grades.
Therefore, there is no principle of suppressing a lower stage while being born into a higher one. How could there be the fault of abandoning a lower stage after having been born into a higher one?

This statement regarding "individual abandonment" applies to the arising [of afflictions] based on internal and external objects, whether coarse or subtle, because there are many distinctions among their categories.
If Bodhisattvas can give rise to this samādhi from the stage of the two vehicles up through all stages, the following clarifies the sequence of its arising.

First, it clarifies the turning of the mind; since they have already attained it previously, they may give rise to it at any point, and there is no further need to discuss the relative high or low of their stages.
If it were not so, there would be cases where [the afflictions] could only be manifested and extinguished after reaching [a certain stage].

If one does not fall back and proceeds directly toward enlightenment as a gradual attainer (*anupūrva-abhisamaya*), then from the final moment of mind in the seventh ground, all afflictions are permanently suppressed.

Although the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm have not yet been permanently severed, one is able—just like those who have attained the state of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*)—to [remain] within this stage.
Regarding the arising of this meditative absorption, the treatise states "below" to cite scriptural evidence:
there are those who, from the very first stage (*bhūmi*), are able to permanently suppress [the afflictions] and are also able to manifest the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

There is a passage from below that clarifies the case of those who attain sudden enlightenment. It states that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, one is able to permanently suppress [the afflictions], just as an Arhat has already severed them.
This meditative absorption arises throughout all ten stages. The sutra provides this citation from below as scriptural evidence.
Regarding those who are in mindless sleep or fainting (up to): "causing the first six consciousnesses to all cease to function.
The phrase "mindless" (*acittaka*) below serves as a general heading for sleep and fainting. The first clause cites the verse; the subsequent portion explains the common name.
Both states are called "mindless" because the six consciousnesses do not function in either case.

The state of the body induced by conditions such as extreme fatigue [continues] until it reaches [a certain point]; because that [state] resembles those [conditions], it is metaphorically designated by their names.
Below "extreme fatigue," there is a separate explanation of sleep (*middha*). First, the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is explained. Below "this sleep," the objection is addressed: [Objection:
Sleep is a mental factor (*caitta*) and is associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*). Since this state is without mind (*acittaka*), how can there be a mental factor? [Response: This sleep...

Although at that time there is no actual entity of dullness or abstraction, because it is induced by that [state] and resembles it, "sleep" is metaphorically designated based upon it; this is not a mental factor (caitta).
The bodily states induced by conditions such as wind and heat are also contrary to the six consciousnesses; therefore, they are called "extremely heavy fainting.
Below, the section on "wind and heat" provides a specific explanation of fainting; the explanation of its characteristics follows the text.
Alternatively, both of these are portions of the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*). Excluding these five states, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises constantly.
Regarding the phrase "or below this," it clarifies the inclusion within the divisions. The word "this" refers to sleep, fainting, and conditions such as extreme fatigue, wind, or heat;
all of these belong to the inclusion within the sphere of tangibles. As for the term "a portion," there are twenty-six types of tangibles: earth, water, fire, and wind—these four...

The [four] elements are substantial entities (*dravya*). All others—such as cold, heat, roughness, smoothness, hunger, thirst, satiety, and fatigue—are conventionally designated (*prajñapti*) based on the specific variations of the four great elements.
Now, both of these two categories arise by taking the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) as their condition;

since one portion is subsumed under the body-faculty, it is called "a small portion. For this reason, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not arise. Apart from these five categories, the mind...
Consciousness is constantly manifest;
even at the time of actual death and rebirth, there is no mental consciousness. Why, then, is it said that [consciousness] does not function during only five states?
Regarding the passage "at the time of actual death," the commentary explains the two characters "and" (及) and "with" (與). First, the question is raised as in the text.

There is one interpretation that the terms "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) and "speech" (*vacana*) manifest [the meaning], and that the terms "manifesting" (*vyakti*) and "speech" manifest the five [factors] without confusion.

There is another interpretation regarding the passage "The following... which provides the answer and explanation. First is the initial interpretation; the passage "That says... provides the subsequent interpretation. The first sentence refutes the previous view. Next is the inquiry and explanation:

since the sacred teachings state that there are six moments of mindlessness (*acittaka*), yet these do not include death and birth, the passage "It should be said... provides the formal explanation. All [of this applies].

As stated in the text: "To clarify that the five [absences] are unmixed" means that the cause of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) and the realm (*dhātu*) appear similar; that both meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) involve the cessation of the mind;
and that sleep and fainting are indistinguishable from an external perspective. The inclusion of the term "and" (*ca*) and the word "with" (*saha*) clarifies their lack of confusion.
This clarifies that after the six consciousnesses have been severed, [the state] reaches [this point]; for this reason, it is not said that one enters the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
This clarifies the following: it addresses an objection. The question asks: "Since you speak of 'six times,' why is the nirvana without remainder not mentioned here?"

The commentary states: These five stages manifest that [the state] arises from its own seeds at a later time; because there is no remaining [seed] and one enters into permanence, they are not mentioned here.
Within these five stages, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have four [stages], up to the point where only one remains, because they have attained [this state] and are free from sleep and fainting.

The following five [states] distinguish between the presence or absence of these states in ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*). Noble ones possess only the latter three. With the exception of the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is absent.
As for the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas, they possess only one [of the remaining states], because they are free from both sleep and fainting.
Therefore, regarding the eight consciousnesses of all sentient beings... this is called a brief explanation of the meaning of the simultaneous transformation of consciousnesses.

The phrase "therefore" below serves as a summary. While the five [sensory consciousnesses] appear according to conditions and do not arise constantly, the mental consciousness (*manas*), although it arises constantly, is absent during the five states;
thus, among the eight consciousnesses, two always transform together. As long as the mental consciousness does not encounter the five kinds of adverse conditions, the preceding...

The five groups of consciousness arise either simultaneously or sequentially according to conditions; thus, three may arise together, up to as many as eight. This is a brief explanation of the principle of the simultaneous arising of consciousnesses.
As for the simultaneous arising of multiple consciousnesses in a single sentient being, [it occurs] because at any given moment, only one [of those specific types] is present.

First, the sixfold analysis. This takes up the previous point that various consciousnesses arise simultaneously as a challenge. First, the question: "In a single sentient being's body, there should be only one consciousness;
multiple consciousnesses arising simultaneously would not constitute a single sentient being, for other vehicles know of only a single consciousness.
Second, the response: The first phrase restates the question. If one establishes the number of consciousnesses based on the basis of a sentient being, [the answer follows].

Regarding your claim that "one who possesses a single consciousness is called a sentient being," the following verse presents a counter-objection: when one reaches the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), a single consciousness does not arise;

at that point, such a person ought no longer to be counted among the category of sentient beings. Furthermore, if the status of a sentient being is established based on consciousness, then while consciousness is associated with the virtue of ethical discipline (*śīla-kusala*), one may indeed be described as a sentient being of the human realm; however, what would happen if one were to give rise to a breach of discipline?
An evil mind belongs to the category of the three miserable realms (*durgati*) and should not be classified as part of the human realm (*manuṣyagati*). Nevertheless, it is established [as such].

When correctly explained, both its establishment based on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and its establishment based on the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) are consistent with reason, because this [consciousness] is always singular.

In a single body, there is only one immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). [The text] speaks of multiple consciousnesses arising together because it is accepted that this condition is manifold.
Regarding "in a single body," there are two questions: "All minds and mental factors arise based on four conditions; while other conditions may perhaps allow for multiplicity..."
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for a single body is unique. How, then, can multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously?

Having first answered regarding the immediately preceding condition, [the author] first provides a response in accordance with the question: "Since these immediately preceding conditions are admitted to project many [results], why not admit that they project multiple minds?

For one [condition] projects one [result], and a collection [projects a collection]. Furthermore, [the section beginning with] "And who... next provides a response that contradicts the question, refuting the [position of] exclusivity.
First: All preceding moments of mind and mental factors that induce succeeding ones are termed "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*). This is because this condition is manifold;
furthermore, it would be illogical for consciousnesses to arise sequentially when one intends to apprehend multiple objects simultaneously.

Furthermore, wishing to address the point below, he next answers the question regarding the simultaneous operation of multiple consciousnesses. First, it is established that based on the equal power of various conditions, all consciousnesses ought to arise together.
As for the previous question—how can multiple consciousnesses operate simultaneously now—the explanation is as follows:
