when the sense faculties are unimpaired, various objects are present before them, the various conditions are harmoniously combined, and attention (*manasikāra*) is correctly arising, yet one wishes to apprehend many [objects], why would the various consciousnesses not arise at once?
They arise together.
Furthermore, although there is no difference in their nature as mental factors (caitta), why would you not allow that minds of different classes arise simultaneously?

Moreover, below [the section on] the mind, one may infer simultaneous arising by analogy with the mental factors. Question: If various consciousnesses arise together, this constitutes different classes [arising together].
"Arising simultaneously. This was raised as an objection based on the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) view that mental states do not arise simultaneously. The present explanation states:

"Furthermore, just as the various mental factors (caitta-dharma), although there is no difference in their nature as mental phenomena, yet—distinguished by categories such as wholesome and defiled—arise together at one time within a single body without mutual contradiction;
so too should it be known that the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) [arise simultaneously] within a single body."
At one time, they arise simultaneously and do not contradict one another.
Furthermore, just as waves and reflections arise from a single basis yet are multiple, so too do multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously based on a single mind.

Moreover, as in the following example, the metaphor illustrates their simultaneous arising: the first phrase uses the metaphor of multiple waves arising from a single body of water, based on a single...
A mirror gives rise to many images; the second phrase applies this analogy to the Dharma. Based on a single storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, if one does not admit that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises together with the five [sensory] consciousnesses—[as it would otherwise be] like a distracted mental consciousness that takes as its object something that has long since ceased—[then this principle is undermined].

Furthermore, the phrase "if [it were] below" refers to the simultaneous consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as proof of co-arising. If within a single body only one consciousness were to function at a time, then it would not be admitted that the mental faculty (*manas*) is concurrent with the five [sensory consciousnesses].
If the mental faculty were not concurrent with the five, its apprehension of their respective objects would not be clear.

This is because the first five [sensory consciousnesses] take the mental faculty as their basis for discernment (*viniścaya*), while the mental faculty takes the first five as its gateways for clarity. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that apprehends an object would not be clear, because it does not operate simultaneously with the five [sensory] consciousnesses—just like the solitary mental consciousness in a distracted state that takes as its object phenomena long since ceased.
Since the mental consciousness does indeed operate simultaneously with the five, this proves that the various consciousnesses arise together.

"How is it that when the five [consciousnesses] are present together, there is only a single mental consciousness? (up to) "because the aspects and the seeing are simultaneously possessed of various characteristics.

"How, below... refers to three questions. Since there is only a single mental consciousness when the five [sensory] consciousnesses are present together, how is it that it takes color-form in the same way as the eye-consciousness, or likewise takes sound and so forth in the same way as the ear-consciousness and others, or takes many objects at once? As stated below, this is raised.

An example and its response: This is because the five consciousnesses apprehend objects in more than one way. By this example, it is shown that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) may apprehend multiple objects.
For instance, a single visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) may, at a single moment, apprehend only a single type of non-distinct color-form regarding a single objective field;
or, at a single moment, it may suddenly apprehend various types of color-forms, as when the visual consciousness perceives a multitude of colors.
In this same way, the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, and body may, at one time, perceive a single object-field, grasping only a single type of non-distinct characteristic;
or they may, at one time, simultaneously grasp many different types of characteristics.

Likewise, the conceptualizing mental consciousness may, at one time, grasp the characteristics of a single object-field, or it may grasp the characteristics of many different types of object-fields. When...

This is also not contradictory to the principle that one knows [the object]. Regarding the phrase "seeing the aspect" (*nimittadarśana*), the subsequent sentence further explains it by taking multiple meanings.

The formal inference (*prayoga*) is as follows: The subject (*dharmin*) is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) co-arising with the five [sensory consciousnesses]. The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it apprehends one or many objects, such as visible forms (*rūpa*).
The reason (*hetu*) is that it possesses various aspects (*ākāra*) simultaneously with the seeing-aspect (*darśanabhāga*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like the visual consciousness and so forth.
Why do cognitions of the same class not arise simultaneously? [The answer continues: Because once one [cognition] has already performed the function of discernment, others would be useless.

Why is this? The following four questions follow upon the preceding inquiry. For example, since a single visual consciousness already possesses various aspects of seeing, there ought to be multiple instances of the same class of visual consciousness arising simultaneously, because the substance and its functions are mutually dependent. How could this not be so?
"Simultaneously. This means that because the function of the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part) is manifold, its substance (*svabhāva*) should also be manifold.
To this, he replies below: "If consciousness cannot cognize its own object, what is the use of it being manifold? If it can cognize it, then one [instance] is already capable of cognizing it;
the others would be useless. Therefore, they do not arise simultaneously. This states that although the *darśana-bhāga* has many varieties, yet...

Although various characteristics such as blue and yellow are perceived, the substance of consciousness is one. This is like the various ministers who assist in governance being each different, while the sovereign remains one.

If this is so, since the five consciousnesses have already perceived their respective objects, why are they not called "conceptualizing" (savikalpa)? The five consciousnesses are not [conceptualizing].

"If that were so," and so forth, constitutes five questions. This also follows upon what preceded: since it was stated that once one [consciousness] has already cognized [an object], the others would be useless, then if the five consciousnesses have already cognized their respective objects, what is the purpose of employing the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)? "Simultaneous with the five," and so forth, is the answer. First, it establishes the mental consciousness as the support for the discrimination of the five [sensory consciousnesses].
Next, it establishes that the mental consciousness is able to clearly apprehend the five objects, whereas the eye-consciousness and the other sensory consciousnesses [cannot do so independently].

Regarding the objective sphere (*ālambana*): it is like a mirror reflecting an object, without separate analysis. Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) identifies and points to [the object] within that [reflection], it is able to apprehend it with clarity.

From this point downward, [the text] establishes the proof: according to the sacred teachings (*āgama*), that which is based on this is called "with conceptualization" (*savikalpa*). The five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are not so; they should not be treated as one and the same.
If multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously, why are they not associated (*saṃprayukta*)? [As stated] "just as the five sensory consciousnesses are mutually unassociated.

Regarding the section on multiple consciousnesses, there are six questions. Since multiple consciousnesses arise together, they should possess the meaning of association just like those belonging to a king;

why is it not so now? [The answer begins with] "It is not the same as... The response is: those associated with a king arise possessing five conditions: they are simultaneous, occurring in a single moment.
They are combined as if they were one; they arise and cease simultaneously; they share the same supporting faculty (*indriya*); and they have a common object of cognition (*ālambana*).

Now, although these various consciousnesses possess the characteristic of arising together momentarily, they do not share the same object. Question: When the mental consciousness (*manas*) is accompanied by the five [sensory] consciousnesses, how can it not be said that they share the same object?
Answer: Even if they shared the same object, the substance and number of their respective supports would differ. As for the support:

This refers to: (1) the faculties (*indriya*), (2) the substance (*dravya*), (3) self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), and (4) mental factors (*caitta*). These are explained by analogy with the five [sense organs], as follows.

For example, although the five sense organs and the five consciousnesses arise simultaneously, they do not correspond to one another because they are distinct from one another; this case should be understood in the same way. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The various consciousnesses arising simultaneously" is the subject (*dharmin*);
"they do not correspond to one another" is the thesis (*pakṣa*); "because they are distinct from one another" is the reason (*hetu*); "just like [the five sense organs]" is the example (*udāharaṇa*).
Regarding the five sense-consciousnesses:
the intrinsic nature of the eight consciousnesses cannot be said to be definitively one, because—like illusory phenomena—they lack a fixed nature.

Following the section on the eight consciousnesses, this concludes that they are neither identical nor different. The first phrase first indicates that they are not definitively one; the subsequent three phrases [elaborate upon this].

This explains the establishment [of the characteristics]. As for the aspects (*ākāra*), they refer to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*). As for the basis (*āśraya*), it refers to the faculties (*indriya*). As for the object (*ālambana*), it refers to the spheres (*viṣaya*).

As for the association (*samprayoga*), it refers to the mental factors (*caitta*). These are all distinct from one another. Furthermore, because this ceases as that arises, there are the four meanings of the perfumer (*vāsaka*) and the four meanings of the perfumed (*vāsya*).

Because their characteristics are each distinct, it is also not "lower. The first phrase first indicates that they are not definitively different; the subsequent three phrases provide the explanation.

It cites the sūtra stating that water and waves are not different. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "The ocean of the ālayavijñāna is eternally abiding," and so forth. As for the nature of cause and effect:
They mutually function as causes and also constantly function as effects. Next, an analogy is raised to clarify that there is no fixed nature. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

The self-nature of the eight consciousnesses is the subject (*dharmin*); it is neither identical nor different, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). Because they lack a fixed nature, this is the reason (*hetu*). Like illusory phenomena and the like, this is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

As previously stated regarding the characteristics of the distinctions among consciousnesses (up to the point where it says): "Because the true nature has no distinct characteristics, and because neither the characterized nor the characterizer exists.
As explained below in the previous section, a doubt is raised: "Since they are not definitively different, why did you previously explain the three transforming consciousnesses in such detail?"
Regarding the characteristics and natures of the distinctions among the six classes of mental factors (*caitta*): the first phrase restates the question, followed by the explanation.

As for "explaining the distinctions," this is according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and not ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). To provide scriptural proof, [the text] cites a verse beginning with "Just as... (the *gāthā*).

Regarding "characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*)," these refer to the defining characteristic and that which is defined. For example, smoke and flame serve as the defining characteristics of fire, while fire in turn serves as the characterized object of those [characteristics]. All... [text continues].
Consciousness is also thus; its characteristics are grasping, deliberating, and discerning, while it itself is the characterized by those [functions].
In the ultimate sense, neither of these can be apprehended. This concludes the explanation of the third transformation.

The characteristics of the three types of transformation have already been extensively analyzed [up to the point of asking]: "By virtue of this, is it the case that all things are merely consciousness?
