Regarding the mutual relationship between manifest arisings and conceptualizations (*vikalpa*), they may serve as all three conditions, as there is no lack of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Below, "Manifestation" (*pratyutpanna*). Next, it clarifies that the manifest acts as a condition to produce the manifest. First, it provides a general indication:

the eight types of manifest discrimination (*vikalpa*), when viewed in relation to one another before and after, act as the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). When the mental consciousness takes other consciousnesses as its object, and the seventh consciousness takes the eighth as its object, they act as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This consciousness exerts an auxiliary power upon that consciousness, or at least does not obstruct it. When self and others are viewed in relation to one another, they act as...

Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*): there is no lack of causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), as this refers exclusively to the present, since all [phenomena] arise from their own seeds.
That is to say, among sentient beings, self and others may mutually act as two conditions, with the exception of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This refers to the following: next, the specific explanation begins by clarifying how self and others act as conditions.

Among the various classes of sentient beings, those who possess the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*) can take the minds of others as their objects of perception (*ālambanapratyaya*). Thus, there is a mutual capacity for assistance between them.

They function as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*). With the exception of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), this is because there is a separation between self and other.

Among the eight groups of consciousness, they relate to one another [as dominant conditions] up to the point where the five sensory consciousnesses rely solely upon the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.

From "From the eighth downward" (*zì bā xià*): This clarifies that one's own aggregate serves as a condition. Within the eight aggregates of consciousness, these look toward one another and possess the capacity to provide assistance or at least not to obstruct;

thus, they certainly possess the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Regarding the absence of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it is because they do not belong to the same category (*sva-jāti*).

From "The object-condition" (*suǒyuán yuán xià*): First, there is a general indication of presence and absence. Regarding "the eighth [consciousness] exists for the seven": this means the seventh consciousness is able to take the eighth as its object.

Because it is seen; because it is the sixth consciousness that takes mental factors as its object; because the first five [consciousnesses] take the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] as their supporting substance (*ālambanapratyaya*);
and because the seventh [consciousness] lacks [the image-part] of the eighth, as the other seven [consciousnesses] are not the supporting substances for the eighth.

Regarding the seventh [consciousness], it lacks [the image-part] of the sixth and the five [sensory consciousnesses] and possesses one [of the eighth]: the five consciousnesses perceive only external form, and therefore they are said to lack it; whereas the sixth [consciousness] is capable of perceiving [it].

The mental faculty (*manas*) exists; therefore, it is said that [the seventh consciousness] exists. As for the other six [consciousnesses], they do not exist in relation to that seventh, because the seventh takes only the eighth as its object and does not take the preceding six as its objects.
As for the sixth [consciousness], it does not exist in relation to the five [sensory consciousnesses], because those five operate externally and do not take the internal as their object;
they rely solely upon the images of the eighth. As for the remaining five, they do exist in relation to the sixth, because the sixth is able to take all eighteen [realms] as its objects.
Because of the realm (*dhātu*).

Within its own class, the preceding and succeeding moments of the sixth [consciousness] can admit three [types of seeds], because they are capable of perfuming and forming the seeds of those [seeds'] image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*).

Regarding "within its own class" and below, this clarifies that its own class acts as a condition. As for "the preceding and succeeding moments of the sixth can admit three": the subsequent moment is able to serve as a condition.
The preceding moment of consciousness is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). The preceding moment induces the succeeding moment; this is the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Because it provides non-obstruction and assists the subsequent moment to arise, it is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Since [the mind] does not arise from seeds, there is no direct cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Of the remaining eight, seven, or five [mental factors], there are only the immediate and dominant conditions, further excluding the object-condition, as they do not take what has already ceased as their object. They grasp [their objects].

Because objects appear [to consciousness], it is accepted that the five [sensory consciousnesses] subsequently perceive moments of the past. In this case, the five and the seven [consciousnesses] function as three conditions for one another across time.

This is because the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of a preceding consciousness serves as the *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition) for a subsequent consciousness. Regarding the possibility of the first seven [consciousnesses] serving as the object-condition for the eighth [the storehouse consciousness]:

those capable of perfuming the seeds of both the objective and subjective aspects (*nimitta- and darśana-bhāga*) are as follows—the first five [sensory consciousnesses] perfume the seeds of the objective aspect of the eighth, while the seventh [mental consciousness] [perfumes the seeds of its own objective aspect].

The eighth consciousness perfumes the seeds of both the aspect (nimitta-bhāga) and the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga). This is because the sixth consciousness perfumes the seeds of both the aspect and the seeing-part, and because it serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for that eighth consciousness.
Furthermore, within the same aggregate, distinct entities are mutually related so that their respective aspects and objects do not differ in substance.
"Same collection" (samprayukta), etc., clarifies that being in the same collection constitutes a condition. Mind and mental factors are conjoined and appear as one; this is called "same collection.

Their characteristics and functions are distinct, which is termed "different entities. Thus, when mind and mental factors are viewed in relation to one another, they possess the capacity to provide mutual assistance.

This is solely an *adhipati* (dominant) condition and lacks an *ālambana* (object-condition). This is because the objective basis they rely upon is the same, and they do not take each other as objects. Alternatively, [the text continues...]

Regarding the section "Based on the lower [level]," this distinguishes and judges the existence or non-existence of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). First, it presents the thesis: "Either based on the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), it is said that they do not mutually take each other as objects;

or based on the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), there is the sense of mutual objectification. Then, regarding the phrase "That is to say, the various [parts]... it explains the meaning: "This means that their respective image-parts arise with one another as the substantial cause (*bimba*).

Finally, regarding the phrase "As in the case of consciousness... it provides an illustration: "It is like the seeds held within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), which serve as the [object-condition] for the five [mental factors], such as contact (*sparśa*)."
It is like the material basis upon which the characteristics of a seed depend. This is because contact and so forth are equal to the objects of consciousness;
because contact and so forth in the formless realm possess objects; and because a direct object-condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*) must necessarily exist.

Otherwise, since there would be no external world, sense organs, or body in the formless realm, contact and so forth would lack an objective sphere. Even if one were to grant that matter is transformed [there], it would still necessarily...

Regarding the seeds as the objective basis (*ālambana-pratyaya*): let there be no [objection] that the objective fields of the various parts (*bhāga*) differ in substance. For contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors] must necessarily transform so as to resemble the aspect of the seed;
thus, when various objective aspects arise mutually as the substantial basis for one another, there exists the sense of being "mutually conditioned" (*anyonya-ālambana*).

The same-substance aspect (sabhāga-bhāga) is divided into two parts, the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) and the object-part (nimitta-bhāga), which serve as conditions for one another; this is stated only because they manifest as mutually acting as conditions.
Below, under "same-substance," it clarifies that the four aspects of the same substance function as conditions. From the above, the progression was from the broad to the narrow;

here, it proceeds from the remote to the intimate. The object-part serves as the dominant objective condition (adhipati-ālambana-pratyaya) for the seeing-part, while the seeing-part [acts] toward the object-part only as...

The *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant condition) is as follows: because the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) necessarily lacks the capacity to act as a cognizer, it cannot serve as a dominant condition for itself;

however, it may serve as a dominant condition and an *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition) for the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect). For the *svasaṃvitti* (self-cognition), the *darśana-bhāga* serves only as a dominant condition, because the *darśana-bhāga*—being sometimes non-valid (*apramāṇa*)—cannot cognize [the self-cognition].
As for the third and fourth [aspects], both serve as both conditions, as they mutually cognize one another and both function as both the cognizer and the cognized.

The preceding section discussed the seeds and the image-aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of those gathered in the same assembly, wherein these may mutually serve as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Here, however, we do not speak according to the seeds and image-aspects; rather, we speak of the four aspects of the same substance (*ekadravya*) arising in the present, which mutually serve as conditions for one another.

It is not the case that the image-aspect and so forth are necessarily always mutually the objects of cognition; therefore, it is said that the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) does not [itself] become the image-aspect.
Regarding the object of cognition (*ālambana*): self-cognition does not function as an object of seeing.

This is because, within the pure assembly of the eight consciousnesses, there is no principle by which they could mutually serve as the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) for one another, nor do they possess the functional capacity to act as a subject that cognizes.

The "Pure Eight Below" clarifies that pure consciousness acts as a condition (*pratyaya*). The assembly of the eight pure consciousnesses arises as discrimination, whether regarding oneself or others, preceding or succeeding moments of the same category, or distinct or identical entities;
when viewed in relation to one another, they all possess an object of cognition (*ālambana*). This is because pure mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are capable of universal cognition.
However, with the exception of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), which is not an object of the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), it is logically impossible for the image-part to be its own object.
Because it functions as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is also taken as an object by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).

Since pure seeing belongs to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), once manifest conceptualization arises from seeds and manifest [dharmas], how many conditions can the manifest and the seeds act as for the seeds?

Having already explained the manifest [consciousness], one now analogously questions the relationship between the manifest and the seeds in producing seeds. The first phrase restates that the preceding seeds and manifest consciousness act as conditions to produce manifest conceptualization;
the second phrase asks by analogy whether seeds likewise arise from the manifest and from seeds; the third phrase concerns the manifest and the seeds.
[The author] asks: How many conditions can the present [seed] and the seed [itself] act as to produce a seed?
A seed necessarily does not arise from the middle two conditions; even in the case of a non-intimate seed, they act only as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The seeds must necessarily be subordinate. Answer: The first phrase first excludes the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);

the second phrase establishes the proof, because the present mind and mental factors are established as having the two intermediate conditions. "Presently, below" clarifies that seeds arise from immediate causes and dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The first two phrases show seeds being produced with the present as their condition; the latter two phrases show [the present] being produced with seeds as its...
Regarding the seeds produced through conditions, all are categorized according to their proximity or remoteness and whether they possess conditions singly or in pairs, as stated in the text.
Based on this, internal consciousnesses mutually function as the arising of conditions; how much more so when it contradicts both scripture and logic—why then do you stubbornly cling to such a view?

"Based on this" and below is the conclusion and critique. The preceding question asked: "If there are only internal consciousnesses and no external objects at all, from what do the various kinds of conceptual discrimination arise?
Therefore, the conclusion states: "Internal consciousness serves as the condition," and so forth. This refers to what is said in the verse:
"By the power of mutual succession, various conceptual discriminations arise."

Although the term "differentiation" (vibhāga) generally indicates the three realms—as extensively differentiated in other treatises—the phrase "although [it is] differentiated" below refers to the detailed exposition.

The second refers to the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*); the third refers to the karma-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), and the manifesting consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*).
The four [consciousnesses] add the consciousness of cognition, and the five add the consciousness of continuity, and so forth; these are explained in detail in other treatises.

It demonstrates that birth and death (*saṃsāra*) likewise do not transcend consciousness. The first phrase acknowledges what preceded; the second phrase poses a question regarding what follows:

sentient beings revolve in birth and death, receiving retribution according to their karma, all of which relies upon external conditions. If there were no external conditions, by what means would birth and death occur?
[The topic of] continuity.

[The word] "below" indicates that the third verse is cited as the answer.

The Treatise says: "Below. There are four expositions; this is the first. First, it explains the initial phrase.

Meritorious karma (*puṇya-karman*) refers to that which can induce the maturation (*vipāka*) of the happy realms, as well as wholesome karma conducive to the experience of humans and devas. Non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-karman*) refers to that which can induce the [maturation of] the evil...
The "karma leading to rebirth" (*gati-vipāka*) refers to unwholesome karma that leads to suffering in the three miserable realms.

As for "immovable karma" (*āniñjya-karman*), it refers to wholesome karma that brings about maturation (*vipāka*) in the form and formless realms, as well as karma that leads to experiences within those realms; it receives the name "immovable" because it is not subject to the distractions of the desire realm.
"Merit," "non-merit," and so forth, are the characteristics of the fruit; thus, the name of the fruit is applied to the cause. The cause itself is "black."
[The text] says: "Superior-superior white karma. These three types of karma all have volition (*cetanā*) as their essential nature;

the other mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) are designated by the name "retinue" because they likewise project and fulfill the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*), and are therefore collectively called "karma.

Regarding the true ripening fruit, it compensates for the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*); as for that which arises from ripening (*vipākaja*), it compensates only for the fulfilling karma (*paripūrakakarma*). Although this [latter] is inferior, it explains the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
[This is] the name. Question: Since karma perishes as soon as it arises, how can it bring about a fruit? Explanation:

Although karma perishes immediately and thus lacks the capacity to directly summon a fruit, it nevertheless perfumes the *mūlavijñāna* (root consciousness), giving rise to its own functional capacity (*śakti*). This very capacity is termed "habitual energy" (*vāsanā*), because it is formed by the perfuming of the karmic constituent parts.
[The phrase] "distinguishing from the past" excludes that which is not currently real; it distinguishes [it] from what is not of the past.

It refers to past karma; it is the residual force (*vāsanā*) of that karma, distinguished from karma currently being performed. As stated below, this correctly clarifies how [karma] serves as a condition to induce results.
Thus, when these habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are repeatedly irrigated until they reach maturity, they summon the ripening result (*vipākaphala*).
This karmic habituation (*vāsanā*) precisely reveals the superior dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) that brings about the future fruit.

Because the karma that produces and manifests [existence] consists of the aspects (*nimitta*), the seeing (*darśana*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), mind (*citta*), and mental factors (*caitta*), it is mentioned first in the verse.
"Regarding 'mutual perception' (*saṃdarśana*) below," this explains the second phrase. First is "mutual perception," which refers to the actual grasping of an actual grasper and an actual grasped;
therefore, it is called the "two graspings. Second is "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): "form" (*rūpa*) refers to the aggregate of form, and "name" (*nāman*) refers to the four [mental] aggregates;
thus, its meaning is the grasping of the five aggregates. That which was previously mentioned as "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) also includes the inclusion of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Because it is the essential nature [of consciousness]. Now, this [definition] specifically reveals the grasping of the immediate object-condition (*sākṣādālambana*), because [consciousness] cannot cognize phenomena external to the mind.
Furthermore, the transformed image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of non-existent things is also subsumed under the name "object," because it is not separate from the mind.
Third, it grasps the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), because all phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are not separate from these two. Fourth, it grasps...
"Root and branch" refers to grasping at the primary fruit (*mūla-phala*). Because the eighth consciousness is the fundamental basis of all maturation (*vipāka*), it is called the "root.

Furthermore, because it constitutes the category of collective retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*), it is termed the "root. The maturation of the other evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) constitutes the category of individual retribution (*viśeṣa-vipāka*), and is thus termed the "branch.

This refers specifically to grasping at a single instance of maturation. Regarding "those graspings," these refer to the four graspings mentioned above; all the graspings mentioned here are likewise [of this nature].

The phrase "subsumed under the two graspings" refers to the two graspings as they manifest. Regarding the passage "those [seeds]... and so forth, it explains the term "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*).
The first instance of the word "those" (*te*) refers to the manifesting perfuming factors; the latter instance of the word "those" refers to the manifesting results produced [by them].

Thus, the former and the latter represent the perfuming factors and the produced results, which are the functional capacities upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). These are, respectively, the perfumed and the productive. The text cites the former and the latter to illustrate this point.

Among these, the differentiation of functional capacity is termed "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*). This indicates what follows: it correctly clarifies how [the seeds] act as conditions to produce results.

These two types of habitual tendencies of grasping (*dvaya-grāha-vāsanā*) specifically manifest the direct causal seeds for the mind of future maturation (*vipāka-phala*) and its associated mental factors.
The phrase "both" (*saha*) below explains the meaning of the word "together": it means that the seeds of karma and the seeds of the two types of grasping exist together. This...

This clarifies the meaning of how the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) assist one another. Question: The verse should place the direct cause first and the remote cause last;
why is the text the reverse? Answer: Although the karmic seed is remote, its manifestation in the resulting retribution is actually evident; therefore, it is mentioned first in the verse.
"Prior maturation" (*pūrvavipāka*) refers to the karmic maturation fruit (*karmavipākaphala*) from one's preceding lives up to one's subsequent lives.
The phrase "prior maturation" below explains the latter two lines. Maturation fruit refers to the collective retribution (*sāmānyavipāka*) in the present life;
it is either produced by the karma of the immediately preceding life, or by karma from two, three, or even hundreds of thousands of prior lives. Combined, these constitute [the present result].
"Prior" refers to the preceding [karma]. "Remaining maturation" refers to the collective retribution (vipāka) to be experienced in the future; relative to the former, it is called "subsequent.
Alternatively, karma that produces results over two or more lifetimes is collectively termed "subsequent-subsequent" (uttarottara).
"Even though the seeds of the two-grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) receive fruits without end, why must they depend on external conditions for their continuity?

This [passage] beginning with "Even though the two... serves as a general rebuttal to an objection. The objection is posed as follows: "The seeds of the two-graspings arise in the very place where they are perfumed, and they perfume that very place where they have arisen.
Thus, arising and arising without ceasing, they receive fruits without end. Why, then, does the verse state: 'Once the maturation (*vipāka*) is exhausted'? Even though... [the fruits continue].
The second part takes up the answer. The first phrase restates the question. The subsequent phrase, beginning with "karmic habit-energy" (*karma-vāsanā*), provides a general response.

For example, based on the wholesome karma of observing the precepts, one receives the present retribution of birth as a human or a deva; yet, if one does not further cultivate practice, the fruits of that human or deva existence will eventually be exhausted. The same principle applies to the causes of evil and their resulting sufferings.

Because these are repaid until they are fully satisfied, they cease of their own accord; thus it is said, "once exhausted. The following section, beginning with "due to maturation" (*vipāka*), provides a further explanation by way of differentiation. Due to maturation...

The phrase "the fruit" [indicates] that there is an exhaustion [of the cause]. First, regarding their distinct natures: karma encompasses both the wholesome and the unwholesome, whereas its fruit is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Since the natures of cause and fruit differ, they do not largely accord with one another. Second, regarding the difficulty of summoning it: although karma may summon its fruit, the fruit necessarily occurs in a different lifetime.
Only when the fruit has fully matured do the karmic latencies (vāsanā) come to an end, just as the fragrance of musk or the stench of *elā* and *uruvūka* fade away.
Regarding the two phrases "equal-flow" (*niṣyanda*) and "predominant" (*adhipati*), they explain the absence of exhaustion. First, their nature is identical;

cause and effect are not distinct, and their essential natures accord with one another. Second, they are easily induced; cause and effect are simultaneous, for they arise from one another. Once this mindfulness has been perfumed...

Because they can produce fruits, the seeds of the two types of grasping easily give rise to an infinite succession. Regarding the simultaneous mention of both "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) and "dominant" (*adhipati*) results:
the dominant result is broad in scope, yet it also includes outflow results. As for "outflow," the seed and the present activity serve as co-arising causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Because the seeds of various [categories] act as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) with respect to their own kind, they are superior;

since they have no distinct substance, they are of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*). Furthermore, because they are outflow fruits, their nature is identical; because they are dominant fruits (*adhipati-phala*), they are easily produced.

Moreover, the seeds of the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha*) are dominant with respect to their own manifest activity, and they are outflows with respect to their own kind of seeds. As for the seeds of karma, with respect to those...
Because both the manifest activity and the seeds are of different natures, they are merely results of maturation (*vipāka*).
When the enjoyment of the previous result of maturation within the present body is exhausted— occurring at the stage when this body is approaching death—
the seeds of karma that have matured therein are further able to produce other results of maturation for future lives.
Result. When prior karma is exhausted and the subsequent seed reaches maturity, its ripened fruit (vipākaphala) arises once more;
this is why birth and death are never severed. From "By this" onwards, the conclusion answers [the question]: because this continuity of karmic fruit is inexhaustible.
Why rely on external conditions outside the mind for the continuity of birth and death?
The meaning of this verse is that it is because karma and the two types of grasping—up to the mind and mental factors—are the very nature of that [continuity].
Below this verse, the general meaning of the verse is explained: one transmigrates through birth and death due to karma and the two types of grasping (*dvaya-upādāna*).

Karma has volition (*cetanā*) as its essence, and the two types of grasping are mental factors (*caitta*); therefore, all are not separate from consciousness (*vijñāna*), because there is no distinct nature apart from the various minds and mental factors.
Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) (up to) acting as the specific causes and conditions for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).

Next, the second explanation follows. First, it provides a general indication that the continuity of birth and death arises from three types of habitual tendencies; next, it explains these three characteristics individually.

Regarding "First, name" (*nāma*): this initial phrase indicates the name [of the first type], which is formed by the perfuming of the portion of habitual tendencies regarding names and expressions (*nāma-vyavahāra*).
Therefore, it is called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*). Because it is the cause for the arising of seeds, it is termed "the habitual tendency of linguistic expression" (*nāma-kāya-vāsanā*).

This means there is a subsequent phrase that establishes its essence, and the phrase "linguistic expression" (*nāma*) below explains its characteristics: first, the vocal sound that expresses meaning; second, the mental factors that manifest objects. Following these two...

They form the causal conditions (*nidāna*). Following the two types of verbal designations (*nāma-vyañjana*), they produce seeds through perfuming (*vāsanā*) and act as the specific, immediate causes (*sākṣāt-kāraṇa*) for each conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Therefore, they are called "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*). Conditioned phenomena refer here to matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

The second is the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), which refers to false attachment (extending to) causing sentient beings and others to differentiate between self and other.
Regarding "the second, the grasping at a self": the first phrase indicates the name; the phrase beginning with "which refers to false" sets forth its essential nature (*svabhāva*). Question:

Since the self is a false conceptual construction (*parikalpita*), how can it infuse seeds? Answer: At the time one grasps the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth as a self, one infuses the seeds of those aggregates and so forth.
This is called the "habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) of self-grasping. Below this, the characteristics are explained: first, innate (*sahaja*); second, conceptual (*vikalpita*).

Following these two, the meaning of their separate establishment is concluded. Question: Since self-grasping is already subsumed under the category of "names" (*nāman*), for what reason is it established separately? Answer:
Because the seeds perfumed by these two types of self-grasping cause sentient beings and others to differentiate between self and other; therefore, it is established separately.

The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the three links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) refer to their being the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the various resultant fruits (*vipākaphala*) that summon [beings] into the three realms.

Regarding "the three existences" and below: the first phrase indicates the name; "referring to what is summoned" clarifies the essential nature (*svabhāva*). The matured results (*vipāka*) of the three realms are that which is summoned.

Karma is that which invites [rebirth]. That which perfumes [the continuum] to form a habitual tendency is called a "seed. Below, under the section on the *bhavāṅgas*, the characteristics are explained:
first, contaminated wholesome karma; second, all unwholesome karma. Below, under the section on "following the two," the distinctions among the destinies (*gati*) are established.

Following the seeds perfumed by the two types of *bhavāṅgas*, they cause the distinction between good and evil destinies for the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*). One should know that, below, it is concluded and determined as a condition. This is termed "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*). The grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Question:

Since the karma of the links of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) is that which invites [rebirth], it may indeed be a dominant condition; however, since the seeds of grasping at a self directly produce the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), they ought to be the direct cause.
Why, then, is it also a dominant condition? Answer: Because it causes oneself and others to be distinct, it constitutes a dominant condition.
Regarding the phrase "karmic latencies" mentioned in this verse (up to the point where it says) "together with," the meaning of the remaining text is as explained previously.

Below this verse, the text concludes by correlating the verse lines according to the literal text. Regarding the phrase "grasping at a self," below that, the text concludes by explaining the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*). Question:

For what reason are both the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the grasping at conventional designations (*nāma-kalpa-grāha*) called the "two graspings"? Answer: Because they grasp at a self and what belongs to a self (*ātman-ātmiya*), and because they grasp at conventional designations.
Because they are perfumed [by afflictions], they are all termed "grasping" (*upādāna*). "Grasping" has the meaning of attachment. The word "both" (*ubhaya*) refers back to the previous explanation.
Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from afflictions, karma, and suffering; [these] act as direct causes and conditions that produce suffering.

Furthermore, [the commentary] below provides the third explanation, clarifying the revolving of the three paths. First, it summarizes that the continuity of birth and death arises from afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*).

Under the heading "The arousal of karma," it provides a detailed explanation of these three characteristics. The verse says: "Feeling (*vedanā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) are afflictions;

Formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) are termed 'karma'; Excluding five, the remaining seven branches Are each termed 'suffering'. Under the heading "The first two," it concludes by classifying them as follows:
Conditions: The two types of afflictions and karma assist in the production of the suffering of birth and death; therefore, they act as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of various sufferings directly produce the suffering of birth and death; therefore, they act as direct causes (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Regarding the verse on the three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), one should understand them as they are presented [in the commentary]. (Up to) the passage "together with," etc., the remaining textual meaning is as explained previously.
Below the third verse, the text concludes by correlating the verses with their commentary. "Afflictions" (*kleśa*) and "suffering" (*duḥkha*) are the two types of grasping (*upādāna*).

Affliction is the grasper (*grāhaka*), while suffering is the grasped (*grāhya*). "Karma" refers to the seeds of karma. Question: Why is karma not called "grasping"? Answer: "Grasping" has the sense of attachment; karma does not [possess this quality].
Regarding the name: the term "both characters" (*juzi*) refers to the previous explanation.
It should be understood that this [category of] afflictions, karma, and suffering subsumes [all factors] up to [the end of the cycle]. However, the twelve links are briefly subsumed into four.

The section beginning with "these afflictions" clarifies the subsumption of the *bhava-aṅga* (existence-link). The first phrase provides a general indication of their mutual inclusion; the second phrase enumerates the twelve links.

The names are explained in detail in the treatise. The essence of ignorance (*avidyā*) refers to delusion (*moha*) within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). The essence of the branch of formations refers to the volitions of body, speech, and mind.

The essence of the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna*) refers to the seeds of the eighth consciousness. The essence of the branch of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): the four aggregates are called "name" (*nāma*), and the aggregate of form is called "form" (*rūpa*).

The essence of the branch of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) refers to the six internal bases, that is, the six faculties (*indriya*). The essence of the branch of contact (*sparśa*) refers to the eighth [consciousness].

Contact (*sparśa*) in its entirety. The first six [types of contact] are maturation (*vipāka*), excluding the seventh, because it is exclusively obscured (*nivṛta*). The essence of the limb of feeling (*vedanā*) refers to the omnipresent (*sarvatraga*) feelings.
The essence of the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) refers to greed (*rāga*) in the three realms. The essence of the limb of grasping (*upādāna*) refers to the grasping of all afflictions (*kleśa*).

The essence of the limb of existence (*bhava*) refers to the seeds of the five [aggregates], beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the seeds of formative forces (*saṃskāra*); for once they have been moistened by craving and grasping, they are designated as "existence. The essence of the limb of birth (*jāti*)...
This refers to the manifestation of the five factors beginning with consciousness; the transformation and cessation of the members of old age and death constitutes the member of old age and death.

It is also termed the twelvefold chain, the twelve-layered city, the twelve-thorned garden, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the four periods across the three times, the twelve hours, and the possession of the twelve factors within a single moment. These twelve factors in their entirety are briefly subsumed into four.
First, the projecting factors (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*) refer to ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*). [From here] up to "distinct auxiliary future karma," all are not the factor of formations;
rather, they constitute the single projecting factor. First, the two factors are indicated in general: namely, ignorance and formations. Next, the meaning of "projecting" is set forth:

these two are projecting because they provide the seeds for the five fruits, from consciousness (*vijñāna*) through sensation (*vedanā*). Below this, the characteristics of the two factors are explained in detail.
First, I shall explain ignorance (*avidyā*). Herein, we take only that which can trigger the wholesome or unwholesome karma that truly brings about a future result;

this future result is what is brought about, while the wholesome or unwholesome karma is what brings it about. Karma is that which is triggered, and ignorance is the trigger. Next, I shall explain the limb of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*):
these are precisely those wholesome or unwholesome karmas that truly bring about a future life, which are triggered by that [ignorance]. This is what is called [volitional formations].

This serves as a qualification by way of exclusion. By this principle, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dr̥ṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*)—namely, that which is performed in the present and experienced in the present—is distinct from auxiliary karma for the future;
that is, it is *paripūrakakarma* (completing karma) which assists in completing the results of future karma. Neither of these two constitutes the member of "formative action" (*saṃskāra*).

This indicates that only karma intended to produce retribution in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*) or subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), as well as karma that directly projects the future result (*ākṣepaka-karma*), is truly the member of formative action.

The second is the "projected factors" (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*), which refers to the eight consciousnesses within the fundamental store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) [up to] because they are projected by the preceding two factors.

These two projected factors first generally designate five factors: the fundamental consciousness, internal consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*).
These five dharmas—consciousness and so forth—are subsumed under the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) and are capable of directly producing [the result] in a future life.
Next, the meaning of what was cited is presented: because these are induced by ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*). Question:

Since karma consists of wholesome and unwholesome conduct, and the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) pertain to both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), how can it be said that karma perfumes these five factors?
Answer: Karma consists of the three types—bodily, vocal, and mental. Because they possess both matter and mind, they perfume the five factors of matter and mind among all formations (*saṃskāra*).
The seeds planted in the mind consist of the five factors, beginning with consciousness, which are accumulated by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) in a single moment and have no subsequent interval.

With respect to these as the seeds of maturation (*vipāka*), they are termed the "limb of the six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*). As the seeds of maturation for contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*), they are termed the "limbs of contact and feeling.
Excluding the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), these three types [of seeds] constitute the essence of the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Furthermore, all...
The remaining seeds of the resultant aggregates are all called the member of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Herein, the seed of consciousness refers to the cause of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). This applies equally to the general and specific cases of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "herein, below," this is a separate explanation of the characteristics of the five members. The seeds of consciousness pervade all eight;

herein, the "seeds of consciousness" refers to the cause of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), thereby distinguishing it from the other seven. The remaining causes are all subsumed within the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The "remaining causes" refers to the causes of the seven [evolving] consciousnesses.

All of these are subsumed under the category of "name" (*nāma*). The causes of the sense faculties and the body are all subsumed under the category of "form" (*rūpa*). Regarding the causes of the final six bases (*āyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*):
according to their sequential order, they correspond to the final three categories. Alternatively, the term "name" may be explained in terms of both the general and the specific.

"Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) serves as the general category, as it subsumes all five causes. Consciousness (*vijñāna*), the mind-base (*manāyatana*), contact, and feeling are thus subsumed within "name. As for the remaining five bases:

It is subsumed within "form" (*rūpa*); the remaining four are established as distinct because they each have their own specific causes. Among these four, whichever is predominant is also established as the others;

thus, although the names of the causes and seeds differ, their meaning is the same. Why, then, are they specifically distinguished in the text? "Cause" (*hetu*) refers to that which has not yet been moistened, while "seed" (*bīja*) refers to that which has manifested.

They are established separately according to what is predominant. The relationship between the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) follows the same pattern of general and specific categories as described above.
Furthermore, there are two layers of general and specific [classifications].

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also a "projecting" [factor]; this is because consciousness is the support for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), yet it is not itself subsumed under name-and-form.

In the latter part of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the scripture and the treatise are reconciled. First, the treatise is reconciled: the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that consciousness is also a projecting factor. Next...

Because the seeds of karma that result in the production of consciousness are designated as the "consciousness link" (*vijñāna-aṅga*) through the explanation of the term. Question: If the seeds of karma are called "consciousness," under what category are the seeds of [resultant] consciousness subsumed?

Answer: Because the seeds of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) are subsumed under "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). Next, we shall reconcile this with the Sūtra. The Sūtra states that the consciousness link encompasses both the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka*) and the projected effect (*ākṣipta*).

This is established by the subsequent phrase, which explains that both the seeds of karma and the seeds of consciousness constitute the consciousness link. Of these, karma belongs to the projecting cause, while consciousness...
Regarding that which is subsumed: Question. The treatise states that consciousness is subsumed under name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). How is this to be reconciled? Answer.

Consciousness is the basis for name-and-form, yet it is not itself included within name-and-form. Therefore, the treatise speaks of name-and-form as the dependent, and thus says that consciousness is subsumed under name-and-form.

The five factors beginning with consciousness arise through the impregnation of karma; [this continues] until "because they necessarily do not coexist at the time of being moistened or not yet moistened.

The section beginning with "Consciousness, etc. clarifies the sequence of the five members. Question: Since the five factors beginning with consciousness arise simultaneously through the impregnation of karma, how are their preceding and succeeding order distinguished?
In the explanation, the first phrase restates the question: although in reality they are identical...
At that time, the subsequent phrases are divided into preceding and following based on their meaning: consciousness is the primary factor and the others are its companions;

name-and-form is the general category while the remaining three are specific instances; the six sense bases are predominant while the latter two are subordinate; the six contacts are the cause and the six feelings are the result.

Based on these four meanings, the sacred teaching provisionally designates a sequence of before and after. Alternatively, it is explained according to the lower [stages] or based on the stage of actual manifestation.
There is a sequence of before and after. From this point downward, the conclusion is provided. At the time of manifestation, there is the sense of a temporal sequence;

therefore, this is stated in reference to the stage of the seed in contrast to the stage of actualization. This is because at the causal stage of initial perfuming, there is certainly no sequential order of actualized phenomena.

Furthermore, it is said that they are simultaneous based on the future stage of actualized results, which are produced and obtained [from the seeds]. When a seed produces an actualized result, it necessarily...

Because it is concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If one relies on the stage of the initial perfuming by consciousness and so forth, it cannot be said that the arising and the projecting [of the seed] occur simultaneously;
for that which has already been moistened and that which has not yet been moistened are necessarily not concurrent.
The three factors that produce [the future] are craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*), because they closely give rise to future birth, aging, and death.
Regarding these three producing factors: first, the three branches—craving, grasping, and existence—are indicated in general; next, the meaning of "producing" is set forth.
They "closely give rise to" birth, aging, and death in a future life because, having moistened the six branches, they combine to form existence (*bhava*), which is precisely what constitutes birth.
Old age and death have ignorance as their proximate seed;
that is to say, because they arise from ignorance regarding internal maturation fruits (up to) the seeds that produce future consciousness and so forth in close proximity.

This refers to the specific explanation of the characteristics of the three members, beginning with "conditioned by [ignorance]" up to "the seeds of the five fruits. Having thus indicated [the sequence], [it continues]: The term "conditioned by" refers to the specific explanation of the characteristics of the three members. That is to say, having conditioned [ignorance] regarding internal [fruits] up to the seeds of the five fruits, this indicates...
The first seven branches are mentioned together because they constitute the fundamental cause and effect for what arises subsequently. That is to say, sentient beings experience two kinds of fruits:

first, internal maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*), which is the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vipāka*); second, the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) consisting of sensations produced by objects, which is the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
Ignorance regarding maturation fruit refers to the branch of ignorance that is deluded with respect to the principle (*tattva*).
Due to ignorance regarding internal maturation results (*vipāka-phala*), one does not know as it truly is the suffering of future births;

thus, one initiates various karmas that are capable of correctly summoning further existence, which is precisely the limb of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). With karma and formations as conditions, there are induced the five limbs beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), which constitute the direct seeds for the five results of the future.
Furthermore, due to the second type of ignorance—ignorance regarding the results produced by objects of experience—that is, ignorance regarding...
Based on ignorance, craving arises conditioned by the experience of objects; this is the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Conditioned by this craving, the four types of grasping arise;

this is the limb of grasping (*upādāna*). One either gives rise to the quest for sensory desires (*kāma*) or the quest for existence (*bhava*), or clings to the grasping of sensory desires (*kāmopādāna*), or clings to views, precepts, and observances, as well as the grasping of self-theories (*ātmavādopādāna*).
Through the conjunction of this craving and grasping, [the karma] that projects [rebirth] is nourished and moistened.

The karmic seeds and the projecting causes are designated as "existence" (*bhava*). This is because both the karmic seeds and the causes are capable of bringing about the immediate presence of future results.

In the passage below [in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*], these two treatises are reconciled: karma is that which directly induces [the result] and is thus called "existence" by way of being a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
the seeds are that which directly produces [the result] and are thus called "existence" by way of being the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The four "branches produced" refer to birth, aging, and death—up until the breaking up of the body and the end of life, which is termed "death.
These are the four produced branches. First, the two branches are indicated in general: namely, birth, aging, and death. Next, the meaning of what is produced is set forth;
these two branches are the immediate productions of the preceding three branches. Thus, from here below, the characteristics of these two branches are explained in detail.

This refers to the period from when one seeks out one's parents in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) until the *kalala* stage reaches the fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*) without yet having undergone decay or transformation.

All such intervals are subsumed under "birth" (*jāti*). Thereafter, decay sets in; the vigor of youth does not remain, its momentum like that of a galloping horse, never abiding as something new, but perishing moment by moment.
This total process is collectively termed "aging" (*jarā*). It is the disintegration and destruction of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). First.
When the period of retribution has ended, it is called death.

Aging is not necessarily present [in every moment], yet it is established as a separate factor (aṅga) in conjunction with death; this is because all things that are about to end possess the characteristic of decay.
Thus, aging is not [included] below [death]. [This is the] detailed analysis. Question: Since birth is established separately, why are aging and death established together? Answer: Aging is not...
It definitely exists. Because neither premature death nor existence in the heavens involves aging, [aging] is established as a factor (aṅga) associated with death.
Question: Since the three characteristics are established as factors, why is illness not also a factor? Answer: Because it does not pervade all realms or destinies, nor is it invariably present;

for example, Bakkula was unaware of headaches. Question: Aging is also not invariably present; why then is it established as a factor? Answer: Although aging is not invariably present, it is pervasive.

The establishment of the members [of dependent origination] is explained in the following verse. With the exception of those who die prematurely, all beings within the various realms, destinies, and births undergo decay as they approach death;

since this decay is itself the characteristic of old age, why is it that *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form) is not established as a member [in those higher realms]? [This is because] it exists partially in all [realms], and in its entirety in the two upper realms.

Question: The four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) are without form, and the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) is without name. Since these two are not universal, why are they established as factors (*aṅga*)? Answer: First, regarding the clarification of meditative concentration:

as long as the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are not yet complete, everything is subsumed under name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Next, regarding the clarification of universality: in the case of beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*), the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) have no function [in that specific stage].

Before the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have arisen, they are still subsumed under name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Since the mental faculty (*manas*), which is formless, has not yet become manifest, it is not yet called the mind base (*mana-āyatana*);

it is still subsumed under "name" (*nāma*). From this point downward, he cites scriptural evidence: in the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*), there is form but no name; in the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is name but no form.
Therefore, it is said that among all the factors (*aṅga*), a portion exists in the two upper realms.
Since feeling (*vedanā*) is not universally present, why is it established as a separate limb? (Up to: The Sūtra states that it is "not present," yet this does not mean it is entirely non-existent.
Question: It was stated above that because [a factor] is universal, it is established as a limb. Since craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is not universally present, why is it established as a separate limb?

The next sentence explains the meaning of its lack of universality. Answer: First, certainty is clarified; because it is certain, it is established separately. Regarding sentient beings in the evil destinies (*durgati*), they do not seek suffering.
Because it is a fruit, one says that [craving] does not exist. Yet, one says, "When shall I attain peace and happiness? This is because there is still craving for oneself;

furthermore, because there is certainly craving for rebirth in the higher realms, one does not return to the lower ones. Question: For a person who has attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), the power of their antidote (*pratipakṣa*) is strong.

Craving certainly does not arise. How could one obtain a happy rebirth while craving definitely exists? Answer: Although manifest craving is absent, because its seeds definitely exist within that link of grasping (*upādāna*).
Furthermore, below the section on craving, it next clarifies pervasiveness: those born in the miserable realms (*apāya*) also possess craving toward their own suffering bodies as objects of the "I.
Regarding the section beginning with "Based on non-existence," the question is: The Sūtra states that the miserable realms...
Question: There is no craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Why, then, is it now said that there is also craving? Answer: First, within the response, the scripture is interpreted generally.
The statement "it is not entirely non-existent" indicates that it exists to some small degree, because one still craves for a self (*ātman*).
For what reason are birth, aging, and death established as that which is produced (*janyamāna*), while the causes are established as five based on this resultant stage (*phalāvasthā*)?

Question: Since the nature of cause and effect is the same for both that which is produced and that which is projected (*ākṣipta*), why is that which is produced limited to two [links], whereas five are established for that which is projected?

Regarding the section "The Stage of the Cause" (*hetu-avasthā*): The answer first clarifies what is being cited. First, it is stated that because the distinctions within the stage of the cause are subtle, hidden, and difficult to know, the five branches are established separately based on their corresponding future fruit (*phala-avasthā*).
Following the phrase "namely, continuity," the characteristics are explained as they appear in the text. Finally, the section concludes with the phrase "based on this."

Because the characteristics of differentiation are easy to understand at the stage of fruition (from "because the characteristics of differentiation are easy to understand at the stage of fruition" to "the five [factors] such as consciousness are taught according to their sequential arising").

Below the section on the stage of fruition, next the produced [results] are explained. First, the heading: because the characteristics of differentiation are manifest and easy to understand at the stage of fruition, two branches are established in total to reveal the three types of suffering.

Birth reveals the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*); aging reveals the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*); death reveals the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkha*). All [three] are present together.
The *Śāstra* says: "The results and causes are abbreviated; by means of the middle [members], the two [extremes] can be inferred. Question:

Previously, it was stated that the five stages of the future result were established in relation to [the present] to establish the five members, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*). Since the result consists of only two members, in relation to what are the causes established? Answer:
However, if the fruit that arises is in the future, the two branches of birth and aging-and-death are taught in order to induce weariness and detachment in sentient beings;
"birth" refers to the manifestation of the five branches, while "aging-and-death" refers to the transformation and cessation of those same five branches.
If it reaches the present, the sequence of the five branches beginning with consciousness is taught in order to bring about an understanding of how the stages arise one after another.
For what reason is ignorance established as the general factor for the initiation of karma, while craving and grasping are established separately within the stage of the moistening of karma?

For what reason are delusions established generally and specifically below [in the stages]? Question: Since both the initiation of karma and the moistening of rebirth are all defilements (*kleśa*), for what reason is ignorance established as the general factor for initiating karma, while craving and grasping are established separately within the stage of moistening karma? First, there is the question regarding the difference in their designations.
Second, there is a difference between the detailed and abbreviated expositions of the questions.

Although all afflictions (*kleśa*) are capable of producing and moistening [the seeds of rebirth], craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is superior in its moistening power; thus it is said that craving increases [rebirth].

Although [all] lower [afflictions]... [The text says: Answer: First, it clarifies the distinction between their functions and their abandonment, answering the initial question regarding how they produce and moisten [seeds] equally, yet according to their respective stages...

Regarding their distinct functions: in the stage of initiating karma, the power of ignorance increases; therefore, ignorance is employed while craving and grasping are set aside. It possesses eleven points of distinction:

first, the distinction of the object, because it universally objects to both the defiled and the pure; second, the distinction of its mode of activity (*ākāra*), because it conceals the real and manifests the false;
third, the distinction of its causal conditions, because it is the root of afflictions, karma, and birth; fourth, the distinction of motivation...
1. The excellence of origination (*utpatti-viśeṣa*), because it can initiate, induce, and give rise to the dependently originated phenomena that are produced.

2. The excellence of transformation (*pariṇāma-viśeṣa*), because of the four types of transformation: latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), association (*saṃprayoga*), and non-commonality (*asādhāraṇya*). 3. The excellence of wrong practice (*mithyā-pratipatti-viśeṣa*).
It is superior in seven ways regarding its characteristics, because it gives rise to activities of exaggeration and depreciation based on the truths;

and because its subtle specific characteristics and pervasive common characteristics—both pleasant and unpleasant—function [therein]. It is superior in eight ways regarding its activity, because it acts as the basis for the process of saṃsāra.
Because it acts as an obstacle to the attainment of *śamatha*, it is (9) distinguished by its obstruction;

because it obstructs the supreme Dharma, it is (10) distinguished by its conformity, for it continues to function even up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); and because it is that which is counteracted by the two kinds of sublime wisdom, it is (11) distinguished by its antidote.
Within the stage of moistening karma, the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is predominant; therefore, craving and grasping (*upādāna*) are employed [as the afflictions].
Abandoning ignorance (*avidyā*). It must be repeatedly applied. Next, the explanation of the different answers regarding the single and the multiple follows the question.

Only after frequent irrigation does the sprout of existence (*bhava*) arise. Furthermore, from the beginning to the end, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are divided into two; therefore, these two are used in combination.
Since the initiation [of existence] is singular and lacks the sense of redundancy, ignorance is established as one at that stage; therefore, it is used singly. Although grasping...
Below, I humbly inquire as follows: There are four kinds of grasping (*upādāna*). First is the grasping of desire (*kāma-upādāna*), which refers to the desire and craving for all objects of desire.
Second is the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*), which refers to the desire and craving for all views other than the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
Third is the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which refers to the desire and greed directed toward those rules and observances arising from false vows.

Fourth is the clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*), which refers to the desire and greed directed toward the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Although the first [the clinging to sensual pleasures] can indeed produce the fruit of suffering in the desire realm, [the others do not].
The other three [grasping-factors] give rise to the fruits of suffering in the three realms, whereas these four collectively encompass all afflictions (*kleśa*).

For what reason is it said that the intensification of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is called grasping (*upādāna*)? Although grasping includes other factors, this is stated by way of emphasizing the predominant over the subordinate. The first phrase restates the question;

because the moistening power of craving is predominant, it is described as the "intensification of craving. This is spoken from the perspective of what is most prominent, not to suggest that other afflictions are absent.
It is not contradictory to the principle that all members of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) depend upon their own respective stages (bhūmi), whether in their manifest state or as seeds.

Regarding the phrase "all depend on lower [stages]," this excludes those of one's own or other stages. Question: Do the members of dependent origination condition one another only within their own stage, or do they also mutually condition those of other stages?
Explanation: All members of dependent origination condition one another exclusively within their own stage. There are instances where there is the activity of projecting [a rebirth].
Regarding the ignorance (*avidyā*) that is dependent on others: it is like the ignorance of a lower stage giving rise to formations (*saṃskāra*) of a higher stage.

If this were not the case, then when one first suppresses the defilements of the lower stage and gives rise to a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the higher stage, that absorption would not be produced by ignorance;

consequently, it would not be the member of "formations" (*saṃskāra-anga*). Why is this? Because the ignorance of that [higher] stage has not yet arisen, and that absorption only manifests after one has attained it. Question: From the upper or the lower...
Regarding those born from a higher stage to a lower stage: with respect to which level of objective sphere do the feelings arise that cause craving to manifest?
Answer: If one descends from a higher stage to a lower stage, one gives rise to the limb of craving by taking the feelings of the lower stage as an object.

From the lower [links] one arises in the upper; by analogy with the upper, this is understood. Because one receives the seeds and receives the manifest, craving arises; all of this is not contrary to reason.
These twelve links consist of ten causes and two fruits; otherwise, they would exceed this number and lead to an infinite regress.

"Below these ten," [the text] distinguishes between those belonging to the same world-period (*adhvan*) and those belonging to different world-periods. Question: Among the various members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), which belong to the same world-period and which belong to different world-periods?

Explanation: It is said that the ten causes and two results definitely do not belong to the same world-period. This is because when the cause is in its present state, the subsequent result has not yet arisen; and when the result is in its present state, [the cause is already past].

The cause must necessarily be past. Among the factors within the cause, the first seven—craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*)—may either differ or be identical [to the effect], because they may or may not have moistened [the seeds] at the time [of the cause], or both, or neither.

Once moistened, one receives the retribution of birth (*janma-vipāka*); in this case, the retribution of birth is certainly identical. If not yet moistened, one receives subsequent retribution (*aparaparyāya-vipāka*); in this case, the subsequent retribution is different.

Regarding the two [factors] of birth and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), birth ultimately returns to extinction. Regarding the three [factors] of craving, grasping, and existence, [craving is as follows: craving...

That which arises must necessarily be moistened. Within the causal stage, the first seven members of dependent origination definitely perfume the seeds; therefore, it is said that each is determined and belongs to the same time period. Question:
Some say that the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) consist of two layers of cause and effect spanning three lifetimes. Why is this [text] only one? The explanation says:

These twelve factors constitute a single layer of cause and effect, which is sufficient to manifest cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and to avoid the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. From cause, fruit is induced; through delusion...
The fruit proceeds from the cause; as the cause ceases, the fruit arises. This continuity is inexhaustible, yet the establishment of two layers [of cause and effect] does not increase its excellence.

As for the distinctions among the categories of these twelve links (from the point where they are distinguished): because the distinctions in their three phases of existence are designated by names such as "birth" (*jāti*) and so forth.

Regarding these ten [factors], they are analyzed according to sixteen thematic categories. First, they are distinguished as being either substantial (dravya) or nominal (prajñapti). The first nine are substantial;
the latter three are nominal.
Five are single entities—namely, ignorance (*avidyā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—while the remaining five are not single entities.

Fifth, the "inferior" [link]. Second, the clarification of the one and the many: the fifth [link] consists of only one factor; the others consist of more than one. Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome;

name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) encompasses both categories. The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) consist of six factors; grasping (*upādāna*) encompasses the four types of grasping; becoming (*bhava*) includes all six factors; and the links of birth and old age and death (*jāti-jarāmaraṇa*) comprise the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*).

"Three are exclusively defiled because they are of the nature of affliction" (up to) "metaphorically said to pertain to both; the others pertain to both types. Regarding "Three are exclusively... and so forth:
this clarifies the defiled and non-defiled. Ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—these three are exclusively defiled.

From consciousness (*vijñāna*) through feeling (*vedanā*), as well as birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—these seven are exclusively non-defiled, because they are of an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature. Alternatively, it is because affliction arises in relation to these seven.

The designation "pervasive" applies to two [factors]. The two members of the process of becoming (*bhava*) are both defiled and non-defiled, as they belong to the categories of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.

Ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are said to have "isolated characteristics," because they do not intermingle with other members; the remaining members have "mixed characteristics."
Below "ignorance" (avidyā), four [links] clarify whether they are solitary or mixed: three are solitary characteristics, while nine are mixed characteristics.
This is because the six moistened factors combine to constitute "existence" (bhava), and because the five factors beginning with consciousness (vijñāna) are designated as "birth" (jāti) and so forth.

Six [factors] are exclusively non-material (*arūpa*), namely: ignorance (*avidyā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*). The others pertain to both kinds. Six are exclusively lower.

Five—form (*rūpa*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—are explained as being both material and non-material. Ignorance and the other five are exclusively mental factors; therefore, they are called "non-material.

Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), name-and-form, the six sense bases, becoming, birth, and old age and death—these six members have meanings that encompass both matter and mind; therefore, they are said to be "both."

2. Both are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) and subsumed under the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are not members of the [twelve] links.
Regarding "both are inferior": 6. This clarifies the contaminated and the uncontaminated. First, the contaminated is explained by means of the conditioned; next, the uncontaminated [is explained].
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is indicated by contrast.

Ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) pertain exclusively to the unwholesome (*akuśala*). [From "throughout" to] "the seven stages," they also arise as wholesome (*kuśala*) or defiled (*kliṣṭa*).

Regarding "ignorance" and below, the seven [links] clarify their three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*): ignorance, craving, and grasping are unwholesome and obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), because they are of the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*).

The formations [of the mind] are exclusively wholesome or unwholesome, because they are of the nature of karma. There are those that are common to both wholesome and unwholesome, as well as the non-obscured neutral, because the seeds of karma and the seeds of fruition combine to constitute existence (*bhava*).

The remaining seven [mental factors] are non-obscured neutral, because they are the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*). Furthermore, within the seven stages [of the life-continuum], wholesome and defiled states also arise;
this is because, by taking these [neutral factors] as objects and depending upon them, wholesome and defiled states are produced.
Although all [of these] pervade the three realms, some are partial and some are complete.

Although all belong to the lower eight [realms], they clarify the distinction between being partial or complete regarding their connection to the realms (*dhātu-saṃyukta*). In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are complete; in the two upper realms, they are partial.

The sphere of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) possesses only form (*rūpa*) and lacks name (*nāman*); the four spheres of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc. possess only name and lack form. Furthermore, among the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), they consist only of the mind-base (*manāyatana*).

The factors of practice (*pratipad-aṅga*) of the higher stages can suppress those of the lower stages; because one seeks birth in the higher [realms] and gives rise to them, the higher stages are superior and the lower are inferior.

Ninth, the clarification of the subduer and the subdued: the factors of practice of the higher stages can suppress the defilements of the lower stages, namely the six contemplations (*ṣaḍ-ākāra-saṃjñā*)—suffering, coarseness, obstruction, excellence, cessation, and detachment—which involve revulsion toward the lower and aspiration for the higher. Because one seeks birth in the higher [realms], these six are brought forth.

Because they are [conditioned] formations (*saṃskāra*), all are exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*). [This applies] up to the arising of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) and so forth; there is no contradiction in principle.

"All below" refers to the ten [factors] which clarify the three trainings (*śikṣā*); all these members are subsumed under that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner. Question: Regarding what is attained by the Noble Ones...

One initiates wholesome karma with outflows (*sāsrava*). Is this course of action not, then, subsumed under the category of "training" (*śaikṣa*)? Answer: The karmic conduct of the Noble Ones (*ārya*) has wisdom as its condition;

because it opposes the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*), it is not subsumed under the factors of existence. This is established by the following two phrases: because it is not subsumed under [the category of] formations (*saṃskāra*). Question:
If the Noble Ones do not create karma that brings about a future existence (*punarbhava*), then by what karma are they born in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*)? Answer:
The cultivation of dhyāna through the intermingling of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) arises from karma that supports the lower stages.

That is to say, when a noble one (*ārya*) uses two slices of the untainted to sandwich and perfume a single slice of the tainted, refining it until it becomes untainted—this is the karma of an *anāgāmin*.

One interpretation holds that ignorance (*avidyā*) is abandoned solely through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), while the remaining nine [afflictions] are all abandoned through both insight and cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Another interpretation holds that the eleven [afflictions] below [ignorance] are abandoned in two ways. First, according to the initial explanation:

ignorance is abandoned solely through insight, because it must delude one regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*) in order to initiate [karmic] activity, and because the afflictions that delude one regarding the principles of the truths are abandoned through insight; for a noble one (*ārya*) will certainly not perform [such actions] again.

Regarding "possessing karma": because there are definitely no afflictions that initiate karma [in this state], this proves that ignorance (*avidyā*) is abandoned only by the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*), while the two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are abandoned only by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). This is because they moisten rebirth through the seeking of future existence;

thus, those above the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) who have not yet exhausted the afflictions of thought (*saṃskāra-kleśa*) must necessarily possess these. As for the nine types of death-minds, it is as in the case of the desire realm...
Upon death in a realm, one may give rise to a mind of the desire realm, a mind of the form realm, or a mind of the formless realm.
Just as three types of minds arise in the desire realm, the same applies to the other two realms; this is because they are all associated with co-nascent craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

This proves that craving and grasping (*upādāna*) are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), while the remaining nine [defilements] are common to both being abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and through cultivation.
