There is one interpretation that all [factors] are common to both types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*); [this applies] up to the three members of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*), which are also common to those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
There is another interpretation [presented below]. Next, the explanation begins: the first sentence clarifies that all are common to both types of abandonment;

next, it cites a treatise (*śāstra*) to prove that once a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) has abandoned a portion of all [defilements], there is no case where they have abandoned them entirely. If [it were otherwise], [the following] refutes the previous view based on the treatise. If [it were the case that] ignorance...

If the members *tṛṣṇā* (craving) and *upādāna* (clinging) were exclusively abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*), then they should be entirely abandoned during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

How then could it be said that a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) has not abandoned them entirely? Furthermore, if these two members were exclusively abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), then they should remain entirely unabandoned during the stage of the path of seeing.

How then could it be said that he has abandoned "one part" of all [the afflictions]? Moreover, regarding the four lower lines [of the verse], the words are arranged in a crosswise correspondence; the word "said" (*ukta*) does not [apply to them].

The characters [in the previous passage] all govern the subsequent sentences. In the treatise, it is only stated that all afflictions (*kleśa*) throughout the entire realm (*dhātu*) are capable of linking birth (*pratisandhi-bandhana*);

it does not say that "moistening birth" (*upapatti-sneha*) is exclusively abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Why, then, is craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) judged to be abandoned only by cultivation?

Furthermore, the treatise only states that the formations leading to the miserable destinies (*durgati-gati*) are produced solely by conceptualized afflictions; it does not claim that all [formations] are [produced in this way].
All subsequent formations are produced by ignorance that is abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). Why, then, is it determined that ignorance is abandoned only through insight?
From this point on, [the text] concludes that these three factors also pertain to both types of abandonment (*ubhaya-prahāṇa*).

However, regarding the factor of ignorance (*avidyā*), while that which directly instigates [the process] is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), its auxiliary factors are not fixed.

Nevertheless, the following explains the established meaning: first, the three factors are explained individually. With respect to those that directly instigate and directly moisten, they are restricted to one abandonment;
with respect to those that assist in instigation and assist in moistening, they pertain to both abandonments.

Furthermore, defiled (*kliṣṭa*) dharmas should be abandoned by their very nature (up to: they are not abandoned by nature because they do not contradict the Path). Furthermore, "defiled" and so forth:
next, the characteristics of the abandonment of the various members are explained in general. First, the difference between the two natures of the members—defiled and non-defiled—is clarified;

hence there is the distinction between those that are to be abandoned and those that are not. The defiled [members] are ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), as well as formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*).
The unwholesome is that which is contrary to the antidotes; since it is eternally severed, it is not defiled by outflows (*āsrava*).

This refers to the remaining nine types of wholesome karma with outflows and the retribution of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), which are not to be abandoned by nature because they do not contradict the Path.

However, there are two senses in which it is said to be "abandoned" (prahāṇa), [extending] up to the state of non-percipient absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), which is abandoned solely through the path of vision (darśana-heya).
Now, below, the meaning of abandonment is explained. The text reiterates the preceding question, saying:

"If wholesome states with outflows (sāsrava-kuśala) and undefiled states (akliṣṭa-dharma) do not contradict the Path, and thus are not to be abandoned, why did you previously say that all [states] are subject to both types of abandonment? In the explanation:

First, because there are two general meanings indicated, it is said that the teaching is common to both types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*). Next, the specific explanation follows: first, regarding the term "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*), it refers to being freed from bondage.

"Bondage" refers to the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. The initial word "those" (*te*) refers to the five factors beginning with consciousness, as well as the two links beginning with birth;
these belong to the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*). [The afflictions] associated with the seventh consciousness, such as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), take these as their object.

Regarding "for me": following that term refers to contaminated wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*). Within the sixth consciousness, the associated and co-emergent afflictions arise in conjunction with those wholesome dharmas;
because they are mixed with and conditioned by those afflictions, one does not attain liberation. Once the afflictions are severed, one is liberated.
Based on being free from these two bonds, it is said that there are contaminated wholesome states and unobscured-neutral states (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
They are abandoned solely through cultivation, because they are innate (*sahaja*). Both types are said to be "abandoned" by virtue of their non-arising.

The term "those" refers to the courses of action leading to the evil destinies, as well as the improper practices such as the meditative attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). The "basis" refers to the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*), which serve as the support for those [actions].

Once those [afflictions] have arisen and the afflictions have been abandoned, they never arise again; it is by way of this abandonment through non-arising that the various evil destinies are said to be abandoned.
The attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth are abandoned only by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), because they are conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

Regarding the statement that the twelve links of dependent origination are abandoned through both [insight and cultivation], one should understand this accordingly in relation to the aforementioned modes of abandonment.

The ten factors are explained as being inferior. This concludes the exposition on the meaning of abandonment (*prahāṇa*). Ignorance, craving, and grasping are explained according to their primary and auxiliary functions;

they are abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). As for the remaining nine factors, they are categorized under the two types of abandonment according to their respective meanings.

Ten [factors] are associated with pleasure and equanimity, but not with sensation (*vedanā*)—up to the eleventh, which is associated with pain and is neither associated with sensation nor dissociated from it.

Ten are associated with pleasure and below; the twelfth clarifies the three types of sensation. Ten members are associated with pleasure and equanimity, excluding sensation, old age, and death, as stated in the text.
Eleven are associated with pain; sensation is neither associated with nor dissociated from [pain].

Eleven [factors] are partially subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); [the range] up to "according to the increase of their respective characteristics, the explanation is not fixed.
(11b). Thirteen [factors] clarify the three types of suffering. Eleven [factors] are partially subsumed under the suffering of change.

Because old age and death lack pleasure, and change is established based on pleasure, they are not mentioned [in this context]. Twelve [factors] are partially subsumed under the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); these are the [five] aggregates of clinging (*upādāna-skandha*).

Because they possess the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*), twelve [links] in their entirety are subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). This is because they undergo transformation through the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

If one speaks of the three types of suffering based on the three feelings (*vedanā*): pleasant feeling is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); painful feeling is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); and neutral feeling is the suffering of conditioned existence.

Therefore, it is said that the suffering of conditioned existence is taught in reliance upon neutral feeling. Eleven [links] are partially subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence; aging and death are not.

Because [the suffering of] change is abandoned, there is no suffering of conditioning (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Regarding the "actual meaning" below: this concludes by clarifying the actual meaning as stated above.

If the characteristics are predominant and indeterminate, all are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering because they possess the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*). Furthermore, the five [aggregates] are also subsumed under the Truth of Origination because they possess the nature of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).

All are suffering. Regarding the inclusion within the four truths: fourteen factors pertain to both matter and mind; all are taken as having the nature of the aggregates and are collectively subsumed under the Truth of Suffering.
Ignorance, craving, and grasping are afflictions (*kleśa*); formative action (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) are karma (*karman*). All of these are that which brings about [rebirth].
Therefore, they are subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

When the various members are compared with one another, their predominance (*adhipati*) is certainly present. (From "up to") the Sūtra relies on this certainty and states that there is only one [predominant condition].

Below the section on the members, fifteen [points] clarify their inclusion within the four conditions (*catasraḥ pratyayāḥ*). First, the four conditions are explained generally. Because the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is broad in scope, it is so stated.

All [the links] definitely exist. The other three conditions are restricted; their presence or absence is not fixed. The Sūtra speaks based on what is certain; therefore, there is only the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Regarding craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in relation to grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) in relation to birth (*jāti*)—and so on up to the mutual relationship between the remaining links—there is no sense of being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Below, regarding craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the three conditions are explained separately to clarify their indeterminate characteristics. First, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is explained: craving intensifying is called grasping (*upādāna*).

Craving is the seed of grasping, capable of producing manifest grasping. "Existence" (*bhava*) refers to the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*); "arising" (*jāti*) refers to the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of consciousness and the other factors.

From the perspective of the seed relative to the manifest, there is the sense of being a causal condition. "Formative action" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the active formative actions of the present; "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to... [the text continues].
Within the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*), the seeds of karma possess the sense of being a causal condition through the perfuming of seeds by their actual manifestation.
As for the other eight links, they lack the sense of being a causal condition when viewed in relation to one another, because they do not directly produce their own specific results.

However, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that in relation to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), ignorance (*avidyā*) is metaphorically designated as such, while in reality it is the seed of the formative forces.

In the subsequent section of the *Samuccaya*, a hypothetical objection is raised: "The *Samuccaya* states that ignorance has the sense of being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) in relation to the formative forces; why is this not accepted?

In the response, the first sentence cites the treatise, followed by the explanation: "The habitual tendencies of karma (*karma-vāsanā*) coexist with ignorance and together give rise [to the formative forces]."

Regarding the limb of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), it is explained in reliance upon the limb of existence (*bhava*). Ignorance as the condition for volitional formations is an *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant condition).

In terms of the seeds of karma, the sense of being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) exists in that seeds give rise to actual manifestations; at that time, the seeds of karma are metaphorically designated as "ignorance," though they are in reality the seeds of volitional formations.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the various members [of dependent origination] have no causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) when viewed in relation to one another; this is based on the teaching that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are present, while existence (*bhava*) consists solely of karma.

In the lower section of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, a question is raised: "If the treatise states that the various members have no causal condition when viewed in relation to one another, why was it previously stated that there is the sense of a causal condition for craving in relation to grasping, and for existence in relation to birth?
In the response, the first sentence restates the treatise’s position, and the subsequent portion provides the explanation. "Present" refers to the current manifestation.

Regarding the formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*), when they are viewed as being of the same category, there is only the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and no causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Only the seeds of karma exist; however, when these are viewed in relation to birth (*jāti*), they possess only the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and lack the sense of a causal condition.
When ignorance is compared to formative action (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*) to grasping (*upādāna*), and so on for the other links, both [conditions] are absent.

Regarding ignorance and below, the next section clarifies the two conditions: ignorance in relation to formative action; since karmic formative action has volition (*cetanā*) as its essence; craving in relation to grasping;

and birth in relation to aging-and-death—all of these are spoken of in terms of active mental factors (*cittadharma*). This refers to the preceding [links] inducing the subsequent existence (*bhava*) and so forth.

There is no interval. The subsequent [moment] takes the preceding mind as its condition; the preceding [mind] serves as the basis for deliberation, possessing the sense of having an object (*ālambana*).

Regarding that which arises from conditions: the seeds of karma and the seeds of fruit arise. Within this arising, the five present fruits—the consciousness and other mental factors (*caitasika*)—are all the subjects that perceive (*ālambaka*), while the seeds are the objects perceived (*ālambana*).
In terms of the relationship between the seeds and the manifest [fruits], it is said that there is no equal or immediate [condition]. One perceives the objective sphere and experiences it.

Birth arises from craving; craving takes its object as its condition, yet it is merely an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Furthermore, between the seeds and their manifestation, there is no immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Regarding the mutual relationship of the other members [of dependent origination], both [types of conditions] are absent.
This explanation is based, for the time being, on immediate proximity; those who are wise should reflect upon it accordingly.
Herein, "below" serves as a summary indication. First, regarding proximity, there is that which is distinct from skipping over: skipping one, skipping two, or skipping many.

Second, regarding the sequential order: this differs from the reverse order, as it proceeds from "ignorance conditions volitional formations" rather than "volitional formations condition ignorance," and so forth.
Third, regarding the absence of confusion: this differs from confusion, as the karmic latencies coexisting with ignorance do not themselves constitute ignorance.
Fourth, regarding the actual dependent origination: because nine [links] are real while three are conventional, these three conditions herein are established in relation to the four [truths].
The explanation of the meaning: when these are viewed in relation to one another, their status as conditions is not fixed.

Regarding the inclusion of the twelve [links] within the three categories of afflictions (kleśa), karma, and suffering (duḥkha): [the text continues] up to "they are included solely within the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) because they are intended to produce revulsion."
Regarding "Delusion and karma" below: the sixteenth section clarifies the inclusion within the three paths (*trivartman*). The first phrase provides a general indication of their mutual inclusion:

the three links of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are subsumed under the path of affliction (*kleśa-vartman*); the entirety of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and one portion of existence (*bhava*) are subsumed under the path of karma (*karma-vartman*);

the entirety of the seven [remaining links] and one portion of birth (*jāti*) are subsumed under the path of suffering (*duḥkha-vartman*). Regarding "In some places" below: this reconciles other treatises. Some say that the entirety of karma subsumes existence (*bhava*).

The members of existence (*bhavāṅga*) pertain to both [defilement and karma], because they consist of karma and suffering. This is because some say that they depend specifically on karmic existence (*karma-bhava*).

Others say that the member of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*) is subsumed under karma; thus, the member of consciousness possesses both: the seed of karma and the seed of consciousness, as they maintain that the member of consciousness depends specifically on the seed of karma.
To preempt an objection: while all twelve members of existence belong to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), why is it now said specifically that they are produced by afflictions and karma?

Why are they designated as "suffering"? The commentary first restates the question in its opening phrase, then provides the explanation: the seven [factors] are exclusively the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and do not extend to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), because they are intended to induce in sentient beings a sense of weary detachment.
Because afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*) constitute the twelve links, these are able to cause the continuity of birth and death.

The phrase "due to afflictions" and so forth summarizes [the preceding]. Since the opening chapter stated that the continuity of birth and death is due to afflictions, karma, and suffering, and the explanation of the twelve links has now been completed, this concludes by returning to the original text: the twelve links are themselves afflictions, karma, and suffering.
Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from internal causes and conditions; because they assist in the production of birth and death, they are described as "conditions.
Next, the fourth explanation begins with a general statement and then proceeds to analyze the causes and conditions.

Regarding the statement that "the two karmas are the cause and the two hindrances are the condition," these two pairs function merely as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Now, however, they are distinguished as cause and condition based on their roles as primary and auxiliary factors.
Furthermore, karma is called a "cause" (*hetu*) because it brings about birth and makes it manifest.
Why is this so? Because there are two types of birth and death: that which has a fixed limit is called "segmented" (*paricchinna*).
The reason for this is that [the text] first poses a general inquiry and then provides a general enumeration. The intent of the inquiry is as follows:

since contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma induces birth and death (*saṃsāra*), how is it that uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma also induces birth and death? Next, the two types of death are explained in detail. First, under the section on "dividing," the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) death is clarified.

The first phrase provides the name; the section beginning with "that which" first explains the characteristics of birth and death: namely, that wholesome and unwholesome karma serve as the cause for induction.

Regarding the causes of birth: the afflictions (*kleśa*) provide the moisture that acts as the auxiliary condition for arising; the matured retribution (*vipāka*) of the three realms constitutes the fruit to be experienced.

When discussing the relative coarseness and subtlety across the three realms and five destinies (*gati*), those [realms] are collectively termed "coarse" in contrast to the *pariṇāmiki-cyuti* (transformation-rebirth). [This refers to] the foul, acrid, and impure [sensations].
Next is the section on "segmented" [birth]. Within the three realms, one discusses the alternating shortness and length;
whether it be the body or the life span, all have varying lengths and fixed limits that cannot be altered or transformed. For this reason, it is called "segmented birth and death."
Second, the inconceivable death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*). [The term] "inconceivable" (*acintya*) refers to its wondrous function being difficult to fathom;

it does not mean that it does not descend. Next, the transformation is explained. The first phrase provides the name; "referring to all" and so forth first explains the characteristics of this death and rebirth.

With untainted conditioned karma as the cause, and the assistance of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) acting as the condition, a distinguished maturation (*vipāka*) is the fruit that is experienced.

Regarding the successive gradations of excellence among the noble ones (*ārya*), they are discussed in terms of coarse and subtle; compared to the *pariccheda* (segmented) existence, these are collectively termed "subtle.
Next, the transformational existence (*pariṇāmika*) is explained: the coarse body is changed into a subtle substance, and a short lifespan is transformed into a long one. Question: Since...
To transform the coarse into the subtle and change the short into the long—what is this called "birth and death"? Answer: The exhaustion of the momentum of conscious awareness is called "death";

entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to provide further sustenance is called "birth. When untainted (*anāsrava*) sustenance brings about transformation through the power of compassion and vows, its wondrous function is difficult to fathom;
it has no fixed measure or limit, and is thus termed "inconceivable transformative birth and death" (*acintya-nirmāṇa-cyuty-upapatti*).
Alternatively, it is called the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*) because it is produced according to one's mental vows. [This leads to] the arising of three kinds of mind-made bodies.

Alternatively, it is called "lower. This section harmonizes various alternative names. First, the "mind-made body" is explained. The first phrase presents the name; the second phrase explains its meaning.
The passage beginning with "As in the Sūtra... cites scriptural evidence. First, the exemplifier is presented; next, the exemplified is presented, as in the text. The three kinds of mind-made...

Regarding the formation of the body: first, the mind-made body produced by the meditative absorption of the bliss of samādhi; second, the mind-made body produced by the awakening to the self-nature of dharmas;
and third, the mind-made body produced by spontaneous birth according to its kind. These are respectively assigned to the three vehicles.

It is also called the "transformation body" (*nirmāṇakāya*) because it is produced by the power of untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), and since it is not a body born of karmic retribution (*vipākaja-kāya*), it does not contradict reason.

It is also called "lower. Next, the transformation body is explained: the first phrase indicates its name; the second phrase explains its meaning. As for the passage beginning with "Just as... [the following is provided].

The introduction poses the question: "If Śrāvakas who have attained the stage of no-more-learning have forever exhausted future existence (*punarbhava*), how can they spend a long time delivering sentient beings and accumulating practices until they realize unsurpassed *bodhi*? If that were the case, there would be something that remains inexhaustible. The answer is:

"They realize unsurpassed awakening by practicing the path through a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) for the benefit of sentient beings, not through a body born of karmic retribution (*vipākakāya*). Therefore, it does not contradict reason."
If the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) assists untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) [to produce rebirth], how can it be that the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) truly brings about suffering?

Regarding the latter point, there is a detailed analysis consisting of one question: If the cognitive hindrance assists untainted karma and is able to bring about birth and death (*saṃsāra*), [how so?]
For those of the two vehicles with fixed natures, this obstacle remains entirely present.

Being constrained by it, they should not enter parinirvāṇa without remainder forever, just as ordinary beings fail to attain liberation because they are obstructed and constrained by the various afflictions. This is the second question.

The accumulation [of karma] can induce suffering, while the path leads only toward cessation. Since untainted concentration and vows are subsumed under the Truth of the Path, how could they truly induce the suffering of birth and death?
Who says they truly induce it? It is not so; for they lack the capacity to project karma or to moisten rebirth.
"Who said [this]? He replied: "I answered the question later. Who said that the meditative vows of the untainted (*anāsrava*) can actually produce suffering? He asked again:

'If that is not so, what then is the meaning? He replied: 'The meditative vows of the untainted support the karma of the tainted (*sāsrava*), causing the results of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) obtained from that karma to continue for a long duration and to become increasingly superior through successive stages. Based on this supportive power, it is metaphorically [designated as such...]"

It is called "maturation. Thus, when an impure (*sāsrava*) karma—supported by fixed vows—reaches the time of producing its fruit, it is not the case that the impure karma alone can produce that fruit.
The cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) acts as a contributing condition; only through the assistance of that [obscuration] can that karma produce such a distinguished fruit.
However, although the cognitive obscuration assists in the production of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), it does not...
It obstructs liberation. Why is this? For nothing possesses the power to activate and moisten [karmic seeds] as afflictions do.
Therefore, although the followers of the Two Vehicles possess objects of knowledge, they nonetheless enter nirvana.
What is the use of providing the conditions for the suffering of birth and death?
What is the use of the three questions below? Since one should cause the oppression of birth and death to be swiftly exhausted, what superior benefit is there in instead causing it to be prolonged?
For the sake of personally realizing *bodhi* and benefiting others (up to) the attainment of unsurpassed *bodhi*.
"Personally realizing" and below is the answer. First, it generally indicates two types of benefits. That is to say, "not inferior" and below is the specific explanation of these two benefits.
First, the persons are cited: not those of the two vehicles, but autonomous *bodhisattvas*. Next, the meaning is explained: afflictions (*kleśa*) are able to moisten birth. If...
By permanently severing and suppressing the afflictions (*kleśa*), one will no longer have a body subject to future suffering.

Perceiving that the end of this segmented retribution (*vipāka*) is near, and fearing that it might interrupt the long-term cultivation of bodhisattva practices, one employs concentration and vows to support the causes of the present body.

This ensures that those altruistic practices continue to yield their fruits without interruption over a long period. By repeatedly providing such support, one attains perfect enlightenment; this constitutes the practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha*).
Regarding the cause for manifesting the body, this refers to contaminated karma (*sāsrava-karma*).
Why, then, would that require the assistance of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)?

Furthermore, below [the text] poses four questions: "Since one has already used uncontaminated meditative concentration and vows to support the cause for manifesting the body, is this not sufficient to bring about its realization?"
What need is there for the assistance of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)? Furthermore, what benefit is there in remaining in this body for a long time?
Since one has not yet fully realized signless great compassion, [the cognitive obstructions] provide great assistance in maintaining the body.

[The questioner] has not yet asked. [The Master] replies: This is explained by way of three meanings. First, it is precisely because of the grasping at the characteristics of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) that compassion and vows arise.

A certain class of beings turns toward the Two Vehicles, while the great Bodhisattvas, having not yet fully realized signless great compassion, are unable to seek within that which is sought-less, nor to deliver within that which is delivered-less.
If it were not for this power of grasping at the objects of knowledge as obstacles...
First, because sentient beings who have grasped at awakening as truly existent lack the basis for generating intense compassion and the vow [to save them], [the Bodhisattva remains].

Second, it clarifies that the intention to retain the body is for the sake of severing obstacles and realizing the principle: the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) obstructs great awakening (*mahābodhi*), and since it is truly difficult to sever suddenly, one retains the body for a long duration in order to ascend to unsurpassed awakening and permanently eliminate it. Third, regarding the dependence of the obstacles upon the body, [the Bodhisattva] retains [the body].
The body is the basis for the obstacles. The body is established in dependence upon the obstacles; the obstacle of the knowable serves as the basis for that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Since the nature of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is with outflows, if this obstacle were absent, that body would not exist, because there can be no supported entity apart from its support.
Therefore, regarding a single phrase, one must conclude that it refers to what is to be known.

As for the "retained body" (āśrita-śarīra), if it is through the power of a contaminated meditative absorption (*sāsrava-samādhi*) or a vow (*praṇidhāna*) [to remain] until one has emerged from the triple world (*traidhātuka*), it is described according to its auxiliary causes.

Regarding the distinctions made in the concluding judgment below: I humbly ask, are all bodies retained [by practitioners] of the *pratisaṃdhi* (segmented) type, or are they of the *pariṇāmika* (transformational) type?
Is the transformational body subsumed within the three realms (*traidhātuka*), or is it not subsumed within the three realms? In the text, the first question is answered first:
"If the body retained is assisted by outflow-tainted meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*) and vows, it is subsumed within the segmented body of the two vehicles."
Because it is an object of knowledge for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and not because it possesses inconceivable and subtle functions.

If the retained body is supported by untainted meditative concentration and vows, it is subsumed under the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), as it is not an object of knowledge for ordinary or inferior beings.
Because its subtle and supreme function is difficult to measure. From this point downward, the subsequent question is answered.

By this, one should know that the death-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) is by nature contaminated (*sāsrava*). It is comprised within the matured fruit (*vipākaphala*) of the three realms, because it is what is directly obtained through contaminated karma.

In relation to uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*), it is comprised within the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*). Its state culminates in the Tathāgata, where the two types of death are eternally extinguished.
"Extinct. Because it is purely untainted (*anāsrava*). From this point downward, all are subsumed within the three realms because they are tainted (*sāsrava*).

Regarding the phrase "There are noble ones," this reconciles other treatises. Some say that the death-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmika-śarīra*) is called "untainted" and "transcending the three realms."
This is explained according to the supporting causes of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma.
Regarding the phrase in the verse beginning with "the latencies of all karmas" up to "together," etc., the meaning of the remaining text is as explained previously.
In the latter part of the verse, the text concludes by correlating the verses; the word "together" (*saha*) is as explained previously.

Although the death-and-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*) lacks the [characteristic] of segmented [rebirth], it nonetheless possesses the sense that what preceded has ended while something else arises again.

Regarding "the death-and-rebirth of transformation" below: [The author] anticipates an objection: In the case of the death-and-rebirth of segmentation (*bheda-maraṇa*), where one abandons a life and proceeds to another birth, one may say that what preceded has ended and there is a subsequent arising.

In the *pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa* (death through transformation), there is no sense of abandoning one state to proceed to another. How, then, could it be that what has previously been exhausted gives rise again to what remains?

In the commentary, the first phrase restates the question; the second phrase provides the explanation: even in the case of "assistance and transformation," there is likewise the principle that what has previously been exhausted gives rise again to what remains.

"Although [the continuity of birth and death] also proceeds from present karma and present grasping, which cause birth and death to continue without end, why is it said that it is solely due to the two types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)? This addresses the underlying question.
In the explanation, the first phrase restates the question, while the subsequent phrase provides the proof. However, the seeds are fixed...

There is [such a cause], yet it does not manifest [as such]. Therefore, the verse specifically mentions "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*). Alternatively, for those of inferior capacity, this is explained by means of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) to reveal the true cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*).
This refers to the seeds of karma and the seeds of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*), which are precisely what can evoke the true fruit of maturation.

Because these are maintained and held by the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), they are not separate from that fundamental consciousness. The true fruit of maturation is, as previously stated...
They all again arise as the sovereign of the collective retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*). These are the fruits summoned and induced by the two preceding causes.

Since these seeds of the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) are also not separate from the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), for this reason, none of them are said to be "present. [The text] below, starting with "the present maturation," clarifies the intent of the selection.
Question: Why are only the seeds taken, and not the present causes? Answer: The present maturation cause refers to that which is presently arising.
Regarding the various karmas and the two types of grasping (*upādāna*): although they can remotely summon future fruits, they only perfume (*vāsana*) when they arise in the present.

After being perfumed, they require moistening; only upon maturation do they induce the fruit, for they do not grant the fruit immediately. Question: Why is it that only the true maturation (*vipāka*) is taken [as the basis], and not that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*)? Answer:

Within the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), that which is born of maturation and is neutral (*avyākṛta*) is subject to transformation, arising, and ceasing; it is not the true maturation.
Because they are [already] explained, both are excluded.
Regarding the cycle of birth and death throughout the prior, middle, and subsequent limits: (up to) "by this one should know that there is only internal consciousness.

The preceding [passage] provides an analogy for pure phenomena; the first sentence concludes the previous section, while the subsequent sentence introduces the following. That is to say, "there is no lower" is the explanation. That is to say:

Within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) there exist untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*). Through the perfuming (*vāsanā*) by the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), these gradually increase and become preeminent.
Eventually, upon attaining Buddhahood, one abandons the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and acquires the pure and stainless [consciousness] that sustains all seeds of merit.

This continues until the end of the future, giving rise to various sublime functions. From this point downward, the text concludes by returning to the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
If there is only consciousness, for what reason did the World-Honored One [state that] "nor is it apart from consciousness"? Why is this? From "If only...

onwards, the next section presents the final three verses to conclude by revealing the return to the source and extensively clarifying *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) to establish the preceding argument.

It clarifies that the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and all phenomena do not depart from consciousness. First, there is a brief inquiry. From "It should be known... onwards, it is a brief [explanation].
Answer: The final line is a re-examination. The verse says:
"Due to various pervasive conceptualizations... [omitted] ...like the nature of impermanence and so forth; it is not that these and those are not seen.
The verse below provides the answer by citing the final three verses. The first line clarifies the nature of pervasive conceptualization regarding the self, phenomena, and existence.
Because [the concepts of] identity and difference lack any substantial reality whatsoever, they are like flowers in the sky, seen by those with cataracts.

Next, the first two lines of the second verse clarify the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*): because the four divisions of all minds and mental factors lack intrinsic nature, they are like illusions produced by various conditions.
The next two lines clarify the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*): it is the true reality upon which all phenomena depend.

The nature (*dhātu*) is the essence of this principle; like a clear, cloudless sky, it is free from existence and non-existence. The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is like the hemp; the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is like the rope;
and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is like the snake. The subsequent verse clarifies that the ultimate and the conventional are neither identical nor distinct.

The Commentary says: It is called "thoroughly conceptualizing" (*parikalpa*) because it circumscribes and universally calculates. (Up to: Because it cannot be found through logical investigation or scriptural inquiry.
The Commentary says: Below, there is an explanation. First, the first line is briefly explained: it refers to circumscribing, being all-pervasive, and calculating or measuring.
Therefore, it is called "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*). With various types and distinct names and forms, they are designated as "this" or "that.

This refers to the very capacity for thorough imagination, which is false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). By means of these various false conceptualizations, one thoroughly imagines the various objects of imagination—namely, the distinctions of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) regarding phenomena (*dharma*) or a self (*ātman*), such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). These are the objects falsely grasped. Regarding the aggregates:

The bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), etc., serve as the support for the notions of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*). As stated in the Sūtra: "All worldly views of self arise based upon the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) exists as if it were real though it is not truly so, because it arises from a multitude of conditions, like magical illusions and the like. The thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is entirely devoid of both essence and characteristics, because it is falsely grasped, like flowers in the sky and the like.
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the ultimate truth revealed [by the former], because it is free from existence and non-existence, like the pupil of the eye.
This clarifies emptiness. Therefore, the following line concludes that [emptiness] is not separate from the mind.
As for what category of nature space, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and so forth are subsumed under:

the section beginning with "Space" clarifies their mutual inclusion in terms of their categories. The intent behind this mutual inclusion is as stated in the preceding heading: "One should know the three..."

The nature (*svabhāva*) likewise does not depart from consciousness. Now, by subsuming all mundane and supramundane phenomena within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it is revealed that everything is inseparable from consciousness.
First, the six unconditioned phenomena (*ṣaḍ-asaṃskṛta*) are subsumed; first, the inquiry is raised:
All three [natures] include the mind and its transformations that appear as such; because they are non-erroneous, they are subsumed under the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).
The phrase "all three" below provides the explanation. The first sentence generally clarifies the inclusion of the three natures. Next, it distinguishes their specific inclusion:

having previously heard names such as "space," there arise appearances of space and so forth according to conceptual construction. Due to the power of repeated habituation, when the mind and its transformations arise, they appear as space...

The characteristics of unconditioned phenomena such as space appear; these manifested characteristics are similar from one moment to the next and are without change, and are thus conventionally designated as "permanent.

These six [phenomena], including space, are therefore merely transformations of the mind and thus belong to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). To falsely grasp them as being truly existent belongs to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
However, if space and other such characteristics are provisionally established based on the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), then they are so designated. Thus it is said.

It belongs to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Regarding the phrase "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) below, this explains that because the aforementioned mind undergoes transformation, it belongs to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

The transforming minds and so forth encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). If they are transformations of a contaminated mind, they definitely belong to the dependent nature.

If they are transformations of an uncontaminated mind, they may be subsumed under two natures: because they arise from pure conditions, they are subsumed under the dependent nature; and because they are free from inversion, they are the perfected nature.
Regarding "actual inclusion": how are these three natures subsumed within the seven suchnesses?
Below this, the seven suchnesses are next subsumed; first, the inquiry is raised.

Regarding the seven kinds of *tathatā* (true thusness): first is the *tathatā* of transmigration, up to the seventh, the *tathatā* of correct practice, which refers to the true nature of the Path (*mārga*).

Below the section on the seven *tathatās*, there is an explanation. First, the characteristics of the seven *tathatās* are set forth; next, their mutual inclusion is clarified. As for the *tathatā* of transmigration:

it means that *tathatā* follows conditions to manifest as all phenomena. Because it is "unchanging while following conditions" and "following conditions while remaining unchanging," it is called "transmigration."
The "transformed true nature" (*parāvṛtta-tattva*): as for the "true characteristic" (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), it is called the true characteristic because it is neither characterized nor uncharacterized.

Since the principle of reality is revealed at the locus where the self and phenomena are empty, it is called the "revealed true nature. The "true nature of consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra-tathatā*): this refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra*) which permeates both the defiled and the pure;
it is the substantial reality that serves as the basis for the dependent, and is thus called the "true nature of consciousness-only. "Establishment" (*vyavasthāna*) refers to the three realms.

Because they are able to establish sentient beings within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), who rise and fall in cyclic transmigration and undergo all manner of suffering—wherein the very nature of suffering is the absence of any characteristic of oppression—this refers to those who practice erroneously;
that is, the afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) which combine and accumulate together.
The gathering of what arises is the absence of any characteristic of aggregation; this is the true nature of gathering.

"Pure" means that both defilement and purity are equally pure, such that all characteristics are extinguished—meaning both arising and ceasing are extinguished—and quiescent cessation manifests before one. This extinction of the characteristic of arising is the true nature of extinction.
"Right practice" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path and so forth, because it remedies that which is to be remedied; thus, the path is non-dual in character. This is...
The reality-nature (*tattva*) of the path.
These seven reality-natures are subsumed under the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). [From "up to" (*yāvat*)] the remaining four are all subsumed under the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*.

Regarding these seven below: this correctly clarifies their mutual inclusion. The reality-nature of these seven is subsumed exclusively under the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*. By the two types of knowledge...

Because they take objects as their conditions, they are subsumed under their respective characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). The flow of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) are subsumed under these three [natures] and two [aspects].

Erroneous attachment to the existence of the three [realms] is subsumed under the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). These three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) are subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). The true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), which is consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) and pure, is [the perfected nature].
Correct practice is entirely subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Regarding how the three natures and the six phenomena mutually subsume one another:
below the section on the three natures, the three subsume the six. First, the inquiry is raised.

Within those six dharmas, all three natures (trisvabhāva) are fully present (up to: because they all possess the nature of being falsely grasped and dependently originated). Regarding "those six" and below:
[it means] that within the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), one conceives of a real self (ātman) and real dharmas; these are subsumed under the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).

The five [aggregates] are all dependently originated and are thus subsumed under the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva). The emptiness of the nature of the five aggregates is subsumed under the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva). The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is as explained above.
Explanation: These also apply to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
How do the three natures and the five categories (*pañcavastu*) encompass one another?

Below the section on the three natures, four [of the five categories] encompass the five categories. First, the inquiry is raised: name (*nāman*), appearance (*nimitta*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), and suchness (*tathatā*).
The various sacred teachings state that the mutual inclusion [of phenomena] is not fixed; (up to: "the four that arise from conditions are all included within the dependent nature.

The passage beginning with "The various sacred... provides the explanation. First, it generally indicates that [the inclusion] is not fixed. Then, the passage beginning with "That is to say" specifically cites the characteristics of non-fixity across four locations.
First, one explanation is cited. That explanation states: "Defiled minds and so forth" refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) that is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).

It comprises the characteristics (*nimitta*), names (*nāman*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*). That which "resembles the signified" (*abhidheya*) refers to the meaning expressed; that which "resembles the signifier" (*abhidhāna*) refers to the various forms of speech.
Regarding "outflow-free mind and so forth": this refers to the pure dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Both subject and object are characteristics of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);

being free from these is collectively termed "correct wisdom" (*samyag-jñāna*). Fourth, the summary from below: whether it be the transforming subject or the transformed object, the signifier or the signified, or whether defiled or purified, all arise from conditions and are subsumed under the dependent nature.
Alternatively, there are places where it is stated that [the dependent nature] is subsumed under the perfected nature because it is non-erroneous regarding both [aspects].

Furthermore, below, two explanations are cited. Regarding "that which is said," the intention is as follows: the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of contaminated minds and so forth is called "characteristic" (*nimitta*);

the remaining subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), as well as the transforming substance itself, is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*); and the dual grasping of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) exists only as a conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).

In principle, these do not exist; they are merely designated as names. Because correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are free from inversion, they are subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*).

Alternatively, some passages state that the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*) is established according to conventional sentiment as the two things: name and characteristic (*nāman* and *nimitta*).

Alternatively, [the text] proceeds next by citing three explanations. Those explanations clarify the underlying intent: within the category of contaminated mental states (*sāsrava-citta*), there are four parts collectively termed "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).
That which is grasped as the signifier (*vācaka*) is the "name" (*nāman*); that which is signified (*vācya*) is the "characteristic" (*nimitta*).

Furthermore, there is another passage which states that [the object] belongs to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)—up to the point where it says—that while its substance is actually non-existent, the designation of its meaning is conventionally established.

Next, four further explanations are cited below. The intent of those [passages] is as follows: the four contaminated parts (*sāsrava-catur-aṃśa*) become the "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*) by the power of names;
therefore, they are called "names. The existence, non-existence, and so forth of the thoroughly imagined nature follow names and are superimposed upon them.

"Imagining" (parikalpa) refers to the provisional designation of names upon objects; "objects" refers to the various notions of existence, non-existence, and so forth that are imagined upon the characteristics (nimitta).

That which is "universally imagined" (parikalpya) belongs to the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), while the "imagined nature" (parikalpita-svabhāva) belongs to the nature of universal imagination (parikalpa-svabhāva). This accords with the first verse of the previous explanation.
The second interpretation is identical in its meaning regarding the dependent nature.
The five categories as explained in the various sacred teachings—up to [the point where it says] "as extensively explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*—should be understood accordingly.
The phrase "the various sacred [teachings]" below concludes the judgment; "as in the *Yogācāra*" below points to the detailed exposition. The treatise asks:

Of the first nature (*svabhāva*), how many of the five dharmas are included? Answer: None at all are included. Of the second nature, how many are included? Answer: Four are included. The third... [and so forth].
How many of the three natures (trisvabhāva) are subsumed [by these]? Regarding "subsumed by one," etc., there is also the question:
how are the five characteristics taught in the holy scriptures (āgama) subsumed within these three natures? Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "Furthermore, the holy...
it states that the five [characteristics] subsume the five aspects. First, the inquiry is raised: 1. the characterized aspect (lakṣya-lakṣaṇa); 2. the characterizing aspect (lakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa); 3. ...
Second is the characteristic of mutual connection; fourth is the characteristic of attachment; fifth is the characteristic of non-attachment.
Both the signified and the signifier each possess the three natures (up to the point where they take uncontaminated wisdom and so forth as their intrinsic nature).

"Regarding that which is expressed" (*so-śūan*) and below is the explanation. The first phrase generally indicates that the expressive (*neng-śūan*) and the expressed (*so-śūan*) each belong to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

"Namely, the false" (*wei wang*) and below assigns them specifically to the three natures. The false imagination of subject and object is subsumed under the *parikalpita-svabhāva*. "Phenomena" (*xiang*) are what is expressed; "names" (*ming*) and "conceptualization" (*fen-bie*) are the expressives.

Therefore, it is said they "correspond accordingly" (*sui ying*) and are subsumed under the *paratantra-svabhāva*. "True Suchness" (*zhenru*) refers to that which is expressed. "Correct Wisdom" (*zheng zhi*)— [The text continues with the definition of correct wisdom as being subsumed under the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*.]

This refers to that which expresses [meaning]. Therefore, it is said to be "according to what is appropriate. It is subsumed under the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). The subsequent phrase, beginning with "subsequently attained" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*), explains that "wisdom" (*jñāna*) belongs to the category of that which expresses meaning;
for although fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is free from subject and object, subsequently attained wisdom manifests as if it were that which expresses meaning.

The characteristic of being associated with these two [aspects] is subsumed solely under the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature); the following phrase explains this. The characteristic of being grasped through attachment belongs solely to the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). Universal...

Because it is that which is universally conceptualized by the mind and its associates, the next phrase provides the explanation: "not adhering to signs" is subsumed solely within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because wisdom is established through the departure from adherence. The subsequent phrase provides the explanation for this.

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "Moreover, in the holy teachings... and so forth: how are the four realities (*catvāri tattvāni*) taught in the sacred scriptures subsumed within these three natures (*trisvabhāva*)?
First, the question is raised. As for the phrase "Moreover, in the holy teachings... and so forth, the six [realities] subsume the four realities. This is the initial inquiry.
The reality established by worldly convention (*loka-prasiddha-tattva*) [extends] up to the latter two realities, which belong exclusively to the third.
Below this, it is explained: first, the reality established by worldly convention; second, the reality established by reasoning (*yukti-prasiddha-tattva*);

third, the reality that is the object of knowledge purified of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara-tattva*); and fourth, the reality that is the object of knowledge purified of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara-tattva*).

Regarding "the reality of the world": it refers to all that is in the world, which, through habitual practice regarding various phenomena, is established as conventional by common designation—namely, earth, water, fire, and wind; and the characteristics of form, odor, taste, and tangibility.

These have been transmitted from of old as fixed terminology, and are mutually regarded as real through the conceptualizations of self and others, rather than being examined through erroneous reflection.
Regarding the "truth of reality as it is" (*yathābhūta-tattva*): this refers to all correct cognitions (*samyag-jñāna*).

For those who practice according to observation, it is the object of knowledge and the sphere of activity of a definitive wisdom that has been thoroughly investigated by means of the three criteria of valid cognition—direct perception, inference, and authoritative scripture—and which is established through the principle of proof based on causes and conditions exactly as they are.
This is the truth of the sphere of activity for the purification of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-gocara-tattva*).

"Those" refers to the uncontaminated preparatory knowledge (*anāsrava-prayoga-jñāna*), the uncontaminated correct knowledge (*anāsrava-samyag-jñāna*), the uncontaminated subsequently attained knowledge (*anāsrva-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), and so forth, belonging to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

these are the spheres of activity and the objects of knowledge for them. "The reality that is the sphere of activity for the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-gocara-tattva*)" refers to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) as they are relied upon by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have entered into the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and those who have already entered into its ultimate purity.
It is beyond the nature of verbal expression, as it is the objective domain of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "the mundane" and below, this explains that the first two realities are subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because they are comprised of the three factors: characteristics (*nimitta*), names (*nāman*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

The latter two realities are subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because they are comprised of the two factors: correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*). From the *Madhyāntavibhāga* and below, this cites scriptural authority regarding the mundane reality.

The [conventional] reality is subsumed under the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because it is commonly clung to as such. The reality of reasoning (*yukti-tattva*) is subsumed under all three natures:

when there is clinging to a principle, it is subsumed under the imagined nature; when the principle follows defiled conditions, it is subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); and when it is free from clinging and purified, it is subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The latter two realities are subsumed exclusively under the perfected nature.
How are the three natures and the four truths mutually inclusive?
[The text] below the section on the three natures states that the seven [categories] subsume the four truths. First, the inquiry is raised:
within each of the four [truths], all three natures are present (up to the point where it says) because they have as their specific characteristic that which is revealed by the absence of "mine."

Among the four [truths], the first is explained below. First, it is generally stated that each of the Four Truths possesses the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Now, regarding Suffering (*duḥkha*), the specific explanation follows.

First, the four contemplations present under the Truth of Suffering—impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnya*), and non-self (*anātman*)—are each shown to possess the three natures.

Regarding impermanence, the three aspects within it are indicated; in each case, the first phrase presents the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), while the second phrase provides the proof. The subsequent sections follow this same pattern.
Regarding these: "absence of intrinsic nature" refers to the emptiness of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because it is eternally devoid of self-nature.

"Arising and ceasing" refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arising and ceasing according to conditions, because it is subject to birth and extinction and does not abide. "Defilement, purity, and transformation" refers to the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) following conditions:

in the stage of ordinary beings, it follows defilement such that defilement appears and purity is concealed; in the stage of the noble ones, it follows purity such that purity arises and defilement ceases. [This concerns] suffering and existence.

Below, the three types of suffering within the category of suffering are indicated. Regarding "the suffering that is grasped": the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are suffering. "Grasping" (*upādāna*) has the meaning of attachment.

Because one gives rise to the two attachments to self and phenomena based upon the five aggregates, they are called the "basis. Because one is attached to the five aggregates, they are called "that which is grasped."

Regarding the suffering of phenomena (*vastu-lakṣaṇa-duḥkha*): there is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). When the mind takes an object of suffering as its condition, and that object of suffering oppresses the mind, the mind and the object arise together;
therefore, it is called the "suffering of suffering. Pleasure is not constant; it abides only for a brief moment. Once the conditions for pleasure have ceased, [it turns into suffering].

This is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). Being invaded by impermanence is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). Since all three types of suffering arise in accordance with conditions, they constitute the suffering of aggregation (*saṃnipāta-duḥkha*).
This refers to the aggregation of the eight sufferings, the five sufferings, and so forth. The nature of this aggregation is empty; its essence is not real.

Below the section on "Emptiness and Existence," there are three headings within the section on emptiness. Regarding "lack of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*): it means that the falsely grasped nature within [the state of] non-existence does not exist.
Therefore, "distinct nature" refers to the fact that the dependent nature and the falsely imagined nature are distinct from one another.

"Self-nature" refers to the fact that its essence is free from false imagination and is manifested by emptiness. Regarding "selflessness" below, it indicates the three [aspects] within selflessness: "signless" because it lacks the signs of grasping at a self;
"distinct sign" because, being provisionally established according to conditions, it is distinct from the falsely imagined real self; and "specific sign" [refers to...]
Because the principle revealed by the contemplation of non-self is its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the three aspects of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*): first, the accumulation of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-samudaya*), up to third, the accumulation of non-separation from fetters (*avisamyoga-samudaya*), which refers to suchness (*tathatā*) that has not yet been freed from obstructions.
Under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), three aspects within the Truth of Origination are indicated. Regarding "the origination of habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā-samudaya*):

this refers to the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), namely the self and dharmas that are grasped. The word "grasping" (*graha*) refers to the mind that performs the grasping; "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) refers to the seeds perfumed by that grasping mind. Question:
Since the mind that grasps constitutes the origination, and this refers to its active manifestation (*pravṛtti*), why is it called "habitual tendency"? Answer: Because it grasps at a self...

The habitual tendencies perfumed by phenomena are provisionally established based upon their actual manifestation; therefore, they are called the "accumulation of habitual tendencies for the grasping at intrinsic nature.
As for "origination," this refers to afflictions giving rise to karma; because karma increases afflictions and they mutually serve as conditions for one another, they are thus brought forth.
"Not yet free from fetters" refers to *tathatā* (suchness) while still enmeshed in bondage.
The three aspects of the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) are: first, cessation by intrinsic nature; [up to] third, cessation by original nature, because it is suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding the truth of cessation, the three within the truth of cessation are indicated. Cessation by intrinsic nature refers to the fact that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is fundamentally non-arisen.

Cessation of the two graspings refers to the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because the two graspings do not arise due to [the absence of] causes and conditions. Cessation by original nature...
This means that the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is fundamentally quiescent.

Regarding the three aspects of the Truth of the Path: first is "universal knowledge" (*parijñā*). Although universal knowledge also extends to the latter two [aspects], within the section on the Truth of the Path, three are designated.
As for "universal knowledge," it refers to the ability to know that the nature of what is grasped is empty, and thus to transcend [grasping] forever.
"Abandonment" refers to the ability to abandon the defiled portion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). "Realization" refers to the ability to realize the true principle (*tattva*).
"Thorough knowledge" applies to both of the latter two, because wisdom thoroughly knows both the dependent nature and the true principle.
The seven triads of the three natures are explained in their respective order; whether they are provisional or substantial, they should be understood according to reason.

Regarding the "seven triads" below, this concludes the correlation with the three natures. As for the "seven triads," it means that within *duḥkha* (suffering) there are four triads, and each of *samudaya* (origination), etc., has three;

thus, there are seven triads in total. Regarding the "explanation in their respective order": all the first phrases belong to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), while the subsequent phrases belong to the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).

The subsequent phrase refers to the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). Regarding whether these are provisional or real: the *saṃgraha* (accumulation) is assigned exclusively to the real, while the remaining six are assigned to the provisional.
How are the objective spheres traversed by the three gates of liberation subsumed within these three natures?
Regarding the three liberations: the eight [liberations] subsume the three. First, the question is raised. In reality, they all apply universally;
yet according to their specific characteristics, each corresponds to one [of the three]. (Up to: This is because these three, respectively, are the objects of those [eight].

In reality, [the three gates] are subsumed below. The first sentence clarifies that each individual gate subsumes all three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Regarding the subsequent sections on their respective distinct subsumptions:

the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) subsumes the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because the imagined nature is empty. The gate of signlessness (*animitta*) subsumes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because that which arises through conditions is signless.
The gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) subsumes the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); once the realized principle has been verified, there is no further seeking or wishing.

Therefore, from "conditioned by this" onwards, it clarifies the objective spheres traversed by the three gates. Conditioned by these three gates, there further arise three types of patience (*kṣānti*): 1.
**Patience regarding the non-arising of intrinsic nature:** By attaining this gate of liberation of emptiness, one realizes that within intrinsic nature there is no self, person, or life-span;
that they are ultimately non-arising. This is because one accepts this [truth] within the mind. 2. **Patience regarding the spontaneous non-arising:**...

Having attained this liberation door of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa-mukha*), one thoroughly understands that dependent origination is like an illusion and devoid of signs, not arising spontaneously;

because this is accepted within the mind, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of the three delusions and suffering (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). As for the patience regarding the non-arising of the fruits of suffering in the three realms:

all such fruits of suffering arise from the afflictions and volitional seeking (*prārthanā*) that produce outflowing karma (*sāsrava-karma*); if there were no volitional seeking, suffering would not exist.
Because they are attained through causes, delusion and suffering do not arise; for these are accepted within the mind. How, then, are these three subsumed under those two truths?

Because [the dependent nature] arises from conditions, it is subsumed within the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature); because [the imagined nature] does not exist as such, it is subsumed within the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature); and because [the perfected nature] is the ultimate reality, all are subsumed within the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).

"These three" and below: the nine [categories] subsume the two truths. "One should know" and below: this is the explanation. The first two lines provide a general indication that the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) possesses all three [aspects], while the ultimate (*paramārtha*) possesses only one.

"The conventional" and below: this establishes the proof. Regarding the "nominal conventional": all phenomena are not real; they exist only as provisional names, for one falsely clings to them according to those names.
Regarding the "functional conventional": the three aggregates (*skandha*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) arise and cease in accordance with conditions.
Regarding "manifesting the conventional through transformation": it is as wisdom understands; because emotional attachments are forgotten, the principle becomes manifest.

First is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*); this is explained in terms of principle. "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the underlying principle, namely *tathatā* (suchness), which is the most supreme meaning.

This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive) compound. Second is the ultimate meaning as attainment; this is explained in terms of the fruit. "Attainment" (*prāpti*) refers to that which is realized and attained, namely the excellence of *nirvāṇa*.
The essence itself is the meaning; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Third is the ultimate as practice (*pratipatti-paramārtha*). This is explained in terms of its cause:

because correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) constitutes the practice, and the sublime noble path (*āryamārga*) constitutes the meaning; this is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound. These three types of ultimate reality are all subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Regarding these three natures, which wisdoms take them as their objects? (From "The perfected nature" down to: "The perfected nature is exclusively the domain of noble wisdom.
Thus, [the text] below begins with a question concerning the ten types of wisdom comprised by both ordinary beings and noble ones. Regarding "The imagined nature," it is explained:

the first phrase clarifies that the imagined nature is not the object of the two wisdoms; the second phrase provides the proof for this. From "Fools" onwards, it clarifies that the imagined nature may also be the object of the two [wisdoms].

The object-domain of the activity of wisdom is grasped as existent by the foolish, whereas the noble ones realize it to be non-existent; thus, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is common to the domains of both ordinary beings and noble ones.

The wisdom of ordinary beings spontaneously takes it as an object, while the wisdom of the noble ones realizes it to be like an illusion. The perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is the exclusive domain of the noble ones.
Among these three natures (*trisvabhāva*), how many are provisional and how many are real? [The text continues: "Because they are not established in dependence upon other conditions.

From "These three" onwards, there are eleven sections concerning the provisional and real status of the three natures. First, the question is raised. From "Universal imagination" (*parikalpita*) onwards, it is explained. First, the provisional and real status of universal imagination is clarified;

next, it is indicated that within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) there are both the provisional and the real. From "Aggregation" onwards, it is explained. "Aggregation" refers to the cause.

"Established by conditions" (pratītyasamutpanna) refers to the conventional nature of being established in dependence upon conditions. "Continuity" refers to the conventionality of continuity, because the preceding moment induces the subsequent one.
"States" refers to the conventionality of mutual dependence, because they are established in relation to others. All these are said to be conventional.

Mental factors, mental concomitants, and form all arise from conditions and are thus said to be substantially existent. [The phrase] "If there were not... serves to anticipate and address a potential objection: that the very essence of phenomena produced by conditions is...
It is like an illusion; how can it be said to be real? This is explained according to the text. This is stated as "real" based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Below, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is clarified as being exclusively real. The subsequent phrase provides the explanation: because its nature is fundamentally true and does not depend on other conditions.
Are these three [natures] different or not different? (Up to: "Because of the false attachment to the distinctness of the true meaning of dependent origination.

Regarding the section beginning with "These three": this concerns the identity or difference of the twelve [links] and the three natures. First, the question is raised; then, starting with "It should be explained," the explanation follows.

The first sentence generally clarifies that they are neither different nor non-different. Based on the "other-dependent" nature, there is false attachment, which constitutes the "imagined" nature; by realizing the emptiness of the other-dependent nature...

That is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Since these three have no separate essence, they are not different. However, because of the false attachment that distinguishes between dependent origination (*paratantra*) and the true meaning (*tathatā*), they are not non-different either.
The meanings and categories of these three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are boundless; fearing that excessive detail might weary the reader, I have briefly presented only the essential framework.

The phrase "Thus, below" refers to the extensive treatment and concludes this summary. Regarding the point here that the extensive explanation of the three natures universally encompasses all phenomena of both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and conventional (*saṃvṛti*) levels:
it was stated in the first question-and-answer section above that "the three natures are also not separate from consciousness. Now, since the three natures are explained extensively...
