The uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) of the Dharma-Truth is the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) that abandons the afflictions of the lower realm of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). 2. The liberation path (*vimuktimārga*) of the Dharma-Truth is the seeing aspect that realizes the principle of the Truth of Suffering.

Since it is thus for the Truth of Suffering, the same applies to the three truths of Origin, Cessation, and the Path. The uninterrupted paths abandon [the afflictions] through their seeing aspects, and the liberation paths realize them.
The same applies to partial realization (*prativedha*). As it is with the four [realizations] below, so it is with the four above. Regarding the "one hundred and twelve":
there are forty for the four truths of the desire realm; for each of the four truths of the two upper realms, anger is excluded, thus eight truths minus eight [afflictions].
Combined, this totals one hundred and twelve.
If one follows the principle of the extensive dissemination of the holy teachings (up to): "By these nine minds, it is called the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*). [The commentary states:

"Regarding 'suffering based on the lower' (*duḥkha-adharāśraya*), the nine minds are collectively synthesized. The first phrase provides a general heading based on the teachings regarding the nine minds. "This is" and below provide the explanation.
The first phrase, stating "based on the previous, twenty-six are separately established," refers precisely to the two types of sixteen [moments] mentioned previously.
This refers to the "lower" [stages] of the dharmas. It correctly clarifies the combined aspects (*saṃprayukta-lakṣaṇa*).

That is to say, among the first sixteen moments, the *dharma-kṣānti*, *dharma-jñāna*, *anvaya-kṣānti*, and *anvaya-jñāna* regarding suffering are combined into a single contemplation (*ekāvalokana*). Likewise, the four regarding origin, the four regarding cessation, and the four regarding the path are each combined into one, totaling four contemplations.
Within the latter sixteen moments, they are likewise combined into four contemplations. Altogether, this constitutes eight mental states (*citta*). Eight.
The corresponding *śamatha* is collectively described as one; these constitute the nine mental states. Although the lower [stages] are seen, they serve to resolve obstacles. Question:
In the Bodhisattva’s stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), where *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are practiced in union, why are there eight types of *vipaśyanā* while *śamatha* is only one?
The explanation for this is as stated in the text. This concludes with the following sentence.
The various aspects of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) are conventionally designated as "real" because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of conceptualization have already been truly abandoned.

[The commentary] below the section on the various aspects concludes by demonstrating that these aspects and the Path of Vision are merely conventional designations. The first phrase provides a direct indication. The two characters "conventionally designated" (*prajñapti*) directly extend from the section on the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) down to the phrase "latent tendencies.
This clarifies the meaning of "conventional designation": they are not real in the manner in which they are described; rather, they are "real" [only in a conventional sense].
The three subsequent lines provide further clarification, which may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the preceding True Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), it realizes the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*); because this is the primary and most excellent among the two [phases], the verse speaks of it specifically.
The preceding section [on] "Reality" (tattva) distinguishes the functions of the two paths. Regarding the fact that the verse specifically speaks of the nature of realization:
because wisdom has nothing whatsoever to be apprehended and is free from the characteristics of the duality of grasper and grasped, this is the most supreme.

The former, the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), is subsumed under fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); the latter, the semblance path of seeing (*pratibimba-darśanamārga*), is subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). Regarding the statement "the former, the true [path]," it is judged that these two types of wisdom each subsume their respective paths.

As for whether subsequently attained wisdom possesses two divisions, one interpretation holds that it possesses neither, because it is free from the dual grasping of subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*).

"Regarding 'All subsequent [cognitions] are inferior,' this turns to explain the subsequently attained cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). First, there is the interrogation. Regarding 'There is one interpretation,' etc., the three schools provide distinct explanations.

First is the initial interpretation: the first phrase establishes that both parts are non-existent; the second phrase explains this by establishing that it is because of being free from the two types of grasping (*grāhya-grāhaka*)."
One interpretation holds that because this wisdom perceives the existence of marks while not clinging to them, it is said to be "free from the two graspings.

To explain this further: the first phrase establishes the perception of the existence of marks, while the following two phrases establish the existence of perception; the subsequent portion [from "not clinging" onwards] explains the latter.

Synthesizing the sacred teachings: Question. Since there is already a subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), the sacred teachings should only state that it is free from the object of apprehension (*grāhya*);
they should not state that it is free from both apprehensions (*dvaya-grāha*). The explanation follows the text.
There is an interpretation that this wisdom possesses both parts (the aspect and the seeing). Because of this, the subsequent wisdom also possesses both parts. This is the third explanation.

The first phrase establishes that the aspect and the seeing exist together. The passage beginning with "This [wisdom]... provides the proof. The word "this" refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
This wisdom takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its objective basis (*ālambana-pratibimba*), transforming it into an aspect for contemplation; it cannot directly realize the essence of True Suchness.
Therefore, that which resembles the aspect of *tathatā* (suchness) is the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect); the mind that performs contemplation is the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect).

Furthermore, the passage below cites scriptural authority to extensively prove the existence of the objective and subjective aspects, as well as the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and the faculties and dispositions (*indriya* and *gotra*) of sentient beings—all of which constitute the *nimittabhāga*. That which is capable of discerning these constitutes the [subjective aspect].
Furthermore, that which is capable of observing is the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect). That which manifests as the body and the buddha-field is the semblance of form (*rūpa*).

The sublime Dharma that is taught is the semblance of sound (*śabda*). These semblances of form and sound constitute the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect). If [the text] does not proceed downward, it serves as a counter-illumination (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*), clarifying that by means of manifesting a body and teaching the Dharma, there is the manifestation of semblances of form and sound.

From "transforming form" (*rūpa-parāvṛtti*) downward, it addresses potential objections. Question: In the stage of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), one has already transformed the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Therefore, it does not manifest as something resembling matter (*rūpa*). In the commentary, the first phrase restates the question; the second phrase provides an illustrative clarification:

if the four aggregates were to transform their basis, there would likewise be no sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth. Since that is not the case, how could this be? As the Sūtra says: "By the cessation of this matter, one attains eternal matter," and so on. Furthermore, the section beginning with "If...
clarifies that because there is an object of cognition (*ālambana*), there is a manifestation resembling the objective realm (*viṣaya*). It transforms into a semblance of the objective realm.

That is to say, the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is the direct object-condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana*). The entity separate from its own nature is the objective essence (*bimba*), which is the indirect object-condition (*paramparā-ālambana*).

If [consciousness] does not transform into a semblance of the object, then there would be no direct object-condition. Since the direct condition would be absent, the indirect condition, being separate from it, would also necessarily not exist;
for we do not observe any phenomenon that possesses an indirect object-condition while lacking a direct object-condition. If there is an object-condition, it should...

"Transforming into something resembling the object. [The text] below "taking form (rūpa) as an object" restates the defense and refutes it by analogy. The defense states: "Although it does not transform into form, it is nonetheless able to take form as its object.
The refutation by analogy states: "Just as when the eye takes form as its object, it does not transform into something resembling sound; yet it should likewise be able to take sound as its object.

Furthermore, below the section on "taking as an object," it clarifies that there must be a resemblance to the object regarding the direct objective support (*ālambana*), yet no such thing exists. This refers to past and future objects, whose essence is not substantially real.

"Because there is no functioning by way of an object. This clarifies that there is no remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana*). If one does not admit that [consciousness] transforms into the semblance of an object, then there is also no immediate object-condition (*sākṣālambana*).
Since both of these are absent, it is said that "there should be no object-condition. The passage beginning with "By this... concludes [the argument].
These two—the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the six clear realizations (*abhisamaya*), up to the wisdom of the ultimate stage such as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).

Below this, it clarifies that the two paths subsume the six clear realizations. First, there is the inquiry. Below "the six clear realizations," there is a general heading followed by a detailed explanation of the characteristics of the six realizations.

First, under "contemplation" (*cintā*), the names are listed; then, under "the most [inferior]," the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is set forth. There are three grades of the wisdom of contemplation (*cintāmaya-prajñā*).

Excluding the middling and inferior grades, one takes the most superior grade. It is associated with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*), excluding the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*), because this [superior grade] is characterized by sharpness.

Its common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—namely, impermanence, suffering, and so forth—induce the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the others, because they are produced through reflection (*cintā*) and cultivated through meditation (*bhāvanā*).

Question: Reflection belongs exclusively to the stage of reflection; it should not be called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). Since "Heat" and the others belong to the stage of cultivation, they should be called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*). Why, then, is the opposite stated here? Answer:

Because this contemplation of the supreme function of all phenomena is the most powerful, it is specifically established as "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*). By specifying "inferior to Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) and so forth, it distinguishes Heat and the other stages from being clear realizations.
By first stating the name "two types of faith" and then explaining "having the lower as its object," its essence is identified as the pure faith in the Three Jewels. Question:

Faith is not subsumed under wisdom; why, then, is it designated by the term "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*)? The explanation states: Faith can assist contemplation so that one does not regress; thus, it is designated by the name "clear observation" (*abhisamaya*).

Below the section on the three types of morality, first the names are indicated, namely: "without inferiority. This provides the essential nature (*svabhāva*), which is the untainted pure morality (*anāsrava-śīla*).

Question: Morality is not subsumed under wisdom; why is it designated by the name "contemplation"? Explanation: Morality can remove defilements and increase clarity; it is likewise called "clear observation."
IV. Manifesting [Knowledge] (mngon par rtogs pa): First, the title is indicated; that is, "manifesting" (*abhisamaya*). Next, the essential nature is set forth:

it is the contemplation of non-conceptually established suchness (*anabhisaṃskṛta-tathatā*) by means of both the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms (*mūla-prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Because it encompasses both types of wisdom, it is called "all-aspect" (*sarvākāra*). V. Manifesting [Knowledge]: First, the title is indicated; that is, "manifesting. Next, the essential nature is set forth:

based on the aforementioned manifest realization, it subsequently arises as the cognition of conceptually established truths (*prajñapti-satya*); this is mundane knowledge with conceptual differentiation (*savikalpa-laukika-jñāna*).

Supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*). Because it universally takes both the ultimate and conventional truths as its objects, [the text] first indicates its name by stating "sixth, the ultimate" (*ṣaṣṭham paryavasānam*). Then, by stating "that which is exhausted," it defines its essential nature (*svabhāva*):
namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) produced by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) subsumes a portion of that fourth [path], yet because it is not of the same nature, they do not mutually subsume one another.

From "This true" below, the actual mutual subsumption is clarified. Regarding "the true path of seeing subsumes a small portion of that fourth": this is because the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is excluded.
Regarding "the path of seeing in its aspects (*ākāra-mārga*) subsumes a small portion of that fourth and fifth": within the fourth, the [wisdom of] the faculties (*indriya*) is excluded.

Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Among the five types of knowledge, mundane knowledge (*loka-jñāna*) is excluded. The two types of faith and precept (*śraddhā-vīrya*) can only assist contemplation (*vipaśyanā*);

they do not have wisdom as their essence and are not subsumed under the two paths. Contemplation through reflection (*cintā-vipaśyanā*) belongs to the causal stage; as long as habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not been extinguished, it remains at the level of the cause. Ultimate realization occurs in the fruit (*phala*), where truth is fully exhausted and delusions are completely eliminated;
thus, neither of these is subsumed [under the aforementioned categories].
When a Bodhisattva attains these two paths of vision (*darśana-mārga*), they are able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings until the end of the future.
[The text] below concludes by demonstrating the superior benefits of these two paths. "All are equal" refers to the three types of equality:
all sentient beings, all bodhisattvas, and all Tathāgatas are entirely equal. "Many hundreds of gates" means that one attains a hundred...
In samādhi, one perceives a hundred worlds, perceives a hundred Buddhas, enters a hundred dharma-gates, manifests a hundred bodies,
and transforms a hundred worlds, and so forth.
What are the characteristics of the subsequent stage of cultivation?

Next is the cultivation of the lower [stages]. This explains the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*). First, the inquiry: "Cultivation" refers to repeatedly taking the truth as an object of cognition.

The verse says: "Non-apprehension and inconceivability... (omitted)... because one abandons the two types of gross heaviness (*dausthulya*), one then realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*)."
The verse says: [The following] cites the verse as the answer.

The commentary states: From the time the Bodhisattva has arisen from the preceding path of vision (*darśanamārga*)—up until [the point where] their wondrous activity is difficult to fathom, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*).

The Commentary states: [This section] explains. First, it explains the initial phrase. The first phrase connects with what precedes; the following two phrases introduce what follows. Regarding "once the Path of Seeing has arisen":
there are three moments of mind within the stage of the Path of Seeing. The first moment of mind eliminates afflictions; this is the Path of Uninterrupted Activity (*ānantarya-mārga*).

The middle moment of mind realizes the principle; this is the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). The final moment of mind initiates cultivation; this is the Path of Progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*). This refers to the final moment of mind.

"Other hindrances" refers to the innate afflictive and cognitive hindrances. The latter two lines provide the direct explanation of the verse. Alternatively, "separated from the lower" provides another explanation;
both are as stated in the text.
This is supramundane non-conceptual wisdom (the portion up to here), which is precisely the non-conceptual wisdom within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
"Is this 'transcending the world'? This explains the second phrase. The first phrase cites the verse. The character "is" (shi) refers back to the aforementioned "unattainable and inconceivable.

The second phrase establishes the transcendental wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*). "Two take the transcending of the world" is a further explanation: first, it concerns the ability to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the mundane;

alternatively, "transcending the world" is explained again as referring to the realization of truth through the untainted (*anāsrava*). "This wisdom... is the final phrase, which provides the conclusion.

It possesses two meanings, whereas other forms of wisdom do not. This is because the essence of the various wisdoms such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth is not untainted (*anāsrava*), and because subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) cannot directly realize the principle (*tattva*).
Because one repeatedly cultivates this [wisdom], the two types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣthulya*) are abandoned; since it causes them to be eternally extinguished, it is said to be "abandonment."
"Repeatedly cultivating below" explains the third line. The first line restates the verse. Regarding "one who repeatedly cultivates this":

based on the aforementioned non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is able to abandon the two types of heavy impediments (*dauṣṭhulya*), one repeatedly contemplates the truth through frequent cultivation of the meditative practice. The two innate types [of impediments] are eliminated stage by stage.
Because the seeds of defilement are heavy impediments, there is a lack of functional capacity (*akarmanya*); whereas the seeds of wholesome, untainted [dharmas] are subtle and light.
Because it possesses capability, it is therefore contrary [to the former].
This is because it can abandon those two types of *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness), thereby realizing such a fruit of the twofold transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
"This can [lead] downward" explains the fourth line. The first line follows from what precedes it; the second line restates the verse.

Regarding "the basis," this first clarifies the basis of defilement and purity. The first phrase identifies the essence: the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), which refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

The second phrase clarifies the meaning of "basis": because it serves as the support for both defiled and pure phenomena. Regarding "defilement," this further explains the meanings of defilement and purity.

The two parts refer to the two aspects of defilement and purity. By the phrase "due to the power of cultivation" (*yō suika*), it reveals the merit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) through the force of practicing the causes.

By the phrase "due to the transformation" (*yō ten*), it clarifies that by transforming the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), one realizes the two fruits. By the phrase "establishing" (*seiritsu*), it concludes by indicating the intent of the treatise:

that the transformation of defilement into purity occurs entirely because of the *paratantra-svabhāva*. It is precisely for this reason that the intent of establishing *vijñapti-mātratā* in this treatise lies herein.
Alternatively, "basis" refers to the suchness of consciousness-only (up to the phrase) "is called the Dharma-body of the Great Muni.

Regarding the basis below: next, the basis for delusion and awakening is explained. The first phrase identifies the essence; it is the suchness of consciousness-only, meaning the essential nature of consciousness.
The second phrase clarifies the sense of being a basis, because it serves as the support for both delusion and awakening. As for the passage beginning with "fools," etc.:

Explanation of the transition: Delusion marks the beginning of birth and death; awakening brings the cessation of saṃsāra. From the phrase "By means of cultivation" (*yō su*) onwards, the text clarifies the power of the transformative basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) through the force of practicing the causes.

From the phrase "Just as" (*nyo su*) onwards, it addresses potential objections. Question: Since the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is inherently pure and fundamentally free from defilement, why is it said that being free from defilement constitutes the transformation of the basis?
The explanation for this follows the text. From the phrase "Although" (*su ni*) onwards, the question is raised: Regarding *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*...

Regarding the fruits and virtues of both [vehicles]: if one attains them, one attains them both. Why is it that here one specifically attains *nirvāṇa* but does not attain *bodhi*? The commentary explains:

the intent of the verse is merely to reveal the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*). This nature of consciousness-only is itself the *nirvāṇa* of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa*).
The subsequent section on the two vehicles clarifies that while both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna rely upon this, their designations differ. For the Śrāvaka, the ultimate is solitary liberation.
Liberated. The Tathāgata’s fruition is fulfilled and the myriad virtues are all perfected.
How is the twofold transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) realized? It is realized by virtue of this [fulfillment].

"How is it that [the transformation of the basis] is explained below? This introduces the detailed exposition of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). First, the inquiry is raised: "Regarding the ten [stages]," etc., which provides the general heading.
As for the "ten stages" (*daśabhūmi*), the first is the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), because it generates great joy by being able to benefit both oneself and others.
The phrase "the ten lower" follows. This is the detailed explanation. The first sentence indicates the name; the subsequent part explains the meaning.

Upon entering this stage, one possesses twenty-five samādhis, destroys the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), and manifests the twenty-five natures of the self (*ātman*). This nature of the self is precisely the nature of the sage (*ārya*).

The nature of the Sage is itself the Buddha-nature. It opens up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, gives rise to the true Middle Way, severs the delusions of ignorance, fully realizes the two kinds of emptiness, and manifests the two bodies of Truth and Response.
When conditions arise, the response is immediate; within a hundred Buddha-worlds, it manifests the bodies of the ten Dharma-realms.
Entering the ground of the wisdom of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, it is able to benefit both self and others. This is the true great celebration, which is called "Joy."

The Joyful Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Second is the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*), so called because it possesses pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and is far removed from the defilements (*mala*) of afflictions that give rise to even subtle transgressions.

The first phrase indicates the name; the subsequent part explains the meaning: it is free from the defilements of afflictions that cause one to violate the precepts through a mistaken mind, and so forth. It is pure.
Because of the fulfillment of pure precepts, there are three types of detachment: first, detachment from the cause, which refers to being free from the afflictions that give rise to transgressions;

second, detachment from the fruit and conduct, which refers to being free from the evil karma of violating the precepts; and third, detachment through antidotes, which refers to the fulfillment of pure precepts.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of delusions: coarse and subtle. There are also two kinds of transgressions: coarse and subtle. By means of coarse afflictions, [transgressions] are initiated.
Regarding intentional transgressions, because they arise from subtle afflictions, even mistaken transgressions do not occur; how much less so intentional ones?
Third, because the Ground of Radiant Light (*Prabhākārī*) accomplishes supreme meditative concentrations and great dhāraṇīs, it is able to emit the light of boundless, wondrous wisdom.

The first phrase indicates the name; the subsequent part explains its meaning. It is called "Luminous" (*Prabhākari*) because, through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, the illumination of the Dharma manifests.

This means that the three types of wisdom illuminate the teachings heard on that particular stage. Furthermore, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is that which brings forth [the light], while retention (*dhāraṇī*) is that which maintains it.

The light of wisdom is that which is produced and sustained by it. Because in the first two stages, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is able to give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and because wisdom is produced from concentration, [the fourth stage] is called the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
This is because one dwells in the most excellent factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), whereby the flames of wisdom increase as they burn away the fuel of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

The first phrase indicates the name; the following explains its meaning. Because it does not forget the fuel of the afflictions and the fire of wisdom is able to burn them, it is called the "Blazing Ground" (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi).
"Blazing" refers to the flame of bodhi-wisdom, which is to say, the fire of fundamental wisdom that can burn the fuel of the two obstacles: the obstacle of afflictions and the obstacle to knowledge.
As the fuel increases, the fire blazes;

because it becomes increasingly superior, the fifth stage, the Extremely Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), is so named because the two cognitions of the ultimate and the conventional are joined and brought into perfect correspondence, making it extremely difficult to conquer.

The first phrase indicates the name; the subsequent part explains the meaning. Because one attains supramundane wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), and is thus able to deliver those who are difficult to deliver, it is called "Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjaya*).

This is because the ultimate truth and conventional truth are non-contradictory, and this state is extremely difficult to surpass. Furthermore, the third ground shares commonalities with the worldly realms.

He had not yet attained liberation. Although he had emerged from the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), he was unable to conform to worldly conventions and remained largely stalled at the two extremes, making it difficult for him to transcend them.

Now, having attained supramundane realization while also being able to conform to worldly conventions, he has skillfully mastered the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*); with no contradiction between the ultimate and the conventional, he is able to overcome partiality and stagnation. Truly, he is difficult to surpass.

In the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), one dwells by means of the wisdom of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-jñāna*) which draws forth and brings into presence the most excellent non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) prajñā.

The first phrase indicates the name; the subsequent portion explains its meaning. Because one thoroughly penetrates dependent arising through conceptual wisdom (*savikalpa-jñāna*), it draws forth the manifestation of great non-conceptual wisdom.
By realizing suchness (*tathatā*)—which is neither defiled nor pure—it is called "Presence."

The seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṃgamā*), extends to the limit of effortful cultivation within the dwelling of signlessness (*animitta-vihāra*), as it transcends both the mundane and the supramundane paths of the two vehicles.

The first phrase indicates the name; the subsequent portion explains the meaning. One who skillfully cultivates the practice of signlessness reaches the culmination of effortful cultivation and is able to transcend both the mundane and the supramundane paths of the two vehicles.
First, by skillfully cultivating signlessness, one reaches the limit of signlessness; second, by [the perfection of] effort...
Because its activity reaches the ultimate limit and surpasses the three realms prior to it, it is called "Far-Going" (Dūraṅgama).
On the eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā), non-conceptual wisdom flows on spontaneously and continuously; because afflictions cannot disturb it, it is so named.

The first phrase indicates the name; the following explains its meaning. In the preceding six stages, one is moved by signs and activity. Although the seventh stage attains signlessness (*animitta*), one still abides in effortful application (*prayoga*).

In this present stage, the practice through maturation (*vipākacaryā*) is fully refined, causing the contemplation of signlessness to proceed spontaneously and uninterruptedly, such that it is unmoved by effortful application; therefore, it is named "Immovable" (*Acalā*).

The ninth stage, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*), is so named because one achieves the four subtle analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and is able to skillfully expound the Dharma throughout the ten directions.

The first phrase indicates the name; the subsequent part explains its meaning. Because one attains the power of non-obstruction in preaching the Dharma and accomplishes practices that benefit others, it is called "Excellent Intelligence.
Merely attaining unobstructed wisdom is not yet sufficient to be termed "excellent"; only when one preaches universally and benefits all universally is it designated as "excellent."

Regarding the phrase "The Great Cloud of Dharma-Wisdom of the Tenth Stage, the Cloud of Dharma" (up to the point) "...the body of dharma is filled with the coarseness [of afflictions] as vast as space":
the first clause provides the title; the subsequent portion explains the meaning. "The great cloud of dharma-wisdom" refers to the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its collective object.
"Multitude of virtues" refers to the gates of dhāraṇī, the gates of samādhi, and so forth. The metaphor of being "like water" means that wisdom is able to store them.
Those manifold virtues are like clouds containing water, for they possess the capacity to produce those supreme functions. "Shading" (*chāyana*) has the meaning of "separating" or "blocking.
It refers to the "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) that is as vast as space, namely a portion of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
This wisdom can obscure this coarseness—which is as expansive as space—so that it does not act as an obstruction. (From the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*)
It is called "cloud" (*megha*) because it is vast like a cloud, covering and obscuring the two obstacles of afflictions and ignorance—which are as expansive and boundless as space.
Furthermore, this wisdom fills the *dharmakāya*, which is the realized reality and the basis of reliance, just as a great cloud fills the void of space.
Thus, these ten stages (bhūmi) collectively encompass all conditioned phenomena; because they cause [virtues] to grow and develop, they are called "stages.

The passage beginning with "Thus, below" explains the meaning of "stage. First, it sets forth their essential nature: conditioned virtues refer to the two wisdoms of equality and discernment among the four wisdoms.
It specifies that they are not the other two because this refers exclusively to the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), whereas the other two exist in the resultant stage (*phala-bhūmi*).
Unconditioned merit refers to the suchness realized within each stage (*bhūmi*). From "with this" below, the meaning of the stages is explained.
A stage possesses the sense of being a support and that which causes growth; therefore, it is so named.
The ten superior practices are the ten [perfections], namely: the wisdom of enjoying the dharma-joy and the wisdom of maturing sentient beings.
Regarding the "ten superior" section below, this part is explained through eleven gates. First, the names and meanings of the ten practices: the first phrase indicates the names of the *pāramitās*.
Under the heading "Giving has," the meaning is explained individually. These ten superior practices each have three aspects in the first six, while the latter...
Each of these four has two aspects; although each is presented with two or three types to demonstrate their distinctions, every single one possesses both self-benefit and benefit for others.

Generosity of material goods (*āmiṣadāna*) refers to relinquishing the necessities of life with a mind free from defilement. Generosity of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*) refers to ceasing harm and rescuing others from trembling fear.
Generosity of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*) refers to teaching the Dharma, such as the sūtras and so forth, according to reality with a mind free from defilement. Discipline (*saṃvara*).
Discipline (*śīla*) refers to the quality of being able to distance oneself from unwholesome states and to maintain them through restraint.
Because it protects against all evil and unwholesome actions of body and speech, this is discipline. It establishes the latter two types of ethical discipline:

the discipline of gathering virtuous qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), because by protecting oneself, one is able to cultivate roots of virtue such as making offerings to the Buddhas, thereby enabling their realization.
All Buddha-dharmas, such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), constitute the morality of benefiting sentient beings.

By guarding oneself, one is able to benefit all sentient beings and cause them to cultivate all dharmas that are roots of virtue. Patience in enduring enmity and harm is patience toward living beings (*sattvākhānti*);
it is the cause for maturing sentient beings. Patience in accepting suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsanākhānti*) is patience toward dharmas (*dharmākhānti*); it is the cause for attaining Buddhahood. Cold...

Because one is able to endure all various forms of suffering, such as heat, hunger, thirst, mosquitoes, and gadflies, without ever turning back, this is the patience of discerning the Dharma (*dharmānupaśyanā-kṣānti*).
It serves as the basis for the two preceding types of patience, for it is capable of enduring the profound and vast Dharma.
Armor-like diligence (*saṃnāha-vīrya*) refers to the initial self-exhortation: "I shall perform such a task.
It is the vow that even if a glowing iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one's head, one would never retreat from what one has undertaken; this vow is itself the donning of armor.
The two types of diligence—gathering virtue and benefiting others—are explained as in the section on the precepts. By means of this personal diligence, one abides securely.
Dhyāna is practiced for the sake of attaining a pleasant abiding in the present life, because it brings about purification by eliminating conceit, views, and craving.
One induces dhyāna in order to manifest the eight supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), which are: (1) becoming minute; (2) becoming vast;
(3) becoming light; (4) mastery; (5) possessing sovereignty; (6) reaching distant places; (7) shaking the earth; and (8) acting according to one's will.

The meditative concentration that accomplishes what is to be done (*kāryakara-dhyāna*) is for the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings by being able to pacify the afflictions of fear, such as famine, pestilence, and epidemics.
Regarding the three aspects of wisdom (*prajñā*), they are as stated in the text. As for the two aspects of skillful means (*upāya*):
because of possessing great wisdom, one does not seek for oneself the virtues and so forth one performs, but dedicates them to sentient beings.

Therefore, because they do not abide in saṃsāra and possess great compassion, they do not abide in nirvāṇa for the sake of rescuing all classes of sentient beings and because they do not seek their own private benefit.
Because they abide in neither of these two, they are called "skillful. "Vow" (praṇidhāna) refers to a solemn oath:
first, the vow to accomplish the unsurpassed path of the Buddha; second, the vow to deliver infinite sentient beings. One initiates the *saṃnāha* (armor) at...
It begins with the resolve for enlightenment and concludes with great compassion rushing to the rescue in times of distress. "Power" refers to capability;
it arises from the power of analytical reflection (*cintā-maya-prajñā*), because through such reflection one correctly discerns what should and should not be done;

and it arises from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya-prajñā*), because the wholesome dharmas thus cultivated possess superior capability and are free from cowardice. Regarding the two types of wisdom: wisdom assists in the perfection of *prajñā*, thereby bringing the practice to fulfillment.
They experience the joy of awakening to the Dharma; furthermore, by means of this wisdom, they bring sentient beings to maturity and cause them as well to experience the joy of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
These ten natures have as their essence the virtues associated with all [perfections], beginning with generosity characterized by non-attachment.

Below this, the nature of the next ten practices is explained. These ten practices must necessarily be cultivated based upon the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, as well as the five object-specific mental factors among the wholesome mental concomitants (*kuśala-caitta*). Their respective meanings and characteristics are explained in accordance with the text. Regarding the final five, all are the discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*);
the treatise states that the sixth is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while the latter four are all subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Regarding "together with its retinue": when practicing generosity, non-attachment constitutes its essence;
it functions in conjunction with non-attachment, while other factors such as faith, shame, and so forth, constitute its retinue. As it is with generosity, so it is with the other practices as well.
Regarding these ten aspects, they must be analyzed through four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) for each of the seven excellences (*saptavidha-paramatā*).
Below these ten, the thirty superior aspects must likewise be subsumed within the seven excellences before one can reach the other shore (*pāramitā*).

This means that although all worldly beings and those of the two vehicles also practice giving and the other perfections, they merely attain the tainted results of gods and humans, as well as the fruits of the two vehicles, and do not reach the other shore.
"Abiding in the bodhisattva lineage" distinguishes this from the other four among the five lineages;
only those with the bodhisattva lineage proceed toward the ultimate fruit. "Relying on the great bodhicitta" is as stated in the sūtra:
It is said: Not generating the bodhicitta is an activity of Māra. One who feels compassion for all sentient beings does not practice giving and so forth without pitying sentient beings;
if one seeks only self-benefit and lacks the benefit of others, it is not a pāramitā.
Regarding the most excellent of activities: if one does not fully perform all virtuous deeds, then practices such as giving will be meager and insufficient.
It is for the sake of fulfilling the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi. That which is encompassed by signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*) means that the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty in essence.
Regarding dedication to bodhi: Question—Since it is said to be "dedication," how does this differ from relying upon the great bodhicitta?
Answer: One may generate the great resolve (*mahācitta*) without necessarily performing dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); yet here, dedication is invariably accompanied by the generation of the resolve.

Furthermore, the generation of the resolve precedes practice, whereas dedication follows practice. For one who is not interspersed with the two obstacles, there is no regret during the three periods [of past, present, and future].

Regret is affliction (*kleśa*), while failing to realize the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). As for the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), the first is...
1. Giving that is not a *pāramitā*: this refers to practicing giving while being devoid of the seven aspects. 2. A *pāramitā* that is not giving:
this refers to the ethical discipline (*śīla*) and other perfections accumulated based on the seven aspects. 3. That which is both giving and a *pāramitā*:
this refers to the practice of giving based on the seven aspects. 4. Neither giving nor a *pāramitā*: this refers to cultivating ethical discipline while being devoid of the seven aspects.
And so forth. Just as it is with these four propositions regarding the precepts, the same principle applies to the nine other sets of four propositions.
These consist of exactly ten, neither more nor less, because they correspond to the realization of the ten aspects of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which likewise neither increases nor decreases.

This refers only to the lower [stages], where there is an increase or decrease of forty [factors]. As for why these ten do not increase or decrease, it is because both the objects to be remedied (*pratipakṣya*) and the realizations (*adhigama*) each consist of ten.
Furthermore, as for why the first six do not increase or decrease—from this point onward—it should be understood as explained in detail in other treatises.
Furthermore, the preceding six [perfections] clarify non-increase and non-decrease by way of counteracting obstacles. To eliminate the six obstacles: generosity counteracts stinginess and greed;
ethical discipline counteracts transgression; patience counteracts malice; diligence counteracts laziness; meditative concentration counteracts distraction; and wisdom counteracts delusion.
The subsequent two phrases concern the maturation of practice through the two benefits (self and others). A detailed explanation is as found in the treatise. Six.

The nature of the perfections (*pāramitā*) consists of six aspects: relinquishing, guarding, enduring, exerting effort, mental abiding, and discernment. The characteristics of these six perfections are as follows:

the giving of what is to be abandoned, the basis, and the recipient is called *dāna* (generosity). Preventing the sevenfold [unwholesome] conduct is called *śīla* (ethical discipline). Not retaliating against being struck or reviled is called *kṣānti* (patience). Carrying out a task from beginning to end is called *vīrya* (diligence).
The four dhyānas and eight samādhis are called *dhyāna* (meditative concentration). Resolving disputes by distinguishing the grounds is called *prajñā* (wisdom). These are the six.

They transcend through mutual generation. This means: leaving the household life; upholding the precepts; enduring insults when encountered; being diligent after having endured; and, once diligent, disciplining the five faculties.
When the faculties are disciplined, one knows the dharma-realm. These six perfections are the remedies for stinginess, transgression, anger, and indolence.
Distraction and impaired wisdom. The fruits of the six perfections are: wealth, [virtue], physical strength, longevity, peace, and eloquence. Furthermore, the retribution of giving is wealth;

the retribution of ethical discipline is rebirth in the happy realms; the retribution of patience is physical beauty; the retribution of diligence is supernormal powers; the retribution of meditative concentration is rebirth in the heavens; and the retribution of wisdom is the destruction of afflictions.
Regarding the merits of the six perfections: giving is subsumed under the state of great wealth and mastery; ethical discipline is subsumed under [rebirth in] great families.
It is subsumed [by these]. Patience is subsumed by a great retinue of followers; diligence is subsumed by the accomplishment of great means of livelihood and activities;

meditative concentration is subsumed by freedom from illness and affliction, few desires, and so forth; wisdom is subsumed by intelligence regarding all fields of arts and sciences (*śilpa-vidyā-sthāna*).
Thus, there is no loss of the wish-fulfilling [nature]—the marks of the fulfillment of the six perfections—as seen in the case of King Śibi who sacrificed himself for the sake of a pigeon.
Dāna was perfected when King Samantaprabha renounced his kingdom; kṣānti was perfected when the seer Kṣāntivādin was dismembered by King Kali without resentment;
and vīrya was perfected when Prince Mahādāna drained the ocean and stood on one foot for seven days praising Buddha Puṣya.
Virtue was perfected when the śrāmaṇera Śaṅkha built a magpie’s nest upon his head; meditation was perfected when the minister Gopaka divided Jambudvīpa into seven parts to quell strife;
and wisdom was perfected [when he attained omniscience].
Furthermore, the three [perfections] beginning with generosity are the path to higher rebirth; for all bodhisattva paths, there are only these two.

Moreover, starting from generosity below, [the text] clarifies their non-increase and non-decrease according to these two paths: generosity brings about great wealth, meaning an abundance of riches and treasures;

ethical discipline brings about a great physical form, meaning a noble body; and patience brings about a retinue, meaning sentient beings who submit and follow one due to one's wealth and superior appearance.
That which involves a large retinue and is preeminent among the realms of existence is called the path of superior birth (*abhyudaya-mārga*).

That which, through diligent vigor, is able to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*), certainly brings forth supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), matures sentient beings, and through wisdom brings about realization and the accomplishment of the Buddha-dharma—possessing these three virtues—is called the path of definitive excellence (*naiḥśreyasa-mārga*).
The paths of all Bodhisattvas consist of only these two; if either one is lacking, [it is not a true Bodhisattva path].
Because the path is not yet accomplished.
Furthermore, the first three types [of giving] benefit sentient beings by permanently subduing and permanently extinguishing all afflictions.

Moreover, the preceding section on the "lower" [levels] clarifies the absence of increase or decrease in terms of the two benefits: the first three primarily benefit others by providing material wealth through generosity.
It benefits others. By maintaining the precepts as one's own guide, one does not harm or afflict them; through patience and non-opposition, one endures their provocations.

The subsequent three [perfections] benefit oneself. Question: Concentration can suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*), and wisdom can sever them; thus, they may both be designated by the name "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*).

Diligence (*vīrya*) is not so; how then is it called an "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*)? The commentary explains: Because one diligently cultivates practices that serve as antidotes to the afflictions (*kleśa*), it also receives the name "antidote.
Furthermore, because [the Bodhisattva] does not abide in *nirvāṇa* through giving and the other [perfections], by virtue of this, the first six [perfections] neither increase nor decrease.

Furthermore, from the perspective of the "lower" [section], non-increase and non-decrease are clarified by means of non-abiding. The first three [great compassion] benefit sentient beings and thus do not abide in nirvāṇa;
the latter three [great wisdom] sever all afflictions and thus do not abide in saṃsāra. Not abiding in these two extremes is the cause of nirvāṇa.
From this "lower" section, the conclusion is shown. The word "this" refers back to the preceding four sections.
The phrase "the latter four alone" means that these serve as aids to the former six; this should be understood as explained at length in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
The section beginning with "the latter four alone" clarifies that there are neither more nor fewer than these four. The first sentence provides a general heading, stating that the four aid the six.

The section beginning with "expedient means" (*upāya*) provides a specific explanation of the characteristics of the aids. The expedient means of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-upāya*) aids the subtle cause of giving by dedicating it toward a supreme fruit, thereby providing rescue and relief.
Skillful means involve enduring affliction without being disturbed by it, for the sake of rescuing others; they assist diligence through vows that seek higher goals and transform those below;
they assist meditative concentration through discernment and cultivation that transforms the inferior into the superior; and wisdom can induce supramundane insight.
Regarding the ten successive stages, this refers to the sequence from the preceding to the succeeding, up to the explanation of the general and specific names, as explained elsewhere.
Following the ten successive stages are the fifty practices in sequence. The first is explained by way of "inducing and maintaining. As for the preceding inducing the succeeding:

being without stinginess regarding one's person or possessions, one is then able to maintain the precepts; in order to protect the prohibitions and precepts, one then cultivates patience; having cultivated patience...
Having been humbled, one is able to arouse diligence; with fierce diligence, one is able to accomplish meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Having possessed meditative concentration, one is then able to arouse wisdom (*prajñā*) and attain supramundane wisdom. Possessing both wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*), one is able to arouse aspirational vows (*praṇidhāna*).
Having made the great vow, because one possesses the capacity and the capability, one is able to obtain the enjoyment of the Dharma-joy and the wisdom that matures sentient beings.
By successively maintaining the purity of what precedes, one upholds that wisdom;

only through such power of purification can one even maintain ethical discipline (*śīla*) so as to make giving pure. Next, the explanation is given according to the coarse and the subtle: the former is coarse, the latter...
Regarding "subtle": generosity is coarse, while maintaining ethical discipline (*śīla*) is subtle. In comparison to patience (*kṣānti*), ethical discipline is coarse and patience is subtle.

Thus, the distinction between coarse and subtle is explained through successive stages. Regarding the ease or difficulty of practice: following the preceding discussion of coarse and subtle, the degree of difficulty is further clarified.

Generosity is easy because it involves external wealth; maintaining ethical discipline is difficult because it requires restraining body and speech. In comparison to patience, however, ethical discipline is easier. Patience... [is difficult].

Because they belong to the mind, the ease or difficulty of their cultivation is discussed through successive transmission: because they are coarse, they are easy to cultivate; because they are subtle, they are difficult to cultivate.

The first eight are all termed "prior-prior," and the last eight are all termed "subsequent-subsequent. Because they are viewed in relation to positions separated by intervals, the repetition of the terms occurs.
The first is not termed "subsequent" because there is nothing prior to it; the tenth is not termed "prior" because there is nothing subsequent to it. The second is only...

The ninth is called "subsequent" (*paścima*), but it is not "subsequent-to-the-subsequent" (*paścāt-paścāt*), because there is no preceding stage in relation to it. The first is called only "prior" (*pūrva*), but it is not "prior-to-the-prior," because there is no subsequent stage in relation to it.
The first and second are called only "prior-to-the-prior," but are not called "subsequent-to-the-subsequent," because there is no prior stage in relation to them.
The ninth and tenth are called only "subsequent-to-the-subsequent," but are not called "prior-to-the-prior," because there is no subsequent stage in relation to them.
The remaining six among these are called both "the preceding" and "the succeeding. Individually, they are named giving (*dāna*) and so forth;

collectively, they are termed *pāramitā*, which here means "reaching the other shore. Since each and every practice accords with the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*), they all reach the other shore.
Regarding these ten cultivations, there are five types of cultivation (up to) as their characteristics are explained in detail in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises.
"These ten" [refers to] the completion of the cultivation of the sixty practices based on the five perfections. The first phrase provides a general heading for cultivating the ten based on the five;

the section beginning with "First, based on... provides a detailed explanation of the five cultivations. As for "cultivation of maintenance," it refers to abiding in the bodhisattva lineage and maintaining it.

One cultivates all the Buddha-dharmas. Cultivation through mental attention (*manasikāra*) refers to cultivating with a mind of resolute determination, aspiration, and delight, vowing to seek enlightenment.

Cultivation through intention (*āśaya*) refers to cultivating by giving rise to a great intention that is free from weariness or complacency, and by generating great compassion and pity for sentient beings, aspiring to deliver them across [to liberation]. Cultivation through skillful means (*upāya*)...
This refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) realizing that the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty in essence, thereby transforming subtle causes into great virtue.

Regarding "practicing with mastery": this means that Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), having partially realized the *dharmakāya*, are able to manifest bodies according to the various types of beings and thus attain mastery;
and having partially attained the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*), they are able to proclaim the Buddha-dharma and thus attain mastery. By means of this mastery...
The cultivation of giving and so forth is concluded as follows. Furthermore, these five cultivations correspond to the seven supreme factors mentioned previously;
among those seven, with the exception of the fourth, the activity, and the sixth, the dedication, the remaining ones correspond respectively to these five cultivations.
Regarding these ten [perfections] as being inclusive: for each one, when compared with the others in turn, four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be formulated.

Below this, regarding the inclusion of the seventy aspects of practice, first, within their own respective classes, they are mutually inclusive. The first proposition generally clarifies that each one universally includes all others because they are mutually concordant.
As the verse says: "The perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) includes the six; it provides the necessities of life... [and so forth].

Fear of [transgressing] the Dharma. Herein, the first, second, and third are called the "abiding in cultivation. Precept (*śīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*) each encompass six perfections (*pāramitā*), as explained in the section on the latter three trainings (*śikṣā*).
The remainder may be understood by analogy. Since the latter four are subsumed within the sixth, these ten dharmas are mutually integrated one with another.
Regarding the phrase "based on cultivation" (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), this clarifies their individual subsumption; based on each preceding stage, each subsequent stage is induced.

Regarding the principle: the preceding is subsumed by the succeeding, because the succeeding must necessarily depend on the preceding for its induction; however, the succeeding does not subsume the preceding, because the preceding does not depend on the succeeding for its induction.
According to the principle that the preceding stages are maintained and purified by depending on the succeeding, the succeeding necessarily subsumes the preceding.
Because that which follows can maintain the purity of what precedes it, the preceding does not subsume the subsequent; this is because the preceding cannot maintain the purity of what follows.

Regarding the four permutations of pure and mixed: first, there is that which is pure but not mixed, such as when one on the first stage practices giving exclusively without practicing the other nine perfections.
Second, there is that which is mixed but not pure, because one practices the remaining practices universally. Third, there is that which is both pure and mixed, [when] one practices correctly...

Because one practices generosity while simultaneously cultivating other practices, the fourth [category] is neither pure nor mixed; this is because, according to the door of distinct practices, one does not cultivate these ten.
Although there are actually ten, they are spoken of as six because the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) subsumes that which takes conventional reality as its object.
Regarding the phrase "This is truly [the section on] the lower": next are the sixty mutual inclusions. The two wisdoms—the fundamental and the subsequently attained—when combined, are said to be six;
when expanded, they become ten.
These ten fruits include four that are with outflows (up to the point where they either mutually support one another or are described as a combination of the two).

Regarding the ten [paths of action] below: eighty types of practice induce results. That is to say, the various practices cultivated during the stages of accumulation (*sambhāra*) and preparation (*prayoga*), which belong to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) level, induce four kinds of results—namely, outflow (*niṣyanda*), dominant (*adhipati*), ripening (*vipāka*), and human effort (*puruṣakāra*)—excluding the result of disconnection (*visamyoga*).

Because they are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), penetration (*prativedha*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) belong to the untainted stage. The various practices cultivated therein also result in four fruits:

namely, the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), and the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*). The fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) is excluded because it is exclusively tainted.

However, there is a lower-level objection that raises a difficulty: "In some places it is said that both tainted and untainted [actions] produce all five fruits; why is this? The answer is as follows:
Alternatively, the outflows (*āsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) may be explained as mutually supporting one another, or the two may be explained in combination.
As for the mutual inclusion of the ten [perfections] and the three trainings (*śikṣā*), they are profound and vast, as explained elsewhere.

Tenth, with the following: the ninety [precepts] subsume the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*). First, the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) is clarified. The first phrase provides a general heading; the subsequent section explains the three meanings in detail.

First, regarding the *pratimokṣa-saṃvara* (the morality of restraint): it includes both the formal ritual of the fourfold motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) and the gravity of the nature of the offenses, as well as those involving censure and reproach, without distinction.

One does not allow the life-preserving float of the precepts to be destroyed by the rākṣasas of craving and false views. Second, regarding the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*):
to feel weary of worldly life and renounce it for the sake of leaving home is *dāna*; to refrain from even the slightest transgression and resist the rākṣasas is *śīla*.
To endure being struck or reviled, and to remain patient amidst the eight winds, is *kṣānti* (patience). To guard the precepts so that no thought of transgression arises is *vīrya* (diligence).
To resolve firmly upon upholding the precepts, without doubt or wavering, is *dhyāna* (meditation).

To know that the precepts are the root of liberation, and not merely like those of cattle or dogs, is *prajñā* (wisdom). Although the six perfections are enumerated here, all six are fully realized within the precepts. III.

The precept of benefiting others is as stated in the text. Regarding which of the three types of precepts are shared with the two vehicles and which are not: the *saṃvara* (restraint) is shared, while the other two are not shared.
This is because the followers of the two vehicles cannot encompass the Buddha-dharma, nor can they extensively benefit sentient beings.

Furthermore, regarding the śrāvaka discipline, there is non-transgression through restraint and transgression through action; however, for the bodhisattva discipline, there may be either permission or prohibition.

Thus, while these are common [to both], they are also uncommon. Only the Buddha alone dwells in the pure precepts; these precepts are profoundly deep, and their essential nature accords with the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
It pervades the entire dharma-realm. This precept is vast;
the training in concentration has four [great] Mahāyāna luminous concentrations (samādhi), which induce karmic activities as explained in other passages.

The Training in Concentration (Samādhi-śikṣā), Part Two. Next, the training in concentration is explained. The first sentence provides a general heading; the following explains four meanings in detail. First, regarding the "concentration of luminosity":
because concentration can give rise to wisdom, it serves as that which illuminates. Based on principle, one establishes the teaching; based on the teaching, one practices.

Attaining the fruit by relying on practice—this is what is illuminated. Because the Light of Samādhi (Dīpaṃkara) is able to comprehend the causes and effects from beginning to end, it is called "Samādhi.

Second, regarding the King of Accumulating Merit (Puṇyasaṃbhārarāja) Samādhi: because samādhi is able to accumulate all practices, while sentient beings are bound and attached to worldly livelihoods and affairs and cannot abandon them even for a moment, the Bodhisattva discards these and enters dhyāna with a single mind; this is called *dāna*. If one does not maintain [this],...
Precepts: When practicing dhyāna, no discursive thoughts arise; entering dhyāna, miscellaneous thoughts do not stir, and one proceeds spontaneously without evil. This is *śīla*.
Restraining body and speech, enduring toil and suffering, subduing external objects so they do not cling, and suppressing internal sense-bases so they do not arise—this is *kṣānti*.

During the first, middle, and last watches of the night, mindfulness is maintained in succession; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the mind is always in samādhi, with no intervening thoughts.
Non-arising is diligence. To have the single mind abiding in concentration—neither distracted nor attached—is concentration.

If, with the single mind abiding in concentration, one can know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena and deeply discern the false and deceptive, this is wisdom (*prajñā*).

Because one can fully possess and give rise to all merits, compassion, and the burden-bearing [of others] within concentration, it is said that "the accumulation of merit is like a king. The latter two are like...

The text states: Regarding these four objects of focus (*ālambana*), they consist of taking the Mahāyāna Dharma as the object. As for the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), it refers to the wisdom that takes the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena as its object;
by means of "using one wedge to extract another," it eliminates all heavy obstructions (*dauṣṭhulya*) within the *ālayavijñāna*.
As for capability (*karmanya*), it refers to abiding in the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and taking birth according to one's wishes. It leads...
"Manifesting" means being able to bring forth unimpeded supernormal powers throughout all worlds.
"Performing actions" means being able to display transformations, coming and going, contracting and expanding, appearing or disappearing with sovereign mastery over what is done.

The training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*) has three parts: first, preparatory non-conceptual wisdom (*prayoga-nirvikalpa-prajñā*). Its objects of focus, modes of activity, and so forth are as explained elsewhere.

Below this, the training in wisdom is further elucidated. The first phrase provides a general heading; the subsequent section provides a detailed explanation of the three meanings. Regarding the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*’s explanation of preparatory wisdom:
it is the wisdom of investigation (*vitarka-prajñā*), and it is also the wisdom of aspiration (*ākāṅkṣā-prajñā*). As for the designation "preparatory" as "non-conceptual," it is due to...
This [wisdom] can produce non-conceptual wisdom and thus also receives this name. Fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) is the wisdom of direct realization; it is the wisdom of internal realization.
Preparatory application (*prayoga*) is the cause of this wisdom, while subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) is its fruit. Subsequently attained wisdom is the wisdom that initiates activity;
it is the wisdom that sustains and maintains. Although these three are designated by different names based on their initial and subsequent stages, their essence is one and the same.
First. Regarding "arising activity and maintaining": it refers to maintaining various meritorious qualities and initiating various transformative activities.

As for "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*): it means that with respect to the true meaning, one does not engage in divergent conceptualization, taking this as the intrinsic nature. As for "the basis" (*āśraya*):...
This refers to that which serves as the basis for non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Because the mind is not an object of discursive thought, it is not a basis that is "non-mind";

rather, because it belongs to the category of mind, it takes the mind as its cause. Through the power of repeated cultivation, one attains this state; thus, it is called "belonging to the category of mind.
This demonstrates that the mind which is the basis of wisdom transcends all conceptualization and discrimination, being the very cause [of such wisdom].
The "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to the hearing of the sounds and words of the Mahāyāna, which perfumes the mind;

it is the specific functional capacity induced by this, as well as such factors as correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*). The "object-condition" (*ālambana*) is the *tathatā* (suchness) manifested by the absence of intrinsic nature, which is liberated from the two extremes of superimposition and denial;
this is the objective sphere of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). As for its "aspect" (*ākāra*)...
That which proceeds in conformity with its object of focus is called an "aspect" (*ākāra*).
Non-conceptual wisdom proceeds in conformity with the object of *tathatā*, taking as its aspect the mental engagement that is free from all signs. This constitutes its aspect.
Thus, within the first two stages of the three types of wisdom (up to the point where both the preparatory and manifest seeds have been relinquished).

Below this, the seeds and manifestations of the three wisdoms are determined according to the stages. Regarding the first two stages—namely, the stage of equipment (*saṃbhāra*) and the stage of application (*prayoga*)—the seeds of all three wisdoms exist therein, because they possess the innate (*dharmatā*) untainted seeds; however, as for the manifest [wisdom], it is only...
Regarding the wisdom of application (*prayoga-prajñā*): because one has not yet realized *tathatā*, there is no fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) nor the two subsequent wisdoms (*pṛṣṭha-jñāna*).

As for the statement that during the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*) only the fundamental and subsequent wisdoms manifest, this is because, upon first realizing *tathatā* in the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the wisdom of application does not yet exist.

Within the Stage of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), there are two distinct meanings: from the beginning of the Path of Seeing up through the seven stages (*bhūmi*), both seeds and manifestations [of these wisdoms] exist.

All [stages] possess three [paths]. This is because from the seventh stage downward, within each respective level, there exist the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

As for why only two [paths] are manifest from the eighth stage onward, it is because they proceed through cultivation without effort (*anābhoga*) and without relying on preparatory application (*prayoga*).
If that is so, by what wisdom does one advance toward the subsequent stages? The explanation states: one employs the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
One performs uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) contemplation because one proceeds spontaneously into subsequent stages. Regarding "both the manifest and the seeds in the ultimate stage":

this refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) following the vajra-path, at which point both the seeds of preparatory application (*prayoga*) and [the seeds of] the [uncontaminated state] are abandoned.

If categorized by their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), ethical discipline (*śīla*) comprises only ethical discipline; concentration (*samādhi*) comprises meditative absorption (*dhyāna*); and wisdom (*prajñā*) comprises the final five [perfections].

Now, to clarify the mutual inclusion (*saṃgraha*) from the perspective of the lower [categories]: herein, there are four types of meaning regarding mutual inclusion. The first is inclusion by intrinsic nature.

They do not include the accompanying factors that coexist with them, but rather speak of each according to its essential nature; therefore, it is said that "precept (śīla) encompasses only precept," and so forth.
Second, if they were to encompass one another along with their accompanying factors, then these three trainings and the ten practices would each encompass all of them.
Third, regarding their mutual inclusion according to their specific functions: precept encompasses the first three [perfections], while giving is the provision for precept.
Morality is the essential nature itself, for patience is a quality that belongs to the retinue of morality. Regarding the inclusion of the characteristics according to their secondary aspects:

morality includes the first four; the first three are as previously explained, with the addition of including diligence. This is because through the power of diligence, one guards against and prevents what is non-virtuous, thereby purifying morality.
The mutual inclusion between meditative concentration and wisdom is as stated in the text.
Regarding these ten stages, all five [stages] possess them; whether manifest or as seeds, they are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).

Below this, "ten by ten" refers to the stages of cultivation where both tainted and untainted [factors] are present. The first phrase indicates that all five stages cultivate the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), and the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*) is most prominent.
As the Sūtra says: "In the first stage, the cultivation of generosity (*dāna*) is preeminent," and so on, up to...
In the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), the cultivation of wisdom (*jñāna*) is preeminent; this is its most manifest meaning.

Nevertheless, from the first stage downward, these ten practices (*daśa-caryā*)—both in their seeds (*bīja*) and their manifestations (*abhinirvṛtti*)—are shown to be categorized across five stages as being either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).

If one considers the stages of the equipment (*saṃbhāra*) and the application (*prayoga*), the superior practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment have seeds that are both with and without outflows, while their manifestations are exclusively with outflows. [However,] the seeds are also without outflows.
"Outflow" (*āsrava*) here refers to the naturally existing untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*). This applies to all untainted seeds in subsequent stages as well.
Regarding the bodhisattva of gradual enlightenment, the superior practices cultivated during the first two stages involve both tainted and untainted seeds and manifestations.

As for those manifestations that are untainted, this refers to the cultivation of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*), by which one has already suppressed the manifest delusions of conceptual discrimination.
Arisen afflictions are associated with the superior practice that accords with contemplation because it penetrates the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
Nevertheless, since the co-emergent (*sahaja*) and manifestly active afflictions have not yet been permanently suppressed, it also penetrates the outflow-possessing (*sāsrava*).

Within the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*), the present [practice] is exclusively outflow-free because the seeds of the two obstacles of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) have already been severed. Within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), there are further divided into two stages. Seven.

Prior to the [eighth] stage, one alternates between entering and emerging from the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena, because the cultivated superior practices must pertain to both their seeds and their manifestations.
From the eighth stage onward, the manifestations are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), because from the stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā*) onwards, they are purely untainted.

As for the seeds that are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*): because the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) has not yet been exhausted, both the seeds and the manifest [states] in the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*) are without outflows (*anāsrava*).

These ten [factors] in the stage of a cause (*hetu-avasthā*) have three types of names: [they are called "impure"] because they include the seeds of afflictions (*kleśa*) and thus are not yet ultimate.
These ten [stages] are alternative names for the eleven stages of the causal path (*hetu-bhūmi*). The Sanskrit term is *asaṃkhyeya*, which here means "incalculable.
Regarding the "first incalculable eon" (*kalpa-asaṃkhyeya*): this is stated provisionally with reference to the causal stage of Śākyamuni.

From the time of the ancient Śākya until the Buddha Śikhin, he encountered seventy-five thousand Buddhas; at that time, he did not yet know that he would become a Buddha. This constitutes the first *asaṃkhyeya*.

*Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*. Regarding the passage "At that time" and below, this explains the names and their meanings. At that time, although the practices are subtle, the afflictions are strong, and one has not yet attained the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state;
relying on the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one cultivates various superior practices. These possess only the name of "reaching the other shore" (*pāramitā*).

In terms of the stages (*bhūmi*), they belong to the provisions (*sambhāra*) and the preparatory application (*prayoga*). As for the second incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), it spans from the Buddha Śikhin to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. In the interim...
He encountered seventy-six thousand Buddhas. At that time, he knew for himself that he would become a Buddha, yet he did not speak of this to others.
This was the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa. At that stage, the names are explained according to their proximate meaning:

because his practice increases and inspires those who submit to him, yet what he cultivates has not yet attained the state of effortlessness (anābhoga), it is called the "near" (*pratyupasthita*) pāramitā. In terms of the stages (*avasthā*), this corresponds to the Path of Application (*prayogamārga*).
Upon reaching [the stage of] cultivation prior to the seventh bhūmi, during the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa—spanning from Dīpaṃkara Buddha to Vipaśyin Buddha—one encounters seventy-seven thousand Buddhas.
At that time, one knows for oneself that one will become a Buddha and also declares it to others, saying:
"This is the third asaṃkhyeya. At this point, the etymology and great significance of the term "Great" (Mahā) are explained. At that time...
The power of practice increases further because it is purely untainted (*anāsrava*); since afflictions never again arise, it is called the "Great Pāramitā.
In terms of stages, this refers to the eighth bhūmi and above. It is still "lower" than the ultimate state, as it is distinguished from final consummation;
for both the seeds and manifestations of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) still persist, and thus it is not yet ultimate.
These ten categories of meaning are infinite in their distinctions, yet they are all subsumed within the ten *pāramitās*.
