From "these ten" below, the extensive is indicated by summarizing the concise. It is said that "one" refers to the mutual increase of each stage (*bhūmi*), while "ten" refers to the categorization of the types of each practice (*caryā*).

Regarding the ten layers of obstructions: first is the obstruction of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*). [This continues] until: "Therefore, there is no fault of the two natures being established simultaneously.

Below this, the ten layers of obstructions are explained. The first two lines state the general and specific names; the phrase "the two" and so forth indicates the essential nature of the obstructions.

That is to say, this obstruction of the nature of an ordinary being is established based on the seeds of afflictions (*kleśa*) and objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) that are conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*). One abandons these two.

[By] "seed," one immediately attains the nature of an ārya. Second, "the two vehicles" and below clarifies that the afflictions severed by the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ in being either single or multiple.
In the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the two vehicles sever only the single category of afflictions (*kleśa*) and are thus said to attain the nature of an ārya.

In the path of seeing, the Bodhisattva severs both afflictions (*kleśa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and is thus said to attain the nature of an ārya. Second, "the two truths" and below addresses an objection. The difficulty is raised: "If it is the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*)..."

[The seeds] are abandoned prior to the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), and the untainted fruit arises; thus, there is no fault of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) and a noble one (ārya) simultaneously possessing [the seeds].
Now, since it is based on the abandonment of the seeds through the path of seeing, there would be the simultaneous presence of the seeds of affliction within the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga).

In that case, the path of seeing would be the noble one, while the seeds of affliction would be the ordinary person—this results in the fault of an ordinary person and a noble one being simultaneously established. In the commentary, first the path of seeing is explained directly by means of the dharmas.

[The state of being] manifest. That seed is not established. "Just as light appears" and so forth; next, an analogy is raised to clarify this: for example, when one says "light arises and darkness ceases," it does not preclude that the arising of light does not coexist with darkness.
Or when one says "the rise and fall of a scale," it does not preclude that at the very moment it rises, it is also falling. Therefore, [the text] applies this to the dharma:
when the noble stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) manifests, the seeds of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) necessarily...
It is not established. Therefore, there is no fault of both natures being established simultaneously.

At the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), the seeds of the afflictions have already ceased, and one realizes the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) pertaining to that category.

"Immediately following" (*anantara*) below [in the text] distinguishes between the two paths. First, the question is posed. "The severing of afflictions" (*kleśa-prahāṇa*) below provides the explanation.

It is due to two meanings that, having already given rise to the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), one subsequently gives rise to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). First, the intention of the path of immediate succession is the severing of afflictions, while the intention of the path of liberation is the realization of the principle (*tattva*).
Second, the path of immediate succession severs the seeds of those afflictions, while the path of liberation abandons their coarse residues (*dauṣṭhulya*). "Immediately following" below...

Addressing the objection: It is asked, "What is the difference between the seeds of affliction (*kleśa-bīja*) and the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*), such that they are severed by two distinct paths? The explanation states:

Although the seeds of affliction no longer exist at the moment of arising in the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*), the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is established for the purpose of abandoning the state of unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*) and realizing the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, the two paths are distinguished. In the text, the terms "seeds," "heavy residues," and "state of unserviceability" appear; these are discussed further in the subsequent passage.
Furthermore, regarding the term "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*), in what sense is this name established? The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

"That which is comprised within the category of the wholesome and possesses the capacity for [spiritual] fitness, as well as that which is comprised within the category of the neutral and that which is comprised within the category of the defiled, are all termed 'seeds' (*bīja*).
That which is comprised within the category of the defiled and that which is comprised within the category of the neutral are termed 'dysfunction' (*dausthulya*). There is no... [end of fragment].
Because it is capable [of producing results]. If it is comprised within the category of defilement (*kliṣṭa*), it is called only a latent tendency (*anuśaya*).

Furthermore, among all the seeds within the various personal existences (*ātmabhāva*), those comprised within the category of affliction (*kleśa*) are called both "heavy dysfunction" (*dauṣṭhulya*) and "latent tendency.
Those comprised within the category of maturation (*vipāka*) and other neutral (*avyākṛta*) categories are called only "heavy dysfunction," not "latent tendency."

Sleep (*middha*), if it is comprised within the category of wholesome factors such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, is not called "heaviness" (*dausthulya*), nor is it a "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*).
Why is this? Because when these factors arise, the basis—the personal continuum (*ātmabhāva*)—possesses only capability (*karmanyatā*) and not incapability.
Therefore, because the entire basis is accompanied by heaviness and produced from heaviness, [it is not itself heaviness].
Because they are coarse and heavy by nature, what is now called the "uninterrupted seed" refers to the defiled category among the seeds of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

As for "liberation through the abandonment of coarse heaviness," this refers to the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) within innate coarse heaviness, as it is subsumed under the same class as the defiled category.
Since these two differ in their degree of gravity, the former is heavy and the latter is light.

"Coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) refers to the state of being unserviceable (*akarmanyatā*). Regarding the term "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*) in the subsequent text, these belong exclusively to the defiled category;
although they are abandoned upon the arising of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), the same principle should be applied to explain the later mention of "coarseness."

Although it appears below, this correctly clarifies that which is abandoned in the first bhūmi. Question: Since the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) also abandons afflictions, as well as the various karmas leading to the miserable destinies (*apāya*) and the various fruits of those miserable destinies, why is it said here only that one abandons the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
In the explanation, the first phrase restates the question. Then, from "Now," the explanation states: Afflictions are the root of the two kinds [of results], namely karma and its fruit. Because...
The root subsumes the branches; it also eliminates karmic results, though this is merely omitted in the text.

From the phrase "By this" onwards, it follows from the preceding point that both are eliminated, and thus states that on the first bhūmi, one universally eliminates the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of two delusions (*moha*) as well as their underlying latencies (*dausthulya*). Regarding the phrase "First, grasping... and so forth, it explains the characteristics of these two delusions.
The delusion of clinging to self and phenomena refers to the conceptualized afflictive and cognitive obstructions, which is precisely the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

Obstruction. Second is the delusion regarding the afflictions of the miserable realms (*durgati-saṃkleśa-moha*). This refers to various karmas and their fruits. It should be understood that [the text] asks below: "Delusion is a portion of ignorance (*moha*);
grasping at self and phenomena can be called delusion. However, karma and its fruits are not subsumed under the category of ignorance;

why are they also called delusion? The explanation states: "The karma and fruits of the miserable realms belong to the class of delusion; they are collectively designated as 'delusion. Subsequent instances should be understood according to this principle."

Regarding the nine subsequent stages (*bhūmi*), any transgressions of the three types of action (*trikarma*) and so forth all belong to the category of delusion (*moha*); they are likewise described as "delusion. Therefore, it is said that for the subsequent stages, one should follow this explanation.

Alternatively, there is another interpretation: when it is said in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) that two types of delusion are abandoned, these refer to the two forms of ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with sharp and dull obstacles.
The "sharp" refers to the five views (*pañcadṛṣṭi*), and the "dull" refers to craving (*rāga*) and so forth. However, [these are] merely two...
Ignorance (*avidyā*) does not include the fruits of karma; thus, the term "dysfunction" (*dausthulya*) reveals the seeds of those two delusions. Furthermore, there is another interpretation:
the term "dysfunction" may not refer to seeds, but rather to the state of unfitness (*akarmanyatā*) arising from those two delusions.
Question: Since "seeds" and "dysfunction" share the same meaning, why is it said that these are not seeds but rather dysfunctions? For example...

[The text] enters the superior [section]. An example is raised to explain: for instance, the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) abandoned by the two mindless absorptions (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti* and *nirodha-samāpatti*) is neither present nor a seed, yet it is termed "dysfunction" (*dausthulya*).
What is abandoned here is likewise not a seed, yet it is termed "dysfunction"; that is, the state of being unserviceable (*akarmanyatā*).
This applies analogously to all cases where the [defilements] of the nine stages are abandoned.
Although what is abandoned at the first stage (*bhūmi*) actually pertains to both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), it is not mentioned here because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are not abandoned.

Although [the text] from "although at the first [stage]" onwards distinguishes [the stages] by means of the two obstacles, first it distinguishes them by means of the two obstacles. Question: Bodhisattvas at the first stage abandon both obstacles;
to which category does the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) belong? In the explanation, the first phrase restates the question. Next...
The phrasing is precise and concise. Regarding the "obstruction of the nature of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*), the intent is to take up the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).

The ten [verses] and the two subsequent lines explain that the ignorance which constitutes the obstruction to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) is precisely this [ignorance], because the objects of knowledge are not defiled. Conversely, it excludes the afflictive obstructions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) because they are defiled.
Question: Why is the severing of the afflictive obstructions not mentioned? Explanation: This [obstruction] is common to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Because they are abandoned together, they are not mentioned [separately]. Next, regarding the distinction between what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):

furthermore, the ten non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*) ignorance refers exclusively to the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) abandoned through cultivation in the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), and does not refer to the conceptualized [ignorance] abandoned through seeing.

Question: In this stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one also suppresses the afflictions (*kleśa*) and abandons their coarse latencies (*dauṣṭhulya*). Why [is it said that the non-afflicted ignorance is abandoned]?

Does this refer only to the abandonment of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)? The first sentence of the commentary restates the question. Regarding the phrase "but not," the explanation states:

Abandoning the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is not the primary intent of the ten stages; therefore, the abandonment of the latent tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśānuśaya*) is not mentioned. This is because the primary intent lies solely in abandoning the cognitive obscurations.
As for the previously distinguished seeds of conceptualized afflictions, although the Bodhisattva abandons them, they differ from those of the two vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas).

They are not mentioned because they have already been abandoned together [with the afflictions]. This excludes the seeds of innate (*sahaja*) afflictions; they are not mentioned because their seeds are retained to assist in the arising [of future existence] and thus are not yet severed.
In reality, within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of the first ground, these are only suddenly severed at the point when one is about to attain Buddhahood.

In reality, this clarifies that each stage (*bhūmi*) eliminates obstacles at both its beginning and its end. Question: Since it is stated that the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the ten stages is explained as being abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), then the first stage must also eliminate a portion of innate (*sahaja*) ignorance.

Why, then, was it previously stated that the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) eliminated in the first stage is that which arises from discrimination (*vikalpa-utpanna*)? Answer: In principle, it is indeed true that the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) also eliminates [obstacles]. However, the previous statement referred to the specific obstacle of the nature of an ordinary person, which is primarily characterized by conceptual discrimination. This does not preclude the fact that other portions of innate ignorance are also eliminated during the process of cultivation. Thus, while the first stage is designated for the elimination of the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary person, it simultaneously effects the abandonment of certain aspects of innate ignorance. Therefore, there is no contradiction between these two explanations.

Regarding the statement that "one portion of the innate [afflictions] is now said to be abandoned through the abandonment of the conceptual," this refers specifically to what is abandoned at the very beginning.

In the first stage (*bhūmi*), there are three moments of mind: the initial moment of mind abandons the conceptual, while the subsequent moments abandon the innate. It should be understood by analogy that in the subsequent stages, two moments of mind are distinguished according to their coarseness and subtlety.
Question: Why is it that after the afflictions have already been abandoned by the initial moment of mind, they are abandoned again by the subsequent moments?

Yes. In the section following "the completion of the stages" (*bhūmi-paripūri*) within the *Śāstra*, the reason why the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) are abandoned upon entering the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) is set forth.

"Completion of the stage" refers to the final moment of mind (*citta*) in the first stage. The obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) that ought to be abandoned are as follows: the obstacle of misconduct (*mithyāpratipatti-āvaraṇa*) is the obstacle to be abandoned in the second stage. Regarding the three periods of the path:

the first period is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), which abandons the delusions of the fundamental stage; the middle period is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), which realizes the reality (*tattva*) of the fundamental stage; and the final period is the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

Regarding the advancement on the path: one advances by severing the afflictions of the subsequent stage. If one did not advance in severance at the final moment of mind of the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), then there would be no distinction between the three phases of the path—beginning, middle, and end.
Since these stages are indeed differentiated, we know that one also severs a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) afflictions.

Thus, as one enters the initial moment of mind of the second stage immediately following the final moment of mind of the first stage, it follows that what was severed at the final moment of the first stage is precisely [the affliction] of the second...

The obstacles severed by the initial mind of the first stage (*bhūmi*) are of only one kind; they are merely divided into two based on their coarseness and subtlety. Therefore, it says "below" to cite scriptural evidence.
First, it proves the severance of the objects of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); this refers to the fourth and fifth of the six types of clear observation (*abhisamaya*).
"Leaving behind afflictions below" clarifies the reason why the afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are not severed.

The second is the obstacle of wrong conduct (*mithyā-pratipatti-āvaraṇa*), which refers to [the portion of] the cognitive obstacle (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) consisting of either the delusion that initiates karma or the delusion regarding the non-understanding of karma.

Regarding the first phrase, it designates the name; regarding the phrase "which refers to," it reveals the essential nature of the obstacle. "Wrong conduct" (*mithyā-pratipatti*) refers to the defiled mind that violates the precepts;
because it obscures pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), it is called an "obstacle. Furthermore, it includes the physical and verbal transgressions that arise based on this obstacle.
Regarding "the karma produced by the mind": the following section clarifies the characteristics of these hindrances.

From the phrase "by this" onwards, it follows that because both [types of hindrance] are abandoned together, the second bhūmi is said to universally abandon the two delusions in their active manifestation (*paryavasthāna*), as well as their corresponding latencies (*dausthulya*). The subsequent section explains the characteristics of these two delusions:

the first delusion is the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its essence; the second delusion is the transgression of the three types of action (*karmapatha*).
It arises based on ignorance; it is a category of delusion, and is generally termed "delusion. Alternatively, it is merely inferior.
Another interpretation is that it is the ignorance capable of producing karma, because one does not understand that the nature of karma is empty.

The third is the obstacle of dullness (*mṛdv-indriyatva-āvaraṇa*), which refers to that within the cognitive obstacles (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) which obstructs the *dhāraṇī* [of] the wisdoms of hearing and reflection.
Regarding "the third obstacle of dullness": the first phrase provides the name; "which refers to" and so forth indicates the essential nature of the obstacle.

It is called "dullness" because it causes the loss of the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. "That obstacle" and so forth clarifies its characteristics; here it is stated generally that it obstructs all three wisdoms.

Within the two delusions of the lower [realm], they are distinguished individually as obstacles. From "By this, the lower... onwards, it follows the preceding statement regarding the abandonment of these two delusions.

First, "Desire for the lower... explains the characteristics of these two delusions: first, desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*), which can obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Question: Above, the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) were indicated; why is the affliction of desire-attachment mentioned here? Answer: It is explained that in former times, those obstacles were frequently associated with desire-attachment.

They arise together. In terms of the meaning of mutual dependence, they are called the delusion of desire and greed (*kāmarāga-moha*). They obstruct the abandonment of desire and its suppression, because desire depends on the obstruction for its manifestation.

Second is the delusion regarding hearing and retention (*śrutadhara-moha*). "Retention" refers to reflection (*cintā*). There are four kinds of retention: retention of the Dharma (*dharma-dhāraṇī*), retention of the meaning (*artha-dhāraṇī*), retention of mantras (*vidyā-dhāraṇī*), and the retention that attains patience (*kṣānti-dhāraṇī*). Delusion universally obstructs these.

The fourth is the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle afflictions (*sūkṣmakleśa-samudācāra-āvaraṇa*). [This continues] until: "thereby one is able to permanently destroy this view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the fourth subtle": the first clause indicates the name; the phrase "that which is" (*yad etat*) below it reveals the substance of the obstacle.

This obstacle is comprised of the innate (*sahaja*) view of a self and other afflictions associated with the sixth consciousness. The final section below explains "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) by way of three meanings.
The "lowest grade" refers to its being obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*). "Without deliberate attention" means it arises spontaneously.

"Distantly following what is currently active" means it has followed and persisted with the body since beginningless time. That which obstructs the lower [stages] clarifies the characteristics of the obstruction. Regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*):
the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) obstructs the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), such that one is unable to contemplate the impurity of the body and so forth. Question:
The previous section spoke of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). Why, then, does this section speak of afflictions (*kleśa*)? The commentary explains:
Because in former times those obstacles arose with the same substance as the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they were designated by the name "affliction" based on the sense of mutual dependence.

When the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) correctly sever the objects of knowledge, these views of self and so forth also cease to function forever. [Question: Why is it that [the afflictions] do not [arise] in the first, second, and third stages?
"It can be severed. This is explained according to the text.
How is it known that this [view] co-exists with the sixth consciousness? (Up to: "Therefore, this is associated only with the sixth [consciousness].

How is it known? Below, there is a distinction made to exclude [others]. First, the question is asked: Both the sixth and seventh consciousnesses possess the innate view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). By what principle...
It is known with certainty that [this view] is associated exclusively with the sixth [consciousness]. Regarding the seventh [consciousness], the commentary explains:

because the seventh consciousness’s view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is contrary to the nature of pure outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states, it can still arise prior to the seven stages (*bhūmi*) when they have not yet become purely outflow-free;
it only ceases forever from the eighth stage onward. This view of self serves as the support for self-love (*ātma-sneha*) and so forth; thus, at the completion of the seventh stage...
Because the mind is suddenly subdued at that point. Furthermore, the sixth consciousness is associated with coarseness, while the seventh is associated with subtlety;
that which is coarse is subdued first, and that which is subtle is subdued later. Therefore, the afflictions subdued in these four stages are associated exclusively with the sixth consciousness.
The phrase "the view of a self" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth also includes [afflictions] from beginningless time; thus, the two types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) will also never again arise.

Below the term "view of a self," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is explained. This term "and so forth" also includes the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), namely craving for meditative absorption (*samādhi-tṛṣṇā*) and craving for the Dharma (*dharma-tṛṣṇā*).

These two cravings—craving for absorption and craving for the Dharma—are names for afflictions because they arise simultaneously with two types of delusion (*moha*); therefore, they are included herein.

"Known objects. From "By this... below, it follows that the two delusions are abandoned as previously described: first, the delusion of craving for meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), which is the object of knowledge associated with craving for concentration;
second, the delusion of craving for phenomena (*dharma*), which is the object of knowledge associated with craving for the teachings.

Because these two delusions, which are subsumed under the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), are abandoned, the two types of craving belonging to the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) also cease to function forever.
Fifth, the obstacle to parinirvāṇa in the Lesser Vehicle (extends to): "those who delight in nirvāṇa herein. Regarding "fifth, in the Lesser": the first phrase provides the name;
"that which is inferior" indicates the substance of the obstacle. To loathe suffering and rejoice in tranquility is identical in meaning to the Two Vehicles.

Not having yet forgotten this longing and loathing, the dichotomy of grasping and rejecting stands opposed. "That obstacle to the inferior" clarifies the characteristics of the obstacle; it is able to obstruct the True [Dharma].

There is no distinction between the mundane and the path, because in this stage the categories of suchness (tathatā) are without differentiation. From here below, following the preceding discussion, it explains the abandonment of two delusions;
these two delusions are precisely [the states of] longing for and aversion toward [the mundane].
The obstacle of the manifestation of the six coarse characteristics (up to: being unable to abide for a long time in signless contemplation).
Regarding "the six coarse [characteristics]" below: the first phrase indicates the name; the phrase "that which is" below specifies the essence of the obstacle.

As for the term "coarse characteristics" (*sthūla-nimitta*): it is called "coarse" in comparison to the subsequent stages. It is termed "manifest activity" (*samudācāra*) to distinguish it from seeds. The twelvefold dependent origination is named...

The coarse aspect of defilement is the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination; this is called the coarse aspect of purity. Regarding "that which obstructs the lower," this clarifies the characteristics of the obstruction:

it refers to the absence of the path of defilement and purity when the most excellent *prajñāpāramitā* manifests. By means of this, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) that is free from both defilement and purity. From "by this" [the text continues].

Continuing from the previous discussion on the abandonment of the two delusions: [the first] is the attachment to the existence of a defiled subject, which is the adherence to the forward progression of dependent origination (*pravṛtti-mukha*) as having causes and conditions for rebirth;

[the second] is the attachment to the existence of a pure subject, which is the adherence to the reverse contemplation of dependent origination (*nivṛtti-mukha*) as having causes and conditions for cessation. "One who practices much with signs" means that their practice of contemplation with signs (*sanimitta-bhāvanā*) is frequent, while their practice of signless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*) is rare.

The Obstruction of the Manifestation of the Seven Subtle Characteristics (up to): being unable to give rise to superior practice within emptiness. "Seven subtle" and below: the first phrase indicates the name;
"that which is" and below, sets forth the essence of the obstruction. As for the term "subtle," it is called subtle because it is compared to the preceding stage.
This also involves the contemplation of causes and conditions; what differs from the preceding [stage] is that the former involved clinging to the process of transmigration and return.

The "characteristics of defilement and purity regarding cessation" refers to the characteristics of arising and ceasing in the cyclic flow and its reversal. The passage beginning with "That obstacle... clarifies the nature of the obstacle. The passage beginning with "By this...
follows the preceding discussion to explain the abandonment of two delusions: first, the attachment to the existence of grasping at birth; second, the seeking of the cessation of non-grasping.
This is because, while one applies mental attention to seek non-existence, one has not yet been able to emerge from emptiness into the provisional (conventional) realm.

The obstacle to applying effort (*prayoga*) within the eight [aspects of] signlessness (*animitta*)—[extending to] the fruit of the knowledge of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*)—is because it does not contradict that [fruit].
"Within the eight [aspects of signlessness], below. The first phrase indicates the name. "That which is to be [attained], below. This sets forth the essence of the obstacle:

because it is an obstacle to application (*prayoga*), it prevents the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-bhāvanā*) from arising spontaneously. "Of the preceding, below. This is explained in detail in contrast to the three preceding stages; in this stage, regarding signlessness...
Because there is still application (*prayoga*) regarding signs, one is unable to spontaneously manifest signs and lands; therefore, this constitutes an obstruction.
The phrase "In this way" and below clarifies the characteristics of the obstruction. The phrase "By this" and below follows from the preceding to explain the abandonment of two delusions:

first, applying effort toward the signless (*animitta*); second, being unable to freely manifest signs and lands. As for the phrase "it also includes signs and lands," these are included within the category of delusion.

"Because it is a partial [removal], it is below the eighth stage. This distinguishes the obstacles to be abandoned; because this stage possesses obstacles to preparatory application (*prayoga-āvaraṇa*), it only abandons the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) within the six consciousnesses, but does not abandon the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the seventh [consciousness].

"The fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) does not contradict that" serves as a counter-indication of the obstacles to preparatory application, which are able to obstruct the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
The obstacle of being unwilling to practice among the nine types of altruistic activity (up to the end) is all subsumed under this ninth obstacle.

Regarding "the nine types of altruism," the first phrase indicates the name; the subsequent phrase "that which is to be... reveals the nature of the obstacle. As for "the obstacle of being unwilling to practice among the nine types of altruistic activity," it is as the Sūtra says:
"The Bodhisattva of the eighth stage, the Immovable, enters the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena). [Regarding] the three periods of time..."

Equanimity; cessation is manifested. If the Buddhas did not grant this bodhisattva the gateways of immeasurable arising wisdom, he would at that time enter ultimate *nirvāṇa* and abandon all activities for the benefit of sentient beings; this is precisely the obstacle.

Below that [section], the characteristics of the obstacle are clarified. This generally indicates the obstacle to the four types of unhindered knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). From "By this" below, it follows...

The above explains the abandonment of two delusions (*moha*). The first delusion obstructs the three kinds of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*); the second delusion obstructs the unimpeded analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

Both are as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "the delusion can [obstruct] below," this concludes the section: this delusion is able to obstruct the four kinds of unimpeded analytical knowledge;
it is comprised within the subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the seventh consciousness within the ninth stage (*bhūmi*).
Tenth, the obstacle regarding the lack of mastery over all phenomena (up to) the great cloud of dharma-knowledge and that which it contains.

"Tenth" indicates the name at the beginning; "regarding the lack of mastery over all phenomena" below specifies the substance of the obstacle; "that obstacle" below clarifies the characteristics of the obstacle.
From "By this" onwards, it follows the preceding discussion on the abandonment of two delusions. First is the obstruction to the undertaking of activities;

that is, the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) for transforming others. As the *Avataṃsaka* says: "O Son of the Buddha, the wisdom of the Bodhisattvas on this stage is clear and penetrating, and their supernatural powers are sovereign.
According to their mental intentions, they can transform a narrow world into a vast world, and a vast world..."
He creates a narrow world, or according to his mental intention, manifests within a single pore all the matters of the adornments of the spheres of all Buddhas, and so forth.

Regarding the two obstacles to the great Dharma-cloud of wisdom: this refers to the wisdom that is capable of containing [the Dharma], and that which is contained therein—namely, the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and all other meritorious qualities. Ignorance (*moha*) is able to obstruct these two kinds.

Although this stage has attained mastery over phenomena (up to the point of) realizing great *nirvāṇa* and great *bodhi*, this section below clarifies the severance of the remaining obstacles on the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*).
The first phrase concludes the preceding; the second phrase introduces what follows. "Namely, there are" below indicates the essence of the obstacles:
the seeds and manifestations of the knowable (*jñeya*), the seeds of afflictions (*kleśa*), and the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), which constitute the tenth stage.
The mind is full; about to enter the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) exhaustively severs the obstructions, being likened to a vajra.

From "by this" [and] below, it follows the preceding to explain the severing of the two delusions (*moha*). Therefore, from "the collection" [and] below, it cites scriptural evidence. This universally proves that those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the three vehicles suddenly sever the two obstructions and suddenly realize the two fruits. — Ninth Scroll.
The Self-Examination of the *Cheng weishi lun*, Fascicle Ten.
Recorded by the disciple Da-hui of the Linju [Temple] in Wulin, Ming Dynasty.
These eleven hindrances are subsumed within the two hindrances.

"Below these ten," etc., concludes the eleven obstacles and subsumes them under the two hindrances (*dvayāvaraṇa*). Although the text generally speaks of the "two hindrances," in meaning it distinguishes between two types of the two hindrances:
first, the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*), which is subsumed under the conceptual (*parikalpita*); and the latter ten types of obstacles.
It is subsumed under the category of innate [afflictions]. Second, among the eleven obstacles, both the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are present.
Within the afflictive obstacle, the seeds to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) cease to function entirely from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward.

Regarding "afflictions below," this generally clarifies the meaning of their abandonment across the various stages. First, it clarifies the afflictive hindrances abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), which are the conceptual delusions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) subsumed under the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).

The seeds of these are abandoned at the first moment of the first stage (*bhūmi*), while their active manifestations (*samudācāra*) are suppressed by the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) prior to the stages.
Regarding "abandoned through cultivation below," this next clarifies the afflictive hindrances abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which are the innate delusions (*sahaja-kleśa*).
Namely, sensual desire, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and so forth. The diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) suddenly severs their seeds;

the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) prior to the stages gradually suppress their active manifestations; and upon the [bodhisattva] stages, they are suddenly suppressed so that they never again arise, just as in the case of an Arhat.

[The author] anticipates an objection by stating "by reason of this" (*ata eva*). The question is: "If, like an Arhat, they are made to never arise again, how is it that the notion of 'self' still arises in the fourth stage?"
[Question: Are there still seeds of the view-obscurations (*dṛṣṭi-āvaraṇa*) associated with desire and greed on the third stage? [Answer: The commentary states:

By the power of intentional effort (*abhiprāya-bala*), etc., the seeds of the view-obscurations among the cognitive obscurations (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*)—having been suppressed by the untainted (*anāsrava*) [wisdom]—are obstructed from manifesting.

Regarding "the objects of knowledge" (*jñeya*) below: first, the objects of knowledge abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) are clarified. Whether as seeds or as manifest states, their meaning is the same as that of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding "the objects of knowledge abandoned through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*) below: next, the objects of knowledge abandoned through cultivation are clarified. Whether as seeds or as manifest states, they are gradually extinguished stage by stage (*bhūmi*), until they are finally and permanently suppressed and exhausted by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Regarding "the eight stages" (*bhūmi*) below: this clarifies the objects of knowledge associated with the various consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) with reference to the final three stages.

There are those that manifest and those that do not. The mind associated with untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-citta*) and the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*)—that is, the sixth consciousness—no longer function because they are diametrically opposed to their respective obstacles.
However, the objects of knowledge associated with the seventh consciousness may still manifest because they are subtle;

these are only suppressed and exhausted by the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) within the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*). As for the factors associated with the five sensory consciousnesses...

Although [afflictions] such as greed and delusion have not yet undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), because they are suppressed by the sixth uncontaminated contemplative mind (*anāsrava-citta*), their obstacles do not manifest.
Although this occurs throughout the ten stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is specifically mentioned here because these three stages are particularly prominent.
Although the meaning of the abandonment of the three stages is explained separately below, a question is raised:

Why is it that within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one only abandons the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), while regarding the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*), one merely suppresses them without abandoning them?

Furthermore, why does the preceding text state that within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one abandons both types of delusion (*moha*) as well as their corresponding heavy residues (*dausthulya*)? Answer: Although within the stage of the path of cultivation one does not abandon the afflictions...
Regarding the seeds of affliction (*kleśa*): when the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are severed, those heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the afflictions are also gradually severed and extinguished.
The seeds of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are comprised within the category of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). "Heavy residue" refers to the state of unfitness (*akarmanyatā*).

As for the severance in three stages: first, at the beginning of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*); second, prior to the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*); and third, after the Vajra-like Path (*vajropama-mārga*). Question: Regarding these various stages...
[Question: All [afflictions] are severed; why then speak only of three stages? [Answer: Because these three stages are manifest, they are specifically mentioned.
Regarding the gradual or sudden severance of the seeds of the two obstacles: [it occurs] because [the antidotes] arise spontaneously within and lack coarse or subtle distinctions.
"Severing the two lower [categories]" explains the sudden and gradual nature of severing the seeds. First, the inquiry: "The seventh... and below provides the explanation.

First, regarding the innate afflictive seeds associated with the seventh consciousness: when those of the Three Vehicles attain the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*), they are severed all at once and simultaneously.

This refers to the common stage of the Three Vehicles; after the Far-Reaching Ground (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*), they sever these seeds together, reaching no further than this ground. They do not surpass it.

Because it is superior, next the co-emergent seeds of the objects of knowledge are explained. Regarding those associated with the seven consciousnesses: they are severed all at once by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Why are they severed all at once? Because they take only the internal eighth consciousness as their object, grasping it as self and phenomena, and thus lack coarse or subtle distinctions.
This applies exclusively to Bodhisattvas; therefore, this occurs upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood.
The seeds of the afflictive hindrances associated with the remaining six consciousnesses (up to) are suddenly severed across the three realms within a single moment.

Regarding the "remaining six" below: first, the seeds of discriminated afflictions associated with the six consciousnesses are all suddenly severed by those of the Three Vehicles upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Next, regarding the seeds of innate afflictions, those of the Two Vehicles are divided into two categories; one category [is severed] in three...

Regarding the nine grades across the nine stages (*bhūmi*) of the realms: this refers to the gradual and sequential severance of eighty-one grades of afflictions of thought (*saṃyojana*), with each stage divided into nine grades.
In one tradition, the nine grades within each of the nine stages of the three realms are combined into a single aggregate, resulting in a total of nine grades that are severed individually.
The Bodhisattva’s diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), however, severs the afflictions of the three realms instantaneously all at once.

Because the seeds of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—ranging from the first thought-moment of the first stage (*bhūmi*) through their various classifications—are manifold, [the text] states "the cognitive [obstacles]" and below.

First, it clarifies the seeds of the cognitive obstacles that are conceptual (*vikalpita*); those associated with the six consciousnesses are severed instantaneously at the first thought-moment of the first stage.

Next, under "the cultivated" and below, it clarifies the seeds of the cognitive obstacles that are innate (*sahaja*); these are severed gradually throughout the ten stages and are finally severed upon attaining Buddhahood.

[They] are exhausted. Why are they abandoned gradually? It is because those [afflictions] associated with the six consciousnesses arise by taking both internal and external, coarse and subtle objects as their conditions;
since their categories and distinctions are manifold, [they are abandoned gradually].
When those of the two vehicles with dull faculties gradually sever the hindrances, [the four paths] may all be present when viewed in relation to one another from beginning to end.

Regarding the two vehicles’ lower [level], this clarifies the four paths capable of severing [afflictions]: the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) refers to the skillful means that induce the path of immediate succession;

the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) refers to that which possesses the power to sever delusions; and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) refers to that which has already attained liberation.
Regarding the obstacles that ought to be abandoned, because one clearly realizes the principle, the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) refers to all remaining paths that gradually advance.
Because these are the path to *nirvāṇa*, they are all called "paths. As for whether the four paths are distinct or collective:

collectively, they occur simultaneously, because the superior progress of a preceding stage is itself the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the subsequent stage. When distinguished individually, they are differentiated as preceding and succeeding, each establishing its own [function].
Because it is established [as such]. When a Bodhisattva does not differentiate between the four paths, they are able to sever and realize [the truth] moment by moment (*kṣaṇa-kṣaṇa*).
Question: The fruit of Buddhahood is only accomplished after passing through immeasurable eons (*kalpa*); why then do you say that realization occurs in a single moment? Answer:

Because the duration of time is protracted, one conceptually designates it as "long. As the verse says: "In a dream, one thinks a year has passed; Upon waking, it is but a brief instant. [The same applies to] the passing [of time]."

Although time is immeasurable, it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa. If one considers each successive kṣaṇa in relation to its predecessor and successor, all four paths are capable of being fully present.
Regarding the ten kinds of *tathatā* (suchness): first is the suchness of universal pervasion (*sarvatraga-tathatā*), because there is not a single dharma that does not abide within it.
Below the section on the ten suchnesses, the text clarifies how the ten stages (*bhūmi*) realize these ten suchnesses. The first two phrases indicate the general and specific names;
the subsequent passage explains their meaning. Specifically, the *dharmadhātu* realized in the first stage is termed "universal pervasion," for suchness pervades all things.
In all places—among all sentient beings and all lands throughout the three periods of time—there is nothing left out, yet no form or image can be apprehended.
The first three phrases signify the meaning of universal pervasion (*sarvatraga*); the last phrase signifies the meaning of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*).
Second, the most excellent *tathatā* (suchness): this means that because this *tathatā* is the most excellent among all phenomena.
Second, the most inferior. The first phrase indicates the name; "this is the inferior" explains the meaning.

The *dharmadhātu* realized in the second stage is called the "most excellent object," because it is far removed from the stains of wrong conduct and transgressions of the precepts. Among great and evil maladies, the precepts serve as the efficacious medicine.
In the midst of great terror, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is the protector; in the darkness of the delusion of death, ethical discipline is the bright lamp;
in the midst of the evil realms, ethical discipline is the valiant general; in the waters of the ocean of death, ethical discipline is the boat and raft. It is the supreme meaning.
The third is the "Superior Flowing True Suchness" (*tathatā-suvyūha*), meaning that this true suchness is extremely superior compared to other teachings.

Regarding the phrase "the third, the superior flow": the first clause provides the name; the phrase "meaning this" and so forth explains the definition. This refers to the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) realized in the third stage, which is termed "superior flow.
From true suchness flows the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); from fundamental wisdom flows the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Thereafter, great compassion flows forth; that from which the twelve divisions of the scriptures flow is the meaning of "superior outflow" (viśeṣa-niḥṣyanda).
True thusness (tathatā) is not grasped by the four kinds of clinging, because it is not an object of appropriation for the grasping of a self and so forth.

"Fourth, there is no inferiority. The first phrase indicates the name; "this [is] below" explains the meaning. The dharma-realm realized in the fourth stage is called "having the sense of non-appropriation.

This means that the suchness realized when the subtle afflictive obstructions are abandoned in the fourth stage is not bound to or dependent upon dharmas such as form, mind, existence, or non-existence; nor is it bound by self-grasping, conceit, self-love, or self-delusion.
Because it is the basis for and the object of apprehension for extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the view of self (*ātmagrāha*), and so forth;
because the five categories have no distinction in their true suchness (*tathatā*), unlike the eye and other faculties which possess distinct categories.

Below the "five categories," the first phrase provides the title; the section beginning with "That is to say" explains the meaning. This refers to the name of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) realized in the five stages.
"Similarity" (jāti) has no sense of differentiation. This means that on the fifth stage, one abandons the obstacles to the parinirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle;
both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equal, unlike the case where categories such as the eye and so forth possess differentiation.
Sixth, the *tathatā* (suchness) that is neither defiled nor pure; it cannot be said that it becomes pure only later.

Regarding "Sixth, no inferiority": the first phrase indicates the name, while the subsequent passage explains its meaning. The *dharmadhātu* realized in the sixth stage is termed "neither defiled nor pure.
This means that in the sixth stage, one abandons the obstacle of the active manifestation of coarse characteristics and realizes that dependently originated phenomena are neither defiled nor pure.

It is not purified; just as the essence of a mani jewel is fundamentally free from defilement and is not made pure through polishing, so too the seven dharmas are no different from true suchness (tathatā), for they are established in various ways yet remain without distinction.

Regarding the "Seven Dharmas," the first phrase provides the title; the subsequent section explains the meaning. The *dharmadhātu* realized in the seven stages is termed "the non-differentiation of dharmas" (*dharma-aviśeṣa*).
Although various teachings are established based upon suchness (*tathatā*), suchness itself is without distinction.

Furthermore, although various names—such as "the true characteristic of the *dharmadhātu*" and so forth—are established within the teachings, these are merely different names for a single essence, while suchness remains without distinction.
Eighth, because of mastery over both the manifestation of signs and the manifestation of lands, there is the *tathatā* (suchness) that neither increases nor decreases.
"Eighth, not below": the first phrase indicates the name; "meaning this, below" explains the meaning.
The dharma-dhātu realized in the eighth stage is termed the meaning of "neither increasing nor decreasing. Because one penetrates this *tathatā*, regarding all pure and defiled phenomena...
One does not perceive a single dharma that increases or decreases. True Suchness (tathatā) manifests as defiled or pure dharmas according to defiled or pure conditions.
When following defiled conditions, there is no increase in defilement, nor is purity diminished. When following pure conditions, there is no increase in purity.
Defilement does not decrease either, because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is equal. From this point downward, different names are set forth.

That is to say, this *dharmadhātu* is the basis for mastery over appearances (*nimitta-vaśitā*). Appearances manifest according to one’s wishes—whether great or small, superior or inferior—and thus it is called mastery over appearances.
That is to say, this *dharmadhātu* is the basis for mastery over lands (*kṣetra-vaśitā*). Whether vast or narrow, pure or impure, they appear according to one’s will.

All are accomplished; this is called mastery over the land (*bhūmi-vaśitā*). "Land" refers to the manifestation of the realm (*dhātu*), while "body" refers to the manifestation of the physical form (*rūpa*).
It is because one attains mastery over the unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) based upon the *tathatā* (suchness), which is the basis for the nine masteries of knowledge.

Regarding "The Nine Knowledges" (*navajñāna*): the first phrase indicates the name; the subsequent section, beginning with "That is to say," explains the meaning. The dharma-realm realized in the nine stages is termed the "mastery of knowledge" (*jñānavaśitārtha*).

This means that because one has abandoned the obstacle to the lack of desire to act for the benefit of others in the nine stages, one is able to skillfully teach the Dharma with effortless mastery through the four kinds of unhindered eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).

Because one attains mastery over the *tathatā* (suchness) that serves as the basis for the ten masteries of action (*karmavaśitā*) and so forth, up to the gates of *dhāraṇī* and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding the "ten masteries of action" below: the first phrase indicates the name; the phrase "that is to say, if... explains the meaning.

The *dharmadhātu* realized in the ten stages is termed the "meaning of mastery of action. This means that in the ten stages, one eliminates the obstacles to mastery regarding all phenomena, and thus the *tathatā* that is realized...
Just as it serves as the basis for the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth, such that all activities of the supernormal powers are attained with mastery;
although the nature of true thusness (*tathatā*) is in reality without distinction, [this is] for the purpose of bringing them to perfection through successive establishments.
[The Opponent] asks: "If the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) is a single Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), its essence being without distinction, how can there be ten [stages]?
[The Commentator] explains: "The names are provisionally established as ten based on the [gradual manifestation of] virtues. [The Opponent] asks:

"In the first stage (bhūmi), one perceives the principle, and since that principle has no dual nature—wherein one is all—why must these ten be established in successive stages? [The Commentator] explains: "In the first..."
Although the stages (bhūmi) are such that one is identical to all, the wisdom that realizes them varies in clarity and dullness;
thus, as long as the practices being cultivated have not yet reached perfection, they are established in successive stages to bring them to completion. These practices are the ten pāramitās.
In this way, the Bodhisattva within the ten stages (bhūmis), up until [the final stage], is able to realize the two types of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Thus, the following explains the two transformations of the basis. In the text, first the preceding section is concluded; then, with the words "in the two," the subsequent section is introduced.

Since it was previously indicated that one relies upon the ten stages, cultivates the ten practices, eliminates the ten obstacles, and realizes the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*), there are these two kinds of transformation of the basis.

Because it is realized through this, there are briefly six distinct stages of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). [This continues] until "and gradually suppressing the active manifestations is also called transformation.

Regarding the phrase "the transformation of the basis," the six types are first indicated in general. First, "diminution" (*hāni*); this is the specific explanation. The first sentence indicates the name; that is, the first stage.

Explanation of the meaning: The seeds of defilement and purity held within the *vipāka-vijñāna*—due to the cultivation of resolute belief (*adhimukti*), shame (*hrī*), and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) during the stages of the accumulations (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*)—possess the power to diminish defilement and the capacity to increase purity. This causes the seeds of defilement to gradually decrease and the seeds of purity to gradually increase.
Question: If this is so, and the seeds of the obstructions have not yet been severed, how can it be called the "transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*)? Answer: [As stated] in the middle...
As stated in the text: this refers to "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) by way of subduing defilements.
Second is "transformation through penetration," which refers to the stage of penetration (up to the point of) realizing a portion of the true transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parivṛtti*).

The second [category] extends downward. The first phrase indicates the name, meaning it "extends downward. This explains the meaning: by severing the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*), one realizes a portion of the true transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
This is termed "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) with respect to its initial realization.

Third, the transformation through cultivation (*bhāvanā-parāvṛtti*) refers to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), wherein [the practitioner] increasingly causes that which is not real to no longer appear.

Regarding "Third, cultivation": the first phrase indicates the name; "refers to cultivation" below explains the meaning. This is based on the gradual abandonment and gradual realization across the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the first six stages are termed "penetration" (*prativedha*), while the latter four are termed "cultivation. This involves the presence of signs (*sanimitta*).

The contemplation of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) penetrates the conventional; the contemplation of the signless (*animitta*) penetrates the ultimate (*paramārtha*). When one enters the contemplation of the signless, the ultimate manifests while the non-ultimate does not manifest.
When one enters the contemplation of the sign-possessing (*sanimitta*), the non-ultimate manifests while the ultimate does not manifest. The "non-ultimate" is precisely the conventional.

In the latter four [stages], one constantly abides in the contemplation of the signless, which mostly causes the non-ultimate not to manifest. However, because remaining afflictions have not yet been eliminated, it still manifests to a small degree, or [this occurs] at the seventh stage.
A small portion is not truly manifest; from the eighth stage upward, it is mostly non-manifest. This refers to "transformation" (parāvṛtti) in terms of partial realization.
The "transformation of the fulfillment of the four fruits" refers to the ultimate stage, wherein benefit and happiness for others continue inexhaustibly until the end of the future.
Regarding the "four fruits" at the bottom: the first phrase indicates the name; the subsequent section beginning with "that is, to exhaust" explains the meaning.

These consist of the cultivation of practice, the severing of delusions, the realization of the fruit, and the benefiting of sentient beings—this constitutes the beginning and end of one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), as well as the agent and object of transforming others (*para-parāvṛtti*). This is designated as "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) in its ultimate sense.
The five types of inferior transformation refer to the stage of the two vehicles (the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). It is called "inferior transformation" because they lack superior capability.
Fifth, the "lowest of the inferior": first, the title is stated; second, the meaning is explained. They exclusively seek their own benefit, like a *ts'ang* deer leaping alone.

Because they have not yet forgotten joy and aversion, they do not accord with equality. Because they only penetrate the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), their realization of principle is not yet complete.

Because the seeds of afflictions have not been severed—since there remains that which has not yet been severed—and because the realization of true analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is not yet Great Nirvāṇa, one lacks superior capability.
Being like one with a deformed ear or a squint eye, and lacking majestic virtue, this is termed "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) in reference to the partial truth (*tattva*).
The sixth is the "vast transformation," which refers to the stage of the Mahāyāna. Reaching a state of superior capability is called the vast transformation.

Regarding the sixth, "vast" and below: the first phrase provides the name; "which refers to the Great [Vehicle]" and below explains the meaning. Its intrinsic nature is the vow to deliver all sentient beings.
Because the Buddha-way of intrinsic nature is vowed to be accomplished, birth-and-death is itself nirvana; because one is free from grasping and abandoning;
because one fully masters the two kinds of emptiness and exhausts the profound depths; because one simultaneously severs the two hindrances and brings the five stages of dwelling to an end;

because one suddenly realizes the two virtues—the sufficiency of merit and the sufficiency of wisdom; and because one possesses supreme capability, with a body adorned by garlands and a majestic virtue that is exceptionally honored.
This refers to "transformation" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) in its broad sense.
Here, the intended meaning is that one realizes transformation by abandoning the two types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Below this, the verse provides a definitive distinction: because the preceding verse states that one abandons the two types of coarse heaviness, one thereby realizes transformation.
Regarding "basis" (*āśraya*): the intention here is to take the sixth, the "vast transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), because its six aspects are preeminent.

Among the first five, the first is designated as "abandonment" only in the sense of suppression; the second is an abandonment that is not yet exhaustive across three parts; the fourth speaks of the fruit in relation to the cause;
