This question is posed based on the fact that although *tathatā* and the unconditioned differ in name, they are identical in essence.
"Analytical cessation is free from bondage because it is not itself a bondage.
Below this, the answer is given: "Analytical cessation is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It is manifested by being free from the bondage of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Since those cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) do not induce rebirth, they are not like the afflictions that bind sentient beings and cause them to dwell in saṃsāra; therefore, [they are abandoned]."

At that time, one merely realizes *tathatā* (suchness) but does not attain *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through discernment). This answer is given in terms of being bound or unbound by the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
Since this is so, how could one attain *nirvāṇa* by severing those [obstacles]?

"Since this is so," and so forth: five questions follow, which continue to inquire based on the identical principle of the two dharmas. The two characters "ji-er" (since this is so) refer back to what preceded.
If the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are not themselves bonds, how can their abandonment result in the attainment of non-abiding nirvana?

This is because, according to the identical principles of both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and nirvana, if one cannot obtain analytical cessation by abandoning those [cognitive obstacles], one likewise should not obtain [nirvana].
Nirvāṇa. Not all nirvāṇas are subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

[The phrase] "not all" below answers by distinguishing the meanings of two types of dharmas; the first sentence provides a direct answer regarding the four kinds of nirvāṇa, some of which are... [is].

There is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Not all *nirvāṇas* are subsumed under cessation through deliberation.

Otherwise, if one were to claim that all *nirvāṇas* are cessation through deliberation, then by way of the analogy of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), it would follow that the first of the four [types of *nirvāṇa*], which is intrinsically pure, would not be *nirvāṇa*, as it does not arise from cessation through deliberation.
The phrase "that which can bind" below correctly judges the difference in meaning regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*).

This [affliction] is a bondage; through the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) one is liberated from bondage. Therefore, when those [afflictions] are severed, one realizes true analytical cessation.
The objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are not bondage, but merely obstruct the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā-tattva*); therefore, when they are severed, one does not attain analytical cessation.

However, when the lower [objects] are severed, the principle of the emptiness of the objects of knowledge is manifested, and it is said that one attains non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*). This single phrase is not a concluding judgment that distinguishes the meanings.

Because the nature of *nirvāṇa* and that of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) differ, the four [types of] *nirvāṇa* are categorized and summarized in relation to the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
The "purity of nature" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and "non-abiding" (*apratiṣṭhita*) are subsumed under *tathatā* (suchness); they are not subsumed under analytical cessation.

The "remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*) are subsumed under analytical cessation. Therefore, the cessation of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) cannot be explained as [merely] extinction.

If the attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) occurs solely through the severing of fetters (*bandhana*), then among the four [types of unconditioned phenomena], in which are the two—namely, the immovable (*āniñjya*) and so forth—included?

If it is only the lower [six], there are six questions. The first phrase restates that analytical cessation is attained through the separation from fetters; the second phrase asks by way of inclusion based on characteristics.

The intent is to show that analytical cessation is exclusively ultimate cessation (*atyanta-nirodha*), namely the immovable unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*).
Regarding the unconditioned of cessation (*nirodha-asamskrta*): among the other four unconditioned phenomena, to which is it subsumed? The other four unconditioned phenomena are namely:
analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), suchness (*tathatā*), and space (*ākāśa*).

It is said that they are included within non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) because they are described as temporary separations; [this is so] up to the point where there is non-analytical cessation that is not an eternal cessation.

Regarding non-analytical cessation, the following provides a direct answer to how these two are included within non-analytical cessation. As for "temporary separation": the fourth dhyāna, characterized by the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, is called "immovable" (*āneñjya*);

yet, because one may fall away from it and return, or be scattered and enter various realms of existence (*gati*), it is only temporarily free from them. As for the "attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), one enters it...

"Temporarily separated. Because [the afflictions] arise again when one emerges from that state. The first phrase of "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) follows upon the preceding "non-deliberative cessation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) to contrast it with the unconditioned cessation through deliberation as a cessation that is eternally ceased.

Furthermore, by means of this ultimate cessation, it is contrasted with non-deliberative cessation, which is subsumed under temporary separation. Thus, the meaning of these two phrases is that they mutually establish one another. "There is a non... [The text continues].
[This] sentence further explains the meaning of the first phrase above: there is a portion of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) that is not an eternal cessation.
Since these two—immovability (*āniñjya*) and so forth—are not eternal cessations, they are subsumed under non-analytical cessation.

To separately indicate that there is a portion of non-analytical cessation outside of this which is an eternal cessation, [the text] refers to the non-analytical cessation regarding the knowable (*jñeya-apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is an eternal cessation.

Therefore, some [states] that lack a place of abiding are also subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Up to the point of ultimate cessation, they are subsumed under analytical cessation.
Alternatively, the preceding section clarifies that non-abiding nirvāṇa is not subsumed under non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because it is not a form of extinction.

Because it is obtained by binding [the mind]. As for the current statement that it is also included within analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), this is because it is obtained by extinguishing hindrances through true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*).

Question: The previous explanation clarified that the extinction of bonds constitutes analytical cessation; why is the present extinction of hindrances also considered analytical cessation? Answer: It is explained as follows:

There are two kinds of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): first, that which is called analytical cessation because it severs bonds; second, that which is called analytical cessation because it eliminates hindrances, as stated in the text.
Therefore, from "the four" below, the answer is given by way of a summary based on their characteristics, correlating the four nirvāṇas with the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

Essential purity is suchness (*tathatā*); the latter three are all analytical cessations. From "immovable" below, the conclusion is reached by correlating the immovable [nirvāṇa] with the temporary cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*).
This clarifies that the latter three types of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are exclusively ultimate cessations.
Since the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) also obstruct *nirvāṇa*, why are they said to be obstructions only to *bodhi*?

Regarding the phrase "Since the [cognitive obstructions]... and so forth: this consists of seven questions. The first phrase cites the preceding point that since the cognitive obstructions obstruct *nirvāṇa*, the second phrase raises the formal objection.
How is it that the holy teachings speak only of [afflictions] as obstacles to bodhi, yet do not say they are obstacles to nirvāṇa?
While it is said that the afflictive hindrances (kleśāvaraṇa) only obstruct nirvāṇa—in reality, both are capable of obstructing both fruits.

Regarding the section on "explaining afflictions" (*kleśa*), the answer is provided by citing an example as in the text. In reality, however, both [afflictions and cognitive objects] act as obstacles; this is stated with partiality based on their specific functions.
The predominant function of afflictions is to bind sentient beings, causing them to dwell perpetually in birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and preventing them from realizing *nirvāṇa*.
The predominant function of cognitive objects (*jñeya*) is to obscure the principle and the objective sphere of what is known, preventing one from realizing *bodhi*.
Among the four types of nirvāṇa thus described, only the latter three are termed "attained through manifestation.

This concludes the preceding section. As for why the first one is not termed "attained through manifestation," it is because its nature is intrinsically pure and is not manifested by means of abandoning obstructions; therefore, this term applies only to the latter three.
"Second, that which is produced and attained refers to Great Bodhi" (extending to "this is the mental complex associated with the four wisdoms").

Regarding "Second, that which is produced...": this next section clarifies what is produced and attained. The first phrase provides the name; the second phrase reveals its essence. *Bodhi* is translated here as "Awakening.

It is called "Great" (*mahā*) to distinguish it from the inferior and middling [awakenings] of the two vehicles. It is able to sever all afflictions completely and is able to realize the principle thoroughly.
Therefore, although this section below explains the meaning of "attainment" (*prāpti*) as that which is produced, it may be asked:

"Since the untainted seeds exist by their very nature (*dharmatā*) and do not arise anew, why is it called 'attainment'? This is explained according to the text, concluding by returning to the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*bodhi*).
What are the mental states associated with the four wisdoms?
[The text asks] "What are they? below, generally inquiring about the four wisdoms. Regarding the term "mental states associated" (*saṃprayukta-citta-varga*):

this refers to the eight purified consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) in conjunction with their twenty-one respective associated mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), which, through their harmonious integration, form a single aggregate; this is termed a "state" (*varga*). A "state" (*varga*) means a category or class.
...and so forth. The following provides a detailed explanation for each point.
First, the mental state associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna), [extending to] "just as a great mirror manifests various forms and images.

Regarding the first section: the initial phrase establishes the name by means of a dharma-illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*); the subsequent passage, beginning with "That is to say," explains the meaning. "Free from all conceptual discrimination" (*sarva-vikalpa-vigata*)...
This means that it is precisely non-conceptual correct wisdom (*avikalpa-samyagjñāna*), because both subject and object are simultaneously transcended.

The single phrase "the object of cognition" (*ālambana*) establishes this, just as it is said that the "appropriation and locus" (*upādānasthiti*) of contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) cannot be known. "Pure" (*śuddha*) means unmixed; "clean" (*viśuddha*) means unstained.
"Perfectly round" (*vṛtta*) signifies fullness. The manifest virtues serve as its basis, while the seeds of virtue serve as its support.

This [mirror-like wisdom] manifests the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) and the land of true retribution; it gives rise to the latter three types of wisdom, just as a great round mirror manifests various forms and images.
The second is the mental state associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), which continues as a single flavor until the end of the future.

[The phrase] "The second, equality" [is divided into two parts]: the first clause indicates the name; the words "that is to say, this... and below explain the meaning. Because one clung to a self during the causal stage, there was inequality between oneself and others;
now that one is free from such clinging, all are equal. "All sentient beings" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) for whom [this wisdom] manifests.

The Enjoyment Body (*sambhogakāya*) and the Land Adorned with True Retribution (*vipākavibhūṣita-kṣetra*) differ in their relative excellence across the various stages (*bhūmi*), and their reflected images likewise possess distinctions.

At the level of the fruit, it still serves as the co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) for the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Not abiding in either extreme is termed "one flavor" (*ekarasa*).
The third is the mental state associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). (Up to: "Causing all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness.
Regarding "The third, wondrous... and below: the first phrase indicates the name; "namely, this... and below explains the meaning.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*) is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*) is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Because wisdom contemplates these, the six perfections and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) serve as...
The Jewel of Merit: because wisdom encompasses this. The Superknowledges and the Ten Powers: these are the differentiation of functional activity; because wisdom manifests this.
Preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of beings is called "raining down the rain of Dharma"; because wisdom speaks this.
The fourth is the mental state associated with the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). From "accomplishing" downwards:

the first phrase indicates the name; "meaning this" and below explain the meaning. It refers to universally manifesting bodies throughout the ten dharma-realms and performing the inconceivable transformations of the three wheels, thereby accomplishing the activities that should be performed according to one's original vows. Because wisdom can accomplish this, it is called "accomplishing."
The wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). Thus, all conditioned merits (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*) are fully encompassed within the mental states associated with these four wisdoms.
[The text] concludes below by establishing the names of these wisdoms. [The opponent] raises an objection: "In each of the four wisdom-mental states, there are twenty [factors]."
2. Regarding the "transforming subject" (*pariṇāman*) and the "transformed object" (*pariṇāmya*), etc., why are they designated solely by the name "cognition" (*jñāna*)? The commentary explains:

These twenty-two factors—namely, the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), the five object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyata*), the eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala*), together with the consciousness upon which they depend—are what constitute the "transforming subject."

This refers to the two internal divisions: the transformed [aspects], namely the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), which are associated with their respective seeds and active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
Herein, because the function of wisdom (*jñāna*) predominates, it is designated by the name "wisdom.

Thus, below this, there is the formal conclusion regarding conditioned qualities (*saṃskṛtakuśala*), namely the twenty-two dharmas, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the ten powers (*bala*), and so forth.

This transformation involves the transmutation of the eight, seven, six, and five consciousnesses that are associated with outflows; therefore, it is said that by transforming the eight consciousnesses, one attains these four wisdoms.

The section beginning with "This transformation" clarifies the essence of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). The first sentence directly explains how the eight are transformed into the four, which may be understood in their respective order.

Although wisdom (*jñāna*) is subordinate, a questioner asks: "Since wisdom is precisely the discernment (*prajñā*) among the five object-specific mental states (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*), one should say that discernment is transformed into wisdom.

Why, then, do you say that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is transformed into wisdom? If that were so, would it not mean that the sovereign [mind] (*citta*) is transformed into the objective [mental factors]?

The explanation says: In accordance with reality, when the sovereign is transformed, it attains the status of a sovereign; when the objective is transformed, it attains the status of the objective. Because wisdom follows the transformation of consciousness and consciousness is the primary factor, it is said that "consciousness is transformed."

It is attained. Furthermore, through transformation, the strong attains the strong. Regarding the strength of contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*): it is because afflictions (*kleśa*) increase and its objects (*viṣaya*) are superior.

Regarding the strength of uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*): it is because afflictions are absent and its objects are empty. It is for the sake of exhorting sentient beings that it is said that consciousness is transformed and attained.
Regarding the mental complex associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśajñāna): [it functions] because it maintains the untainted seeds so that they are not lost.
Below the section on the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the stages of the manifestation of the four wisdoms are clarified.

The first school asserts that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom first manifests at the time of the path of immediate succession (ānantaryamārga), because the seeds within the maturation consciousness (vipākavijñāna) and [the new seeds] are simultaneously empty [of defilements]. Once the maturation consciousness has been relinquished...

Since the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) has not yet arisen, there is no consciousness capable of sustaining the pure seeds. The next school asserts that it first arises precisely at the time of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
Regarding the phrase "matured [consciousness]" (*vipākaja*) and below: this refutes the previous claim that seeds are abandoned immediately [upon the path of seeing].

As for the statement that they are "not yet suddenly abandoned," it means that while the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are abandoned, the seeds of contaminated virtue (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and inferior uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-hīna-bīja*) have not yet been abandoned. This is [the view] of the Uninterrupted [School].
Because the Vajra-like Wisdom does not contradict [the seeds], it is not an obstacle; rather, they are abandoned only when liberation is attained.
This is because these seeds are definitively contradictory to the fruition of perfect Buddhahood. Regarding "Vajra" below, this clarifies the Path of No-Interval (*ānantarya-mārga*).

If the matured fruit (*vipāka*) were abandoned, there would be no consciousness to serve as the substrate for perfuming (*vāsana*). If there were no substrate for perfuming, the untainted [qualities] would not increase; at that time, one would immediately...
Having attained Buddhahood, what further need is there to arise through the path of liberation? From this point downward, it is concluded:
the mental state associated with the wisdom of equality (continues) as a mutual dependence and continuity until the end of the future.

The *Samatā* [wisdom] is at the lower level. It transforms during the seventh cause, because by means of the sixth consciousness one enters the contemplation of the dual emptiness (*ubhaya-śūnyatā*), thereby severing the two types of conceptual grasping (*vikalpa-graha*).
At the initial arising of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the verse says: "When the *manas* that grasps only one [aspect] resides in the state of seeds, the *Samatā-jñāna* does not manifest.
When the *manas* that grasps both [aspects] returns to the state of seeds, the *Samatā-jñāna* finally manifests. [This occurs] subsequently during the ten...

Within the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), these [factors] are co-emergent and remain unsevered. Upon exiting and re-entering meditative equipoise, they alternate between being contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Therefore, there is an interval between their concealment and manifestation. The final moment of mind in the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) serves as the simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) for the pure eighth consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*);
it continues in succession without end until the limit of the future.
The mental states associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) may manifest at all times, including during periods when there is no mind.

This [wisdom] also functions within the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*). The category of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) is common to the three vehicles, whereas the category of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) belongs exclusively to Bodhisattvas.

Even for those of the two vehicles, it can first arise during the stage of the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) regarding the emptiness of persons; subsequently, upon reaching the stage of no... [text truncated].

Regarding the training: for a Bodhisattva of gradual awakening, it arises at the conclusion of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*); for a Bodhisattva of sudden awakening, it arises from the initial path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) up to the eighth bhūmi.

It is not a defiled mind (*sāsrava-citta*), nor is it [indicated by] characters that extend downward; it is not during a state of no-mind (*acittaka*). "No-mind" refers to the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);
this implies that it is an uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*). Only during states of having a mind (*sacittaka*) is its manifestation permitted. If a Bodhisattva...

The view of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) first arises precisely at the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), continuing until the final moment of the tenth ground (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the phrase "not [associated with] outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth," the character "not" (*fei*) governs what follows. Outflows are contrary to wisdom; the view of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) does not contradict the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*);

and in the absence of mind, there is no mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Therefore, these three periods do not manifest. This serves to clarify that it is the uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) [that perceives] phenomena.
The fruit of the knowledge of emptiness arises only when there is a mind; although this cause of illumination may occasionally be interrupted during its transformation,
the mental state associated with the wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) does not frequently interrupt it, because it arises through deliberate attention (*manasikāra*).

Regarding the phrase "attained upon becoming a Buddha" (*cheng suo xia*), there are two masters' interpretations. The first master says: It is identical to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses in that it also transforms within the causal stage;

during the path of cultivation, being induced by the subsequent realization (*prṣṭhalabdha*) of the sixth consciousness, it is also able to arise for the first time. The second master says: It arises only upon becoming a Buddha.

This is because, as indicated by the passage beginning with "with the ten [powers]," its supporting faculty (*āśraya*) is not untainted (*anāsrava*); therefore, it does not transform within the causal stage. It is not...

"Common" (*sādhāraṇa*) means that the eye-faculty serves exclusively as the support for the visual consciousness. "Necessarily coexistent" (*sahabhū*) refers to the coexistent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), because the faculty and the consciousness arise simultaneously.
"Sharing the same object" (*samālambana*) means that the faculty and the consciousness take one and the same object as their cognitive domain.

These three names differ, yet all belong to the five faculties; they are all subsumed under the category of the "coexistent support" among the three types of supports. Since the supporting faculty is itself contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Therefore, it cannot give rise to untainted consciousness and wisdom (*anāsrava-vijñāna-jñāna*). Tainted faculties are dull, while untainted consciousness is luminous;

because they do not accord with one another, this wisdom—which is concluded and manifested below—only arises upon the attainment of Buddhahood. That which is intermittently interrupted does not proceed in a continuous succession like the former two types of wisdom.
Although these four types of nature are all inherently present (until: "lest the virtues of a preceding Buddha be superior to those of a subsequent Buddha").

Regarding the section beginning with "These four," a question is raised: Since these four categories of wisdom are all produced from inherently present untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), if they were to manifest as active states (*samudācāra*), they should all at all times uniformly constitute the untainted. How, then, can there be a sequence of cause and effect?

Is the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) not uniform? The commentary explains: Although [the consciousnesses] arise from seeds, there are degrees of excellence and inferiority in their perfuming (vāsanā).

The sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] gradually increase during the stage of the cause (hetu-bhūmi), while the fifth and eighth are perfected upon the stage of the fruit (phala-bhūmi). Furthermore, it is asked: Why is it that at the stage of Buddhahood there is neither increase nor decrease?
The commentary explains: It arises solely from seeds and no longer perfumes seeds. If it were to perfume seeds further, then the preceding Buddha would have perfumed many more.
Thus, it is superior; later, when the Buddha’s熏 (vāsanā/impressions) are slight, it is inferior.
This should be understood by analogy for the remaining one part and two [parts] associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśajñāna).

Below "Great Perfect Mirror" (mahādarśajñāna): the function of the object-conditioning of clear wisdom. Regarding the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, there are two masters' interpretations. The first master says: it takes only suchness (tathatā) as its object;

among the two types of wisdom, it is exclusively fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna). This is established by the phrase "the aspect of activity," because it is non-conceptual (nirvikalpa), it is fundamental wisdom.
The second master says: it also takes conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) as its object. First, he cites sacred scripture to provide proof.

This establishes the mundane conditions, as stated in the text. Furthermore, from this point downward, it cites reasoning to prove the cause: since the result already takes three types of objects as its conditions, it is also capable of taking them as its objects.
The verse says: The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, stainless and arising simultaneously, Universally illuminates the lands and atoms throughout the ten directions.
Its activity takes subtle objects and is said to be unknowable; It is not without discernment, yet it is called "non-conceptual."

This can be understood. For example, because the *ālayavijñāna* takes both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) as its objects, the section "taking the ultimate as its object" below is judged to belong to the two wisdoms:

the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) takes the ultimate as its object, while the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) takes the conventional as its object. Regarding the term "subsequently attained," it means that it is obtained after the fundamental wisdom has realized the ultimate.

By analogy with other cases such as the equality-wisdom (*samatā-jñāna*) and the wondrous observation-wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), one should understand that their essence is single while their aspects are divided into two. This should be known accordingly.
The mental state associated with the Wisdom of Equality (samatājñāna), up to its inclusion within the two [other] wisdoms, does not contradict the principle.

Regarding the section on "Equality," there are three masters' interpretations. The first master says: "It takes only conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) as its object, because it takes the purified eighth consciousness as its object."

For example, the first master says that in the defiled state, it takes the ālayavijñāna as its object. The second master says that it takes only *tathatā* (suchness) as its object, because it takes the nature of equality as its object.

The third master says that it takes both the ultimate and the conventional as its objects universally; he cites a sūtra to prove that it takes the ultimate as its object and cites a śāstra to prove that it takes the conventional as its object.
Because it manifests according to others as the image of a Buddha, the verse says: "The Tathāgata manifests the Enjoyment Body for others;

it is the object for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages. From "By this" onwards, the conditions for the ultimate and conventional truths are concluded: the fundamental [wisdom] takes the ultimate as its object, while the subsequently attained [wisdom] takes the conventional as its object.

First, the self-nature body (*svābhāvika-kāya*): it refers to all Tathāgatas, because it is the basis for the dharmas of great merit.

First, from below: initially, there is the formal explanation of the three bodies (*trikāya*). The first phrase indicates their names; the phrase "which are all... sets forth their essential nature (*svabhāva*); and the phrase "the enjoyment [body], etc.
uses the dependent to manifest the excellence of the basis. From "free from characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-vinirmukta*) onwards is the explanation of the meaning.
Profoundly serene, it transcends all discursive thought; utterly still, its names are severed. It serves as the basis for the appearance of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
Whatever has characteristics is entirely false and illusory; this very self-nature is also called the *dharmakāya*. The second phrase explains it by way of its meaning as a "basis" (*āśraya*).

That which provides a standard and sustains is "Dharma" (*dharma*); the Buddhas take this as their standard and thereby attain Buddhahood. Because it is the basis for all merits, it is called "Body" (*kāya*).
Regarding the designation of the first two fruits of transformation as the *dharmakāya*, this is explained by way of combination (*samuccaya*).

Regarding the designation of this true, pure *dharmadhātu* as the *dharmakāya*, this is explained by way of singularity (*kevala*). When there are three distinct aspects within the *dharmakāya*, this is explained by way of differentiation (*vibhāga*).

When the first two fruits of transformation are designated as the *dharmakāya*, this is explained by way of synthesis (*saṃgraha*). Although there are thus distinctions between the singular and the combined, and between the differentiated and the integrated...
The synthesis of the distinct [bodies]. These three bodies are neither vertical nor horizontal; they are neither unified nor separate.
Although the text belongs to the distinct [teachings], the meaning is harmonized within the comprehensive and perfect [teaching], because the Dharma-body fully possesses these three characteristics.
Second, the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). This has two types (up to: these two types combined are called the Enjoyment Body. "Second, the enjoyment" [refers to the section].
The first phrase indicates the general name; the second phrase lists the two types: first, the self-enjoyment body, because it constantly enjoys for itself the bliss of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Regarding "As for the various... [and so on], this explains the meaning: "true merits" refers to the four wisdoms of the Buddha.

"Ti" refers to the extremely perfect, pure, and eternally pervasive form-body (*rūpakāya*), which is none other than the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*). Because wisdom is in profound accord with principle, the light of its insight illuminates the immeasurable.
Attained through long-cultivated practice, it is called the "body of self-enjoyment reward" (*svasaṃbhoga-vipākakāya*). "Body" (*kāya*) here means the basis of support.
The meaning of continuity (*saṃtāna*): because it is the basis for conditioned virtues, its continuity remains serene, extending to the end of the future.
Second, the body of enjoyment for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*): because it causes others to enjoy the bliss of the Mahāyāna Dharma, it is a body of subtle and wondrous virtues.
This is precisely the sublime, distinguished, and responsive body (saṃbhogakāya), and its pure land is the land of actual retribution and adornment (*vipākālaṃkāra-kṣetra*).

This body and land are manifested for the sake of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). The Tathāgata manifests this as the "other-enjoyment" (*parasaṃbhoga*) for those Bodhisattvas of the ten stages who serve as the receptive capacity (*adhikāra*).
This is what is manifested by the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). When these two aspects are combined, it is called the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
The third is the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), which refers to the various Tathāgatas [providing] each being with all manner of beneficial and blissful matters.
Regarding the "three transformations" below: the first phrase indicates the name; "refers to the various... explains the meaning. As for "transforming according to types," there are three:

first, the great transformation (*mahā-nirmāṇa*), manifesting a body one thousand *zhang* tall that pervades the great trichiliocosm, intended for those whose faculties have not yet reached the stage of the *bhūmi*; second, the small transformation (*parīttā-nirmāṇa*), manifesting a body one *zhang* tall...

The six bodies: First, the king of one four-continent world; second, those who are recipients of the two vehicles and ordinary beings; third, transformation according to species, such as appearing as a monkey among monkeys and appearing as a deer among deer.
Regarding pure and impure lands: they may be suppressed or gathered, transformed into purity or transformed into impurity;

these are for the sake of those in the three stages of worthiness, the two vehicles, ordinary beings, and so forth. As for what is called the "transformation body" (nirmāṇakāya), it differs from the "response body" (sambhogakāya). Contemplate this.

The *Yinshu* (Commentary on Sound) states: "Transformational [bodies] appear suddenly and vanish suddenly; they are merely temporary manifestations for the benefit of sentient beings. As for 'responding':

it means responding to questions and sharing the beginning and end of beings. For example, while the lifespan of the people in Sukhāvatī is incalculable, the Buddha there likewise has an immeasurable lifespan;
whereas in this land the lifespan is short, the Buddha likewise has a span of eighty years. There is a day of his descent and birth, and there is a day of his entry [into parinirvāṇa]."

At the time of cessation, he is precisely the Buddha of the eight aspects. Regarding the phrase "transforming according to types" used herein, it encompasses both *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation) and *nairmāṇika* (transformation).
If one responds to humans and devas, this transformation belongs to the *nirmāṇakāya*; if one responds to other realms of existence (*gati*), this response belongs to the *nairmāṇika*.
Regarding the inclusion of the three bodies within the five natures of phenomena (up to): "Therefore, one knows that the three bodies all possess real wisdom.
From "By the five... onwards, the second section clarifies how the five phenomena subsume the three bodies. There are two interpretations. First is the explanation of the pure dharma-dhātu.

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśajñāna) subsumes the Svabhāvakāya. Next, a sutra is cited to prove that True Suchness (tathatā) subsumes the Dharmakāya, and a treatise is cited to prove that Mirror Wisdom subsumes the Svabhāvakāya.
True Suchness is the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and the Dharmakāya is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva); these are merely different names for the same essence.
The phrase following "Perfect Mirror" serves as a further explanation of the preceding one, harmonizing and clarifying that the transformation of the ālayavijñāna is [the Mirror Wisdom].
Because of the *ādarśa-jñāna* (mirror-like wisdom), the middle two [wisdoms] equally observe and encompass the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body).

Next, citing a treatise to prove that the *samatā-jñāna* (equality wisdom) manifests the body and the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (discerning wisdom) expounds the Dharma: "By transforming the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), one attains the enjoyment [body].

This phrase generally proves that both wisdoms encompass the enjoyment body. The last [wisdom], the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom), encompasses the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (transformation body). Next, citing a treatise...
This establishes the proof. Furthermore, the phrase "and wisdom" (智) and those following it clarify that the four wisdoms collectively encompass the three bodies.
Thus, the phrase "therefore one knows" and those following it conclude that all three bodies possess actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

There is one interpretation that the first [of the four wisdoms] subsumes the *svābhāvika-kāya* (self-nature body), because it is without marks (*animitta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and thus neither form nor mind.
There is another interpretation which explains it as follows: the pure *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) subsumes the *svābhāvika-kāya*.

This explanation excludes the *ādarśa-jñāna* (mirror-like wisdom), because the category of mirror-like wisdom is not eternally fundamental, possesses arising and ceasing, and is produced by causes of birth.
Therefore, these possess characteristics and are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), as they consist of the dharmas of form and mind (*rūpa-citta*). Their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the opposite of this;

therefore, they do not subsume one another. Nevertheless, it is said that those who attain [the state] by transforming the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) cannot be described as being material or mental entities.
"However, it is said below. This refers back to the first school’s citation of the treatise; the first phrase restates the preceding citation of the treatise.

"However, the first school says that by transforming the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), one attains the self-nature body (svabhāvakāya). Regarding "it is because of," this correctly explains the intent of the treatise:

by transforming the seeds of the two obstacles within the storehouse consciousness, the Dharma-nature body (dharmatākāya) is manifested. One must not claim that the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) is also subsumed under the self-nature body. Wisdom...

[The commentary] below [the word] "extraordinary" (*viśeṣa*) applies generally to the subsequent phrase. Question: Since it is stated that mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) does not encompass its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how can it be said that this extraordinary wisdom fully encompasses the three bodies (*trikāya*)?
Explanation: It is because the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the support for those four wisdoms and is the actual nature (*tattvasvabhāva*) of those four wisdoms;
therefore, it is said to fully encompass the three bodies. In reality, however, mirror-like wisdom does not encompass the Dharma-body.

"Body" refers exclusively to the body of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*). Below the section on "Self-nature," the reason why the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) does not include the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is set forth.
Question: It was previously stated that within the self-nature body there are infinite, true, and eternal merits.
Does this not mean that wisdom exists within the Dharma-body? Why, then, is it said that the mirror-like wisdom does not include the Dharma-body? Explanation: Within the self-nature body...
Although these possess merit, because they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and are neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*), they are not included [within the aggregates].
Among the four types of wisdom, true merits [up to] various bodily forms include the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Regarding the four wisdoms below: the wisdom of clarity subsumes the latter two bodies; that is to say, the self-enjoyment body is subsumed by all four wisdoms as well as the form body arising from the mirror-like wisdom;
the enjoyment-for-others body is subsumed by the wisdom of equality; and the transformation body is subsumed by the wisdom of accomplishing tasks.

It is taught that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is the Enjoyment Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*). [The passage from] "In reality" up to "form and mind are all subsumed under the Enjoyment" provides the scriptural evidence.

Regarding the phrase "It is taught that the Great... and below: the first clause cites evidence that Mirror Wisdom is for one's own enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*), while the second clause cites evidence that the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) is for the enjoyment of others (*parasaṃbhoga*).

Regarding the phrase "Although it transforms... and below: this addresses a potential objection. An anticipated question asks: "Does this statement refer to the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)?"

The Mirror-like Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) is accomplished, and one also attains self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*). Why was it stated previously that the transformation of the eighth consciousness reveals the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), yet it did not mention the attainment of self-enjoyment?

The explanation states: although this passage mentions that through the transformation of the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) one also attains enjoyment, the preceding text only spoke of the transformation of the store-consciousness revealing the Dharma-body and did not state the attainment of enjoyment; such is the text.

This is a brief summary. One should understand that the transformation of the *ālayavijñāna* has two meanings: first, by transforming away the seeds of the two obstacles within the *ālayavijñāna*, the *dharmakāya* is manifested;
second, by transforming the defiled *ālayavijñāna* into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), one attains the enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*).
The preceding text spoke only of manifesting the *dharmakāya*; it briefly omitted the meaning of attaining the enjoyment body through the transformation of the defiled into the pure.

Furthermore, it says "below. When inferred through reasoning, the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) should only be subsumed under the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), not the dharma body (*dharmakāya*).
Previously, the characteristics of being without birth or cessation within the dharma body were cited as an example; the mirror-like wisdom is the opposite of this.

If it were not the enjoyment body, to which body would it belong? Furthermore, it says "below" regarding the "enjoyment," clarifying that the self-enjoyment body subsumes the four wisdoms, which are conditioned and real.
"Virtue" refers to the four wisdoms. Therefore, [the text] concludes with "the four...
Furthermore, the Enjoyment Body for Others (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*) and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*)—up to this point—are subsumed under these two wisdoms of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*).

Furthermore, the phrase "Moreover, others below" refutes the first school’s position that all three bodies possess real wisdom (*jñāna*). The initial passage directly refutes the [Sambhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya] two bodies by stating that they do not have wisdom as their essence.
Regarding the phrase "Although it is said below," this refers to the general intent of the argument. Question: The scriptures state that the Nirmāṇakāya is subsumed within the excellence of wisdom;

why then do you now say it is not wisdom? Answer: Although the treatise states that the Nirmāṇakāya is subsumed within the excellence of wisdom, it is merely a semblance of wisdom (*jñāna-pratibimba*).
Because they manifest, or because they arise based on wisdom (*jñāna*), they are metaphorically designated by the name "wisdom," though their essence is actually not wisdom. Furthermore, it is asked:

"The Noble Ones have taught that the two bodies (*kāya*) are the manifestations of the two wisdoms; why now do you say their essence is not actual wisdom? This is merely a statement [of the objection].
The subsequent explanation of the meaning follows the text. Therefore, this final phrase concludes [the argument]: since the two wisdoms are not the two bodies, one knows that [the bodies] are...
One should understand that the *svābhāvikakāya* (nature body) is subsumed within the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment body).

The *svasaṃbhogakāya* is like the surface of a mirror, while the *sāmbhogikakāya* (other-enjoyment body) and the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) are like the reflections appearing therein. Light and the surface are neither identical nor different.
Without the face, the light is not manifested; without the light, the face is not manifested.

This is a metaphor for the mutual merging of wisdom and principle (*jñāna* and *tattva*), which are non-dual yet dual, and dual yet non-dual, such that they cannot be established as separate or distinct. The latter two bodies are like the reflected image.

Although the image appears in dependence upon the face and the light, and although no image can be obtained apart from the face and the light, it does not follow that the image is ultimately [non-existent].
The radiance of the face cannot be established as being identical [to that of the Transformation Body]. Therefore, these two bodies may only be said to be manifestations of wisdom;
they do not have wisdom as their substance.
However, because the Transformation Body and the Body of Enjoyment for Others possess functions such as [the absence of] sense organs and so forth, they are not said to exist [in those respects].

However, the following section addresses a general objection. It asks: "If the latter two bodies do not have wisdom as their essence, but are like puppets made of wood or clay, how can they preach the Dharma and transform beings for their benefit?
This is explained according to the text; there is nothing above or below it. Furthermore, it asks:

"While the body and so forth possess substance and can thus be manifested through transformation, the mind and so forth are formless; how could they possibly be manifested through transformation? This is explained according to the text.
If it were not so, it would conversely reveal that [the Tathāgata] is able to manifest them.

If one were to claim that the Tathāgata cannot manifest mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) that lack physical form, then since the Tathāgata has long since severed greed, hatred, and so forth, how could he further manifest the existence of the three poisons?
As for śrāvakas and animals who know the Tathāgata’s mind, this is a manifested (nirmāṇa) mind and not a real mind.
The Tathāgata’s true mind is such that even Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment—like rice, hemp, bamboo, or reeds—cannot yet know it.
For instance, when the Buddha once deeply censured the assembly of monks and later thought of taking them back, Brahmā King knew it entirely.

Furthermore, at another time, when he thought of becoming a king to transform the world according to the Dharma, Māra King immediately knew it and came to offer an exhortation. It was as if the Buddha were about to take mud...
At that time, Āniruddha knew the sequence of the various *dhyāna* and *samādhi* states into which the Buddha had entered.
From this point downward, the text cites evidence to show that emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) appearing according to the capacities of beings all possess consciousness.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that although a million humans and devas provided the final offering, it was only the offering of Cunda that the Buddha received in person; the others were all offered to an emanation Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*), yet all appeared as if they possessed consciousness.

It causes those humans and devas to each think, "The Buddha has accepted my offering. The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) manifests as the three types of action; "mind" here refers to the mental faculty (*manas*).
Furthermore, because it takes the dependent real mind as its substance and transforms it into the aspect-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), the mind appears.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Although it is said...": an objection is raised: "The Sages state that those who undergo transformation possess neither sense-faculties (*indriya*) nor mind (*citta*); why then do you now say they are capable [of such actions]?"

Regarding the transformation of faculties, mind, and so forth, the commentary states: "The claim that emanated beings lack faculties and mind refers to those emanated for the sake of other vehicles, such as the two vehicles and non-Buddhists.

Furthermore, when the Noble Ones say they lack faculties and mind, this is because the faculties do not possess the function of generating consciousness, and the mind and its associates lack any real defiled or virtuous activity;
therefore, they are said not to exist [in that sense], but it does not mean they are not manifested through transformation.

Although these three bodies are all fully endowed with the merit of the transformative marks that benefit and bring joy to others, [the text] below clarifies the distinctions among the virtues of the three bodies.
The first phrase provides a general indication of the differences in the virtues of the three bodies; the subsequent section provides a detailed explanation.
Regarding the *svābhāvikakāya* (self-nature body), it possesses only permanence, bliss, self, and purity, being free from all defilements—this is the meaning of "purity."
That which is the basis of all virtues is the meaning of "self" (ātman). Unconditioned merit is the meaning of "permanence" (nitya).

The absence of form, mind, and so forth is the meaning of "bliss" (sukha). The self-enjoyment body (svasaṃbhogakāya) possesses sublime form, mind, and so forth; its true merits are the four wisdoms (*jñāna*).
As for the latter two bodies possessing what resembles form, mind, and so forth, these are manifestations resembling wisdom, for they do not have wisdom as their essential substance.

Furthermore, the *svābhāvika-kāya* (Self-nature Body) is primarily comprised of self-benefit; however, it belongs exclusively to the category of benefiting others because it manifests for the sake of others.
Furthermore, from the passage below, the distinction between self-benefit and benefit for others is clarified. Regarding the *svābhāvika-kāya* acting as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*):

this means that True Suchness (*tathatā*) pervades the bodies of all sentient beings, serving as an internal perfuming influence. Therefore, it simultaneously accomplishes the benefit of others. This is the "self-experience" [of the Buddha].

The Body of Essential Nature (svābhāvika-kāya) benefits only oneself because its wisdom is in profound accord with the principle (*tattva*). The latter two bodies benefit only others because they manifest in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
Furthermore, the Body of Essential Nature abides in the Dharma-realm land (*dharmadhātu-kṣetra*), pervading all places like space.

Furthermore, from this point downward, [the text] explains the lands (*bhūmi*) upon which the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) rely. The first phrase indicates that the *svabhāvakāya* (self-nature body) relies upon the *dharmatā-bhūmi* (land of the nature of phenomena).

Although the following section provides the explanation, a question is raised: "Since the body is itself the *dharmadhātu* and the land is the *nitya-prabhāsvara* (eternal radiant light), their essence is non-dual;

why then distinguish between body and land? The explanation states: "Although there is no differentiation, they are differentiated despite being undivided. The Buddha is the aspect of characteristics (*nimitta-artha*); thus, there are two bodies."
Because it is the self-substance; because it is the basis for the merits of the four wisdoms; because it is the gathering of all virtues.

"Dharma" has the meaning of "nature," because it maintains its own nature, because it is the self-nature of merit, and because it is the self-nature of all phenomena. Regarding "being boundless according to the objects":

since the objects of the three bodies and three lands—such as the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth—are indeed boundless, [the Dharma-realm] takes these as its nature; how could there be...?

[The opponent] objects: "It is partial. [The proponent] establishes the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: The Dharma-nature body and its land are the subject (*dharmin*). Their magnitude is infinite, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Because they are not subsumed under the category of matter (*rūpa*), this is the reason (*hetu*). The analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like space.
The body of self-enjoyment (svasaṃbhogakāya) likewise relies upon its own land; it may also be said to pervade all places. [The phrase] "the body of self-enjoyment" and below marks the initial point.
"Its own land" refers to the untainted aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Sentient beings are the subjective support (*āśraya*), belonging to the reward body (*vipākakāya*);

the environment is the objective support, belonging to the reward land (*vipākabhūmi*). This is the land of actual retribution. [The phrase] "meaning perfect" and below provides the explanation; that is, it is stainless.

Consciousness, through the maturation of seeds for self-benefit and the pure land previously perfumed, transforms from the moment of initial Buddhahood into a purely pure Buddha-land that is circular and boundless.
As explained below regarding "purity," this is analogous to the body-faculties and marks; like the dimensions of the pure land, each is infinite.
Every faculty and every object pervades the entire realm of sands. Below, "merit" provides the explanation.
An objection is raised: "The body of self-enjoyment is itself wisdom and is not a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*).

How, then, can it be described as being 'perfectly round and immeasurable' in terms of its shape and magnitude? The explanation states: "Although the shape and magnitude of wisdom cannot be described," [it is so designated through metaphor].
Furthermore, with respect to the realized principle and the body upon which it relies, it may also be said that [the enjoyment body] pervades all.
The Enjoyment Body of Others (parasaṃbhogakāya) likewise relies on its own land; thus, even the dimensions of the supported body have no fixed limit.

The following section explains the "reception by others. The first phrase serves as the heading. "One's own land" refers to the Land of True Reward Adornment (*sambhoga-kāya-vyūha-bhūmi*). However, this is exclusively a Pure Land. This is the explanation:

it means that through the maturation of the seeds of the pure land—which are untainted (*anāsrava*) and for the sake of benefiting others—the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) transforms into a Pure Land according to what is appropriate for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). As for the changes and transformations in scale, excellence, inferiority, and temporal sequence: [these occur] accordingly.

Because the stages (bhūmi) are compared to one another, their relative superiority and inferiority differ from stage to stage. Regarding the basis below, if we take the land as an analogy for the body, there is likewise no fixed limit.

Though the moon does not descend [to the earth] nor do a hundred waters rise [to it], yet according to the length or shortness of rivers and the squareness or roundness of vessels, it appears everywhere at once—without before or after. This is the inconceivable, wondrous response.
If the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) relies upon a transformation land (*nirmāṇabhūmi*), the dimensions of that supporting body are likewise without fixed limit.

If it transforms into a lower [realm], the first phrase indicates the transformation land; this refers to the two lands of Expedient Means (*upāya*) and Common Dwelling (*sahā*). This explains the lower transformation.

Commentary: This refers to the wisdom that accomplishes activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). Through the maturation of the seeds of pure and impure Buddha-fields for the sake of benefiting others, it manifests as Buddha-fields according to what is appropriate for sentient beings who have not yet ascended to the [bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*). Generally speaking, the spiritual capacities (*indriya*) of great beings and lesser sages differ.

Each perceives differently according to the power of their respective karma. As for the variations in purity and defilement, smallness and greatness, and prior and posterior transformations, these arise because the modes of grasping and breaking [the aggregates] differ;

thus there is purity and defilement. Because they accord with the superior or inferior capacities of sentient beings, there is smallness and greatness. Regarding the statement that the untainted (anāsrava) is "defiled": [it refers to the fact that even the untainted is perceived as such by those whose faculties are dull].

He manifests according to capacities and perceives impurity; yet the Buddha is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*). As a sutra says: "When the great fire burns, this land of mine remains peaceful and secure"—this is precisely that meaning.
Regarding the phrase "the dependent [body] below": using the land as an analogy for the body, it likewise has no fixed limit.

The latter two bodies correspond to the three lands; all are said to undergo transformation and transition from beginning to end. This is discussed horizontally in terms of the four teachings, while vertically it refers to the three lands.
The four teachings are co-existent. The two provisional teachings constitute the stage of skillful means (*upāya*), while the one perfect teaching constitutes the stage of true retribution.

They are distinguished in broad outline because they respond differently to the capacities of sentient beings: the sudden teaching is for those with sharp faculties, while the gradual teachings are for those with dull faculties.

To discuss this in detail, within the sudden teaching there are both the dull and the perfect/sharp; within the gradual teaching, there are the perfect/sharp and three types of dull. Furthermore, one may also discuss sharpness and dullness through the successive transmission of the four teachings regarding what is taught.

The Dharma arises and ceases according to the capacities of sentient beings. Whether in terms of capacity or response, these aspects shift and transform at every stage; they cannot be fully detailed in words. One should reflect upon them according to the teachings.
From the self-nature body and land of all Tathāgatas [down to] the fact that a single Buddha can benefit all sentient beings.
Below the section on "Self-nature" (*svabhāva*), the six bodies and lands are explained together. Regarding the self-nature body and land:
their essence is *tathatā* (suchness), and there is no distinction between one's own and others' bodies and lands. Regarding the self-enjoyment body and land:

although each Buddha transforms them individually, they do not obstruct one another, like the light from many lamps. As for the remaining two bodies and lands, they are either common or uncommon depending on the sentient beings to be converted.

"Common. Regarding "common to those being transformed," the *Qingliang shi* (Commentary by Qingliang) states: "As for the statement that 'the Buddhas each manifest transformations,' it is like the present Śākyamuni’s transformation body.
If a class of sentient beings has a karmic affinity with both [Śākyamuni] and various Buddhas such as Akṣobhya, they should receive their transformation.
The bodies of those being transformed cannot be divided; it is as when one Śākyamuni attains Buddhahood and saves sentient beings, so do all Buddhas."

At the same time, they all manifested their own bodies as Śākyamuni and attained Buddhahood simultaneously beneath a single Bodhi tree, causing all sentient beings to perceive them as but a single Śākyamuni Buddha.
It is like many lamps illuminating a single object together, producing a single reflection;
yet in reality, each lamp emits its own light, and because these lights intermingle, one speaks of a single reflection. In this regard...

Regarding "not shared": it means that what is manifested is by only one Buddha. Even if one sees hundreds of thousands of transformation Buddhas in the ten directions, these are likewise merely the various bodies manifested by a single Buddha.
From "All those who... onwards, there is a double conclusion that explains the meaning of being both shared and not shared.
It should further state: "or many belong to one," "or one belongs to many," "or many belong to many," and "or one belongs to one. These [latter] phrases are not present in the text.

This is a brief summary. Due to the distinction between common and uncommon characteristics, although all ordinary beings and sages share the same mind, there is a difference between seeing and not seeing one another.
Although they equally transform lands, there is a distinction between those who experience them together and those who do not.
Therefore, while Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa constantly shines, one perceives the trees as hidden luster; the six-foot golden body appears again as earth and ash of various colors;
the lotus-flower jeweled temple is instead called a mound of soil; and the adorned jeweled ground is perversely described as sand and gravel.
This is because they are both common and uncommon.

Whether these various bodies and lands are pure or defiled (until "it would not be so"), otherwise there would be no [distinctions such as] the fifty-two [stages] and so forth. From the phrase "These various...

below, it clarifies the distinction between the transformed outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) [realms]. First, it clarifies the transformation of non-outflowing consciousness; that is, the aforementioned four...

Regarding the various bodies and lands—whether pure or defiled—that are manifested upon the Buddha’s untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*), they are identical to that which manifests them (the consciousness) in being purely untainted.
The final three phrases explain this by establishing that they are purely wholesome. Question:

If that which manifests is untainted and that which is manifested is also untainted, then by analogy, if that which manifests is consciousness (*vijñāna*), that which is manifested should likewise be consciousness.
If it were consciousness alone, there would be no distinction between the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. The commentary explains:

"The aggregates and so forth that are transformed do not necessarily coincide with the transforming consciousness, because the three dharmas—the aggregates and so forth—are produced through the combined influence of various causes and conditions.

Next, the transformation of contaminated (*sāsrava*) consciousness is clarified: these various bodies and lands, whether pure or impure, exist upon the contaminated consciousnesses of all sentient beings.

Regarding "transformational manifestation" (*nirmāṇa*): it is identical to that which undergoes transformation; both are contaminated (*sāsrava*). This is established through the three preceding phrases alone.

Below the section on "wholesome" (*kuśala*) and so forth, there is another question: "If that which is manifested is identical to that which manifests it, then the nature of the manifesting consciousness must be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)."
The transformed [objects] should also belong to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); there should not be a distinction of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). The commentary explains:

"The three natures—wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth—do not necessarily share the same characteristics as the transforming consciousness (*pariṇāmin-vijñāna*), because they are produced through the diverse drawing-forth of causes and conditions for each of the three natures.

Regarding the section on the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth: [the opponent] asks, "The transforming [agent] is consciousness; the transformed [object] should likewise be identical to that consciousness. There should not be [a separate category of] aggregates and so forth..."

[The answer is] different. The commentary explains: "The transformed [objects] and the transforming [consciousnesses] do not necessarily correspond to one another, because the three dharmas are produced through the combined drawing-forth of causes and conditions.

Otherwise, if the transformed [objects] had to be identical to the consciousness, there would be no distinction between the five aggregates (skandhas), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the eighteen elements (dhātus)."

However, the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and so forth manifest based on consciousness; [this is said] because it is admitted that both consciousness and its internal objects are substantially real.
Now, regarding the phrase "However, the objective aspect" and below: this follows from the preceding to clarify the reality or unreality of the four transformed parts. First, the initial explanation:

the two divisions of the objective and the subjective (*nimitta- and darśana-bhāga*) are transformations of consciousness and are subsumed under the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); thus, they are unreal. The substance of the transforming consciousness itself is subsumed under the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*); thus, it is [real].

It is real. Were it otherwise, if one were to claim that the two external parts are also real, then there would be real dharmas existing outside of consciousness, and the principle of "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) would consequently fail to be established.
Alternatively, [the objection is: "If the aspects and the seeing-part of consciousness arise from conditions... (up to)... otherwise, even True Suchness (*tathatā*) would not be real.

Regarding the passage "Alternatively, consciousness... and below, the next section provides the explanation: Because the two parts—the aspect (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*)—arise from conditions, both are *paratantra* (dependent origination).

As for the statement "whether false or real, they are like consciousness," this is said in terms of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Since consciousness is like a magical illusion or a dream, the aspects and the seeing-part that are transformed by it are likewise like consciousness.

"Empty. This is said in terms of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). If the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is not non-existent, then its characteristics and perceptions are as real as consciousness itself.
If this were so, would it not follow that there are real objects? The explanation says: the word "only" (*kevala*) excludes phenomena external to the mind, but it does not negate internal objects.

If it were otherwise, then when subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) transforms appearances to take suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, these internal objects would likewise have to be unreal.
Since both internal objects and consciousness are neither false, why do you speak only of "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) and not of "objects-only"?

[The section] beginning with "Internal objects" addresses this objection. Question: Since both objects and consciousness are neither false, one should instead say "only consciousness and only objects.
Why do you speak only of "consciousness-only" and not of "objects-only"?
"Consciousness exists only internally, while its objects extend to both the internal and external" (up to "because mind and mental factors are necessarily associated").

Regarding "consciousness exists only [internally]," the answer is given by way of three meanings. First, it is said that consciousness exists only internally, whereas its objects extend to both the internal and external.

If one were to say only "objects," there is a fear that the ignorant might erroneously calculate that phenomena exist outside the mind; therefore, it is simply called "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*). Alternatively, various...

[The Master] said: "Secondly, it is because foolish people cling to the existence of external objects, giving rise to delusions and creating karma that causes them to sink into the cycle of birth and death.
Out of compassion for them, I negate their external calculations and cause them to contemplate their own mind; this does not mean that internal objects do not exist either.

There are two ways of contemplating the mind. First is the contemplation of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), which means realizing that the essence of consciousness is fundamentally quiescent, wherein the three thousand [worlds] are perfectly present and are themselves emptiness."

In the provisional middle [truth], there are two types of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) contemplation. One contemplates that the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) are produced by the transformations of the arising mind;

because the four natures (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) are unobtainable, [one realizes emptiness]. Or, as stated below in the third [section]: "The two divisions of appearance (*nimitta-bhāga*) and seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) both have consciousness as their nature.

Through the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*), they arise resembling the four parts [of consciousness], yet in reality they are a single essence. Question: If the nature of consciousness is conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and True Suchness (*tathatā*) is ultimate (*paramārtha*), would this not mean that [the ultimate] exists outside of the mind?

"There is a dharma. The commentary explains: Suchness (*tathatā*) is the true nature of consciousness (*vijñapti*). Since there is no separate dharma apart from consciousness, [it is said that] there is a dharma.

Question: If objects are transformations of consciousness, they may be considered a single consciousness. However, since the various mental factors (*caitta*) each possess their own distinct substance, could they also be a single consciousness?

The explanation for this follows the text. The preceding section concludes the explanation of the stage of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). This concludes the main purport of the Great Chapter on the True Doctrine.
This treatise, established in three parts, achieves the perfection of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra), being neither deficient nor redundant.

Having distinguished the meaning of the nature and characteristics of Consciousness-Only based upon the sacred teachings and correct reasoning, I dedicate the merit thus obtained to all sentient beings. May we together swiftly ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment.
Below this treatise, the section on the conclusion of the exposition and the dedication of merit is explained.

Below this treatise, the meaning is explained because it establishes the three parts, clarifies the principles with purity, fulfills the root verses, and manifests both name and reality. Thus, based on what follows...
The concluding text: "Relying upon the teachings and principles" refers to the basis; "discriminating the nature and characteristics" refers to the analysis.

"That which is obtained below" refers to the dedication, as it involves turning oneself toward others and turning phenomena toward principle. "May we together below" refers to the aspiration, wherein those who see, hear, or rejoice therein rely on these causes to achieve the fruit.

Postscript to the *Self-Examination of the Weishi*:
This record of self-examination was composed by Dharma Master Lingyuan. The Master had long planted roots of goodness and manifested his form in this world.
In his prime, he attended the lectures of Dharma Master Shao, where he extensively studied the Tiantai school and mastered the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.

Soaring through the gates of the Dharma, he was already renowned as a "dragon or elephant" among the great disciples. Subsequently, he withdrew from the capital to refine his studies for many years; it was there that the layman preached the Dharma.
The Master’s eloquence was vast and profound. For a long time, the monastic community within the realm had looked toward the single school of Vijñaptimātratā (Consciousness-Only).

Although the tradition of the "Lotus Abode" alone transmitted this lineage, after the Master had undergone tonsure, he traveled south in the spring of the Bingyin year to seek instruction. There, he happened to examine the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā* by Haichang;

although it followed the phonology and meanings of the original treatise, its analysis of complex terminology was not without errors, and its expansion upon the great principles lacked the depth of personal realization. Indeed...
Since the sacred compositions were difficult to elucidate clearly, yet the faithful maintained their devotion to the distant lineages of their masters, I lamented for a long time.
One night, at the request of the host of Longju, I took up my brush and spread out my paper to record what I remembered.

In less than a few months, the text was completed in a thousand fascicles, its meaning encompassing the entire collection. I traveled between the north and south and ascended the lion throne once again. As for that...

Regarding the lectures and those who participated in their compilation, there is almost no room for further comment. Guang previously encountered Dharma Master Xiang in Chang’an, where he heard the introductory discourses;
ten years have passed since then. This spring, I was once again able to read the draft manuscript under the guidance of Master Lianju, as if having obtained a precious jade tablet.
Unable to bear concealing it within its casket so that later students would have nothing to follow or revere, I have contributed my funds...

It has been committed to the press. Bearing this responsibility alone, although it cannot be said that its lofty carriage matches the proofs of the original meaning, it joins the long with the short and is quite worthy of being considered a sibling to other works.

Compared to the *Sūcī* (Explanations for the Laity), it is more precise; compared to the *Jishie* (Collected Explanations), it is more concise. Thus, those of shallow learning will not find its profound phrasing tiresome.

Even for those who have attained awakening from past lives, it is difficult to find the remaining meaning [of this work]. May those of excellent wisdom come later to continue the life-force of the Buddha’s grace;
thus, one may perhaps be free from shame.
Written on the day of the Winter Solstice in the first year of the Chongzhen era, the Wuchen year, by the layman Guǎnggù of Hǎicháng, with respectful greetings.
